unit-01.jnhwtx2p70: Strip away the screen, the keyboard and the apps, and a computer is a machine that does exactly one kind of thing: it transforms information by following instructions. A photo, a song, a web page, a video game, a spreadsheet: to a computer, all of these are just information, and all of that information is stored as numbers.
unit-01.yjksc16k9u: That's the big idea of this whole unit, so let it sink in. When you edit a photo, the computer is doing arithmetic on numbers that describe the colour of each dot. When you type the letter A, the keyboard sends a number. When you play a song, a list of numbers describing air pressure is sent to your speaker thousands of times a second.
unit-01.obfjsgpg57: So the first question a computer scientist asks is: how does a machine store and work with numbers?
unit-01.1fcjh7ja0g3: Why two states? Switches, not dials
unit-01.v7fm1rr9q3: Inside every chip are billions of microscopic switches called transistors. A transistor is an electrically controlled switch: it is either letting current through (on) or not (off). We usually call these two states 1 and 0.
unit-01.q5who62vkn: Why only two? Why not build switches with ten levels, one for each decimal digit? Because the real world is noisy. Voltages wobble, components heat up, and wires pick up interference.
unit-01.hsdqmj2h5: Analogy: Imagine reading a light switch versus a dimmer from across a dark room. You can always tell whether the switch is on or off. But is the dimmer at 60% or 70%? Hard to say, and easy to get wrong. Computers use the light-switch approach because "on vs off" stays readable even when things get messy.
unit-01.2dqdqf5mfm6: With only two states, a chip can tolerate lots of noise: anything above a threshold voltage counts as 1, anything below counts as 0. That reliability is what lets a phone do billions of operations a second without mistakes. The price is that we have to represent everything using just two symbols. That system is called binary.
unit-01.1ewao1wx9jb: A single 0-or-1 value is called a bit, short for binary digit. One bit on its own can only say two things: yes/no, on/off, true/false.
unit-01.faw0gdyfuf: Group bits together and the possibilities multiply. Every extra bit doubles the number of patterns, because each existing pattern can be followed by either a 0 or a 1:
unit-01.18hplixvl6p: There is a table here. Have a look at it on screen.
unit-01.fh2o476tun: Key idea: n bits can represent 2ⁿ different values. If those values are the whole numbers starting at 0, the biggest one is 2ⁿ  minus  1 (because counting starts at 0, not 1).
unit-01.2b9j3x4ss0: A group of 8 bits is called a byte. One byte has 2⁸ = 256 patterns, so it can store any whole number from 0 to 255. Bytes are the standard unit for measuring memory and file sizes:
unit-01.2dbxee4bac7: 1 kilobyte (KB) ≈ a thousand bytes, a short text file
unit-01.2eg9jl67phj: 1 megabyte (MB) ≈ a million bytes, a photo or a minute of music
unit-01.21g6vmap71g: 1 gigabyte (GB) ≈ a billion bytes, about an hour of HD video
unit-01.20ub5s33zxi: 1 terabyte (TB) ≈ a trillion bytes, a whole laptop drive
unit-01.28rbyt9nfmw: Note: Because computers work in powers of 2, memory is often measured in units of 1024 rather than 1000 (2¹⁰ = 1024). Strictly, 1024 bytes is a kibibyte (KiB), but many people still say "kilobyte" for both. In this course, when a question needs the exact number, it will say which one it means.
unit-01.2f8eodpasmp: Also watch the capital letters: a lowercase b means bits and an uppercase B means bytes. Internet speeds are sold in megabits per second (Mbps), so a "100 Mbps" connection downloads at most about 12.5 megabytes per second.
unit-01.u7t40deyqv: You already know a number system that uses place values: decimal. In the number 352, each position is worth ten times the one to its right:
unit-01.1qvd2qpin66: So 352 means 3 times 100 + 5 times 10 + 2 times 1. We call decimal base 10 because it has ten digits (0 to 9) and each place is worth 10 times more.
unit-01.225juu88hmc: Binary works exactly the same way, but in base 2: there are only two digits (0 and 1) and each place is worth 2 times more than the one to its right. Reading from the right, the place values are 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, and so on.
unit-01.w2thqzx3td: Binary to decimal: add up the place values that have a 1. Take the binary number 1011:
unit-01.rniauuygnq: Decimal to binary: repeatedly divide by 2 and keep the remainders. To convert 13:
unit-01.21zq6wgpu6v: Read the remainders from the bottom up: 1101. Check: 8 + 4 + 0 + 1 = 13.
unit-01.dgc92gnhfs: Why: Each remainder tells you whether the number is odd (1) or even (0) at that step, which is exactly whether the current lowest place value is "on". Dividing by 2 then shifts every bit one place to the right, so the next remainder reveals the next bit.
unit-01.1m9ik9dr1ke: There's a second method many people find faster for small numbers: find the biggest power of 2 that fits, write a 1 there, subtract, and repeat. For 13: 8 fits (13  minus  8 = 5), 4 fits (5  minus  4 = 1), 2 doesn't fit, 1 fits. So 8, 4 and 1 are on: 1101.
unit-01.1xfotkr7m6g: Throughout this course you'll check your understanding by running real code. Python is a programming language that reads almost like English, and it runs right here in your browser. You will learn it properly in Unit 2. For now you only need three tiny pieces:
unit-01.skaijlt5b3: print(something) shows a value in the output panel.
unit-01.f0wjpqe2g: answer = 13 stores a value under the name answer. Exercises will ask you to set a name like this, and the tests will look at it.
unit-01.2fxuvp5ws5a: Numbers in binary are written with a 0b prefix: Python reads 0b1101 as the number thirteen. Without the prefix, 1101 means one thousand one hundred and one.
unit-01.253dezatuf7: Python can also convert for you: bin(13) gives the text '0b1101', and int("1101", 2) reads the text "1101" as a base-2 number. You'll use these to check your hand calculations, but in the exercises, do the conversion by hand first. The goal is for binary to feel natural, not for Python to do it for you.
unit-01.bcwojhsxh5: A line that starts with # is a comment: a note for humans that Python ignores.
unit-01.y75c0zldyr: Python understands binary directly. Notice how the same value can be written in different ways.

unit-01.1zlw2hcemn1: Here's the divide-by-2 method from the lesson written as code. Two new operators: // divides and throws away any fraction ("floor division"), and % gives the remainder of a division.
unit-01.1jbonftxlwy: Reading place values from the wrong end
unit-01.1fs2llw9mqg: Place values grow from right to left. The rightmost bit is always worth 1. In 1000, the 1 is worth 8, not 1. If you write the place values above the bits starting from the right (1, 2, 4, 8...), you won't mix them up.
unit-01.k7jxz8o5gw: Thinking n bits can store numbers up to 2ⁿ
unit-01.1gwz7i8olwg: n bits give 2ⁿ patterns, but one of them is zero, so the largest value is 2ⁿ  minus  1. A byte holds 0 to 255, not 0 to 256. This off-by-one error is one of the most common bugs in all of programming, so it's worth getting right now.
unit-01.1dms10ab94a: Python assumes numbers are decimal unless told otherwise. 1011 is one thousand and eleven; 0b1011 is eleven.
unit-01.e7sdkn8nf4: Network speeds use bits (Mbps), file sizes use bytes (MB). There are 8 bits in a byte, so to know how long a 100 MB download takes on a 100 Mbps line, divide by 8 first: about 12.5 MB per second, so roughly 8 seconds, not 1.
unit-01.az4pl5q4y9: Computers store all information as numbers, and store numbers using bits: 0s and 1s.
unit-01.1my511jplsa: Two states are used because transistors are switches, and on/off is reliable to read despite electrical noise.
unit-01.1tqmk8i0lu4: n bits give 2ⁿ patterns; as whole numbers starting at 0, that's 0 to 2ⁿ  minus  1. A byte is 8 bits (0 to 255).
unit-01.11d8r5d1kib: Binary is base 2: place values are 1, 2, 4, 8, 16... from the right. Convert to decimal by adding the place values that hold a 1.
unit-01.qkf6e645lu: Convert decimal to binary by dividing by 2 repeatedly and reading the remainders bottom-up.
unit-01.26slr3o91hi: In Python, 0b1101 is a binary number, bin(n) shows binary, int(text, 2) reads binary, and print displays values.
unit-01.f48hfirqmj: You can now store any whole number in bits. But computers also store text, negative numbers, colours, images and sound. In Lesson 1.2 you'll learn the clever encodings that turn all of those into bits, plus hexadecimal, the shorthand programmers use to write binary without going cross-eyed.

unit-01.1e1jkcbjl5e: Bits don't mean anything until we agree what they mean
unit-01.2dpdy7iekd1: In Lesson 1.1 you learned to treat bits as whole numbers. But look at this byte:
unit-01.1vophouddgl: Is it the number 65? The letter A? A shade of dark blue? A tiny piece of a song? It's any of these. The bits are identical; what differs is the encoding, the agreed-upon rule for what a pattern means.
unit-01.wdfwwmd8pc: Key idea: Bits have no meaning on their own. Meaning comes from interpretation. A file extension like .txt or .png is partly a hint to programs about which encoding to use when they read the bits.
unit-01.pxi7b1uh7q: This is why opening an image in a text editor shows gibberish: the editor is interpreting colour data as if it were letters. Every kind of data you'll meet in computing (numbers, text, images, programs themselves) is just bits plus an encoding. In this lesson you'll learn the most important encodings.
unit-01.1zrdnw66429: Binary gets long fast. The number 2025 is 11111101001. Programmers needed a compact way to write bit patterns, and decimal is awkward because 10 is not a power of 2. The answer is hexadecimal ("hex"): base 16.
unit-01.hn1rfi4nb7: Hex needs 16 digits, so after 0 to 9 it borrows letters: A = 10, B = 11, C = 12, D = 13, E = 14, F = 15.
unit-01.vmhvlzsz9v: The magic is that 16 = 2⁴, so each hex digit stands for exactly 4 bits. That makes conversion a matter of grouping rather than arithmetic:
unit-01.1jnu3kmsv1z: Binary to hex: split into groups of 4 from the right, then translate each group. 1101 0110  to  D 6  to  D6.
unit-01.2fzcbisv64d: Hex to binary: expand each digit into 4 bits. 3F  to  0011 1111.
unit-01.mu7bvj11gk: Hex to decimal: place values are powers of 16 (1, 16, 256, ...). So 2F = 2 times 16 + 15 times 1 = 47.
unit-01.14k5ubuxkgq: A byte (8 bits) is always exactly two hex digits, from 00 to FF (0 to 255). That's why hex is everywhere: memory addresses, error codes, and web colours like #FF8800. In Python and most languages, hex numbers start with 0x, just as binary starts with 0b.
unit-01.22kcq04jpja: To store text, we number every character. In the 1960s, American engineers agreed on ASCII (the American Standard Code for Information Interchange), which uses 7 bits to number 128 characters: English letters, digits, punctuation, and some control codes like "new line".
unit-01.joi76634sm: Notice the patterns: letters are in alphabetical order, so B is one more than A; and every lowercase letter is exactly 32 more than its uppercase partner. In binary, 32 is a single bit, so changing case means flipping one bit. That was a deliberate design choice.
unit-01.mrmdwtz9xy: Warning: The character '7' is not the number 7. The character '7' has code 55. When your program reads digits that someone typed, it gets characters and must convert them to numbers. You'll do this constantly in Unit 2.
unit-01.2c23w46nq6g: 128 characters is fine for English but useless for 你好, Привет, नमस्ते, or 😀. Unicode fixes this by giving every character in every writing system its own number (its code point), over 150,000 so far. Code points are usually written like U+1F600 (that's 😀, in hex).
unit-01.22cu1pftcdw: Unicode code points are stored as bytes using an encoding called UTF-8, the encoding of the modern web. It's cleverly variable-length: the original 128 ASCII characters take just 1 byte (and use the same codes as ASCII, so old files still work), while other characters take 2, 3 or 4 bytes.
unit-01.1d0cmkrh6ub: In Python, ord("A") gives a character's code, and chr(65) gives the character for a code.
unit-01.2cnalvyw6s: How do you store  minus 5 when all you have is bits? A first idea is a sign bit: use the leftmost bit for the sign (1 = negative) and the rest for the size. It works but causes problems: there are two zeros (+0 and  minus 0), and the circuits for adding become complicated because they need special cases.
unit-01.1ry81iqwzc: Nearly every computer instead uses two's complement. In an 8-bit two's complement number, the leftmost place value is negative:
unit-01.10rz3uf94ti: Check:  minus 128 + 64 + 32 + 16 + 8 + 2 + 1 =  minus 5. An 8-bit two's complement number holds  minus 128 to 127.
unit-01.d7mq0ouqe8: To negate a number: flip every bit, then add 1. For  minus 5: 5 is 00000101, flipped is 11111010, plus 1 is 11111011.
unit-01.1hpul8rrvgy: Why: The beauty of two's complement is that ordinary binary addition just works, negative or not. 5 + ( minus 5) is 00000101 + 11111011 = 1 00000000. The 9th bit falls off the end of the 8-bit box, leaving 00000000: zero. The same adding circuit handles positive and negative numbers, with no special cases.
unit-01.e24ydmnxy1: A handy shortcut: in 8 bits,  minus x is stored as the same pattern as the positive number 256  minus  x. So  minus 5 is stored like 251, which is 11111011.
unit-01.1m8qv6crmwo: A fixed number of bits can only hold a fixed range. What happens when a calculation goes past it? The extra bits are lost and the number wraps around, like a car's odometer rolling from 999999 back to 000000. This is called overflow.
unit-01.93s1odxw4k: In an 8-bit unsigned byte, 255 + 1 = 0. In 8-bit two's complement, 127 + 1 =  minus 128 (the pattern 10000000).
unit-01.107fvbpqe5a: Overflow has caused real disasters. In 1996, the Ariane 5 rocket exploded 37 seconds after launch because a 64-bit number was squeezed into 16 bits and overflowed. The video game Pac-Man breaks on level 256 because the level counter is one byte. And many computers store time as a 32-bit count of seconds since 1970, which overflows on 19 January 2038.
unit-01.1lw3ohen2pq: Note: Python's whole numbers grow automatically, so you won't see overflow in Python code: 2 ** 1000 works fine. Most other languages, including C in Unit 9, use fixed-size numbers where overflow is very real. Understanding it now will save you from serious bugs later.
unit-01.1xlt0g2dm7o: What about fractions like 3.75? Computers store them in a format called floating point, a binary version of scientific notation. A surprising consequence is that some simple decimals, like 0.1, can't be stored exactly in binary (just as 1/3 can't be written exactly in decimal). You'll see this in action in Unit 2.
unit-01.16v8qdypki0: Colours. Screens mix red, green and blue light. A common encoding gives each of the three channels one byte (0 to 255), so a colour takes 3 bytes, or 24 bits. That's 2²⁴ ≈ 16.7 million colours. In web code, a colour is written as six hex digits: #FF8000 means red = FF (255), green = 80 (128), blue = 00 (0), which is orange.
unit-01.vyzhn204ie: Images. A digital image is a grid of tiny coloured dots called pixels. An uncompressed 1920  times  1080 image with 3 bytes per pixel needs 1920  times  1080  times  3 = 6,220,800 bytes, about 6 MB. A minute of 60-frames-per-second video at that size would be over 22 GB! That's why formats like JPEG, PNG and MP4 compress data, using clever maths to store the same picture in far fewer bytes.
unit-01.1m8qbum18oq: Sound. Sound is a wave of air pressure. To record it, a microphone measures the pressure thousands of times per second; each measurement is a sample. CD-quality audio takes 44,100 samples per second, each stored as a 16-bit number, for each of 2 stereo channels.
unit-01.1hxjyftz36f: Key idea: Everything follows the same recipe: measure something, turn the measurements into numbers, store the numbers as bits, and agree on an encoding so the bits can be turned back into the original thing.
unit-01.2d4u5pigho5: Python writes hex with a 0x prefix, mirroring 0b for binary.
unit-01.1twesuvzjvn: ord() turns a character into its code, chr() turns a code into a character, and + joins pieces of text.
unit-01.cw2t9z9yt0: Example 3: Two's complement with the 256 trick
unit-01.ddzwgja03b: In 8 bits, a negative number  minus x is stored with the same bits as 256  minus  x. Let's see the bit pattern for  minus 5 and check it.
unit-01.qsj9puxg4h: Example 4: How big is a photo?
unit-01.2avotx59lbg: Calculating storage needs is everyday engineering arithmetic.
unit-01.22eaqitryos: Confusing the character '5' with the number 5
unit-01.y9hfvex72z: Text digits are characters with their own codes ('0' is 48). "5" + "5" joins text to give "55", while 5 + 5 gives 10. This trips up beginners constantly when reading user input in Unit 2.
unit-01.2afdi06gjc: Grouping bits from the left when converting to hex
unit-01.30yjsy1lh9: Always group bits into fours from the right, padding the left with zeros. 110101 is 0011 0101 = 35, not 1101 01...
unit-01.q36tiyi61t: Forgetting to add 1 in two's complement
unit-01.20nsjevzhza: "Flip the bits" alone gives a different system (ones' complement) that has two zeros. Two's complement is flip, then add 1. Check your answer by adding the place values with  minus 128 on the left.
unit-01.5d4jl1o9m2: Thinking hex digits go past F
unit-01.233fjz8qdx1: Hex digits are 0 to 9 and A to F (15). There is no G. After F comes 10 (which is 16).
unit-01.1emk6v4n85g: Bits mean nothing without an encoding: an agreed rule for interpreting them.
unit-01.2blxoxo334a: Hexadecimal is base 16 (digits 0 to F). Each hex digit is exactly 4 bits, so a byte is two hex digits (00 to FF).
unit-01.oihxgcu9lw: Text is stored as character codes: ASCII for English, Unicode for every language, usually stored as UTF-8 bytes. Use ord() and chr() in Python.
unit-01.pf3sx122c2: Negative numbers use two's complement: flip the bits and add 1. The leftmost bit is worth  minus 128 in 8 bits, giving a range of  minus 128 to 127.
unit-01.275faf18xpx: Fixed-size numbers can overflow and wrap around. Python's whole numbers grow as needed; most languages' don't.
unit-01.22a8tym5twf: Colours are usually 3 bytes (RGB), images are grids of pixels, and sound is a stream of samples. All of it is just numbers.
unit-01.6odj6xgtay: You now know what computers store. Next you'll discover how they compute with it. In Lesson 1.3 you'll meet logic gates, tiny circuits that make decisions about bits, and you'll build a working adding machine out of nothing but AND, OR and XOR.
unit-01.13torrirvcr: Understand the basic logic gates (NOT, AND, OR, XOR, NAND), describe them with truth tables, and see how combining gates produces circuits that can add binary numbers, the foundation of every CPU.

unit-01.1435v6mhanw: In the 1850s, long before computers existed, the mathematician George Boole invented an algebra of logic where every value is either true or false, and the operations are words like AND, OR and NOT. It was considered a curiosity for almost a century.
unit-01.sao8im92a7: In 1937 a 21-year-old student named Claude Shannon noticed something remarkable: electrical switches behave exactly like Boole's algebra. Two switches in a row (in series) only let current through if the first AND the second are closed. Two switches side by side (in parallel) let current through if the first OR the second is closed. Treat "current flows" as true (1) and "no current" as false (0), and circuits can compute logic.
unit-01.2evt8tnupmc: Key idea: Boolean logic is the bridge between maths and machines. Any yes/no question you can express with AND, OR and NOT, you can build as a circuit, and the circuit will answer it at the speed of electricity.
unit-01.iv6wu0g9c3: A logic gate is a small circuit, built from a handful of transistors, that takes one or more input bits and produces one output bit according to a fixed rule. We describe each rule with a truth table: a list of every possible input combination and the output for each.
unit-01.7bhfoeu0tb: NOT (also called an inverter) has one input and flips it.
unit-01.lfenog18pi: AND outputs 1 only when both inputs are 1. Think of a bank vault that needs two keys turned at once.
unit-01.26p4thir8c5: OR outputs 1 when at least one input is 1. Think of a car's interior light, which comes on if the driver's door OR the passenger's door is open.
unit-01.27vo91v5pex: Note: With two inputs there are 2² = 4 rows; with three inputs, 2³ = 8 rows. That's the "n bits give 2ⁿ patterns" rule from Lesson 1.1 again. A truth table simply lists every pattern.
unit-01.25dyg84a0z0: XOR, NAND and the universal gate
unit-01.l2aaxgzbne: XOR ("exclusive or") outputs 1 when the inputs are different: one or the other, but not both. A light controlled by two switches at the top and bottom of a staircase works like XOR: flipping either switch changes the light.
unit-01.1y00j8kj63z: NAND is "NOT AND": it gives the opposite of AND, so it outputs 0 only when both inputs are 1. NOR is "NOT OR".
unit-01.163iq1m1hlj: Here's a surprising and important fact: NAND is universal. Every other gate, and therefore every possible digital circuit, can be built from NAND gates alone. For example, NOT A is just NAND(A, A). Because NAND is also very cheap to make from transistors, real chips are built from enormous numbers of NAND-like gates. A modern CPU contains billions of transistors, but it is, in a real sense, "just" NAND gates connected in very clever ways.
unit-01.14xgdlvn4ay: Gates become powerful when you wire the output of one into the input of another. Consider this circuit: (A AND B) OR (NOT C). To find its truth table, work through each of the 2³ = 8 input rows, computing the inner parts first:
unit-01.18uayt11vbz: Adding helper columns for the intermediate results is the professional way to do this. It's slow but almost impossible to get wrong.
unit-01.1woj17mn6sb: Two famous rules, De Morgan's laws, let you rewrite circuits: NOT (A AND B) is the same as (NOT A) OR (NOT B), and NOT (A OR B) is the same as (NOT A) AND (NOT B). In words: "not both" means "at least one isn't"; "neither" means "this isn't and that isn't". You'll use these laws all the time when writing conditions in code.
unit-01.a81pqxh7s: Now for the payoff. Let's add two single bits, A + B:
unit-01.22p3a7vijaa: Look at the last two columns. The sum bit is 1 when exactly one input is 1: that's XOR. The carry bit is 1 only when both are 1: that's AND. So a one-bit adder, called a half adder, is just one XOR gate and one AND gate.
unit-01.r2dbk5l6gt: To add multi-bit numbers, each column must also add the carry coming in from the column to its right, just like carrying a 1 in pencil-and-paper addition. A full adder adds three bits (A, B and carry-in) and produces a sum and a carry-out:
unit-01.1lg48dfx49n: sum = A XOR B XOR carry-in
unit-01.2ee4zcqjmsb: carry-out = (A AND B) OR (carry-in AND (A XOR B))
unit-01.1vb14l6mu1e: Chain four full adders together, with each carry-out feeding the next carry-in, and you have a 4-bit ripple-carry adder that adds numbers from 0 to 15. Chain 64 and you have the adder inside a 64-bit CPU. You'll build the 4-bit version in the Unit 1 project.
unit-01.dw554h9kee: Why: This is the moment where "computers are just switches" stops being a slogan. Switches make gates, gates make adders, and adders (plus a few more circuits) make a processor. Nothing magical is hiding in the box.
unit-01.15t8kxz756: When values are the bits 0 and 1, Python has operators that act like gates:
unit-01.1r0grs6xk0u: (Python also has the words and, or and not, which work on True/False values. You'll use those in Unit 2 when your programs make decisions.)
unit-01.1m7l0pcj0ru: In the exercises you'll write tiny functions. A function is a named recipe:
unit-01.4v70lol0t0: Read it as: "define a recipe called AND that takes two inputs, a and b, and gives back a & b." After defining it, AND(1, 1) gives 1. The indented line (4 spaces) is the body of the recipe. That's all you need to know for now; Unit 2 covers functions in depth.
unit-01.xdirbnhnmj: Example 1: Truth tables with Python operators
unit-01.1lwytb4lbax: Each print shows one gate's output for the four input rows 00, 01, 10, 11.
unit-01.13wjiescmhy: Wrapping each gate in a function gives it a readable name, just like a labelled component on a circuit board.
unit-01.2538zadwxe3: Adding two bits gives a sum bit (XOR) and a carry bit (AND).
unit-01.17ipada2v8m: In everyday English, "or" is often exclusive ("tea or coffee?"). In logic, OR is inclusive: 1 OR 1 is 1. Only XOR excludes the "both" case.
unit-01.1mo467rpfob: 1 - a & b is not NAND. Python computes 1 - a first, then ANDs it with b. Use brackets to make the wiring explicit, just as a circuit diagram shows which gate feeds which.
unit-01.1qkinrarn81: Missing rows in a truth table
unit-01.21vhwg6zb94: With n inputs there are always 2ⁿ rows. A systematic order (count up in binary: 000, 001, 010, ...) guarantees you don't skip one.
unit-01.1krcc7ngoia: Adding bits column by column without passing the carry along is like doing long addition and forgetting to carry the 1. Every column except the rightmost needs a full adder, not a half adder.
unit-01.1l0y79e6ikc: Boolean logic works with true/false (1/0). Shannon showed that switch circuits compute it, linking maths to machines.
unit-01.1mieia5ojef: NOT flips, AND needs both, OR needs at least one, XOR needs exactly one (inputs differ).
unit-01.1iqnpwqvc4c: NAND (and NOR) are universal: any circuit can be built from them alone.
unit-01.1akgxmknqfu: Combine gates by wiring outputs to inputs. Work out truth tables with helper columns. De Morgan's laws rewrite NOT-AND and NOT-OR.
unit-01.15dvkqo2dex: A half adder is XOR (sum) + AND (carry). A full adder also adds a carry-in. Chained full adders add numbers of any size.
unit-01.140f126club: In Python, on 0/1 values: & is AND, | is OR, ^ is XOR, 1 - a is NOT.
unit-01.19blw2oab30: You've seen how gates compute. But a pile of adders isn't a computer: something has to decide which operation to perform, on which data, when. In Lesson 1.4 you'll open up the CPU, meet its registers and its arithmetic logic unit, and follow the fetch-decode-execute cycle that runs every program ever written. You'll even program a tiny simulated CPU yourself.
unit-01.1ojzkalug96: Understand what the CPU is made of (ALU, registers, control unit, program counter, clock) and how it runs a program one simple instruction at a time through the fetch-decode-execute cycle, including how jumps create decisions and loops.

unit-01.v1nacx34ik: The CPU is a fast, literal clerk
unit-01.10i9n822pbe: The CPU (central processing unit, or processor) is the part of the computer that actually carries out programs. People often call it the "brain", but that's misleading: a CPU doesn't understand anything. A better picture is an incredibly fast, perfectly obedient clerk with a tiny desk, following a numbered list of very simple instructions, one at a time, never skipping ahead and never questioning anything.
unit-01.1shtlvocnss: Analogy: Picture the clerk with a list of instructions like "Write 7 on your notepad", "Add the number in box B to your notepad", "If your notepad shows zero, go to step 12". Each instruction is trivial. The clerk's superpower is speed: a modern CPU follows billions of them per second.
unit-01.2bgt18otxa7: Every program you've ever used, from a calculator to a 3D game, is ultimately a long list of such tiny instructions. In this lesson you'll learn the parts of the clerk's desk and exactly how instructions are followed.
unit-01.1tou2wrm8gm: ALU (Arithmetic Logic Unit). The calculator. It performs arithmetic (add, subtract) and logic operations (AND, OR, NOT, compare). It's built from the gates you met in Lesson 1.3: its adder is a chain of full adders.
unit-01.p5h02jwfgo: Registers. A handful of tiny, ultra-fast storage slots inside the CPU, each holding one number (typically 64 bits). They are the clerk's notepad. Data must usually be in a register before the ALU can work on it.
unit-01.pn20etm8kw: Program counter (PC). A special register that holds the position (address) of the next instruction to run. It's the clerk's finger, keeping their place in the list.
unit-01.2458yav0e3t: Control unit. The manager. It reads each instruction, works out what it means, and sends signals that make the ALU, registers and memory do the right thing.
unit-01.2emsvbf3gcx: Clock. A crystal that ticks billions of times per second. Each tick moves the CPU forward one step. A 3 GHz (gigahertz) CPU ticks 3 billion times per second.
unit-01.24cv8lcts8f: The CPU works closely with memory (RAM), where programs and data are kept while running. You'll explore memory in Lesson 1.5. For now: instructions live in memory, and the PC says which one is next.
unit-01.nrnpf4enys: Each kind of CPU understands a fixed vocabulary of instructions called its instruction set architecture (ISA). The two you'll hear about most are x86-64 (most Windows PCs and servers) and ARM (phones, tablets, and Apple's M-series Macs). A program compiled for one won't run directly on the other, because they speak different languages.
unit-01.j7bllrqi25: Real instruction sets have hundreds of instructions, but they fall into a few families:
unit-01.1lqn4a4chqs: Every instruction is itself stored as a pattern of bits, called machine code. For example, on an x86 CPU the bytes 05 07 00 00 00 mean "add 7 to register EAX". The CPU's control unit is a circuit that recognises these patterns.
unit-01.93saa9ww9j: A CPU spends its entire life repeating three steps, billions of times per second:
unit-01.17ijmz3m5lg: Fetch. Read the instruction at the address in the program counter from memory. Add one to the PC so it points to the next instruction.
unit-01.215irv187a4: Decode. The control unit works out what the instruction means: which operation, and which registers or values it uses.
unit-01.1p9cuqa8k84: Execute. Do it: the ALU adds, a register gets a new value, data moves to or from memory, or the PC is changed by a jump.
unit-01.14peuz0vr0f: Then repeat, forever, until the program ends or the power goes off.
unit-01.28292eifx3p: Key idea: Because the PC normally just goes up by one, instructions run in order, top to bottom. The only way to break that order is an instruction that changes the PC: a jump. That single idea is behind every if statement and every loop in every language.
unit-01.1nr935pfoz5: Real machine code is hard to read, so in this lesson you'll program TOY, a simplified CPU with four registers named A, B, C and D, all starting at 0. A TOY program is a list of instructions written in square brackets. Each instruction is in round brackets with its parts separated by commas, and instructions are numbered from 0:
unit-01.1n6pxb62p27: run_cpu(program) runs a program and returns the final registers. run_cpu(program, show=True) also prints a trace: one line per step, showing the PC and every register after the instruction runs. Traces are how engineers see what a processor is really doing.
unit-01.jnbudexs6s: Notice that TOY's ADD and SUB only work between registers. To add 1 to C, you first put 1 in another register, then add that register. Real CPUs have similar restrictions, which is part of why compiled programs contain so many instructions.
unit-01.1t9x8amnv2p: With JZ (jump if zero), a CPU can choose between two paths, which is a decision. With JUMP back to an earlier instruction, it can repeat work, which is a loop. Combine them and you can compute anything a computer can compute.
unit-01.9ndjdoye89: Here's a countdown loop that prints 3, 2, 1:
unit-01.x7svdjxubp: Instructions 2 to 5 are the loop body. Instruction 4 is the exit condition: without it, the loop would run forever. When you write while loops in Unit 2, Python turns them into exactly this pattern of compare-and-jump.
unit-01.jqiwvpryg8: If a 3 GHz CPU completed one instruction per tick, it would run 3,000,000,000 instructions per second. Light travels only about 10 cm in the time of one tick!
unit-01.1c9a7pch67j: Real CPUs are both slower and faster than this simple picture:
unit-01.v0e9qf012z: Slower because some instructions take many ticks, and waiting for memory can take hundreds of ticks (Lesson 1.5 explains why).
unit-01.1svr4g47gkw: Faster because of pipelining (like a laundry line: while one instruction executes, the next is being decoded and the one after is being fetched), running several instructions at once, and having multiple cores: several complete CPUs on one chip, each running its own instructions.
unit-01.19ee0nw2gz8: Deep dive: For decades, CPUs got faster mainly by raising the clock speed. Around 2005, chips hit a wall: faster clocks made them too hot. Since then, speed gains have come mostly from more cores and smarter designs. That's why modern software must do many things in parallel to use the hardware fully, a topic you'll study in Unit 10 (Operating Systems).

unit-01.1q0hmkle1pd: This program computes 7 + 3 and prints it. The trace shows each fetch-decode-execute step.

unit-01.1tepygek3ht: How many instructions could a CPU run in the blink of an eye (about 0.1 seconds)?
unit-01.c56abrd529: Forgetting that instructions are numbered from 0
unit-01.zb2vpytym4: The first instruction is number 0, so a jump to 4 runs the fifth instruction. Writing the number in a comment beside every instruction prevents off-by-one jump targets. Counting from zero is standard throughout computing, and you'll see it again with Python lists in Unit 3.
unit-01.22jt2smhsow: A loop needs an exit condition that will definitely become true. Testing for an exact value (JZ) when the counter can skip past it causes an infinite loop, as in exercise 4. The CPU won't warn you; it just keeps going.
unit-01.1ydg35gtdsg: Thinking the CPU understands the program
unit-01.rnwygilw3m: The CPU follows instructions mechanically. If the program says to add when you meant subtract, it will add, perfectly and instantly. Almost every bug you'll ever write is a case of the computer doing exactly what you said rather than what you meant.
unit-01.1sq1tx4mxax: Registers are a few tiny slots inside the CPU; memory (RAM) is a huge separate store. Data is loaded from memory into registers, worked on, and stored back. Lesson 1.5 covers memory.
unit-01.25p0agl6jbo: The CPU runs programs one simple instruction at a time: ALU (calculator), registers (tiny fast storage), control unit (manager), program counter (which instruction is next), clock (the heartbeat).
unit-01.20dm60gy5cf: Each CPU family has an instruction set (e.g. x86-64, ARM). Instructions are stored as bit patterns called machine code.
unit-01.1b6sacmmhd4: The CPU repeats fetch  to  decode  to  execute billions of times a second.
unit-01.kuoeapv9pd: Instructions run in order unless a jump changes the PC. Conditional jumps give decisions; backward jumps give loops.
unit-01.1p1pk143zu3: Clock speed (GHz) is ticks per second, but real performance also depends on pipelining, multiple cores, and waiting for memory.
unit-01.22ce1ipma9i: Your TOY CPU kept everything in four registers. Real programs need to store millions or billions of values. In Lesson 1.5 you'll explore memory: how every byte gets an address, why memory is organised as a hierarchy from tiny-and-fast to huge-and-slow, and why that hierarchy matters for the speed of every program you'll write.
unit-01.q3bhxrby7p: Understand how memory stores bytes at numbered addresses, how programs and data share that memory, and why computers use a hierarchy of storage (registers, caches, RAM, disk) that trades speed for size.
unit-01.11uez1840by: Explain addresses and calculate how much memory an address size can reach
unit-01.12dz2zytk9h: Work out where multi-byte values and sequences of values sit in memory

unit-01.1mcrb308d3g: Memory is a very long row of numbered boxes
unit-01.ykljsrj8r8: Your TOY CPU had four registers. A real program needs to keep track of far more: every character of a document, every pixel of an image, every variable in a game. That's what memory is for.
unit-01.2eb3ntiqxa3: Picture memory as an extremely long row of boxes. Each box holds one byte (8 bits), and each box has a number painted on it, called its address, starting at 0. A computer with 16 GB of RAM has about 16 billion of these boxes.
unit-01.z2xtak14ys: The CPU talks to memory with just two operations:
unit-01.keinmzxn45: Analogy: Think of a huge hotel where every room holds a single byte. To deliver or collect something, you need the room number. The CPU never says "the user's name"; it says "the bytes starting at address 5,382,104".
unit-01.2ay13wjavgc: This kind of memory is called RAM, for random access memory. "Random access" means any address can be read in the same amount of time, whether it's box 0 or box 15 billion, unlike a cassette tape where you'd have to fast-forward. RAM is also volatile: it forgets everything when the power goes off. That's why unsaved work is lost in a power cut.
unit-01.qmqq6wq45b: Addresses are numbers too, and that sets limits
unit-01.1evxw2fdba4: An address is just a number, and the CPU stores it in a register with a fixed number of bits. That puts a hard limit on how much memory the CPU can reach. With n-bit addresses there are 2ⁿ different addresses, so 2ⁿ bytes can be addressed.
unit-01.1u4ax0dwj8h: This is exactly why 32-bit computers couldn't use more than 4 GB of RAM, and why the industry switched to 64-bit processors in the 2000s. 64-bit addresses can reach more memory than all the computers on Earth combined.
unit-01.7ysvu0c0ge: A byte only holds 0 to 255, so bigger values are spread across several consecutive boxes. A 32-bit (4-byte) number stored "at address 1000" actually occupies addresses 1000, 1001, 1002 and 1003. A 64-bit number takes 8 boxes.
unit-01.y2np5xw9uo: When a program stores many values of the same size one after another, finding any one of them is simple arithmetic:
unit-01.28i39tfb3jh: Key idea: address of item i = start address + i  times  size of each item (counting items from 0). This formula is how arrays, lists and strings are found in memory, and it's why going to the 1,000,000th item is just as fast as going to the 1st: the CPU computes the address directly instead of searching.
unit-01.v7fpzw9crv: Which byte of a multi-byte number goes first? Most modern CPUs (x86 and usually ARM) are little-endian: the least significant byte (the "little end") goes at the lowest address. So the 16-bit number 0x1234 is stored as 34 then 12. Network protocols traditionally use big-endian (most significant byte first). The name comes from Gulliver's Travels, where two nations go to war over which end of a boiled egg to crack.
unit-01.x21lugvyu3: Here's a profound idea from the 1940s, usually credited to John von Neumann and his colleagues: store the program itself in the same memory as the data. Instructions are just bytes (machine code), so they can sit in memory boxes like any other bytes. This is called the stored-program design, and nearly every computer since has worked this way.
unit-01.1iymfjc5pb: Before this, "reprogramming" a computer meant physically rewiring it, which could take days. With stored programs, loading a new program is just copying bytes into memory. It's why your computer can switch from a web browser to a game in a second.
unit-01.22cix1pnnw8: Warning: It also creates risk. If instructions and data share memory, a bug that lets an attacker write data into the wrong place might let them write instructions, which the CPU will then run. This is the root of many famous security attacks, which you'll study in Unit 16.
unit-01.28yhdan0gg: Engineers face a frustrating trade-off: memory can be fast, large, or cheap, but not all three. Fast memory must be physically close to the CPU and built from expensive circuits; large memory must be dense and cheap per byte, which makes it slower. So computers use a hierarchy:
unit-01.1883w7xlmmx: (Numbers vary between machines; the ratios are what matter.)
unit-01.1345oj6dy65: Look at that last column. If an add took one second, fetching from RAM would take five minutes, and reading from a hard disk would take a year. Waiting for data, not computing, is often what makes programs slow.
unit-01.ooru3ee89j: SSDs and hard disks are storage, not memory: they're non-volatile (they keep data without power), but they're far slower. Files live in storage; to work on them, programs load them into RAM.
unit-01.vtdfoky8q7: Caches are small, fast memories between the CPU and RAM that automatically keep copies of recently used data. When the CPU needs an address, it checks L1 first, then L2, then L3, and only then goes to RAM.
unit-01.1jpy4qrvhqd: A cache hit means the data was found in the cache: fast.
unit-01.64tluzieav: A cache miss means it wasn't, so the CPU must wait for a slower level.
unit-01.ewv43vjb00: Analogy: Your desk (registers and L1) holds the few papers you're using right now. The bookshelf behind you (L2, L3) holds things you've used recently. The library across town (RAM) has everything but takes a trip. The warehouse in another city (disk) has everything ever, but takes days.
unit-01.g0k5utviq7: Caches work astonishingly well (often over 95% hit rates) because real programs show locality:
unit-01.1k13pf74zsw: Temporal locality: something used recently will probably be used again soon (like a loop counter).
unit-01.16nvyo9ipx4: Spatial locality: things near something used recently will probably be used soon (like the next item in a list). So when a cache fetches one byte, it grabs a whole cache line (typically 64 neighbouring bytes).
unit-01.1tl2llv75uf: We can estimate performance with the average memory access time:
unit-01.hi8b9eatt6: AMAT = hit time + miss rate  times  miss penalty
unit-01.4po6j3hkfo: With a 1 ns cache, a 5% miss rate and a 100 ns trip to RAM on a miss: 1 + 0.05  times  100 = 6 ns on average. Without the cache, every access would take 100 ns: the cache makes memory look about 16 times faster.
unit-01.1dyhf14gkdp: This is why, later in the course, you'll find that reading a list in order is much faster than jumping around it randomly, even though both read the same number of items.
unit-01.ffosorim83: Python's bytearray is a row of byte-sized boxes, so it makes a good model of RAM. The number in square brackets is the address.
unit-01.1634rcyg3jl: to_bytes shows exactly which bytes a number is stored as, in either byte order.
unit-01.1k9v3f8n4xd: Example 3: Finding item i in memory
unit-01.41ugodyzt7: The address formula that makes arrays fast.
unit-01.5dsw48h9sn: How much does a cache help?
unit-01.m7cvh5fv0p: RAM is fast and temporary; storage (SSD, hard disk) is slow and permanent. "My laptop has 16 GB of memory and 512 GB of storage" describes two different things. Running programs use RAM; saved files live in storage.
unit-01.1ma49j5jqkw: Forgetting that multi-byte values take several addresses
unit-01.jzxc1jwoxg: A 4-byte number at address 1000 also uses 1001, 1002 and 1003. The next 4-byte item starts at 1004, not 1001. Forgetting this leads to overlapping data, one of the nastiest bugs in languages like C.
unit-01.2do3rkqzkmu: Counting items from 1 in the address formula
unit-01.101ze0vhs2f: With the formula start + i  times  size, the first item is i = 0. Item "number 3" in everyday speech is i = 2. Most programming languages count from 0 precisely because of this formula.
unit-01.z5ugql2kdx: Assuming all memory accesses cost the same
unit-01.1gdpfdip0b5: A cache hit can be 100 times faster than a trip to RAM. Two programs doing the same amount of work can differ hugely in speed depending on how they access memory. Keep locality in mind, and you'll write faster code later.
unit-01.2dlzsi5gunb: Memory is a row of byte-sized boxes, each with a numbered address. The CPU reads and writes by address.
unit-01.1pjzj2oeztl: RAM is random access (every address equally fast) and volatile (lost without power).
unit-01.10hcgp6ydn6: n-bit addresses reach 2ⁿ bytes, which is why 32-bit machines were limited to 4 GiB.
unit-01.1k6bprcp3w5: Multi-byte values use consecutive addresses. Item i is at start + i  times  size. Byte order is little-endian on most CPUs.
unit-01.1no7hbxq81p: In the stored-program design, instructions live in memory alongside data.
unit-01.arceg3jxa1: The memory hierarchy (registers, caches, RAM, SSD, disk) trades speed for size. Caches exploit locality; AMAT = hit time + miss rate  times  miss penalty.
unit-01.1eq7mnse3ec: You now understand the hardware: bits, gates, the CPU and memory. One mystery remains. You write code in a language like Python, but the CPU only understands machine code. In Lesson 1.6, the last lesson of this unit, you'll discover how human-readable code becomes instructions, through assemblers, compilers and interpreters, and you'll peek at the instructions Python itself creates from your code.

unit-01.2bzn1y4xed: You now know that a CPU only understands machine code: bit patterns for simple instructions like "add register B to register A". Writing real software that way would be unbearable. A web browser contains tens of millions of lines of code; imagine writing that as raw numbers.
unit-01.phmvu6ggsb: So computer scientists built layers of languages, each one easier for humans and each one translated into the layer below:
unit-01.1e48t25xlpo: Key idea: This is abstraction, the most important idea in computer science. Each layer hides the messy details of the layer beneath, so you can think about what you want without worrying about how the transistors do it. You've just climbed the whole tower: transistors  to  gates  to  adders  to  CPU  to  machine code  to  assembly  to  high-level languages.
unit-01.1fp0qnk5jz4: Assembly language gives each machine instruction a short readable name called a mnemonic (like ADD, MOV, JMP) and lets you name registers instead of using bit patterns. There's a near one-to-one match between assembly instructions and machine code instructions, so translating is straightforward. The program that does it is called an assembler.
unit-01.m3fuco567g: Your TOY programs from Lesson 1.4 were essentially assembly. Here's what similar code looks like in real x86-64 assembly:
unit-01.10di9qmmsm2: Assembly is still used where every instruction counts: parts of operating systems, device drivers, and speed-critical code. Because it's tied to one instruction set, x86 assembly won't run on an ARM chip. You'll read and write some assembly in Unit 9.
unit-01.27inhxnzj50: A compiler translates an entire program written in a high-level language into machine code (or another lower-level language) before it runs. The output is an executable file you can run again and again without the compiler. C, C++, Rust, Go and Swift are usually compiled.
unit-01.50sfgln843: A compiler works in stages, a bit like how you'd translate a sentence from French:
unit-01.1tvgefln247: Lexing (tokenizing). Break the text into tokens, the "words" of the language. total = price * 3 + tax becomes 7 tokens: total, =, price, *, 3, +, tax.
unit-01.9x0foiabjc: Parsing. Check the grammar and build a syntax tree that shows how the pieces fit together. Because * binds tighter than +, price * 3 is grouped first: = / \ total + / \ * tax / \ price 3If the grammar is wrong (say you wrote total = price * + tax), the parser stops with a syntax error.
unit-01.1v1i3kn9ks7: Analysis and optimisation. Check meanings (does price exist?) and improve the code: for example, x = 60 * 60 * 24 can be computed once by the compiler as 86400, so the CPU never has to.
unit-01.1hloy7ps96w: Code generation. Walk the tree and emit instructions: load price, multiply by 3, add tax, store in total.
unit-01.lutczkdufj: Note: The first compiler for a popular language was built by Grace Hopper's team in the 1950s. Many people at the time didn't believe a computer could write programs. Today's compilers produce code that's usually faster than what an expert would write by hand in assembly.
unit-01.28zihxtu1iw: An interpreter takes a different approach: instead of translating the whole program first, it reads the program and carries it out directly, statement by statement, as it goes.
unit-01.2624iuxchxg: Analogy: A compiler is like translating a whole book into English and then handing over the translation; readers never need the translator again. An interpreter is like a live interpreter at a conference, translating each sentence as it's spoken; nothing is written down, and the interpreter must be there every time.
unit-01.87sqy912lb: In practice the line is blurry. Most modern "interpreted" languages first compile to an in-between form, and many use a JIT (just-in-time) compiler that compiles the busiest parts of a program to machine code while it runs. JavaScript engines in web browsers do this, which is why JavaScript became fast enough to run full applications.
unit-01.11nzd8hbjr7: Your TOY CPU stored values in named registers. Another popular design for an instruction set uses a stack instead.
unit-01.1lyyjktun4i: A stack works like a pile of plates: you can only push a new plate onto the top, or pop the top plate off. A stack machine's arithmetic instructions pop the top two values, combine them, and push the result back.
unit-01.1kjdcnso7kv: No registers are named at all; everything happens at the top of the stack. That makes stack instructions short and easy for a compiler to generate: just walk the syntax tree, pushing values and then applying the operator after both its operands. For subtraction, the value pushed first is the left side: PUSH 10, PUSH 4, SUB gives 10  minus  4 = 6.
unit-01.1ew79w3u103: In this lesson's exercises, run_stack(program) runs stack programs using ("PUSH", n), ("ADD",), ("SUB",), ("MUL",) and ("PRINT",) (print the top value), and show=True prints the stack after each step. The register CPU run_cpu from Lesson 1.4 is also available.
unit-01.xxnlks6i3z: So is Python compiled or interpreted? Both! When you run a Python program with the standard Python (called CPython, because it's written in C):
unit-01.1asumuer2tn: Python compiles your source code into bytecode: compact instructions for an imaginary computer, not for any real CPU.
unit-01.jzhprq4f6r: The Python virtual machine (VM), an interpreter loop written in C, then runs the bytecode one instruction at a time, in its own fetch-decode-execute cycle.
unit-01.plog45eb4g: The Python VM is a stack machine, just like the one above. And the VM itself is a C program that was compiled into machine code for your actual CPU. In this app, there's one more layer: that C code was compiled to WebAssembly, a portable instruction set that your web browser translates into your device's machine code. Layers on layers, each one hiding the one below.
unit-01.2deos37tgvr: Python's dis module ("disassemble") lets you see the bytecode Python makes. You'll see instructions like LOAD_NAME (push a variable's value), BINARY_OP (pop two, compute, push the result) and STORE_NAME (pop into a variable): the same push, compute, pop pattern as our stack machine.
unit-01.1arvbjy0ut9: Why: Bytecode makes Python portable: the same bytecode runs anywhere the VM has been built, on Windows, Mac, Linux, phones, or a browser. The cost is speed: simulating a CPU in software adds overhead, so pure Python is often 10 to 100 times slower than compiled C. For most programs, being quick to write matters far more than that difference, and libraries written in C handle the heavy number-crunching.
unit-01.578apknweo: Understanding translation explains the two kinds of error you'll meet constantly in Unit 2:
unit-01.6mwozhwk17: A syntax error is found while Python is compiling your code into bytecode, before any of it runs. Nothing runs at all, not even the lines above the mistake.
unit-01.2b3karpnbhj: A runtime error (an exception) happens while the program is running, when a line does something impossible, like dividing by zero. Lines before it have already run.
unit-01.2ac5z6pnfkz: Try both in the playground below. Seeing when an error happens tells you a lot about what's wrong.

unit-01.1uuqw92zw5l: Python's own tokenize module shows how Python splits a line into tokens, the first stage of compiling.
unit-01.log53kctkr: Each token has a kind: NAME (a name like price), OP (an operator), or NUMBER. Spaces aren't tokens at all; they just separate them.

unit-01.1soaljybm04: Thinking "Python is interpreted, so it's never compiled"

unit-02.19tzrz4sb2w: An int is a whole number, positive, negative or zero. Unlike the fixed-size integers of Lesson 1.2, Python's ints grow as big as they need to: 2 ** 1000 works fine and gives a 302-digit number. Python quietly uses more memory as the number grows, so ints never overflow.

unit-02.2bk7x3vp6qu: A float (floating-point number) holds numbers with a fractional part. Any number written with a decimal point is a float, even 2.0. Very big or small floats can be written in scientific notation: 6.02e23 means 6.02  times  10²³.
unit-02.1dwnjvcide0: Mixing an int and a float gives a float: 3 + 0.5 is 3.5, and 2 * 1.0 is 2.0.
unit-02.1k67x9se4ih: Now the famous surprise. Try print(0.1 + 0.2) and Python says 0.30000000000000004. This isn't a Python bug; every language using standard floats does the same. Here's why:
unit-02.thtpaq6o2n: Floats are stored in binary, in 64 bits (a standard called IEEE 754).
unit-02.1jvwqovxnu6: In decimal, 1/3 can't be written exactly: 0.3333... goes on forever, so any fixed number of digits is slightly off.
unit-02.1vf3321c0an: In binary, 0.1 is like 1/3: it's 0.000110011001100... repeating forever. Squeezed into 64 bits, it's stored as a number extremely close to, but not exactly, 0.1.
unit-02.5iiys019xn: Add two slightly-off numbers and the tiny errors can show up in the result.
unit-02.2b8rg32p70t: Never compare floats with ==. Instead check whether they're close enough: abs(a - b) < 1e-9. (abs gives the absolute value: the distance from zero, ignoring the sign.)
unit-02.x5kpd9plfw: Don't store money as a float. Store whole pennies (or cents) as an int: £19.99 is 1999 pennies. Banks and shops do exactly this, because a rounding error multiplied by millions of transactions is real money.
unit-02.ha3f5o1z2c: Deep dive: A 64-bit float stores a sign bit, an 11-bit exponent and a 52-bit fraction: binary scientific notation. That gives about 15 to 17 significant decimal digits of precision, and a range up to about 10³⁰⁸. In Unit 9 you'll look at the actual bits.

unit-02.1i432snzdgs: Key idea: Programming is mostly about managing complexity, and functions are your main tool for it. A large program is a few big functions built from smaller functions built from smaller ones still, just as a CPU is adders built from gates built from transistors.

unit-02.27vrr57sayr: Parameters are the names in the definition (name). Arguments are the actual values passed in a call ("Ada"). When you call greet("Ada"), Python binds the parameter name to the argument "Ada", then runs the body.
unit-02.1mpmw8gyhfs: A function can have zero parameters (def show_menu():) or several (def area(width, height):). Arguments are matched to parameters by position: the first argument goes to the first parameter, and so on.

unit-02.1pjsmu3ok4g: Functions can call other functions. Python keeps track using the call stack, the same push/pop structure you met in Lesson 1.6:
unit-02.cetxlwf8tw: Each call pushes a frame; each return pops one. When an error happens inside a function, Python's traceback shows this stack, listing every call that led to the error. You'll use that to debug in Lesson 2.9.
unit-02.zwbbb3u0wm: Scope, what a function can see
unit-02.kb7mqgcagb: Variables created inside a function, including its parameters, are local: they exist only in that call's frame and vanish when the function returns.
unit-02.10tye8sldjp: This is a feature, not a limitation. You can use any names you like inside a function without worrying about clashing with names elsewhere. Two functions can both have a variable called total and they never interfere.
unit-02.19w20ht1x8v: Variables created at the top level of a program are global. A function can read a global variable, but if it assigns to a name, Python treats that name as local to the function. Relying on global variables makes functions hard to understand and test, because their behaviour depends on something outside them.
unit-02.drv4m0tqkr: Tip: A good function gets everything it needs through its parameters and gives back its result with return. Then it behaves like a mathematical function: same inputs, same output, every time. Such functions are easy to test, easy to reuse, and easy to reason about.
unit-02.1jfg68xmn44: Parameters can have default values, used when the caller doesn't pass that argument:
unit-02.15ge2pzsl6j: Parameters with defaults must come after those without. Callers can also name arguments explicitly, using keyword arguments: greet(name="Ada", greeting="Hi"). You've already used these: sep= and end= in print are keyword arguments with default values.
unit-02.2e5qgnmuyde: A docstring is a string written as the first line of a function's body. It documents what the function does, what it takes, and what it returns:
unit-02.st0udiwob7: Docstrings are what Python's help() shows, and editors display them when you hover over a call. Every function you write from now on should have one.
unit-02.xjtymwx4dx: Good functions share a few qualities:
unit-02.25l4inzrsm1: One job. If you need "and" to describe it ("reads the input and calculates and prints"), split it up.
unit-02.198upkq38sw: A clear name, usually a verb or a question: calculate_tax, is_valid_email, count_vowels.
unit-02.1o49euw3mch: Short. Most good functions fit on one screen, and many are just a few lines.
unit-02.1mko7yhc82u: Decomposition means breaking a problem into functions before writing them. To "print every prime below 100 that's also a palindrome", you might write is_prime(n), is_palindrome(n), and then a short loop that uses both. Each piece is simple, can be tested on its own, and can be reused elsewhere.
unit-02.1mgu4l55wft: Think of functions as building blocks. In the exercises you'll build several small ones and then combine them, exactly the way professionals build real programs.

unit-02.1j2chyhh6ca: If a function prints its result, the caller gets None and can't use the value. Return it, and let the caller print if needed.

unit-02.47b7u37ymr: def name(parameters): defines a function; calling name(arguments) runs its body with the parameters bound to the arguments.

unit-02.15ar0s4cyqk: In 1947, engineers working on the Harvard Mark II computer found a moth trapped in a relay, taped it into their logbook, and wrote "First actual case of bug being found." (Grace Hopper, who you met in Lesson 1.6, loved telling this story.) The word "bug" was older than that, but the name stuck.
unit-02.1v505b8qlkh: Here's the truth every programmer learns: you will write bugs constantly, no matter how experienced you become. Professionals often spend more time debugging than writing new code. What separates beginners from experts isn't writing bug-free code; it's finding and fixing bugs calmly and systematically.
unit-02.1xqnvka6dei: Key idea: Debugging is the scientific method applied to code. Observe what happens, form a hypothesis about why, design an experiment to test it, and repeat. Guessing and randomly changing things is the opposite of debugging, and it usually adds new bugs.
unit-02.134w2t45r8b: Syntax errors are the easiest: Python tells you exactly where they are. Runtime errors come with a traceback that usually points straight at the problem. Logic errors are the hardest, because the program runs happily and produces the wrong answer. The only way to catch them is to know what the right answer should be and check, which is why testing matters so much.
unit-02.11o1rv8q4du: When an exception isn't handled, Python prints a traceback: a report of the call stack (Lesson 2.8) at the moment of the error.
unit-02.1tfqxkw11ct: Read it from the bottom up:
unit-02.cw1ht9muth: The last line says what happened: the exception type (ZeroDivisionError) and a message.
unit-02.12jpbfeblry: The line just above says where it happened: line 2, inside average.
unit-02.opvst7pc67: Further up is how you got there: line 8 called report, which on line 5 called average.
unit-02.2gb02kfo39x: The line where the error appears isn't always where the bug is. Line 2 is correct code; the real problem is that report was called with 0 people. Following the traceback upwards helps you find where the bad value came from.
unit-02.w29rc397f5: You'll meet IndexError and KeyError in Unit 3, when you work with collections.
unit-02.zasfnzfv6t: Tip: Copy the last line of an unfamiliar error message into a search engine. Millions of programmers have hit the same error before you, and the explanation is usually one search away. Reading error messages carefully is a skill that pays off for your whole career.
unit-02.36lqek41lf: When a program misbehaves, work through these steps:
unit-02.1597y0zanao: Reproduce it. Find an input that reliably causes the problem. A bug you can't trigger, you can't fix (or confirm you've fixed).
unit-02.2141rg64nct: Read the error message and traceback, if there is one.
unit-02.1evez5mc2oz: Hypothesise. What could cause exactly this behaviour? Be specific: "the loop stops one iteration early" is a hypothesis; "it's broken" isn't.
unit-02.1z86e2hi8pv: Experiment. Gather evidence to confirm or rule out your hypothesis: Print debugging: add temporary prints showing variable values at key points. The f-string form print(f"{total=}") prints both the name and the value, like total=42. Trace by hand: make a table of variables, line by line, as you did in Lesson 2.2. Compare what you expect with what the prints show. The bug is where they first differ. Divide and conquer: check halfway through the program. Is the value right there? Then the bug is in the second half; otherwise the first. Keep halving. This is a binary search, and it finds the bug in a 1000-line program in about 10 checks.
unit-02.1s3agqcax2f: Fix the cause, not the symptom. If a total is 1 too small, adding + 1 at the end hides the bug; fixing the loop's range removes it.
unit-02.958l987l02: Verify the fix with the input that failed, and with other inputs too, to check you haven't broken something else.
unit-02.u6kaoz8tmz: Prevent: add a test for that case so the bug can never quietly return.
unit-02.ydzh5ky0ce: Analogy: Rubber duck debugging is a real technique used by professionals: explain your code, line by line, out loud, to a rubber duck (or a patient friend). Very often, halfway through explaining what a line "obviously" does, you realise it doesn't.
unit-02.1kmpiu94pcv: An assert statement checks that something is true, and raises an AssertionError if it isn't:
unit-02.26p4u5vt7vv: If every assert passes, nothing happens. If one fails, the program stops with your message. This is exactly how the automatic tests in this course work: every test you've passed was a set of assert statements run against your code.
unit-02.1gto30lggu8: Typical cases: ordinary inputs, with answers you've worked out independently.
unit-02.1lbaeoecpui: Edge cases: zero, negative numbers, empty strings, one item, the biggest allowed value.
unit-02.v2b5nm4kx4: Boundaries: values on each side of every condition (Lesson 2.5).
unit-02.10h33ut9r75: A good way to judge your tests: imagine someone made a small mistake in the function (< instead of <=, a missing round, a wrong constant). Would at least one of your tests fail? If not, your tests aren't strong enough. Deliberately introducing small bugs to check that tests catch them is called mutation testing, and you'll do it in exercise 5.
unit-02.1dx81ypkkv4: Writing tests before fixing a bug, or even before writing the function, is a professional habit called test-driven development. You'll study testing in depth in Unit 14.
unit-02.1lt2g11rnr0: Handling errors with try and except
unit-02.wgn34l5m6w: Some errors aren't bugs in your code but problems with the outside world: a user types "twelve" where you asked for a number, a file is missing, the network is down. A program should cope with these gracefully rather than crash. Python's try / except statement does this:
unit-02.2es1uxnitg2: Python runs the try block. If a ValueError happens anywhere inside it, Python immediately jumps to the except ValueError: block instead of crashing. If no error happens, the except block is skipped.
unit-02.26ni063swua: Combined with a loop, this gives robust input reading:
unit-02.nbsa2itvt9: Warning: Always name the exception you expect (except ValueError:). A bare except: catches everything, including errors caused by your own bugs (a misspelled variable becomes a silent failure instead of a helpful NameError). Catch only what you know how to handle, and keep the try block as small as possible.
unit-02.15dabugs33h: You can also raise errors yourself when a function receives something it can't handle: raise ValueError("percent must be between 0 and 100"). That's often better than returning a strange value like None, because it can't be accidentally ignored.
unit-02.1byaq9kof1a: Run this in the editor and match each line of the traceback to the code. The error appears in average, but the bad value comes from the call on the last line.

unit-02.ozw6hiqr77: Tests that pass are silent; a failing test stops with your message.

unit-02.1l2tft24gsz: Changing code randomly until it works
unit-02.25ocnmqkp8l: Random changes might make one example pass while breaking others, and you won't understand why it works. Form a hypothesis, test it, and only then change code.
unit-02.1oa4oc10zb0: Reading only the top of a traceback
unit-02.1kckqcc01t9: The most useful information is at the bottom: the exception type, the message, and the line where it happened. Start there and work upwards.
unit-02.cznijfn6t3: A bare except: hides real bugs, such as a misspelled variable name. Catch only the specific exception you expect, around only the line that can raise it.
unit-02.1pvapjr4vjo: Tests that use only typical values (and especially "special" values like 0, 1 or 100 that hide bugs) give false confidence. Include edge cases and boundaries, and ask "what mistake would this test catch?"
unit-02.1znq1g6hqnn: Fixing the symptom instead of the cause
unit-02.c96mvwmk6d: If a loop adds one number too few, adding + n at the end makes the output right but leaves the faulty loop in place. Find why the value is wrong and fix that.
unit-02.1nyz7opf1ff: Three kinds of error: syntax (found before running), runtime/exceptions (stop the program with a traceback), and logic (wrong output, no message).
unit-02.xp25nqm932: Read tracebacks bottom-up: the exception and message, then the line, then the chain of calls that led there.
unit-02.2edtb1xdggl: Common exceptions: NameError, TypeError, ValueError, ZeroDivisionError, IndentationError, AttributeError.
unit-02.1ipowvbhbyv: Debug systematically: reproduce, read, hypothesise, experiment (print, trace, divide and conquer), fix the cause, verify, prevent.
unit-02.1xx4tz721tl: assert turns expectations into tests. Good tests cover typical cases, edge cases and boundaries, and would catch plausible mistakes.
unit-02.1fi9d3nvn7: try/except SpecificError: recovers from expected problems like bad input. Keep the try block small; never catch everything blindly.

unit-03.6uazprb97g: How can a dictionary find a key without searching? The trick is called hashing. When you store a key, Python computes a number from it, its hash, using a function that always gives the same number for the same value. The hash decides which slot in a hidden internal table the entry goes into. To look a key up later, Python hashes it again and goes straight to that slot. The time taken hardly depends on how many entries there are: looking up one name among a million is about as fast as among ten.

unit-04.2dtc0erjjko: By now you know a lot of Python: loops, functions, lists, dictionaries, files. Yet many learners hit a wall at this point. They can read code, and they understand every line of a solution when they see it, but faced with a blank editor and a new problem, they don't know where to start.
unit-04.tmfdhhh7as: That's because knowing a language and solving problems are different skills. Knowing Python is like knowing the rules and pieces of chess; solving problems is knowing how to play. The good news is that problem solving can be learned like any other skill, and it starts with having a method, so you always know what to do next.
unit-04.2dwuevu88ia: The method in this lesson comes from the mathematician George Pólya, whose 1945 book How to Solve It described four phases:
unit-04.1226mlsyevc: Beginners usually skip straight to step 3, typing code before they really understand the problem. Experienced programmers spend most of their time in steps 1 and 2, and their code comes out shorter and with fewer bugs.
unit-04.9h83vqlcct: You can't solve a problem you don't understand, and most problems are stated less precisely than they seem. Before writing anything, answer these questions:
unit-04.5v7b1cal8u: What are the inputs? What types are they? What range of values?
unit-04.nkxcp0s807: What is the output? A return value, printed text, a file? In exactly what format?
unit-04.1ya4eja86dk: What are the edge cases? An empty list, a single item, zero, negative numbers, duplicates, the largest possible input?
unit-04.o51hkrhvjp: Can I restate it in my own words?
unit-04.1lq1l58tcw3: Then do the single most useful thing in all of problem solving: work some examples by hand, on paper, slowly. Choose small inputs, including an edge case, and write down the answer you expect. If you can't solve it by hand, you can't tell a computer how to.
unit-04.i0wggqdyfb: Analogy: A builder reads the plans and walks the site before ordering any bricks. Ten minutes understanding the job saves days of knocking down walls.
unit-04.dfdevs8a2w: For example: "Write a function that returns the length of the longest run of increasing numbers in a list." What's a "run"? Do equal neighbours count as increasing? What does an empty list return? Working an example, [3, 4, 7, 2, 5, 6, 8, 1], you find the runs 3-4-7 (length 3), 2-5-6-8 (length 4) and 1 (length 1), so the answer is 4. Doing this by hand, you'll probably notice how you did it: you moved along the list, extending the current run while numbers went up and starting a new run when they didn't. That's the algorithm.
unit-04.1x0hs1xmwqw: Now decide how to solve it, still without writing Python. Useful questions:
unit-04.1dvj4mgze30: Have I seen a similar problem? Most problems are variations on patterns you know: filter, transform, search, count, group (Unit 3). The longest run is a "track state as you go" problem, like run-length encoding in Lesson 3.3.
unit-04.n3u055evj7: Can I break it into smaller problems? This is decomposition: split a big problem into parts that are each easy to solve, often one function per part. "Is this a valid date?" splits into "is this year a leap year?" and "how many days are in this month?".
unit-04.1gqvua18vet: Can I solve a simpler version first? Ignore an awkward requirement, solve the rest, then add it back.
unit-04.16w7qeoggib: Write the plan as pseudocode: structured English that reads like code but ignores Python's exact rules. There's no standard syntax; it just has to be clear to you:
unit-04.xgjwawfezf: Here is some code. Have a look at it on screen.
unit-04.2bcch2bwagx: Pseudocode lets you think about the logic without worrying about colons and brackets. If the pseudocode is wrong, it's much cheaper to fix than code.
unit-04.17i2x4xvkg5: Step 3. Carry out the plan, in small steps
unit-04.1r9ethk4f16: Now translate the plan into Python, but not all at once. Write a little, run it, check it, then write a little more. Each step should be small enough that if something breaks, you know exactly which lines caused it.
unit-04.1srg7y1my30: A powerful habit is to write the tests first, using the examples you worked by hand in step 1 (and the assert statements from Lesson 2.9):
unit-04.1ja9bsrbqd6: Now you have a definition of "done": when every assert passes. This is the idea behind test-driven development, a practice used widely in industry (Unit 14).
unit-04.n4gcmx83v9: With decomposition, build and test the small functions first, then the functions that use them. When a small function is tested, you can rely on it and stop thinking about its insides, the same way you rely on len without wondering how it works. That's abstraction (Lesson 1.6), applied to your own code.
unit-04.j48wc85oeh: A working program isn't the end. Look back and ask:
unit-04.11yrpuntys0: Does it handle every edge case? Run it on the tricky inputs from step 1.
unit-04.1v6g9nrrawk: Can I check the result another way? For example, compare with a slow but obviously correct brute-force version on many random inputs. The tests in this course often do exactly this.
unit-04.1h97ovysgnm: Can it be simpler? Can a loop become a comprehension, or a chain of ifs become data (like the tic-tac-toe lines in Lesson 3.4)?
unit-04.12bz1xvdnqu: What did I learn? Is there a pattern here you'll meet again?
unit-04.20bt3qda36u: Key idea: When you're stuck, go back a step. Stuck writing code? Your plan is incomplete: go back to pseudocode. Stuck on the plan? You don't understand the problem well enough: go back and work more examples by hand. "Stuck" almost always means you skipped something earlier.

unit-04.18b1r1ym78x: Two programs can give exactly the same answers while one takes a second and the other takes a week. In Lesson 3.7 you saw this happen: checking for a pair with a given sum took 20 billion steps with nested loops, and 200,000 with a set. Both were correct; only one was usable.
unit-04.26pjws1pedq: How do we compare algorithms? The obvious answer is to time them, but a stopwatch measures the computer as much as the algorithm. The same code runs at different speeds on a phone and a desktop, and even on the same machine from one run to the next. What we want is a measure of the algorithm itself.
unit-04.1arb347tnmz: The answer is to count steps: the basic operations the algorithm performs, such as comparisons, additions or loop iterations. A step takes roughly constant time on any machine, so the step count captures the algorithm's work independent of the hardware.
unit-04.ej5wfenxgn: And we care most about one question: how does the number of steps grow as the input grows? An algorithm that does 5n steps and one that does 3n steps behave similarly: double the input, double the work. One that does n² steps is in a different league: double the input, quadruple the work.
unit-04.zh05x7ubvb: The simplest way to count steps is to add a counter to the code. Here's linear search (Lesson 3.2), counting comparisons:
unit-04.i487433t16: If the target is first, it takes 1 comparison: that's the best case. If it's missing, it takes len(lst) comparisons: the worst case. On average, if the target is equally likely to be anywhere, about half the list.
unit-04.spyjxrngr5: We usually focus on the worst case, because it's a guarantee: "this will never take more than n comparisons". Average cases are useful too, but harder to define (average over what inputs?).
unit-04.ny21s93tvn: Most algorithms you'll write in this course fall into a handful of families. Let n be the size of the input:
unit-04.2db5u8e9ip: Constant: the work doesn't depend on n at all. Indexing a list jumps straight to the address (Lesson 1.5); a dictionary lookup jumps to the hashed slot (Lesson 3.6).
unit-04.17g4galqndw: Linear: one pass over the data, doing a constant amount of work per item. Summing a list, linear search, counting words.
unit-04.j09yfeqjpi: Quadratic: for each item, look at every item (or every later item). Comparing all pairs, the n² dedupe from Lesson 3.2. A loop over all pairs i < j does n(n  minus  1)/2 steps, which is still quadratic: for large n it's about n²/2, and halving doesn't change the family.
unit-04.23nelc01qdx: Logarithmic: each step halves the remaining problem. Starting from n, how many halvings until you're down to 1? That's log₂ n: about 10 for a thousand, 20 for a million, 30 for a billion. You met this number in Lesson 1.1: n items need about log₂ n bits to number them, because each bit halves the possibilities.
unit-04.y2y0uf7sye: Key idea: At a million items, a logarithmic algorithm takes about 20 steps, a linear one a million, and a quadratic one a trillion. If a step takes a nanosecond, that's 20 nanoseconds, a millisecond, and 17 minutes. The family an algorithm belongs to matters far more than how carefully its loop is written.
unit-04.14so8tdkpr2: These families have standard names in Big-O notation: big O of 1, big O of log n, big O of n, big O of n². You'll study Big-O formally in Unit 8; for now, the idea of growth is what matters.
unit-04.hospfm8i1h: A neat way to identify an algorithm's family, even without reading its code, is to double the input and see what happens to the step count:
unit-04.dbdyrevdgy: Scientists use the same trick: run an experiment at two sizes and compare. It works with real timings too, as long as n is big enough that the timing noise is small.

unit-04.1rurfqy2fve: For example, this looks like one loop, but in result searches a growing list each time, so it does about n²/2 steps:
unit-04.safx81hjli: Swapping the list for a set (Lesson 3.7) makes it linear.
unit-04.1ytpo9ty70d: Tip: You don't need to optimise everything. For a list of 100 items, even quadratic code finishes instantly. Think about growth when the data might be large, or when code runs inside another loop. "Make it work, then make it fast (if it needs to be)."

unit-04.242a2zo2apn: Two loops one after another add (n + n = 2n, linear). Only nested loops multiply.
unit-04.1kbfnc9on3s: Clear, correct code comes first. Worry about growth when data can be large or the code is inside another loop, and measure before and after.
unit-04.y3xyd5ljvu: Measure algorithms by counting steps, not with a stopwatch, and focus on how the count grows with input size n.

unit-04.12n2hdzbn4x: Common growth families: constant (1), logarithmic (log₂ n, halving), linear (n, one loop), quadratic (n², nested loops).
unit-04.bs3wt2v45i: Sequential loops add; nested loops multiply. n(n  minus  1)/2 is still quadratic.

unit-04.2c477as3uyb: Watch for hidden loops: in on a list, insert(0, ...), remove, slicing and string +=.
