unit-04.128ryw13bv2: I'm thinking of a number between 1 and 100. Each time you guess, I'll say "higher", "lower" or "correct". What's your strategy?
unit-04.1iturg8i7gy: You could guess 1, 2, 3, ... (linear search), which might take 100 guesses. But almost everyone quickly realises the best first guess is 50. Whatever I answer, half the numbers are ruled out at once. Then guess the middle of what's left: 25 or 75. And so on. Each guess halves the possibilities: 100, 50, 25, 13, 7, 4, 2, 1. At most 7 guesses, guaranteed.
unit-04.27tbkn5r9m5: That strategy is binary search, and it works on any data that is sorted. Searching a sorted list of a million names for "Lovelace", you check the middle name. If "Lovelace" comes alphabetically before it, the answer must be in the first half; otherwise the second half. One comparison throws away half a million names. About 20 comparisons finish the job, where linear search could need a million.
unit-04.1sbz05ksvah: Analogy: Looking up a word in a paper dictionary: you open it near the middle, see you've landed on "M", and flip left because you want "F". You never read every page from the start.
unit-04.3lciggmsnr: Binary search relies on one fact: if the middle item is smaller than the target, every item to its left is smaller too, so they can all be skipped. That's only true if the list is sorted. On an unsorted list, binary search will happily skip right past the target and wrongly report it missing.
unit-04.seg7m92t8s: Sorting costs time (you'll see how much in Lessons 4.4 and 4.7), so binary search pays off when you sort once and search many times, like a phone book, a dictionary, or a database index.
unit-04.1ex610qy2ao: We keep track of the part of the list where the target could still be, between two indexes lo and hi (inclusive):
unit-04.2b46fg85swf: Each pass looks at the middle of the remaining range. If it's the target, we're done. If it's too small, the target can only be to the right, so the new range starts just after mid. If it's too big, the range ends just before mid. When lo passes hi, the range is empty and the target isn't there.
unit-04.65u123or21: In pseudocode (Lesson 4.1), it's just: look at the middle; if it's not the answer, throw away the half that can't contain it; repeat until found or nothing's left.
unit-04.1bw5gj4if95: Binary search is famously easy to get almost right. When the computer scientist Jon Bentley asked professional programmers to write it, about 90% of their versions had bugs. The traps are all off-by-one errors:
unit-04.cosugdepy3: while lo < hi instead of lo <= hi: misses the case where the range has shrunk to one item, so a target in that last position isn't found.
unit-04.2ekj47pq8lo: lo = mid instead of mid + 1 (or hi = mid instead of mid - 1): when lo and hi are neighbours, mid equals lo, the range never shrinks, and the loop runs forever.
unit-04.zkwz8f8y9x: Forgetting the empty list: hi starts at  minus 1, so the loop never runs and  minus 1 is correctly returned. Check that yours does too.
unit-04.1ad74ios6sc: The way to reason about it confidently is a loop invariant: a statement that's true before the loop starts and stays true after every pass. Here it is:
unit-04.14crqe2penu: Key idea: If the target is anywhere in the list, it is somewhere in lst[lo..hi]. At the start, the range is the whole list, so it's true. Each branch only throws away items that can't be the target, so it stays true. When the range is empty, the invariant says the target isn't in the list. And because the range shrinks every pass (by at least one item, thanks to the + 1 and - 1), the loop must end.
unit-04.124frvfdkl7: Invariants are how computer scientists prove that loops are correct, rather than just hoping. You'll use them more formally in Units 6 and 8.
unit-04.y5pybhyhez: Each comparison halves the range (or ends the search). Starting with n items, after k comparisons at most n / 2ᵏ remain. The search must end once that drops below 1, so it takes at most about log₂ n + 1 comparisons: the "halvings" count from Lesson 4.2.
unit-04.1wg51ngchy2: Doubling the data adds just one comparison. That's logarithmic growth, and it's why binary search is one of the most important algorithms ever devised.
unit-04.2gi08b21qll: Insertion points and the bisect module
unit-04.2gf3aw1ahv1: Often the question isn't "is it there?" but "where would it go?": the index of the first item that is greater than or equal to x. This is called the lower bound or insertion point, because inserting x there keeps the list sorted. A small change to binary search finds it:
unit-04.1u0vrfb9ylu: Here the invariant is different: everything before lo is less than x, and everything from hi onwards is at least x. When lo meets hi, that's the boundary. (Note hi = mid, not mid - 1, because mid itself might be the answer; that's safe here because the loop condition is lo < hi, which guarantees mid < hi.)
unit-04.1503ln2yytd: Python's standard library has this ready-made in the bisect module: bisect.bisect_left(lst, x) is exactly lower_bound, and bisect.insort(lst, x) inserts while keeping the list sorted. Use them in real programs; write your own here to understand them.
unit-04.p9ku8uj5fm: The halving idea works even without a list. Suppose you want the integer square root of a big number n: the largest whole number r with r  times  r  less than or equal to  n. unit-04.v89pli1ut5: Python already has sorted and list.sort, and you should use them in real programs. So why write your own?
unit-04.1yaholwk3r2: Because sorting is the perfect laboratory for algorithms. It's easy to state ("put these in order"), there are dozens of ways to do it, and the ways differ enormously in speed. Learning them teaches you how to design, trace, analyse and compare algorithms, skills you'll use on problems no library solves for you. Sorting also matters in practice: binary search (Lesson 4.3) needs sorted data, and so do many other algorithms.
unit-04.15y8sccysqp: In this lesson you'll meet two simple methods that people use naturally when sorting things by hand. In Lesson 4.7 you'll meet a cleverer one that's dramatically faster on big lists.
unit-04.222xix38zfg: Imagine sorting a hand of playing cards laid out on a table. One natural method: find the smallest card and put it first. Then find the smallest of the rest and put it second. And so on.
unit-04.atn9glpuor: That's selection sort. On a list, "put it first" means swapping it with whatever is in the first position:
unit-04.1jgscz1b0v1: The list is split into a sorted part (on the left, growing by one each pass) and an unsorted part (on the right). That's the loop invariant: after pass i, the first i + 1 items are the smallest items, in order.
unit-04.1kuen1shc23: It sorts in place (Lesson 3.4): it rearranges the list it's given, using no second list, and returns None like list.sort().
unit-04.dqciwf0nh2: How much work? The first pass compares n  minus  1 items, the next n  minus  2, and so on: (n  minus  1) + (n  minus  2) + ... + 1 = n(n  minus  1)/2 comparisons. That's the triangular loop from Lesson 4.2: quadratic. And it does that many comparisons every time, even if the list was already sorted, because it can't know the minimum without looking at every remaining item.
unit-04.h6wn5j2sgy: Now imagine picking cards up one at a time from the table and keeping your hand sorted. Each new card is inserted into its correct place among the cards you already hold, sliding the bigger cards along to make room.
unit-04.1be1bhyot2j: The invariant: before pass i, the first i items are sorted (but, unlike selection sort, they aren't necessarily the smallest items overall).
unit-04.21hvt5laxzn: How much work? It depends on the input:
unit-04.eutwi2wbpd: Worst case, a list in reverse order: every new item slides all the way to the front. That's 1 + 2 + ... + (n  minus  1) = n(n  minus  1)/2 comparisons: quadratic.
unit-04.brkaxqdwd1: Best case, an already sorted list: every new item is compared once with its left neighbour and stays put. That's n  minus  1 comparisons: linear!
unit-04.1jf5x50tofb: So insertion sort is excellent for lists that are nearly sorted, such as a sorted list with a few new items added at the end. That's why real-world sorting libraries use insertion sort for small or nearly sorted pieces of data.
unit-04.1rf0vue87i: When you sort records by one field, what happens to records with equal keys? A stable sort keeps them in their original relative order.
unit-04.27u0tex16cl: Sorted by age with a stable sort: Bob, Di, Ada, Cy. Bob still comes before Di, and Ada before Cy, as in the original list. An unstable sort might give Di, Bob, Cy, Ada.
unit-04.u2za5vg1qx: Why care? Because stability lets you sort by several keys in steps. To sort people by age, and alphabetically within each age, first sort by name, then do a stable sort by age: the name order survives inside each age group.
unit-04.1klwub8440: Insertion sort is stable: an item only slides past items that are strictly bigger (lst[j] > item), never past an equal one. Selection sort is not: its long-distance swaps can jump an item over an equal one. Python's sorted and sort are guaranteed stable (you relied on this in Lesson 3.5).
unit-04.1xiea01v5xd: Both algorithms are quadratic in the worst case: sorting a million items would take around 500 billion comparisons. That's far too slow, which is why Python's built-in sort uses a more advanced algorithm called Timsort (a blend of merge sort, Lesson 4.7, and insertion sort).
unit-04.gvi57i5rwz: There's also a completely different idea. If you're sorting small whole numbers (exam marks from 0 to 100, say), you don't need to compare items at all. Just count how many times each value appears, then write the values out in order. This is counting sort: it makes one pass to count and one pass over the possible values, so its work grows linearly. The catch is that it only works when the range of possible values is small; you'll try it in the last exercise.
unit-04.121hodk7wyd: Key idea: There's no single "best" sorting algorithm. The right choice depends on the size of the data, whether it's nearly sorted, whether stability matters, and what kind of values you're sorting. Asking "what do I know about my data?" is the heart of algorithm design.

unit-04.5awj4dmd9p: In-place sorts return None, like list.sort(). Sort, then use the list.
unit-04.1s639ogsvfh: In insertion sort, sliding past items that are equal (>=) reorders equal keys, making the sort unstable. Use >.
unit-04.dtzk4c86hf: Selection sort: repeatedly find the minimum of the unsorted part and swap it into place. Always n(n  minus  1)/2 comparisons; not stable.
unit-04.1uxokmpbcmt: Insertion sort: take each item and slide it left into the sorted part. Quadratic in the worst case, linear on sorted or nearly sorted data; stable.
unit-04.1hf4fu7zh45: Both sort in place, using no second list, and are described by loop invariants about the sorted part.
unit-04.27pgii7m0hv: A stable sort keeps equal keys in their original order, which allows sorting by several keys in steps.
unit-04.2bztncl3ifr: Insertion sort's work is about n plus the number of inversions (out-of-order pairs).
unit-04.1jtrf6q8h4l: Counting sort sorts small whole numbers in linear time without comparisons, by using values as indexes.
unit-04.13xc76vltfi: Both simple sorts are too slow for big lists. The faster method in Lesson 4.7 depends on a powerful idea: a function that solves a problem by calling itself on smaller versions of the same problem. In Lesson 4.5 you'll learn this idea, called recursion, from the ground up.

unit-04.1l5kcmg61si: Solving a problem with a smaller version of itself
unit-04.1sv50ihq12d: Imagine you're in a long queue at a cinema and you want to know your position, but you can't see the front. You could ask the person in front of you: "what's your position?" They don't know either, so they ask the person in front of them, and so on. Eventually the question reaches the person at the very front, who knows the answer without asking anyone: "I'm number 1." That answer travels back down the line, each person adding 1, until it reaches you.
unit-04.2eru8g165p7: That's recursion: solving a problem by reducing it to a smaller version of the same problem, until you reach a version so small that the answer is obvious.
unit-04.2gkmwyg371t: Every recursive solution has two parts:
unit-04.68tnphgbvk: A base case: an input small enough to answer directly, without recursion. (The person at the front.)
unit-04.2djrrui1zul: A recursive case: an answer built from the answer to a smaller input. (My position is the position of the person in front, plus 1.)
unit-04.12icxgr9ci6: Mathematicians define things this way all the time. The factorial of n, written n!, is 1  times  2  times  ...  times  n. It can also be defined recursively:
unit-04.1dfscsy7wh5: n! = n  times  (n  minus  1)! for n  greater than or equal to  1 (recursive case)
unit-04.13fnluznrpu: In Python, that definition becomes a function that calls itself:
unit-04.scjz2jmied: It reads almost exactly like the mathematical definition. That directness is recursion's great strength.
unit-04.uj7mn5072s: How it runs: the call stack
unit-04.17bz80i2uq2: How can a function call itself without getting confused? The answer is the call stack you met in Lesson 2.8. Every call to a function gets its own frame: its own private copy of the parameters and local variables. Calling factorial(3) creates a frame where n is 3; inside it, the call factorial(2) creates a new frame where n is 2. The two ns are completely separate, just like the local variables of two different functions.
unit-04.r0wserznue: The calls go down until the base case, pushing a frame each time; then the answers come back up, each frame finishing its multiplication and being popped off. Each frame waits, paused in the middle of its return line, until the call it made returns. This is exactly the stack machine idea from Lesson 1.6: last in, first out.
unit-04.1n2fejeip5: Analogy: Russian nesting dolls. You open each doll to find a smaller one inside, until you reach the smallest solid doll (the base case). Then you close them up again in reverse order.
unit-04.1aezwk0zc0t: Tracing every call is useful for understanding, but it's a terrible way to design recursive functions: for anything bigger than factorial, the trace becomes overwhelming. Instead, experienced programmers use a mental trick often called the recursive leap of faith:
unit-04.p89fqpxfo0: For the recursive case, assume the function already works for smaller inputs. Don't think about how.
unit-04.1lxjxeq5zjo: Ask: "if I had the answer for the smaller input, how would I build the answer for this input?"
unit-04.1ry02gd069r: For example, to sum a list recursively: "if I already had the sum of everything except the first item, the total would be the first item plus that sum."
unit-04.1x7dr2l2vwl: You trust total(lst[1:]) to be right, just as you trust len or sum, because it's solving a smaller instance of a problem you've already shown how to solve. (Mathematicians call this kind of argument induction, and you'll study it properly in Unit 6.)
unit-04.1e5c4quayop: Key idea: Three questions design almost any recursive function. What's the simplest input, and its answer? How do I make the input smaller? How do I turn the smaller answer into the full answer?
unit-04.18fj6gzwr4s: Every recursive call must make progress towards the base case. If it doesn't, the calls never stop:
unit-04.1yfadju95k7: Each call pushes another frame. Memory for the stack is limited, so Python sets a limit, by default about 1,000 frames deep, and stops with:
unit-04.ilir7prs46: This is recursion's version of the infinite loop from Lesson 2.6. Common causes:
unit-04.2d3cp078g7z: A base case that's never reached: factorial(-1) counts down  minus 2,  minus 3, ... and never hits 0. Guard against bad inputs, or make the base case n <= 0.
unit-04.165lqiia2wk: Not shrinking the input: calling total(lst) instead of total(lst[1:]).
unit-04.1jredrcmev8: The depth limit also means plain recursion can't process a list of 10,000 items one item at a time. Python isn't designed for very deep recursion; some languages are.
unit-04.22dupmu68i0: Everything you can do with recursion you can also do with loops, and vice versa. factorial and total are actually simpler and faster as loops: recursion makes a new frame for every step, and lst[1:] copies the list every time (a hidden linear cost, Lesson 4.2).
unit-04.9x0voky1no: So why bother? Because some problems are naturally recursive, and for those, recursive code is dramatically clearer:
unit-04.228t4fghxf4: data that contains smaller copies of itself: folders inside folders, lists inside lists, the tree structures of Unit 7,
unit-04.1gkw9hskm0u: problems that split into smaller copies of themselves: merge sort (Lesson 4.7), the Towers of Hanoi puzzle, exploring every possible arrangement (Lesson 4.6).
unit-04.ya8ohc2yaw: The next lesson is all about those. For now, practise on simple problems where you can check the answers easily.
unit-04.mgxxldcxi1: Some recursive definitions use more than one smaller case. The famous Fibonacci numbers start 0, 1, and each later number is the sum of the two before: 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, ...
unit-04.1s85pbg2sig: It's correct, and beautifully short. But each call makes two more calls, which make two more, and so on: the calls form a branching tree. fib(5) calls fib(3) twice, fib(2) three times, and so on; the same values are recomputed again and again. The number of calls grows exponentially: about 1.6 times as many for each increase of n by 1. fib(30) makes over a million calls; fib(100) would take longer than the age of the universe.
unit-04.gy77jhggtq: That's not a reason to avoid recursion; it's a reason to count the work, as in Lesson 4.2. In Unit 8 you'll learn memoisation, a one-line fix that remembers answers already computed (a dictionary, Lesson 3.6, does it) and makes fib(100) instant.

unit-04.1mrmgkr95f3: A recursive function calls itself on a smaller input. It needs a base case (answered directly) and a recursive case (built from a smaller answer).
unit-04.172itkhoueg: Each call gets its own frame on the call stack; calls go down to the base case, then results come back up in reverse order.
unit-04.m21hadry5a: Design with the leap of faith: handle the base case, assume the function works on smaller inputs, and build the answer from that.
unit-04.1gh10kbasbi: Missing base cases or inputs that don't shrink cause RecursionError (Python's limit is about 1,000 frames).
unit-04.1qt0qpehwqq: Simple linear problems are often better as loops; recursion shines on naturally recursive problems and data.
unit-04.bsbuli20a4: Functions that make several recursive calls can repeat work and grow exponentially, like naive Fibonacci. Count the calls.

unit-04.1wio3leipmj: Some data contains smaller copies of itself. A folder holds files and other folders, which hold files and other folders. A list can hold numbers and other lists:
unit-04.jflrhj241l: How would you add up every number in that? A loop handles one level; two nested loops handle two levels. But the nesting could go any number of levels deep, and you can't write a loop for each level you don't know about.
unit-04.1mnmw1sfo5d: Recursion handles it naturally, because the data's shape is recursive: a nested list is a list whose items are either numbers or nested lists. The function follows the same shape:
unit-04.f6cmdh92ec: isinstance(item, list) asks "is this item a list?" (it's True for lists and False for numbers, strings and so on). Notice this function mixes a loop and recursion: the loop walks along one level, and recursion dives into deeper levels. The base case is hidden: a list containing no lists makes no recursive calls.
unit-04.24g54rj0tzb: Key idea: When data is defined in terms of itself, the code that processes it should be too. This is why recursion is everywhere in Unit 7, where you'll meet trees: structures made of smaller trees.
unit-04.l8mdda2xg1: In Lesson 4.5, power(base, exp) made exp recursive calls. There's a much faster recursive idea, based on halving, like binary search:
unit-04.oaij6laekq: b¹⁰ = (b⁵)². To get b¹⁰ you only need b⁵, then one multiplication.
unit-04.n76dptoh2z: b⁵ = b  times  (b²)². An odd power is b times an even power.
unit-04.2c8ll24f642: Each call halves e, so it makes about log₂ e calls instead of e: 20 calls for an exponent of a million, instead of a million (which would also crash, far beyond the recursion limit). This is fast exponentiation, and it's how computers raise numbers to enormous powers in cryptography (Unit 16).
unit-04.qq59h3zo4a: Notice half is computed once and used twice. Writing fast_power(b, e // 2) * fast_power(b, e // 2) would make two calls at every level, and all the benefit would be lost.
unit-04.lnmwy3vhzj: Binary search is naturally recursive too: search the middle; if it's not there, search the correct half, which is a smaller version of the same problem. But slicing (lst[:mid]) copies half the list on every call, a hidden linear cost (Lesson 4.2) that would destroy binary search's speed. Instead, pass the boundaries as extra parameters:
unit-04.ca6yk9snax: You call it as search(lst, target, 0, len(lst) - 1). The list is shared by every call (no copies); only the two numbers change. A default parameter (Lesson 2.8) can hide the extra arguments from callers: def search(lst, target, lo=0, hi=None): and then if hi is None: hi = len(lst) - 1.
unit-04.dyqc4bhsfn: Compare this with the loop version in Lesson 4.3: lo and hi play exactly the same roles. The loop's "update and go round again" has become "call again with new values".
unit-04.270jgymioge: Many problems require trying every possible combination: every way to pack a bag, every order to visit some cities, every combination of toppings. Recursion is the natural way to generate them.
unit-04.1akd5hqa9c0: Take subsets. What are all the subsets of [a, b, c]? Think recursively about the first item: every subset either leaves out a or includes a. And in both cases, the rest is just a subset of [b, c], a smaller version of the same problem. So:
unit-04.ndvy5s27ei: Recursively find all subsets of the rest, [b, c]: [], [c], [b], [b, c].
unit-04.1hyr9kyjotr: The answer is those subsets, plus each of them with a added: [a], [a, c], [a, b], [a, b, c].
unit-04.hsim87d1yx: The base case: the empty list has exactly one subset, the empty list itself.
unit-04.1zl1x30gboh: Each item doubles the number of subsets, so n items have 2ⁿ subsets, the same 2ⁿ patterns of n bits from Lesson 1.1 (each bit says "in" or "out" for one item).
unit-04.22cgag3kc7m: Arrangements (also called permutations) work similarly: to arrange [a, b, c], choose which item goes first (3 choices), then arrange the remaining items behind it (a smaller version of the problem). n items have n  times  (n  minus  1)  times  ...  times  1 = n! arrangements: the factorial from Lesson 4.5.
unit-04.27uu788b9xm: Both counts grow terrifyingly fast. 2³⁰ is about a billion subsets; 20! is about 2.4 quintillion arrangements. Generating everything is called brute force. It's simple and always correct, and only practical for small inputs. Lesson 4.8 looks at when brute force is good enough and what to do when it isn't.
unit-04.1z7ex5libn0: A classic puzzle: three pegs, and a stack of n discs of different sizes on the first peg, largest at the bottom. Move the whole stack to the third peg, moving one disc at a time, and never putting a bigger disc on a smaller one.
unit-04.1vgg7g42k5m: With 3 discs, people usually solve it by trial and error. With 8, it's very hard without a method. But recursively, the solution is three lines:
unit-04.1mc1z2klht1: To move n discs from source to target, using spare:
unit-04.1z9346z07f9: Move the top n  minus  1 discs from source to spare (recursively, using target as the spare).
unit-04.2g7dtr1wplu: Move the biggest disc from source to target.
unit-04.1mv8zy386lt: Move the n  minus  1 discs from spare to target (recursively, using source as the spare).
unit-04.lmqth156qv: The base case: moving 0 discs needs no moves at all.
unit-04.1faw7csb3w6: This is the leap of faith (Lesson 4.5) at its most impressive: you don't need to know how the n  minus  1 discs get moved, only that a smaller version of the same problem can be solved. Counting moves: M(n) = 2  times  M(n  minus  1) + 1, which gives 2ⁿ  minus  1 moves. A legend says monks are moving 64 golden discs; at one move a second, they'll finish in about 585 billion years.

unit-04.blcvziqzo1: Divide the problem into smaller subproblems (usually two halves).
unit-04.ph1w63x52y: Conquer each subproblem by solving it recursively. Very small subproblems are solved directly (the base case).

unit-04.bs8oqz2tp8: Analogy: A teacher has 32 exam papers to sort alphabetically. They split the pile in two and give each half to a teaching assistant. Each assistant splits their pile in two and passes it on again, until someone gets a single paper (already "sorted"). Then the sorted piles come back up, and at each step two sorted piles are merged into one.

unit-04.1enx5gw5bt7: Suppose you have two sorted piles of cards face up, and you want one sorted pile. You only ever need to look at the top card of each pile: the smaller of the two must be the smallest card remaining overall. Take it, put it on the output, and repeat. When one pile runs out, the rest of the other pile goes on the end.
unit-04.tqjouudib2: This is the two-pointer technique from Lesson 3.2: i moves along left, j along right. Each comparison places one item, so merging lists with a combined length of n takes at most n  minus  1 comparisons: linear time.
unit-04.1gdm58laq2o: Using <= (take from the left on a tie) keeps equal items in their original order, which makes the merge, and the whole sort, stable (Lesson 4.4).

unit-04.rx5qhzshf: How much work does merge sort do? Picture the splitting as a tree of levels:
unit-04.o55u9u6fax: How many levels? Each level halves the pieces, so after about log₂ n levels every piece has size 1 (the halving count from Lesson 4.2).
unit-04.1zw1cck2g5e: How much work per level? On every level, all the pieces together contain all n items, and merging is linear. So each level costs about n steps.
unit-04.19j4jcdgt16: Total: about n  times  log₂ n steps. Compare that with the n²/2 of selection sort:
unit-04.1jbftd2e04g: At a million items, merge sort is about 25,000 times faster. And unlike insertion sort, its time doesn't depend on the input order: it's n log₂ n in the best, worst and average cases. n log n growth is so common it's often called linearithmic: a little worse than linear, enormously better than quadratic.
unit-04.25s0lee3iey: Deep dive: Can any sort that works by comparing items do better than n log₂ n? No. There are n! possible orders of n items, and each comparison has two outcomes, so at best it halves the possibilities; telling n! orders apart needs at least log₂(n!) comparisons, which is about n log₂ n. Merge sort is, in this sense, optimal. (Counting sort escapes the limit by not comparing at all.)
unit-04.20m2p4vynqo: The cost is memory: merge sort builds new lists as it merges, needing extra space proportional to n, where insertion and selection sort work in place.
unit-04.3l9z1o8vc0: The other famous divide-and-conquer sort is quicksort, invented by Tony Hoare in 1959. It puts the work in the divide step instead of the combine step:
unit-04.8c9nnogbs8: Pick an item called the pivot (say, the first one).
unit-04.2b2d3yaquv7: Partition the rest into items smaller than the pivot and items greater than or equal to it.
unit-04.2f9yqiapmxm: Recursively sort the two parts. The answer is: sorted smaller items, the pivot, sorted larger items. No merging needed.
unit-04.1rkacw9ux9: When the pivot splits the list roughly in half, quicksort has about log₂ n levels of linear work, n log₂ n again, and in practice it's very fast. But if the pivot is always the smallest or largest item (for example, using the first item on an already sorted list), one side is always empty: n levels of work, which is quadratic. Real implementations choose the pivot randomly, or as the middle of three samples, to make that worst case extremely unlikely.
unit-04.mzipk432f6: Python's own sorted uses Timsort, designed by Tim Peters in 2002: a carefully tuned merge sort that finds runs that are already sorted and uses insertion sort for small pieces. It's stable, n log n in the worst case, and close to linear on nearly sorted data, combining the strengths of everything in this unit.

unit-04.1b1ktyeevs0: The most straightforward strategy of all: try every possibility and keep the ones that work (or the best one). This is called brute force or exhaustive search. You've already used it: finding all subsets with a given sum (Lesson 4.6) generated every subset and filtered them.
unit-04.16vu5dxdadg: It's simple to write and easy to convince yourself it's correct: if every possibility is checked, the answer can't be missed.
unit-04.2aqc1ht8gif: It's often fast enough. Checking a million possibilities takes a fraction of a second.
unit-04.14xln10vwg1: It makes a perfect reference solution for testing cleverer code, as many tests in this course do: compare the fast version with brute force on lots of small random inputs.
unit-04.2d1utpoitha: Its weakness is that the number of possibilities often grows explosively. Before using brute force, estimate the count:
unit-04.1dz2ydpeel3: A rough rule: Python manages around 10 million simple steps a second. Up to a few million possibilities, brute force is fine. Up to a few billion, it's slow but possible. Beyond that, you need a better idea.
unit-04.179bsc3ccv0: Tip: Brute force often improves dramatically with pruning: stopping early on paths that can't possibly work. If you're choosing items to fit in a bag and the bag is already over-full, there's no point trying to add more.
unit-04.lpzmqqhnwf: A greedy algorithm builds a solution step by step, at each step taking whatever choice looks best right now, and never reconsidering.
unit-04.21r9s2rt7pw: The classic example is giving change. To pay 68p with UK coins (50p, 20p, 10p, 5p, 2p, 1p), a shop assistant takes the biggest coin that fits, again and again: 50p (18p left), 10p (8p left), 5p (3p left), 2p (1p left), 1p. Five coins, which is the fewest possible.
unit-04.2czy9pspyxm: Greedy algorithms are usually fast (this is linear in the number of coins used) and simple. The catch: they aren't always right. Suppose a country had coins of 1, 3 and 4. To make 6, greedy takes 4, then 1, then 1: three coins. But 3 + 3 is just two. Taking the biggest coin first looked good, but it led somewhere worse.
unit-04.pho544k29j: For UK and euro coins, greedy change-making happens to always give the fewest coins; for the 1-3-4 system it doesn't. A greedy algorithm is only correct when the problem has special structure, and proving it needs an argument, not just a few examples that work.
unit-04.29y482b7fj: Some problems have a greedy solution that's provably optimal. A famous one is scheduling: you have a list of meetings, each with a start and end time, and one room. What's the largest number of meetings you can hold, if none can overlap?
unit-04.1ugvpz8m0rq: pick the shortest meeting first? (Fails: a short meeting can overlap two others that would both fit.)
unit-04.18gfau9eytw: pick the meeting that starts earliest? (Fails: an early meeting might last all day.)
unit-04.2f2pzbo8p5o: pick the meeting that ends earliest, then the next one that ends earliest among those that start after it, and so on? (Correct!)
unit-04.g9z4eghsj5: Why does "ends earliest" work? Whatever the best schedule is, its first meeting can be swapped for the meeting that ends earliest without causing any clash (it ends no later, so it can't collide with anything after it), and then the same argument applies to the rest. This kind of exchange argument is how greedy algorithms are proved correct; you'll see more in Unit 8.
unit-04.2a8seowx60: Greedy ideas appear all over computer science: finding shortest routes on a map (Dijkstra's algorithm), compressing files (Huffman coding), and connecting networks cheaply (Unit 8).
unit-04.h9649z9d8f: When greedy gives wrong answers and brute force is too slow, there's a powerful third option called dynamic programming: solve every smaller subproblem once, store the answers (as with memoised Fibonacci, Lesson 4.5), and build up. Dynamic programming finds the true minimum number of coins for any coin system efficiently. It's a major topic of Unit 8; for now, it's enough to recognise the symptoms that greedy isn't safe: an early choice that looks good can block a much better combination later.
unit-04.1nnnjhgxl8m: Greedy can still be useful even when it isn't optimal: a quick answer that's "pretty good" can be valuable when the perfect answer is too expensive. The travelling salesperson problem (visit every city once and return home, by the shortest route) is a famous example: brute force means trying all n! routes, and nobody knows a fast method that's always optimal. A greedy "always go to the nearest unvisited city" route is quick and usually reasonable, though rarely perfect.

unit-05.1smw7vo8jv: Python comes with types for numbers, text, lists and dictionaries. In Units 3 and 4 you built everything else out of those: a book was a tuple ("Dune", "Frank Herbert", 1965), a student's grades were a dictionary of dictionaries. That works, but it has problems you've probably already felt:
unit-05.2fzgcowuxwd: Meaning is hidden. What is book[2]? You have to remember that position 2 is the year. Type book[3] by mistake and you get an IndexError far from the real bug.
unit-05.1eh8jo6k6hc: Nothing keeps the data valid. Nothing stops someone writing a dictionary with "scroe" instead of "score", or a negative price.
unit-05.253nopuvtkq: Data and behaviour live apart. The functions that work on books (title_key, find_title) are scattered around the program, and nothing says which functions go with which data.
unit-05.1c9nl14jjrv: Object-oriented programming (OOP) solves these problems by letting you define your own types. A Book type can have named fields (book.year instead of book[2]), rules that keep its data valid, and its own functions built in. Almost every large program you use (games, browsers, phone apps) is organised this way.
unit-05.obve6xper3: A class is a blueprint that describes a kind of thing: what data it holds and what it can do. An object (also called an instance) is one particular thing built from that blueprint.

unit-05.1y1gkfdjpan: class Dog: defines the blueprint (class names use CapitalisedWords by convention, unlike functions). Calling the class like a function, Dog(), builds a new object. __main__ just means "defined in this program".

Instead, a class defines a special function called __init__ (two underscores each side, said "dunder init") that Python runs automatically every time a new object is created:

unit-05.16rtjw7visd: self is simply the name, by strong convention, of the first parameter of every method: it refers to the particular object the method is working on. One Dog class serves many dogs, so methods need to know which dog. When you write rex.describe(), Python quietly turns it into Dog.describe(rex), passing rex as self.

unit-05.1x3y9alt7u0: Queries answer a question and leave the object unchanged: account.can_afford(30), rect.area(). They return a value.

unit-05.88x41ehbd5: Encapsulation applies the same idea to classes: an object exposes a small set of methods and attributes for the outside world to use (its public interface) and keeps the details of how it works (its implementation) to itself. This gives two big benefits:
unit-05.g3bq3melte: Protection. If outside code can only change the balance through deposit and withdraw, the invariant "balance is never negative" (Lesson 5.2) can't be broken.
unit-05.jflyvqfskm: Freedom to change. If outside code never touches the internals, you can redesign them (store transactions instead of a balance, use a dictionary instead of a list) without breaking anything that uses the class.
unit-05.1ld23vaq91d: In big programs the second benefit is huge: thousands of lines may use a class, and encapsulation lets you improve it without rewriting them.
unit-05.8y8bd5cb1f: Many languages (Java, C++) let you mark attributes private and the compiler forbids outside access. Python takes a gentler approach based on a convention: a name starting with one underscore means "internal, please don't touch":
unit-05.gzmkb4y483: Python doesn't stop you from writing acct._balance = -500, but every Python programmer knows the underscore means "you're on your own if you do this". The motto in the Python community is "we're all consenting adults here".
unit-05.ky9t7qc6jx: You may also see two leading underscores, self.__balance. Python then renames the attribute behind the scenes (to _Account__balance), mostly to avoid accidental clashes in subclasses (Lesson 5.6). It's still reachable, and most code just uses one underscore.
unit-05.16djoz0yarv: Suppose you want acct.balance to be readable, as before, but not settable from outside. Or you want circle.area to be worked out from the radius each time it's read. Python's tool for this is the property: a method that's used with attribute syntax.
unit-05.1auemmmrlbn: @property on the line above a def is a decorator: a label that changes how the function behaves. Here it turns the method area into something you read like an attribute. unit-05.28o98t2vwci: A property with no setter is read-only: c.area = 100 raises AttributeError. That's exactly what you want for derived values.

unit-05.2ehwgwrqqdb: Now c.radius = -1 runs the setter and raises an error, while code that uses the class still just writes c.radius. Even the assignment in __init__ goes through the setter, so an invalid circle can't be created either.

unit-05.1akb36akikz: Now the same Car class works with any kind of engine that has the right methods, and in tests you can pass in a simple fake engine. This is called dependency injection, a grand name for a simple idea: give an object its collaborators instead of making it build them.

unit-05.n7mpqulbwz: There's also issubclass(SavingsAccount, Account) for classes. Use these sparingly: code full of if isinstance(x, Dog): ... elif isinstance(x, Cat): ... usually means a method should be overridden instead. The next lesson shows how.
unit-05.37hl8ybudu: Inheritance is powerful but easy to overuse. Three tests help:
unit-05.1rcfcpzxggf: "Is a": is a SavingsAccount really a kind of Account? Yes. Is a Car a kind of Engine? No: a car has an engine, so use composition (Lesson 5.5).
unit-05.1a27xthkpp3: Substitution: can a subclass object be used anywhere a base class object is expected, without surprises? This is the Liskov substitution principle. A SavingsAccount passed to code that deposits and withdraws behaves like any account: fine. But a subclass that overrides withdraw to always raise breaks code that expects accounts to allow withdrawals.
unit-05.1pj7pcskx9j: Shallow hierarchies: one or two levels are usually plenty. Deep chains (A  to  B  to  C  to  D  to  E) become hard to follow, because a method might be defined at any level.
unit-05.1151q8tyniq: A famous trap: mathematically, a square is a rectangle. But if Rectangle lets you set width and height independently, a Square subclass must either break that promise (set one and the other changes too, surprising code written for rectangles) or stop being square. "Is a" in everyday language doesn't always mean "is substitutable" in code.
unit-05.1rxcw4gyp75: Key idea: A widely quoted guideline is "favour composition over inheritance". Use inheritance for genuine, substitutable "is a" relationships, especially when the base class is designed to be extended; use composition for everything else.
unit-05.5l9j2skbmb: (Python also allows multiple inheritance, class C(A, B):, inheriting from several bases. It has uses, but it adds complexity; you won't need it in this course.)
unit-05.1ffmjnssdfm: A subclass reuses everything and adds one method.

unit-05.xyn533nrrn: One inherited method, three different results.
unit-05.2c8uwus3pfj: A manager is an employee with a team and a bonus.
unit-05.wiclkki3rm: If a subclass defines __init__ but doesn't call super().__init__(...), the base class's attributes are never created, and inherited methods fail with AttributeError.
unit-05.1bxyslbbic5: Copying base class code into the subclass
unit-05.2g8yu63oq1j: Re-implementing a calculation the base already does defeats the purpose and lets the two drift apart. Call super().method() and add only the difference.
unit-05.avhl7peds0: class Car(Engine) claims a car is an engine, and gives cars every engine method. A car has an engine: use composition.
unit-05.1k3fixuykgn: Overrides that break the base class's promises
unit-05.1t5v56teoaf: A subclass should be usable wherever the base class is expected (the substitution principle). Overriding a method to do something unrelated, or to always fail, breaks code written for the base class.
unit-05.tzc2ipjsqe: Long if isinstance(x, A): ... elif isinstance(x, B): ... chains are usually better replaced by a method that each subclass overrides.
unit-05.20pb0hxkcw6: Inheritance models "is a": class SavingsAccount(Account): gets all of Account's attributes and methods.
unit-05.21wibaajt6z: Python looks up attributes on the object, then its class, then each base class in turn, up to object. The first match wins.
unit-05.2d69k7wkpg5: A subclass overrides a method by redefining it. Base class code that calls self.method() uses the subclass's version.
unit-05.1xktd9n4pyp: super() reaches the base version, to extend rather than replace: super().__init__(...) sets up inherited attributes.
unit-05.1y3v0lp1hau: isinstance(obj, Base) is true for subclass objects too.
unit-05.1rqnmb1xaka: Use inheritance only for genuine, substitutable "is a" relationships, and keep hierarchies shallow. Favour composition otherwise.
unit-05.1kfwaqehcvq: You saw in this lesson that one piece of code, like introduce or total_payroll, can work on many different classes as long as each provides the right methods. That idea, polymorphism, is the heart of object-oriented design. Lesson 5.7 explores it: abstract base classes, interfaces, and Python's relaxed "duck typing".

unit-05.1yrr08o9f3e: Polymorphism (Greek for "many forms") means one piece of code can work with objects of many different types, as long as they all support the operations it uses. You've seen it already:
unit-05.2erysqemzj2: len() works on strings, lists, dictionaries and your own Playlist (Lesson 5.3).

unit-05.ir25fk9j6t: for loops work on anything iterable.
unit-05.wb7dwe9dne: The set of methods that code relies on is called an interface. total_payroll relies on one method, monthly_pay(). Any object with that method can be passed in, including classes written years later by someone who never saw total_payroll's code.
unit-05.7t6o38cwua: Analogy: A wall socket defines an interface: two or three pins of a certain shape. Kettles, laptops and lamps all work in it, and inventors keep making new appliances that work too, without anyone rewiring the house. The socket doesn't know or care what's plugged in.
unit-05.2taiq05a58: This is the big payoff of object-oriented programming: you can add new kinds of things without changing the code that uses them.
unit-05.1ny3x3sit9f: Here's code without polymorphism: shapes stored as dictionaries, with a function that checks the kind:
unit-05.1oq58ida2m5: Every function that handles shapes (area, perimeter, draw, save...) has its own if/elif chain. Adding a hexagon means finding and editing every one of them, and missing one is a bug.
unit-05.1svaqje1syi: With polymorphism, each class carries its own version:
unit-05.1bg7uspjgfp: Adding a hexagon now means writing one new class, and nothing else changes. Everything about hexagons lives in one place. This is sometimes summed up as the open/closed principle: code should be open for extension (new classes can be added) but closed for modification (existing code needn't change).
unit-05.e22rxst0l9: To make the shared interface explicit, define a base class that declares the methods without implementing them. Such a class is called abstract: it exists to be inherited, never to be used directly.
unit-05.2gj1f10gdro: describe is concrete: it works for any shape, because it only relies on area(). Subclasses fill in area and get describe for free. (type(self).__name__ is the name of the object's actual class, such as "Circle".)
unit-05.2c034ogxjhb: Python's standard library has a stricter tool in the abc module ("abstract base classes"):
unit-05.luryuts0hi: Now Python refuses to create a Shape, or any subclass that hasn't implemented every abstract method: Shape() raises TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class Shape.... The mistake is caught the moment someone tries to create an incomplete object, rather than later when area is finally called. (from abc import ... loads names from a module; Lesson 5.8 explains modules properly. The ... is Python's "nothing here" placeholder, like pass.)
unit-05.2e3079x4sle: Languages like Java require a class to formally declare which interfaces it implements. Python is more relaxed. It uses duck typing, from the saying "If it walks like a duck and quacks like a duck, then it's a duck."
unit-05.1827w0pjx8u: Python never checks what class an object is when you call a method. It just tries the method. If the object has it, it works:
unit-05.1ytzcldthrz: Duck and Robot share no base class, yet the loop works for both. Inheritance from a common base is optional in Python; what matters is having the right methods.
unit-05.19h599y1y94: Python's built-in protocols work this way too. Anything with __len__ works with len(); anything with __iter__ or __getitem__ works in a for loop; anything with a write method can be passed where a file is expected:
unit-05.1q93rhiq0x2: print doesn't check that its file is really a file; it just calls .write(). That's duck typing.
unit-05.gyiw5bdhjr: So when should you write an abstract base class? Use one when it adds value: it documents the interface in one place, can provide shared concrete methods (like describe), and with abc it catches incomplete subclasses early. For small, informal interfaces, duck typing alone is perfectly Pythonic.
unit-05.2cjcj78idoc: Polymorphism really shines with recursive structures (Lesson 4.6). Consider an arithmetic expression like (2 + 3) * 4. It can be represented as a tree of objects: a multiplication node whose left child is an addition node (with children 2 and 3) and whose right child is the number 4.
unit-05.2dulfr9050b: Give every node class an evaluate() method. A number returns itself. An addition node evaluates its two children and adds the results; a multiplication node multiplies them. Each node only needs to know about itself; the recursion and the polymorphism together do the rest. This is exactly how compilers and interpreters (Lesson 1.6) represent and run programs: as syntax trees of node objects, each with an evaluate or compile method. You'll build one in the last exercise.

unit-05.1qa5ndmtetm: Subclasses implement one method and inherit the rest.
unit-05.s29r0tobk8: Incomplete classes can't even be created.
unit-05.2ciettbb974: No shared base class needed, just the right method.
unit-05.13ewh64wtzv: Type-checking instead of calling a method
unit-05.26k44nxrrdz: if isinstance(s, Circle): ... elif isinstance(s, Square): ... must be edited for every new class. Give each class the method and just call it.
unit-05.2dx76u9t8c8: Forgetting to implement an abstract method
unit-05.kpwmpdq31f: With a plain NotImplementedError base, the mistake only shows when the method is called. Using abc.ABC and @abstractmethod catches it as soon as the object is created.
unit-05.26npny56l7j: Polymorphism only works if every class's method takes the same arguments and returns the same kind of value. One area(self, units) among many area(self) breaks the shared code.
unit-05.1zccuxr95kc: Abstract classes exist to be inherited. Create one of the concrete subclasses instead.
unit-05.1k8bac2d44g: Thinking duck typing means no rules
unit-05.7op3qz8ber: Duck typing removes the need for a common base class, not the need for a consistent interface. Document which methods your code expects its objects to have.
unit-05.2ah22p8p107: Polymorphism: one piece of code works on many types through a shared interface (a set of methods).
unit-05.v941ohee5j: Replacing if/elif type checks with methods means new types can be added without changing existing code (the open/closed principle).
unit-05.1jrut85b91g: An abstract base class declares the interface and can share concrete methods. abc.ABC with @abstractmethod prevents incomplete subclasses from being created.
unit-05.2tx72qrpwa: Duck typing: Python only cares whether an object has the method, not what class it is. Built-in protocols (len, for, files) work the same way.
unit-05.1msnnoekc1p: Polymorphism plus recursion gives tree structures such as expression trees, the basis of interpreters and compilers.

unit-05.10pjcx7y481: Real programs grow to thousands of lines, far too many for one file. Python lets you split code into modules: a module is simply a .py file whose functions, classes and variables other files can use. A folder of related modules is called a package.
unit-05.mqelmbc00z: You've already used modules a few times (import random, from abc import ABC). There are three common forms of import:
unit-05.1bcpy7pk02z: import math loads the module and gives you one name, math; everything inside is reached with a dot. This is usually the clearest, because a reader can see where each name comes from.
unit-05.11ul5my8v5s: from math import sqrt copies specific names into your program, for convenience.
unit-05.za367hib4x: as gives a module a shorter or clearer name.
unit-05.1j4dcmmavhh: (Avoid from math import *, which dumps every name from the module into your program: you can't tell where names came from, and it may silently replace your own variables.)
unit-05.62sxqwf3hy: Modules give each file its own namespace: math.log and a log function in your own code can't clash. They also let you reuse code across programs, and they're how teams split work: one person owns payments.py, another inventory.py.
unit-05.2ab10kq5a16: Analogy: A module is like a toolbox with a label. import math puts the "math" toolbox on your bench; math.sqrt means "the sqrt tool from that box". from math import sqrt takes just that tool out and puts it on the bench by itself.
unit-05.2ckxhf4ojkv: Python comes with a huge standard library: hundreds of modules, installed with Python, ready to import. This is what people mean by Python's "batteries included" philosophy. A few you'll use constantly:
unit-05.17z6s4jtddm: Two from collections replace patterns you've written by hand since Unit 3:
unit-05.uvg1hkx0x5: Before writing a utility yourself, it's worth a quick search: "Python standard library ". Beyond the standard library are hundreds of thousands of third-party packages installed with a tool called pip (you'll meet them in Unit 14). Writing it yourself is still valuable while learning, which is why this course often asks you to.
unit-05.hejhxjlezd: Any .py file is a module. If you save functions in geometry.py, another file in the same folder can import geometry and call geometry.area(...). (This browser editor runs a single file, so you'll practise this properly when you set up a local project in Unit 14.)
unit-05.1x77zv8y0oq: When Python imports a module, it runs the whole file, top to bottom, defining its functions and classes. That causes a problem if the file also contains test code or a main() call: importing it would run them too. The fix is a famous idiom:
unit-05.21376ll5eao: Every module has a variable __name__. When you run a file directly, Python sets it to "__main__"; when the file is imported, it's set to the module's name ("geometry"). So the block runs when you run the file as a program, but not when someone imports it. You'll see this at the bottom of most Python programs.
unit-05.1c3iojetrm1: Many classes exist mainly to hold data: a point, a product, a book. Writing them means a lot of repetitive typing: __init__ with self.x = x for every field, __repr__, __eq__. The standard library's dataclasses module writes all of that for you:
unit-05.23ky30fkgna: The fields are listed with type hints: name: str means "name is expected to be a string". Python doesn't enforce hints, but they document intent, and the dataclass uses them to know which fields exist. Fields with defaults must come after fields without.
unit-05.wltmsrurcw: You still write methods and properties as normal; the decorator only generates the boring parts. Useful options:
unit-05.20snb47sqvj: @dataclass(order=True) also generates __lt__ and friends, comparing fields in order like a tuple, so objects sort naturally.
unit-05.dla0en4qk9: @dataclass(frozen=True) makes objects immutable (assigning to a field raises an error) and hashable, so they can be set members and dictionary keys. Remember from Lesson 5.3 that defining __eq__ normally removes hashability; frozen dataclasses solve that.
unit-05.a8kzhca178: For a mutable default, use field(default_factory=list) rather than = [], which would be the shared-list trap from Lesson 5.2 (dataclasses actually refuse = [] with an error).
unit-05.t70ddby404: Tip: Use a dataclass when a class is mostly data with a little behaviour. Use a regular class when __init__ needs real logic or validation, or when the internal data should be hidden. (A dataclass can run checks in a method called __post_init__, which it calls after setting the fields.)
unit-05.704xswlp94: So far you've raised Python's built-in exceptions, mostly ValueError and KeyError. In a larger program it's better to define your own, because they describe errors in your program's own terms and let callers catch exactly the ones they can handle.
unit-05.ac4x1wsr5b: Exceptions are classes, and they form an inheritance hierarchy. ValueError and KeyError both inherit from Exception, and except Exception: catches both. To make your own, inherit from Exception:
unit-05.106yi1kqd57: A body containing only a docstring (or pass) is fine: the new class inherits everything it needs. Custom attributes like needed let a handler respond intelligently ("you're 20 short"), and calling super().__init__(message) sets the text shown when the error is printed.
unit-05.1fhrcuky4vl: The hierarchy pays off when catching:
unit-05.mtr9dy5f0f: except clauses are checked in order, and each catches its class and all subclasses, so put specific ones first. A whole library can be wrapped with one except BankError by code that just wants to know "did banking fail?", while other code catches individual errors. Python's own exceptions are organised this way: except LookupError catches both KeyError and IndexError.
unit-05.5jyb0e56h7: Two more pieces of try complete the picture: an else: block runs only if no exception happened, and a finally: block runs no matter what, which is ideal for cleaning up (closing files and connections).

unit-05.2ghlumvin40: Custom exceptions should inherit from Exception (or one of its subclasses). BaseException also covers things like Ctrl+C, which ordinary handlers shouldn't swallow.

unit-05.e517tkkv9s: @dataclass generates __init__, __repr__ and __eq__ from type-hinted fields. order=True adds comparisons, frozen=True makes objects immutable and hashable, and field(default_factory=list) gives safe mutable defaults.

unit-05.ulnziw62hz: Any working program solves today's problem. A well-designed program can also absorb tomorrow's changes without a rewrite. Requirements always change: the shop adds a new payment method, the game gets a new kind of enemy, the report needs a CSV version. Good design means each change touches as few places as possible.
unit-05.er7s8rp0j7: Everything in this unit has been heading here. Encapsulation (5.4) hides details so they can change. Composition (5.5) builds systems from replaceable parts. Polymorphism (5.7) lets new kinds of thing be added without editing old code. This lesson collects those ideas into habits for designing a program from scratch.
unit-05.14un1bfi58u: Analogy: A house with plumbing behind removable panels, standard sockets and modular kitchen units can be renovated room by room. A house with pipes cast into the concrete has to be demolished to fix a leak. Both are "working houses" on the day they're finished.
unit-05.18w4ljtcpgo: A simple, surprisingly effective starting technique: write a short description of the problem, then underline the nouns (candidate classes and attributes) and the verbs (candidate methods).
unit-05.1h7hvywxrfa: A library has books and members. A member can borrow up to three books and return them. A book has a title and an ISBN. The library can report which books are overdue.
unit-05.hbbxcw2bgk: Nouns: library, book, member, title, ISBN. Verbs: borrow, return, report. Some nouns are big enough to be classes (Library, Book, Member); others are just attributes (title, isbn). Each verb becomes a method on the class that has the data it needs: borrowing changes both books and members, so it belongs on Library, which coordinates them (exactly as you built in Lesson 5.5).
unit-05.1rpjuny015j: Next, write a one-sentence responsibility for each class. Designers sometimes use index cards called CRC cards (Class, Responsibilities, Collaborators): the class name on top, what it knows and does on the left, and which other classes it works with on the right. If you can't describe a class in one sentence without using "and" several times, it's probably doing too much.
unit-05.1c7ev7rlz1p: Two measures judge almost any design:
unit-05.w5ijnphws: Cohesion: how closely related the things inside one class are. A Fraction class whose every method is about fractions is highly cohesive. A class Utilities with methods for dates, emails and fractions has low cohesion.
unit-05.29nlvmryqle: Coupling: how much one class depends on the details of others. If changing how Book stores its title forces changes in five other classes, coupling is high.
unit-05.2g21anmxdf: Aim for high cohesion and low coupling. Each class should do one thing well and depend on others only through their public interfaces. The Law of Demeter (Lesson 5.5) and encapsulation (5.4) are tools for reducing coupling; giving each class one responsibility raises cohesion.
unit-05.24drfd5fhrr: In the early 2000s, the software engineer Robert C. Martin popularised five principles for object-oriented design, remembered by the acronym SOLID. You've already met most of them in action:
unit-05.q1cjbt2yfo: These are guidelines, not laws. Applied blindly to a 50-line script they add needless classes. But as a program grows, violations show up as pain: one change breaking distant code, classes that are impossible to test, or if/elif chains that grow with every feature.
unit-05.oq0iei3f0b: A code smell is a surface sign that a design might have a deeper problem. It doesn't prove anything is wrong, but it's worth a look:
unit-05.18exn1sj9ij: God class: one huge class that knows and does everything. Split it by responsibility.
unit-05.1l11q3810kd: Duplicated code: the same logic in several places will eventually be fixed in only one of them. Move it into one function, method or base class.
unit-05.1efqu97cgt: Long parameter lists: make_order(name, street, city, postcode, phone, email, ...) suggests the parameters belong together in an object (Customer, Address).
unit-05.26zkwroi0i: Feature envy: a method that mostly uses another object's data (order.customer.discount_rate * order.customer.loyalty_years ...) probably belongs in that other class.
unit-05.13q1ul6ygwj: Type switches: if kind == "a": ... elif kind == "b": ... repeated in several places is a sign polymorphism is missing (Lesson 5.7).
unit-05.wbl7n9q21v: Primitive obsession: using strings and tuples where a small class would add meaning and validation (prices as floats instead of a Money class).
unit-05.7s459cfb5y: Improving the structure of code without changing what it does is called refactoring. It's safe only when you have tests to confirm the behaviour hasn't changed, which brings us to testing.
unit-05.1kokhry1sya: A class that creates its own collaborators is hard to test. Imagine a WeatherAlert that reads a real thermometer inside its methods: how do you test what it does at 40°C in winter? The answer is dependency injection (Lesson 5.5): pass the thermometer in.
unit-05.20y69bkceds: FakeSensor is a test double: a simple stand-in with the same interface (duck typing, Lesson 5.7). Thanks to dependency inversion, WeatherAlert doesn't care whether its sensor is real hardware, a web service or a fake. The same trick makes randomness testable: instead of calling random.randint inside a game, pass in a "dice" object or function, and in tests pass one that returns fixed numbers. You'll use exactly this in the last exercise and the unit project.
unit-05.onjxg4m1d6: Finally, two pieces of advice that balance all the principles above. KISS, "keep it simple": the simplest design that meets today's needs is usually best. And YAGNI, "you aren't gonna need it": don't build flexibility for changes you only imagine. Refactor when a real change arrives, with tests protecting you.
unit-05.513yz7z79u: Calculating and formatting are separate jobs, so they get separate classes.

unit-05.12q98ak2rgt: Starting to code before deciding which classes exist and what each is responsible for leads to tangled designs. Spend a few minutes with nouns, verbs and one-sentence responsibilities first.
unit-05.15mrif7es23: Ten classes and three layers of abstraction for a 40-line problem make code harder, not easier. Apply principles in proportion to the size of the program (KISS, YAGNI).
unit-05.13j2av2yprs: A class that builds its own sensor, database or random generator can't be tested in isolation. Pass collaborators in.
unit-05.2daaqnwy4b6: Ignoring smells because the code works
unit-05.a081yiz7ri: Duplication and god classes don't cause bugs today; they cause them during the next change. Refactor while the code is fresh in your mind, with tests to protect you.

unit-06.t6agfrcd05: A tautology is a formula that is true in every row of its truth table, whatever its variables are. p ∨ ¬p ("either it's raining or it isn't") is a tautology. A contradiction is false in every row, like p ∧ ¬p. A formula that's true in at least one row is satisfiable.

Because a formula with n variables has only 2ⁿ rows, a computer can check any claimed equivalence by trying every row: a perfectly respectable proof for small n.

unit-06.aw1jj6osw8: "x > 5" isn't a proposition, because its truth depends on x. Statements like this are called predicates: they become propositions once you fill in their variables. We write them like functions: let P(x) mean "x > 5". Then P(7) is true and P(2) is false.
unit-06.18r8shcgc5u: You already write predicates all the time: they're just Python functions that return a boolean.
unit-06.ui2q4k1t5g: A predicate always has a domain: the set of values its variables can take, such as "all whole numbers", "all students in the class" or "every item in this list". The same predicate can be true for every item in one domain and false for some item in another, so the domain must always be clear.
unit-06.1sccsxr3ljg: Quantifiers turn a predicate into a proposition by saying how many values it holds for:
unit-06.2cl2jj4xz26: Universal quantifier: ∀x P(x), "for all x, P(x)". True if P holds for every x in the domain.
unit-06.1gzjgg9qogi: Existential quantifier: ∃x P(x), "there exists an x such that P(x)". True if P holds for at least one x.
unit-06.11vmv2ddii2: Over a finite domain, these are exactly Python's all and any (Lesson 3.8):
unit-06.20mlclsjfzt: One way to picture it: ∀ is a giant and (P(x₁) ∧ P(x₂) ∧ P(x₃) ∧ ...), and ∃ is a giant or (P(x₁) ∨ P(x₂) ∨ ...). That's why all stops at the first false item and any at the first true one: short-circuiting (Lesson 2.5).
unit-06.7ayur1brs: What about an empty domain? all([]) is True and any([]) is False. "Every unicorn in this room is purple" is vacuously true, because there are no unicorns to break the rule, just like an implication with a false hypothesis (Lesson 6.1).
unit-06.1b65ztu7meo: What's the opposite of "every student passed"? Not "every student failed", but "some student failed". In symbols, De Morgan's laws extend to quantifiers:
unit-06.1t1d2t1mq7s: To negate, flip the quantifier and negate what's inside. In Python: not all(p(x) for x in xs) is the same as any(not p(x) for x in xs).
unit-06.23xpiiwmeoe: This gives a powerful tool. To disprove a "for all" claim, you need only one counterexample. To prove it, you must show it for every element, which for an infinite domain needs a proof (Lessons 6.4 and 6.5) rather than testing. A famous example: n² + n + 41 is prime for n = 0, 1, 2, ..., 39, forty values in a row, which might convince you it's always prime. But at n = 40 it's 1681 = 41  times  41. Lots of confirming examples never prove a universal statement; one counterexample always disproves it.
unit-06.11dgb2f9v5m: Predicates with several variables can have several quantifiers, and their order matters. Let L(x, y) mean "x loves y", with the domain being people:
unit-06.64no21ss5: ∀x ∃y L(x, y): "everybody loves somebody" (each person may love someone different).
unit-06.najv9f6ax4: ∃y ∀x L(x, y): "there is somebody whom everybody loves" (one single person loved by all).
unit-06.18t6qquus7h: The second is much stronger: it implies the first, but not the other way round. In code, the order of quantifiers becomes the nesting of loops (or of all and any):
unit-06.2a3kn5jblnb: Programmers meet this distinction all the time. "Every request is handled by some server" is very different from "some server handles every request". Specifications, database queries (Unit 12) and security rules (Unit 16) are all built from nested quantifiers, and getting the order wrong is a classic source of bugs.
unit-06.1rpj238uifn: Negation works through nested quantifiers one at a time: ¬∀x ∃y L(x, y) becomes ∃x ¬∃y L(x, y), which becomes ∃x ∀y ¬L(x, y): "there's someone who loves nobody".
unit-06.1y8fnrmx3gl: Turning a vague English requirement into a precise quantified statement is a core skill, for maths and for writing correct programs. Some patterns:
unit-06.28slmtcb72h: Notice that "all A are B" uses  to  but "some A are B" uses ∧. "All students in year 1 passed" is ∀x (Year1(x)  to  Passed(x)); writing ∀x (Year1(x) ∧ Passed(x)) would claim that everyone is in year 1. In Python, "all A are B" restricts the domain with a filter: all(passed(s) for s in students if s.year == 1).
unit-06.2b0t3tild34: Tip: When translating, first decide the domain, then the predicates, then the quantifiers, from the outside in. Then test your formula on a small example where you know the answer.

unit-06.1as98w5agbm: Any number of examples where a "for all" claim holds proves nothing about the cases you didn't check. One counterexample, though, disproves it.
