unit-06.s0boi79uux: A set is an unordered collection of distinct objects, called its elements. You met Python's set type in Lesson 3.7; mathematics uses exactly the same idea, with its own notation:
unit-06.19oirlz9ltu: For large or infinite sets, set-builder notation describes the elements by a rule: {x ∈ ℤ | x > 0 and x is even} means "the set of integers x such that x is positive and even". (ℤ is the set of all integers, ℕ the natural numbers 0, 1, 2, ..., ℝ the real numbers.) Python's set comprehensions (Lesson 3.8) are set-builder notation in code: {x for x in range(1, 20) if x % 2 == 0}.
unit-06.1a4nn25s70r: Sets are the foundation on which almost all of mathematics is built: numbers, functions, relations and graphs can all be defined as sets. They're also the foundation of databases (Unit 12), where tables are sets of rows and queries are set operations.
unit-06.1w4zwsmvowm: Two ways of building new sets come up constantly:
unit-06.29hgref74zk: The power set 𝒫(A) is the set of all subsets of A. For A = {a, b}, 𝒫(A) = {∅, {a}, {b}, {a, b}}. Each element of A is either in a subset or not, two choices per element, so a set with n elements has 2ⁿ subsets (the same count as truth table rows and bit patterns: they're all the same idea). You generated subsets recursively in Lesson 4.6.
unit-06.tjbsud64es: The Cartesian product A  times  B is the set of all ordered pairs (a, b) with a ∈ A and b ∈ B. For A = {1, 2} and B = {x, y}: A  times  B = {(1, x), (1, y), (2, x), (2, y)}. Its size is |A|  times  |B|. Pairs are ordered, so (1, x)  not equal to  (x, 1); in Python they're tuples. itertools.product(A, B) generates them. A chessboard's squares are {a, ..., h}  times  {1, ..., 8}, which is 64 pairs; a database table's possible rows are a Cartesian product of its columns' possible values.
unit-06.1p18gbg7u3z: In Python, a set of sets needs frozensets: ordinary sets are mutable and therefore unhashable (Lesson 3.6), so they can't be elements of another set. frozenset({1, 2}) is an immutable, hashable set.
unit-06.1sh8bb7gb5a: A relation R from A to B is any subset of A  times  B: a set of pairs saying which elements are related. We write a R b, or (a, b) ∈ R. Relations are everywhere:
unit-06.1zqephcrz2j: "is enrolled in" between students and courses.
unit-06.o5q33o7elk: In Python, the simplest representation is a set of tuples: follows = {("ada", "bo"), ("bo", "cy")}. A relation on a single set A (a subset of A  times  A) can have important properties:
unit-06.1meoygdhw96: "Follows" on social media is not symmetric (you can follow someone who doesn't follow you back), while "is friends with" on many sites is. "Is a prerequisite of" is not transitive as a list of direct requirements, but "must be taken before" is. Each property is a quantified statement (Lesson 6.2), so each becomes an all(...) check in code.
unit-06.g9mv4ivghz: A relation that is reflexive, symmetric and transitive is called an equivalence relation. It captures the idea of "the same in some respect": "has the same birthday as", "has the same remainder when divided by 3", "are anagrams of each other" (Lesson 3.8).
unit-06.1u32hfgrob1: An equivalence relation splits its set into equivalence classes: groups of elements that are all related to each other, and unrelated to anything outside the group. Every element is in exactly one class. Such a split is called a partition. For "same remainder mod 3" on {0, ..., 8}, the classes are {0, 3, 6}, {1, 4, 7} and {2, 5, 8}.
unit-06.1hqi7kicsg9: You've already computed equivalence classes without the name: grouping words by their sorted letters (anagrams), or students by year, is exactly this. The grouping pattern of Lesson 3.6 with a canonical form as the key finds the classes in one pass.
unit-06.16zncnfoizt: A function f: A  to  B is a relation in which every element of A is related to exactly one element of B. A is the domain, B the codomain, and f(a) is the image of a. A Python dictionary whose keys are exactly A is a function; so is a Python function that always returns a value, as long as it gives the same output for the same input.
unit-06.ssxapq2wmx: Injective (one-to-one): different inputs give different outputs. No two keys of the dictionary share a value. Example: student  to  student ID number.
unit-06.1n0xas05fqn: Surjective (onto): every element of B is the image of something. Every possible value is used. Example: student  to  year group, if every year has at least one student.
unit-06.1f73z5mtzsb: Bijective: both injective and surjective, a perfect pairing between A and B. A bijection has an inverse function f⁻¹: B  to  A, which in Python is the dictionary with keys and values swapped.
unit-06.q53xm9cuth: Why should a programmer care? An injective function is exactly what you need for a key: database IDs (Unit 12) and good hash functions (Unit 7) aim to be injective. Encryption (Unit 16) must be a bijection, or messages couldn't be decrypted. And counting arguments (Lesson 6.6) rely on bijections: if there's a bijection between two finite sets, they have the same size.
unit-06.ti4p0oozin: Functions can be composed: (g ∘ f)(x) = g(f(x)), "apply f, then g". With dictionaries, that's g[f[x]].
unit-06.3wfuaasfhk: Suppose a course catalogue lists each course's direct prerequisites: Algorithms needs Data Structures, which needs Programming. To take Algorithms you actually need both, because "needs" chains. The transitive closure of a relation adds every pair implied by chains: if a R b and b R c, add (a, c), and keep going until nothing new appears.
unit-06.157npeccum3: A simple algorithm: repeatedly look for pairs (a, b) and (b, c) whose combination (a, c) is missing, and add it. When a full pass adds nothing, the relation is transitive. This "repeat until nothing changes" idea, called a fixed-point iteration, is very common in computer science. (Faster algorithms exist, such as Warshall's, which you'll see in Unit 8.) If the closure ever contains (a, a), then a course is its own prerequisite through some chain: a cycle, which makes the catalogue impossible to complete. Lesson 6.9 treats such relations as graphs.
unit-06.1o182xdcehr: Building them in Python and checking their sizes.
unit-06.1ojn51m4x72: Each property is a quantified statement over pairs.
unit-06.1srhputo5ka: Dictionaries as functions, with injective, surjective and inverse.
unit-06.1rdrwomhslj: {{1, 2}} raises TypeError: unhashable type: 'set'. Elements of a set must be hashable, so use frozenset({1, 2}).
unit-06.n57mpaffo2: In a Cartesian product or relation, (1, 2) and (2, 1) are different pairs. "Follows" from Ada to Bo says nothing about Bo to Ada.
unit-06.12z3v7pm8cx: Checking reflexivity only on elements that appear in pairs
unit-06.vc8sz299r6: Reflexive means every element of A is related to itself, including elements that appear in no pair at all. You need A itself to check it.
unit-06.1ft9vo7lkm0: A function must give every element of its domain exactly one image. A dictionary missing some keys, or a relation with two outputs for one input, isn't a function on that domain.
unit-06.1ana3r3x47s: Injective is about inputs (no two share an output); surjective is about outputs (every possible output is used). A function can be either, both or neither.
unit-06.l7k3lc1cpv: Sets: ∈, ⊆, ∪, ∩,  minus , |A|; set-builder notation {x | P(x)} is a set comprehension. Sets of sets need frozensets.
unit-06.9xm52n7298: The power set of an n-element set has 2ⁿ subsets; the Cartesian product A  times  B has |A|·|B| ordered pairs.
unit-06.6dv5w6kbxi: A relation is a set of pairs. Key properties: reflexive, symmetric, antisymmetric, transitive.
unit-06.1iiilow4cx3: An equivalence relation (reflexive, symmetric, transitive) partitions a set into equivalence classes; grouping by a key finds them.
unit-06.nknb3bwkys: A function gives each input exactly one output. Injective: no repeated outputs; surjective: every output used; bijective: both, so it has an inverse.
unit-06.57rv8fe5bq: The transitive closure adds all chained pairs; repeat until nothing changes. A pair (a, a) in it reveals a cycle.
unit-06.yzl41r6xt9: So far you've checked claims by computing: trying every row, every element, every pair. That works for finite cases, but how can you be sure something holds for every integer, or for lists of any length? Lesson 6.4 introduces proof: direct proof, proof by contrapositive, proof by contradiction, and how to write an argument that convinces anyone, forever.
unit-06.2flmjb9qo23: Read and write mathematical proofs using four core techniques (direct proof, contrapositive, contradiction and cases), prove existence by construction, disprove claims with counterexamples, and connect proofs to programs through loop invariants, using code to explore and check ideas before proving them.
unit-06.rgrt8x9izw: Explain what a proof is and why testing alone can't replace it
unit-06.ajtd68ej3v: Write a direct proof from precise definitions (even, odd, divides)
unit-06.12aub5y6aqf: Prove an implication through its contrapositive
unit-06.15xfx4g0984: Prove a statement by contradiction, including that √2 is irrational and that there are infinitely many primes
unit-06.2d1bckg1az0: Prove a statement about all integers by checking a finite number of cases
unit-06.1w4jpia198x: Use a loop invariant to argue that an algorithm is correct
unit-06.yh9eurifhr: A proof is an argument that shows a statement must be true, with every step following logically from definitions, from facts already proved, or from earlier steps. Once proved, a theorem stays true forever: Euclid's proof that there are infinitely many primes is over 2,300 years old and as valid today as when he wrote it.
unit-06.1muwwpfn7cr: Computer scientists need proofs because programs handle inputs nobody tested. A sorting function tested on a thousand lists might still fail on the thousand-and-first; a proof that it's correct covers every list. Proofs also explain why something is true, which often leads to better algorithms.
unit-06.13igr1w5579: Proofs start from precise definitions. For whole numbers:
unit-06.du9e6wbhsd: n is even if n = 2k for some integer k; n is odd if n = 2k + 1 for some integer k.
unit-06.240yb52h9p3: a divides b, written a | b, if b = a·k for some integer k. (So 3 | 12, but 5 ∤ 12.)
unit-06.16355rt5ufd: n > 1 is prime if its only positive divisors are 1 and n.
unit-06.or13j34tfu: a real number is rational if it equals p/q for integers p and q with q  not equal to  0.
unit-06.nocmwyamt3: Code is an excellent exploration tool: test a claim on thousands of cases first, and if it survives, look for a proof. But the code's output is evidence, not proof (Lesson 6.2's n² + n + 41).
unit-06.1de3piu6i5: To prove "if P then Q" directly: assume P is true, then use definitions and algebra to reach Q.
unit-06.154jmvkwq48: Claim. The sum of two odd numbers is even. Proof. Let a and b be odd. By definition, a = 2j + 1 and b = 2k + 1 for some integers j and k. Then a + b = 2j + 1 + 2k + 1 = 2j + 2k + 2 = 2(j + k + 1). Since j + k + 1 is an integer, a + b is two times an integer, so a + b is even. ∎
unit-06.1rsd67oz52l: Notice the pattern: unwrap the definitions of the hypothesis (odd means 2k + 1), manipulate, then rewrap into the definition of the conclusion (even means 2  times  something). Use different letters (j and k) for different numbers: writing a = 2k + 1 and b = 2k + 1 would wrongly assume a = b. The symbol ∎ (or "QED") marks the end of a proof.
unit-06.ht3rks6rr4: Another example: if a | b and b | c, then a | c. Proof: b = a·j and c = b·k for integers j, k, so c = (a·j)·k = a·(jk), and jk is an integer, so a | c. ∎ (That's the transitivity of "divides" from Lesson 6.3, now proved for all integers rather than checked for 1 to 12.)
unit-06.1k78h7fjrik: Sometimes "if P then Q" is hard to prove directly, but its contrapositive "if not Q then not P" is easy. Since they're logically equivalent (Lesson 6.1), proving one proves the other.
unit-06.1d2om8ei8j: Claim. For any integer n, if n² is even, then n is even. Proof. We prove the contrapositive: if n is odd, then n² is odd. Let n = 2k + 1. Then n² = 4k² + 4k + 1 = 2(2k² + 2k) + 1, which is odd. ∎
unit-06.f9nrjzfq7i: Trying the direct route, you'd start from "n² = 2m" and get stuck trying to take a square root. The contrapositive turns it into a simple calculation. Look for the contrapositive whenever the conclusion is easier to assume false than the hypothesis is to use.
unit-06.28kdj8twpu6: To prove a statement S by contradiction: assume S is false, and show that this leads to something impossible, like 1 = 0 or "x is both even and odd". Since a valid argument can't reach a false conclusion from true assumptions, the assumption must have been wrong, so S is true.
unit-06.10io3x8xbqa: Claim. √2 is irrational. Proof. Suppose, for contradiction, that √2 is rational: √2 = p/q, where p and q are integers with no common factor (any fraction can be reduced to lowest terms, Lesson 5.3). Squaring, 2 = p²/q², so p² = 2q². So p² is even, and by the claim above, p is even: p = 2m. Then 4m² = 2q², so q² = 2m², so q² is even, and q is even. But then p and q are both even, sharing the factor 2, which contradicts their having no common factor. So √2 is irrational. ∎
unit-06.skj82os46c: Claim (Euclid). There are infinitely many primes. Proof. Suppose there are only finitely many primes, p₁, p₂, ..., pₙ. Let N = p₁·p₂·...·pₙ + 1. N > 1, so it has some prime factor p. But dividing N by any pᵢ leaves remainder 1, so p is none of p₁, ..., pₙ. That contradicts our list containing every prime. ∎
unit-06.1pdfhzymrmx: Note that N itself needn't be prime: 2·3·5·7·11·13 + 1 = 30031 = 59  times  509. The proof only needs N to have a prime factor missing from the list. Contradiction is powerful but use it with care: if a direct proof exists, it's usually clearer.
unit-06.cqa2ouid27: If every possibility falls into one of a few cases, prove the claim separately in each case.
unit-06.wal6k34nqj: Claim. For every integer n, n² leaves remainder 0 or 1 when divided by 4. Proof. Every integer is even or odd. Case 1: n = 2k, so n² = 4k², remainder 0. Case 2: n = 2k + 1, so n² = 4k² + 4k + 1 = 4(k² + k) + 1, remainder 1. ∎
unit-06.gfy9kx2uzl: A neat consequence: a sum of two squares leaves remainder 0, 1 or 2 when divided by 4, never 3. So 4,000,003 is not a sum of two squares, proved without searching.
unit-06.rk18qku7h1: Here's where computers help honestly. The remainder of n² when divided by m depends only on the remainder of n (Lesson 6.8 explains why). So to learn every possible value of n² mod m for all integers, it's enough to check n = 0, 1, ..., m  minus  1. That's a finite proof by exhaustion, and a computer can do it. The famous Four Colour Theorem (any map can be coloured with four colours so neighbours differ) was proved in 1976 by reducing it to about 1,900 cases checked by computer.
unit-06.1bangc5lkyz: To prove "there exists an x with P(x)", the most satisfying method is construction: show a specific x and check it. For example, "for every n, there are n consecutive composite (non-prime) numbers": take (n+1)! + 2, (n+1)! + 3, ..., (n+1)! + (n+1). Each (n+1)! + k is divisible by k (because k divides (n+1)!), so none is prime. A constructive proof is also an algorithm for finding the thing. You'll code this one.
unit-06.1uf5sjx4b9f: To prove "for all x, P(x)" is false, give a single counterexample (Lesson 6.2), and check it carefully.
unit-06.2bey68cu8a9: Common logical errors to avoid in proofs:
unit-06.1kbtod81hy9: Proof by example: "it works for 3 and 5, so it's true for all odd numbers."
unit-06.g1ddy8iawe: Affirming the conclusion: proving Q  to  P when you needed P  to  Q (the converse, Lesson 6.1).
unit-06.xxjn03l18v: Circular reasoning: using the claim itself somewhere in the argument.
unit-06.1o07jw1icfn: Hidden assumptions: dividing by something that might be zero, or assuming two different numbers are the same.
unit-06.2cfszkw2zsq: Proofs aren't only about numbers. You can prove that a loop is correct using a loop invariant (first met in Lesson 4.3): a statement that's true before the loop starts and stays true after every iteration. Take finding the maximum:
unit-06.10enebfa94t: Initialisation: before the loop, best = xs[0], the largest of xs[0..0]. Maintenance: if best is the largest of xs[0..i minus 1], then after comparing with xs[i] and keeping the larger, it's the largest of xs[0..i]. Termination: when the loop ends, i has covered every index, so best is the largest of the whole list. ∎
unit-06.s28ejzp0wi: This three-part pattern is the backbone of algorithm correctness proofs in Unit 8. Python's assert (Lesson 2.9) can check an invariant while the program runs, a useful bridge between testing and proving. The next lesson, on induction, shows that this pattern is a proof technique in its own right.
unit-06.uh1dulth7t: Check claims on many cases first; if they survive, look for a proof.
unit-06.1b0hlpx2bun: Multiply the known primes, add 1, and find a new prime factor.
unit-06.22dslumd5hf: An assert inside the loop checks the invariant on every iteration.
unit-06.1jdjsjrj52m: Showing a claim for several values isn't a proof of "for all". A general proof works with an arbitrary value, such as "let n = 2k + 1".
unit-06.1rzqkep6abv: Reusing a letter for different numbers
unit-06.1sov5h0goh5: Writing both odd numbers as 2k + 1 silently assumes they're equal. Use different variables: 2j + 1 and 2k + 1.
unit-06.5hhgjiagl1: To prove P  to  Q, start from P. Starting from Q and reaching P proves Q  to  P, a different statement.
unit-06.130r7w3q2ii: Assuming what you want to prove
unit-06.viy1uwmbi7: Circular arguments use the conclusion as a step. In a proof by contradiction, you assume the negation of the claim, not the claim.
unit-06.28ialynbrcx: A proof by cases must cover every possibility (every integer is even or odd; every remainder mod 4 is 0, 1, 2 or 3). Missing one leaves a gap.
unit-06.1zo5yr8fgqw: A proof shows a statement must be true, using definitions, known facts and logic. Testing provides evidence; proof provides certainty.
unit-06.1uyy865f54i: Direct proof: assume P, unwrap definitions, reach Q.
unit-06.cj9z6uncvx: Contrapositive: prove ¬Q  to  ¬P instead of P  to  Q.
unit-06.1impxmj4atb: Contradiction: assume the statement is false and derive something impossible (√2 is irrational; there are infinitely many primes).
unit-06.1jj9ujj5guw: Cases / exhaustion: split into cases that cover everything; a finite check can prove facts about all integers when only remainders matter.
unit-06.5ms13hul0j: Construction proves existence by exhibiting an example; one counterexample disproves a universal claim.
unit-06.1hg9a7441go: Loop invariants (initialisation, maintenance, termination) prove algorithms correct.
unit-06.14320unn5wh: The loop invariant argument had a familiar shape: true at the start, and if true at one step then true at the next, so true at every step. That shape is a proof technique in its own right, mathematical induction, and it's the natural way to prove things about recursion. It's the subject of Lesson 6.5.
unit-06.1dewxgxhfzc: Prove statements about every natural number using mathematical induction and strong induction, prove recursive algorithms correct with the same reasoning, solve simple recurrences, and apply structural induction to recursive data such as trees.
unit-06.1udx2nf2lir: State the principle of induction and explain why it works
unit-06.2322mfg0m0d: Write an induction proof with a clear base case, inductive hypothesis and inductive step
unit-06.18l6n0myd8p: Use strong induction when the step needs more than the previous case
unit-06.22cgtkjli8c: Prove a recursive function correct by induction on its input
unit-06.1haaasl4f5q: Find and verify closed forms for recurrences such as T(n) = 2T(n  minus  1) + 1
unit-06.21qao7j3yqt: Use structural induction on recursively defined data like binary trees
unit-06.1x3t6xy23zl: Imagine an infinitely long row of dominoes. You want to be sure they will all fall. Two facts are enough:
unit-06.2a0xtl5cb60: Whenever a domino falls, it knocks over the next one.
unit-06.sk4wav290t: Then domino 1 falls, so domino 2 falls, so domino 3 falls, and so on forever. No domino is left standing.
unit-06.bubz6uaqwb: That's mathematical induction. To prove a statement P(n) for every natural number n  greater than or equal to  some starting value b:
unit-06.194dl0qqx2g: Inductive step: prove that for every k  greater than or equal to  b, if P(k) is true, then P(k + 1) is true. The assumption "P(k) is true" is called the inductive hypothesis.
unit-06.y357r9qgek: Then P(n) holds for all n  greater than or equal to  b. The inductive step is an implication (Lesson 6.1): you don't prove P(k) is true; you prove that if it is, the next case follows. Infinitely many cases, proved with two finite arguments.
unit-06.g6we1lq6aq: If this feels like recursion, it should: a recursive function solves a base case directly and reduces every other case to a smaller one (Lesson 4.5). Induction is recursion's twin in mathematics, and it's the way to prove recursive programs correct.
unit-06.68dppzls0c: Claim. For every n  greater than or equal to  1, 1 + 2 + 3 + ... + n = n(n + 1)/2. Base case (n = 1). The left side is 1; the right side is 1·2/2 = 1.  Inductive step. Let k  greater than or equal to  1 and assume the inductive hypothesis: 1 + 2 + ... + k = k(k + 1)/2. We must show 1 + 2 + ... + k + (k + 1) = (k + 1)(k + 2)/2. Starting from the left: 1 + 2 + ... + k + (k + 1) = k(k + 1)/2 + (k + 1) (by the inductive hypothesis) = (k + 1)(k/2 + 1) = (k + 1)(k + 2)/2.  By induction, the formula holds for all n  greater than or equal to  1. ∎
unit-06.1sghf3ofzbm: The key move is in the second line: you spot the sum up to k inside the sum up to k + 1 and replace it using the hypothesis. Almost every induction proof works this way: find the smaller case inside the bigger one.
unit-06.1uvelzroxe9: This formula matters for programmers: a loop that does 1, then 2, then 3, ..., then n steps (like insertion sort's worst case, Lesson 4.4) does n(n + 1)/2 steps in total, which is big O of n².
unit-06.1sgunnlgyka: Before attempting a proof, it's sensible to test the claim in Python for, say, n up to 1,000. If it fails, you've saved yourself trying to prove something false. If it passes, you know what to aim for.
unit-06.1nzz7i98nh4: Sometimes P(k + 1) depends not on P(k) but on some earlier case, or several. Strong induction lets you assume P is true for all values from the base up to k, and use whichever you need.
unit-06.eewfapqfxi: Claim. Every integer n  greater than or equal to  2 can be written as a product of primes. Proof (strong induction). Base: 2 is prime, a product of one prime. Step: let n > 2 and assume every integer from 2 to n  minus  1 is a product of primes. If n is prime, done. Otherwise n = a·b with 2  less than or equal to  a, b < n. By the hypothesis, a and b are both products of primes, so n = a·b is too. ∎
unit-06.mjyx5bxrce: Here n  minus  1 is no help at all: you need the factors a and b, which could be anywhere below n. Strong induction gives you every smaller case. (This is the existence half of the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic; the other half says the factorisation is unique.)
unit-06.23dd9kdi6km: Another classic: with 4p and 5p stamps, you can make every postage amount from 12p upwards. Check the bases 12 = 4+4+4, 13 = 4+4+5, 14 = 4+5+5, 15 = 5+5+5 directly; then for n  greater than or equal to  16, n  minus  4  greater than or equal to  12 can be made (by the hypothesis), so add one 4p stamp. Notice the four base cases, because the step reaches back four places. A recursive function that builds the answer follows the proof exactly.
unit-06.gk473w0g5a: Induction is how you prove that a recursive function does what it claims, for every input. Take fast exponentiation from Lesson 4.6:
unit-06.2cyrg17zkv0: Claim. power(x, n) = xⁿ for all n  greater than or equal to  0. Proof (strong induction on n). Base: power(x, 0) returns 1 = x⁰. Step: let n  greater than or equal to  1 and assume power(x, m) = xᵐ for all m < n. Since n // 2 < n, the hypothesis gives half = x^(n//2). If n is even, n = 2·(n//2), so half·half = xⁿ. If n is odd, n = 2·(n//2) + 1, so half·half·x = xⁿ. ∎
unit-06.1upqstiozlx: The structure mirrors the code: the base case of the proof is the base case of the function, and the inductive hypothesis is exactly the "leap of faith" from Lesson 4.6, that the recursive call on a smaller input works. Induction is what makes the leap of faith legitimate.
unit-06.wyiho3myjj: The running time or output of a recursive process is often described by a recurrence: a formula defining each value in terms of earlier ones. For the Towers of Hanoi (Lesson 4.6), moving n discs means moving n  minus  1 discs, moving the largest, then moving n  minus  1 again:
unit-06.26f48ylpfyu: Computing a few values, 0, 1, 3, 7, 15, 31, suggests the closed form T(n) = 2ⁿ  minus  1. Induction confirms it: T(0) = 2⁰  minus  1 = 0 , and if T(k) = 2ᵏ  minus  1, then T(k + 1) = 2(2ᵏ  minus  1) + 1 = 2ᵏ⁺¹  minus  1 .
unit-06.mxrpmu54dq: This is a standard workflow: compute small values, guess a pattern, prove it by induction. You'll use it constantly in Unit 8, where the running time of merge sort, T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n, turns out to be big O of n log n, just as you measured in Lesson 4.7.
unit-06.19rjlu46wuu: Induction isn't only about numbers. Any recursively defined structure supports it. A full binary tree is defined like this:
unit-06.6ymap965yp: a single leaf is a full binary tree;
unit-06.13jus221dtq: if L and R are full binary trees, then a node with left child L and right child R is a full binary tree.
unit-06.qe2tnwjqi2: To prove a property for all such trees, structural induction proves it for a leaf (base case), then proves that if it holds for L and R, it holds for the tree built from them. For example:
unit-06.yjca52hs9t: Claim. In every full binary tree, leaves = internal nodes + 1. Proof. Leaf: 1 leaf, 0 internal nodes.  Node: if L has iₗ internal nodes and iₗ + 1 leaves, and R has iᵣ and iᵣ + 1, the combined tree has iₗ + iᵣ + 1 internal nodes (counting the new root) and iₗ + iᵣ + 2 leaves, one more.  ∎
unit-06.18dx52khkrb: The proof follows the shape of the recursive definition, just as a recursive function on trees follows it. Lists, expression trees (Lesson 5.7) and nested folders all work the same way.
unit-06.51waxcgnvb: A famous fake proof "shows" that all horses are the same colour. Base: one horse is the same colour as itself. Step: given k + 1 horses, remove one: the remaining k are the same colour (hypothesis). Put it back and remove a different one: those k are the same colour too. The two groups overlap, so all k + 1 are the same colour.
unit-06.ttbgt2h06h: The flaw is in the step from k = 1 to k = 2: with two horses, the two groups of one horse each don't overlap, so the argument collapses. The inductive step must work for every k  greater than or equal to  b, including the smallest. Other common errors: forgetting the base case (then you've proved nothing, like dominoes that each knock over the next but none of which is ever pushed), or assuming P(k + 1) while trying to prove it.
unit-06.jhmz49v130: Check closed forms numerically before proving them.
unit-06.uiblbkn43n: Postage from 4p and 5p stamps, built exactly the way the proof argues.
unit-06.1kfx7rp3bnf: Example 3: Guessing a recurrence's closed form
unit-06.22mcboqd60: Compute small values, spot the pattern, then check it.
unit-06.fiby0jdch: An inductive step without a base case proves nothing: every domino would knock over the next, but none is ever pushed. Always check the starting value.
unit-06.2876cmi1qhx: The inductive hypothesis is P(k), and you must derive P(k + 1). Using P(k + 1) along the way makes the proof circular.
unit-06.1ntepxwuhi4: A step that fails for small k
unit-06.awoxzm0v0s: The step must work for every k from the base upwards. The "all horses are the same colour" argument breaks exactly at k = 1.
unit-06.1pmm0pmtvb4: Too few base cases for strong induction
unit-06.n7sdp2od0x: If the step uses P(k  minus  3), you need enough base cases (three in a row) so every value is reached.
unit-06.sqqlmlw5bg: Treating numerical checks as the proof
unit-06.19zd25y47mz: Testing a formula for n up to 1,000 is a good way to find what to prove, but the proof must handle a general k with algebra.
unit-06.wx002pibec: Induction: prove a base case P(b), and that P(k)  to  P(k + 1) for all k  greater than or equal to  b. Then P(n) holds for every n  greater than or equal to  b.
unit-06.1nu3orsj2zf: The key move in the step is to find the smaller case inside the larger one and apply the inductive hypothesis.
unit-06.1yse68j6j9j: Strong induction assumes P for every value up to k; it suits steps that reach further back (factorisation, postage).
unit-06.xrwvc09kvy: Induction proves recursive functions correct: the base case matches, and the hypothesis justifies the recursive call (the leap of faith).
unit-06.6ta1iue445: Recurrences: compute small values, guess a closed form, prove it by induction.
unit-06.7ul025fsue: Structural induction proves properties of recursive data, such as trees, by following their definition.
unit-06.19og8mkb5qq: Several results in this lesson were really about counting: subsets, tilings, trees, regions. Lesson 6.6 develops counting into a systematic toolkit: the sum and product rules, permutations and combinations, the binomial theorem, the pigeonhole principle and inclusion-exclusion, so you can count possibilities without listing them all.
unit-06.1fb7socbnbs: Count possibilities without listing them, using the sum and product rules, permutations, combinations and binomial coefficients, the pigeonhole principle and inclusion-exclusion, and check every count against brute-force enumeration with itertools.
unit-06.1y6jc7o6t0s: Apply the sum rule and product rule, and count using complements
unit-06.140fsoc61va: Count arrangements (permutations) and selections (combinations), with and without a size limit
unit-06.1mtpv4935tt: Compute binomial coefficients and relate them to Pascal's triangle and the binomial theorem
unit-06.m58tftq64n: Use the pigeonhole principle to prove that a collision must exist
unit-06.16mcagdpimz: Count unions of overlapping sets with inclusion-exclusion
unit-06.7mt2aznknh: Verify a counting formula by brute-force enumeration on small cases
unit-06.2dm7yszu3po: How many passwords would an attacker have to try? How many steps can an algorithm take? How many test cases cover every combination of options? How likely is a collision in a hash table? All these questions are counting questions, and the answers are usually far too large to find by listing every possibility. Combinatorics, the mathematics of counting, gives formulas instead.
unit-06.13ezt5crli3: You've already counted in this course: 2ⁿ bit patterns (Lesson 1.1), n² steps for nested loops (Lesson 2.7), 2ⁿ subsets and n! orderings for brute force (Lesson 4.8). This lesson organises those ideas into a toolkit. Throughout, a computer gives you a safety net: for small cases, itertools can generate every possibility, so you can check a formula before trusting it.
unit-06.iyb3igjo9d: Sum rule: if a task can be done in one of m ways or one of n ways, with no overlap, there are m + n ways. A café with 4 cold drinks and 6 hot drinks offers 4 + 6 = 10 drinks.
unit-06.1zynea247ae: Product rule: if a task is done in two independent steps, with m ways for the first and n for the second, there are m  times  n ways. A starter (4 choices) and a main (6 choices) give 4  times  6 = 24 meals.
unit-06.2fdxwloizvb: The product rule extends to many steps. A UK car number plate pattern of 2 letters, 2 digits, then 3 letters gives 26  times  26  times  10  times  10  times  26  times  26  times  26 = 1,188,137,600 plates. A password of 8 characters from 62 letters and digits gives 62⁸ ≈ 2.2  times  10¹⁴: at a billion guesses per second, that's under three days to try them all, which is why security advice favours longer passwords (Unit 16).
unit-06.1kh16ommty8: Often the easiest way to count something is to count its complement and subtract. How many 8-character passwords contain at least one digit? Counting directly means handling "exactly one digit, exactly two, ...". Instead: all passwords minus those with no digits = 62⁸  minus  52⁸.
unit-06.1ij4g140eee: A permutation is an ordered arrangement. How many ways can n different items be arranged in a row? The first position has n choices, the second n  minus  1 (one item is used), and so on down to 1. By the product rule:
unit-06.29s33iw1l6t: n! = n  times  (n  minus  1)  times  ...  times  2  times  1 ("n factorial", with 0! = 1)
unit-06.1268drormjy: Arranging 5 books on a shelf: 5! = 120 ways. 52 playing cards: 52! ≈ 8  times  10⁶⁷, more than the number of atoms in the Earth, so every well-shuffled deck is almost certainly an order that has never existed before.
unit-06.cqtizk5pdu: If you only fill k of the positions (a podium of 3 from 10 runners), there are n  times  (n  minus  1)  times  ...  times  (n  minus  k + 1) ways, the first k factors of n!. This is written P(n, k), and equals n! / (n  minus  k)!. Podiums from 10 runners: 10  times  9  times  8 = 720.
unit-06.vbnimi81g5: itertools.permutations(items, k) generates them all (Lesson 4.8), and Python's math.perm(n, k) computes the count.
unit-06.127qc9anxtz: A combination is a selection where order doesn't matter. Choosing 3 people from 10 for a committee: the 720 ordered podiums count each committee 3! = 6 times (once for each order of the same three people). So there are 720 / 6 = 120 committees.
unit-06.jna44441ny: In general, the number of ways to choose k items from n is the binomial coefficient:
unit-06.1mq0471pk0k: C(n, k) = n! / (k! (n  minus  k)!) (read "n choose k", also written as n over k in brackets)
unit-06.28acmnix4cu: Some values to know: C(n, 0) = C(n, n) = 1 (one way to choose nothing, or everything); C(n, 1) = n; C(n, 2) = n(n  minus  1)/2, the number of pairs, which is why comparing every pair of n items takes about n²/2 steps (Lesson 4.2). And C(n, k) = C(n, n  minus  k): choosing k to include is the same as choosing n  minus  k to leave out.
unit-06.25ujinkqtje: Combinations count subsets of a given size, so adding them up over all sizes counts all subsets: C(n, 0) + C(n, 1) + ... + C(n, n) = 2ⁿ (Lesson 6.3). The UK National Lottery chooses 6 numbers from 59: C(59, 6) = 45,057,474 possible tickets.
unit-06.wm20qchiby: Key idea: Ask two questions. Does order matter? (permutation or combination) Can items repeat? (with or without repetition). With repetition and order mattering, it's just nᵏ, as with passwords.

unit-06.1w6mt11x8io: Roll a fair die. What's the chance of an even number? You probably said one half without thinking: three of the six equally likely faces are even. That's the whole idea of classical probability:
unit-06.53yidjmnfo: P(event) = (number of outcomes in the event) / (total number of outcomes)
unit-06.rw9ubptut6: when all outcomes are equally likely. So probability, at first, is just counting (Lesson 6.6) followed by a division.
unit-06.1znysr13993: Programmers need probability everywhere: randomised algorithms like quicksort's random pivot (Unit 7), hash table collision rates, testing with random inputs, games, simulations, networking (how likely is a packet loss?), and the whole of machine learning (Unit 17), which is built on probability.
unit-06.2b5tdzqws08: An experiment is something with an uncertain result: rolling two dice.
unit-06.1qit1drhuz9: The sample space S is the set of all possible outcomes: the 36 pairs (1, 1), (1, 2), ..., (6, 6).
unit-06.1nlrcw4mh7f: An event is a subset of S: "the total is 7" is the set {(1, 6), (2, 5), (3, 4), (4, 3), (5, 2), (6, 1)}.
unit-06.1kjn9eel94y: With equally likely outcomes, P(total is 7) = 6/36 = 1/6. In Python, itertools.product(range(1, 7), repeat=2) builds the sample space, and an event is a filter over it.
unit-06.2bzqx2nf2ct: Probabilities are always between 0 (impossible: the empty event) and 1 (certain: the whole sample space). Because events are sets, set operations give the rules:
unit-06.qfy0fzbauc: Complement: P(not A) = 1  minus  P(A). The chance of not rolling a six is 5/6.
unit-06.14g5ajtxrrb: Addition rule: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B)  minus  P(A and B). That's inclusion-exclusion from Lesson 6.6, divided by |S|.
unit-06.6s7zpqf7yb: Watch out for outcomes that aren't equally likely. The totals 2 to 12 of two dice are not equally likely (7 can happen 6 ways, 2 only one way), so you can't say P(total 7) = 1/11. Always go back to a sample space whose outcomes really are equally likely.
unit-06.ib27zew9gd: Python's fractions.Fraction keeps probabilities exact: Fraction(6, 36) is Fraction(1, 6), with no floating-point rounding (Lesson 2.3).
unit-06.1nazc24m3vp: Sometimes you learn something that changes the odds. You roll two dice and a friend peeks and says "at least one is a six". Now what's the chance the total is 12?
unit-06.8ui1syc6q4: The new information shrinks the sample space to the 11 outcomes containing a six. Only (6, 6) gives 12, so the answer is 1/11, not 1/36. This is conditional probability, written P(A | B), "the probability of A given B":
unit-06.27fl4tozhfv: P(A | B) = P(A and B) / P(B)
unit-06.sv0l8sryp0: In counting terms: |A ∩ B| / |B|. You restrict attention to B, and ask what fraction of it is also in A.
unit-06.1ehne2vv2e5: Order matters: P(A | B) is usually not P(B | A). The probability that someone who speaks French lives in France is quite different from the probability that someone living in France speaks French. Confusing the two is a famous error, sometimes called the prosecutor's fallacy.
unit-06.214h0flpem3: Two events are independent if knowing one happened doesn't change the probability of the other: P(A | B) = P(A). Equivalently:
unit-06.1232h04o5cl: P(A and B) = P(A)  times  P(B)
unit-06.24fp7vzttii: Two separate coin flips are independent: the first doesn't influence the second. This is why the chance of 10 heads in a row is (1/2)¹⁰ = 1/1024, the product rule of Lesson 6.6 in probability form.
unit-06.1xih2te1w68: The coin has no memory. After 9 heads in a row, the chance of a 10th head is still 1/2. Believing that tails is "due" is the gambler's fallacy.
unit-06.1lfgm1083bc: Independence makes "at least one" problems easy, using the complement. If each of 20 servers fails on a given day with probability 0.01, independently, the chance at least one fails is 1  minus  0.99²⁰ ≈ 0.18. Small risks add up quickly across many components, which is why large systems are designed to tolerate failures (Unit 11).
unit-06.22amwt6p5yy: Bayes' rule turns a conditional probability around:
unit-06.ux5pmb5a6c: P(A | B) = P(B | A)  times  P(A) / P(B)
unit-06.qaxlytbn8d: Its classic use is updating a belief when evidence arrives. Suppose a disease affects 1 in 100 people. A test catches 90% of real cases, but also gives a positive result for 5% of healthy people. You test positive. How worried should you be?
unit-06.1mmuzfuh99i: Think about 10,000 people. 100 have the disease, and 90 of them test positive. Of the 9,900 healthy people, 5% = 495 also test positive. So 90 + 495 = 585 people test positive, and only 90 of them are ill:
unit-06.1k97dv02o0k: Most people guess around 90%. The surprise comes from the base rate: the disease is rare, so false positives from the large healthy group swamp the true positives. Spam filters work exactly this way, combining the base rate of spam with how much more often words like "winner" appear in spam (Unit 17).
unit-06.ocd1g5v8p6: A random variable is a number that depends on the outcome: the total of two dice, the winnings from a bet. Its expected value (or mean) is the average you'd get over many repeats: each possible value weighted by its probability.
unit-06.pttomb3b1z: For one die: (1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6)  times  1/6 = 3.5. You'll never roll 3.5, but it's the long-run average.
unit-06.7olxr4c5fx: Expected values add: E[X + Y] = E[X] + E[Y], even if X and Y aren't independent. So two dice average 3.5 + 3.5 = 7 without listing 36 outcomes.
unit-06.10yf60r0wr7: A game costs £1 to play. You roll a die and win £5 on a six. Expected winnings: 5  times  1/6 = about 83p, so you lose about 17p a game on average. That's how every casino profits.
unit-06.1e53za2a42i: Variance measures spread: the expected squared distance from the mean, E[(X  minus  μ)²]. Its square root is the standard deviation. In algorithm analysis, expected value gives the average-case running time: quicksort with random pivots takes big O of n log n steps on average, even though its worst case is big O of n² (Unit 7).
unit-06.24nlng39let: Some probabilities are hard to calculate but easy to simulate: run the random experiment many times with the random module and count how often the event happens. This is called the Monte Carlo method.
unit-06.18i2dtx5m9s: random.seed(42) makes the "random" sequence repeatable, which is essential for testing and debugging. The law of large numbers says the estimate gets closer to the true probability as the number of trials grows. The error typically shrinks like 1/√n, so to get one more correct decimal place you need about 100 times as many trials.
unit-06.mqmspfi8ki: Simulation is also a superb way to check a calculation. If your formula and your simulation disagree, one of them is wrong, just like checking a counting formula against brute-force enumeration in Lesson 6.6.

unit-06.1zezrzog07u: Number theory studies the integers: whole numbers and how they divide each other. It was long considered the purest, most useless branch of mathematics. Then computers arrived, and it became the foundation of hashing, checksums, random number generators and all of internet security.
unit-06.1i09ipdpamf: You met the basic tools in Lesson 2.2. For integers a and d > 0, there's exactly one way to write
unit-06.2cml3eqeevv: a = q  times  d + r with 0  less than or equal to  r < d
unit-06.2cchsnwkqxx: where q is the quotient (a // d) and r is the remainder (a % d). divmod(a, d) gives both. Python keeps r between 0 and d  minus  1 even for negative a: -7 % 3 is 2, because  minus 7 =  minus 3  times  3 + 2.
unit-06.1k7e8olbmf0: We say d divides a, written d | a, when the remainder is 0. Useful facts, which you can prove from the definition (Lesson 6.4): if d | a and d | b then d | (a + b) and d | (a  minus  b); and if d | a then d | (a  times  c) for any c.
unit-06.10m6111fa0u: A prime is an integer greater than 1 whose only divisors are 1 and itself: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, ... The Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic says every integer above 1 is a product of primes in exactly one way (apart from order): 360 = 2³  times  3²  times  5. Primes are the atoms of multiplication. You proved part of this with strong induction in Lesson 6.5, and that there are infinitely many primes in Lesson 6.4.
unit-06.12y89wfk5ah: To test whether one number n is prime, try divisors up to √n (if n = a  times  b, one of a and b is at most √n). To find all primes up to n, the sieve of Eratosthenes, over 2,000 years old, is far better:
unit-06.tud4xd0lbh: Write out 2, 3, ..., n, all marked "possibly prime".
unit-06.fvoa2u9ufb: Take the smallest number p still marked. It's prime. Cross out its multiples p², p² + p, p² + 2p, ... (smaller multiples were already crossed out by smaller primes).
unit-06.269m8574nsf: Repeat until p² > n. Everything still marked is prime.
unit-06.1qyc7ajpfw4: Each number is crossed out once for each of its prime factors, so the total work is about n log log n steps, which is practically linear. Finding the 664,579 primes below ten million takes a few seconds in Python.
unit-06.1dd1id07r7: The greatest common divisor gcd(a, b) is the largest number dividing both: gcd(48, 18) = 6. You need it to simplify fractions (48/18 = 8/3) and to compute the least common multiple, lcm(a, b) = a  times  b / gcd(a, b), used for inclusion-exclusion in Lesson 6.6.
unit-06.29e83y2gbu0: Factorising both numbers works, but factorising is slow for big numbers. Euclid's algorithm (around 300 BC) is much faster, and it rests on one fact:
unit-06.1pcl71dm68y: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a mod b)
unit-06.u87rb4lf2l: Why? If d divides a and b, it divides a  minus  q  times  b = a mod b. Conversely, if d divides b and a mod b, it divides q  times  b + (a mod b) = a. So the two pairs have exactly the same common divisors. Repeat until the second number is 0, and since gcd(a, 0) = a:
unit-06.24okxaby4rb: The numbers shrink fast: every two steps, the larger one at least halves, so it takes big O of log n steps. Even 300-digit numbers need only around a thousand steps. Python provides math.gcd, but you'll write your own.
unit-06.1ufgibuywfc: Modular arithmetic is clock arithmetic. On a 12-hour clock, 4 hours after 10 o'clock is 2 o'clock: (10 + 4) mod 12 = 2. We say a ≡ b (mod m), "a is congruent to b mod m", when a and b have the same remainder, that is, when m divides a  minus  b. So 14 ≡ 2 (mod 12).
unit-06.1wu2qm6etyq: The key property: you can take remainders at any stage of adding, subtracting or multiplying, and the final remainder is the same:
unit-06.17vvwovk5ld: (a + b) mod m = ((a mod m) + (b mod m)) mod m (a  times  b) mod m = ((a mod m)  times  (b mod m)) mod m
unit-06.243cvxedv4m: That keeps numbers small. What's the last digit of 7¹⁰⁰? Work mod 10 and you never need the 85-digit number. Applications are everywhere:
unit-06.1y4uk8r8cjv: Calendars: if today is Wednesday (day 2, with Monday as 0), the day 100 days from now is (2 + 100) mod 7 = 4, a Friday.
unit-06.1c72tcfb13a: Hashing: a hash table with m buckets puts a key in bucket hash(key) % m (Unit 7).
unit-06.10mfpi2y7f9: Check digits: barcodes, ISBNs and card numbers include a digit chosen so a weighted sum is divisible by 10 or 11, so most typing errors are detected.
unit-06.240p9kik7w0: Random numbers: simple generators compute xₙ₊₁ = (a  times  xₙ + c) mod m.
unit-06.1gndsgzeccb: Division is the tricky one. You can't simply divide remainders, as you'll see below.
unit-06.epa23tpnpv: Cryptography needs things like 5^(10³⁰⁰) mod m. Multiplying by 5 a googol-cubed times is impossible. Square-and-multiply (also called fast exponentiation) uses the binary form of the exponent (Lesson 1.1):
unit-06.27i9l4ep8jr: 5¹³ = 5⁸  times  5⁴  times  5¹, because 13 is 1101 in binary.
unit-06.20qvp0r3jx0: 5², 5⁴, 5⁸, ... come from repeated squaring, each one the square of the last.
unit-06.ajoegqz6od: The algorithm walks through the exponent's bits, squaring each time and multiplying in when the bit is 1, taking the remainder after every step so numbers stay below m². It needs about 2  times  log₂(n) multiplications, so even a 1,000-bit exponent needs only around 2,000. It's the same halving idea as binary search and divide and conquer (Unit 4). Python's built-in pow(base, exp, mod) does exactly this.

unit-06.t118sln91h: Dividing by a mod m means multiplying by an inverse: a number x with a  times  x ≡ 1 (mod m). 3  times  5 = 15 ≡ 1 (mod 7), so 5 is the inverse of 3 mod 7. An inverse exists exactly when gcd(a, m) = 1, and the extended Euclidean algorithm finds it. Alongside the gcd, it finds integers x and y with
unit-06.1rbzhekr5el: a  times  x + m  times  y = gcd(a, m)
unit-06.1knyi6ib31l: If the gcd is 1, then a  times  x ≡ 1 (mod m), so x is the inverse. Python's pow(a, -1, m) computes it too.
unit-06.hnk1u1cznx: These pieces build RSA, the public-key encryption invented in 1977 that still secures much of the internet:
unit-06.cudvfog1yo: Choose two large primes p and q, and let n = p  times  q.
unit-06.12ivwzslug0: Let φ = (p  minus  1)(q  minus  1), and choose e with gcd(e, φ) = 1. The public key is (n, e).
unit-06.1lg8t0k5jso: The private key d is the inverse of e mod φ.
unit-06.2ggglmqt116: To encrypt a message number M: C = Mᵉ mod n. To decrypt: M = Cᵈ mod n.
unit-06.14u34yq6q5s: Anyone can encrypt with the public key, but decrypting needs d, and finding d needs φ, which needs the factors p and q. Multiplying two 300-digit primes is instant; factorising their product is, as far as anyone knows, practically impossible. The security rests on that gap. (Why decryption works is Euler's theorem, which Unit 16 covers alongside real-world cryptography. Never use toy RSA for real secrets.)

unit-06.1rqvnj93ynw: Modular arithmetic: reduce at every step of +,  minus  and  times . It underlies clocks, calendars, hashing and check digits.
unit-06.2144w8u1iuf: Square-and-multiply computes base^exp mod m in big O of log exp multiplications, like pow(b, e, m).
unit-06.i6ws0yo1ly: The extended Euclidean algorithm finds modular inverses, which make RSA possible: easy to multiply primes, hard to factor.
unit-06.1xhr2fgrgsx: So far Unit 6 has dealt with numbers, sets and logic. Lesson 6.9 turns to the most useful structure in computer science: graphs, made of vertices joined by edges. Social networks, road maps, the web and course prerequisites are all graphs, and you'll learn their vocabulary, how to store them, and how to explore them.
unit-06.93ahiwdrfa: Model connections with graphs: use the vocabulary of vertices, edges, degree, paths, cycles, connectivity and trees, prove and use the handshake lemma, store graphs as adjacency lists and adjacency matrices, and find everything reachable from a vertex.
unit-06.pnin8lid7y: Describe a situation as a graph, choosing undirected or directed edges
unit-06.mk6bdkv4fh: Compute degrees and use the handshake lemma to check and reason about graphs
unit-06.22ofpzlmmcl: Store a graph as an adjacency list or an adjacency matrix, and explain the trade-offs
unit-06.jws9hqkn56: Recognise walks, paths and cycles, and count walks with matrix multiplication
unit-06.lt237z1zyn: Find the vertices reachable from a start vertex, and split a graph into connected components
unit-06.1yclvc717lw: Recognise trees, and decide whether a graph has an Euler path or circuit
unit-06.ihgtxhmzu4: In 1736 the people of Königsberg had a puzzle. Their city had seven bridges joining two river banks and two islands. Could you walk through the city crossing every bridge exactly once? Leonhard Euler realised the shapes and distances didn't matter, only which land masses were joined by which bridges. He drew each land mass as a dot and each bridge as a line, and invented graph theory.
unit-06.hckdgwg00e: A graph G = (V, E) is a set V of vertices (also called nodes) and a set E of edges, each joining a pair of vertices. Graphs model anything made of things and connections:
unit-06.2aaw5wxehsq: Once a problem is a graph, decades of graph algorithms apply to it. That's why graphs may be the most useful idea in this whole unit. Units 7 and 8 build their main algorithms on the foundations here.
unit-06.1yz6hmvlfun: In an undirected graph, an edge {u, v} goes both ways, like a friendship. In a directed graph (a digraph), an edge (u, v) goes one way, like a web link or a prerequisite (Lesson 6.3's relations are digraphs).
unit-06.5krdv8nrsu: Two vertices joined by an edge are adjacent, or neighbours.
unit-06.sgycjg5xbn: In a weighted graph, each edge carries a number such as a distance or cost (Unit 8).
unit-06.1ntmumdage5: A simple graph has no loops (edges from a vertex to itself) and at most one edge between any pair. We'll use simple graphs unless we say otherwise.
unit-06.sqc3nyv5de: The degree of a vertex is its number of edges. In a digraph, the in-degree counts edges arriving and the out-degree counts edges leaving.
unit-06.1o8ltbojfqx: A graph where every pair of vertices is joined is complete. The complete graph on n vertices has C(n, 2) = n(n  minus  1)/2 edges (Lesson 6.6). The density of a graph is the fraction of those possible edges actually present.
unit-06.2bqrvzjl6wz: At a party, everyone counts how many hands they shook, and you add up the counts. The total is always even. Why? Each handshake involves two people, so it's counted exactly twice. In graph terms:
unit-06.cmj3mtegwo: Handshake lemma: the sum of the degrees of all vertices = 2  times  (number of edges).
unit-06.11wwcb6tufb: You can count edges from degrees: a graph with degrees 3, 3, 2, 2, 2 has (3 + 3 + 2 + 2 + 2) / 2 = 6 edges.
unit-06.25llvfa5uer: The number of vertices with odd degree is always even. (The odd degrees must add to an even number, since the total is even.) So no group of 7 people can each have exactly 3 friends among themselves: 7  times  3 = 21 is odd.
unit-06.1zrwc664k8r: It's an excellent sanity check for graph code. If your degrees don't sum to twice your edge count, there's a bug.
unit-06.2853q9xi3cs: For a digraph, the sum of in-degrees and the sum of out-degrees both equal the number of edges.
unit-06.19tai05ea3t: There are two standard representations. Label the vertices and take the graph with edges A–B, A–C, B–C, C–D.
unit-06.1td1um6z51y: An adjacency list maps each vertex to the set of its neighbours. In Python, a dictionary of sets:
unit-06.1x0sr0rz60f: An adjacency matrix is an n  times  n grid of 0s and 1s, with a 1 in row i, column j when vertices i and j are adjacent (a list of lists, Lesson 3.4):
unit-06.13s5jlldi42: For an undirected graph the matrix is symmetric: entry (i, j) equals entry (j, i).
unit-06.1b9bagli9qs: Most real graphs are sparse: a social network with a billion people where each has a few hundred friends. A matrix would need 10¹⁸ entries, mostly zeros, while an adjacency list needs space for only the actual edges. So adjacency lists are the usual choice; matrices suit small or dense graphs, and have neat mathematical properties, as you'll see.
unit-06.1kt1wn18fxq: A walk is a sequence of vertices where each consecutive pair is joined by an edge: A, B, C, A, B is a walk.
unit-06.k6ugf8l0ew: A path is a walk with no repeated vertices: A, B, C, D. Its length is its number of edges, here 3.
unit-06.px4efog4cq: A cycle is a walk of length at least 3 that returns to its start, with no other repeated vertices: A, B, C, A.
unit-06.mra62eh2qw: The distance between two vertices is the length of a shortest path between them. Finding shortest paths efficiently is breadth-first search (Unit 7) and Dijkstra's algorithm (Unit 8).
unit-06.1v3inz08mbk: Here's a lovely link between graphs and the nested lists of Unit 3. Square the adjacency matrix M with matrix multiplication: entry (i, j) of M² counts the walks of length 2 from i to j, because each one goes i  to  k  to  j through some middle vertex k, and the sum Σₖ M[i][k]  times  M[k][j] counts exactly those. In general, Mᵏ counts walks of length k, which can be proved by induction on k (Lesson 6.5).
unit-06.21l388jf6zs: Vertex v is reachable from u if there's a path from u to v. An undirected graph is connected if every vertex can reach every other. If not, it falls into separate pieces called connected components: in a social network, groups with no friendship links between them.
unit-06.2a8nz75mhk8: To find everything reachable from a start vertex, keep a set of visited vertices and a to-do list:
unit-06.9tdrlarie0: Put the start vertex in both.
unit-06.fyn3sp3dh1: While the to-do list isn't empty, take a vertex out, and for each neighbour not yet visited, mark it visited and add it to the to-do list.
unit-06.1dg51ctgjw6: When the to-do list is empty, the visited set is everything reachable.
unit-06.1tpu0aeheuj: Each vertex enters the to-do list at most once and each edge is examined at most twice, so this takes big O of V + E time. If the to-do list is a stack (take from the end with pop()), this is depth-first search; if it's a queue (take from the front), it's breadth-first search. Units 7 and 8 study both in depth; for now, either finds the same set. Running the search again from each unvisited vertex finds every connected component.
unit-06.27g3tl86gic: A tree is a connected graph with no cycles. Trees appear all over computing: file systems, the Python syntax trees you've used with ast, family trees, and the search trees of Unit 7. Trees have a remarkable property:
unit-06.bjknwn1kjg: A tree with n vertices has exactly n  minus  1 edges.
unit-06.13zuet5cvqm: Proof by induction (Lesson 6.5): a tree with at least 2 vertices has a leaf (a vertex of degree 1; follow a longest path, and its end can't have another neighbour without making a longer path or a cycle). Removing the leaf and its edge leaves a tree with n  minus  1 vertices, which by the inductive hypothesis has n  minus  2 edges. So the original had n  minus  1. In fact, a graph with n vertices is a tree exactly when it's connected and has n  minus  1 edges. Add any edge to a tree and you create a cycle; remove any edge and it disconnects.
unit-06.27ovjbczqpu: Back to Königsberg. An Euler path uses every edge exactly once; an Euler circuit also ends where it started. Euler proved:
unit-06.r7arnacvss: A connected graph has an Euler circuit exactly when every vertex has even degree. Each visit to a vertex arrives along one edge and leaves along another, using edges in pairs.
unit-06.t5jr7wt95c: It has an Euler path exactly when it has 0 or 2 odd-degree vertices (the path must start at one and end at the other).
unit-06.u5xveub0se: Königsberg's four land masses had degrees 5, 3, 3 and 3: four odd vertices, so the walk was impossible. Euler answered the puzzle without trying a single route, by reasoning about degrees.

unit-06.146p3zu6xyn: That makes n references to the same row, so setting one entry changes a whole column. Use [[0] * n for _ in range(n)].

unit-06.rl1czaivl9: Mark a vertex as visited when it's first discovered and added. Otherwise the same vertex can be added many times, wasting time and possibly memory.
unit-06.29jl96j55o2: A walk may repeat vertices; a path may not. A cycle needs at least 3 edges, so going along one edge and straight back isn't a cycle.

unit-06.1km1rmsqbvd: A matrix needs V² entries. With a million vertices that's a trillion entries, nearly all zero. Use an adjacency list.
unit-06.4itexg5bai: A graph has vertices and edges; edges may be undirected or directed, and may carry weights.
unit-06.zrhzi0lgwr: Handshake lemma: the degrees sum to 2  times  the number of edges, so the number of odd-degree vertices is even.
unit-06.jxhjxpj3mf: Adjacency lists use big O of V + E space and suit sparse graphs; adjacency matrices use big O of V² and give instant edge lookups.
unit-06.4g44o5y1ow: Walks may repeat vertices, paths may not, and cycles return to their start. Entry (i, j) of Mᵏ counts walks of length k.
unit-06.27b1524k4ud: A visited set plus a to-do list finds everything reachable in big O of V + E; repeating it finds the connected components.
unit-06.2803euaxe5m: A tree is connected with no cycles, and has exactly n  minus  1 edges. A connected graph has an Euler circuit iff every degree is even, and an Euler path iff 0 or 2 degrees are odd.
unit-06.kg8h1r36t8: That completes the discrete maths toolkit: logic, sets, proof, induction, counting, probability, number theory and graphs. Unit 7, Data Structures II, puts it to work. You'll build stacks, queues, linked lists, hash tables (using modular arithmetic and the pigeonhole principle), trees and heaps (with induction to prove their properties), and graphs with breadth-first and depth-first search, analysing each with the counting and Big-O tools you now have.

unit-07.g5v6vhmtc: In Unit 3 you used Python's built-in structures: lists, dictionaries, sets and tuples. In this unit you'll build them, and some that Python doesn't include, from the ground up. Why build something Python already provides?
unit-07.1h6pue6ddo8: To choose well. The right data structure can turn a program that takes hours into one that takes a second. You can only choose well if you know what each structure costs, and you understand costs best by building the structure.
unit-07.11lw7ykxm7r: To build what isn't provided. Real systems need priority queues, trees, graphs and caches tailored to the problem.
unit-07.m5c0hlesul: Because interviews and exams expect it. Data structures are the core of a CS degree, and the most common topic in technical interviews.
unit-07.mptlxkuea6: Each lesson follows the same pattern: what the structure is for, how it works, its costs in Big O (Lesson 4.2), and how to build it as a class (Unit 5).
unit-07.vktd87agr1: Think of a car. To drive, you need to know its interface: steering wheel, pedals, gear stick. You don't need to know whether the engine is petrol, diesel or electric. Different engines can sit behind the same interface.
unit-07.2f8ud83tcqq: An abstract data type (ADT) is the interface of a collection: which operations it supports and what they mean, with nothing said about how they work. A data structure is a concrete way of implementing an ADT in memory.
unit-07.18hplixvl6p: There is a table here. Have a look at it on screen.
unit-07.1465gseaq5p: This is encapsulation (Lesson 5.4) applied to collections. Code that uses a Map only calls its operations, so you can swap a slow implementation for a fast one without changing that code. The choice of implementation decides the cost of each operation, and that's what this unit is about.
unit-07.oin996m9cd: Underneath almost every data structure is the array: a fixed number of slots in one contiguous block of memory (Lesson 1.5). If each slot takes 8 bytes and the array starts at address 1000, then slot i is at address 1000 + 8  times  i. The computer finds any slot with one multiplication and one addition, however big the array is, so indexing is big O of 1. This is also why indexes start at 0 (Lesson 3.1).
unit-07.pz3gv0smus: The catch: an array's size is fixed when it's created, because the memory just after it may be in use by something else. To make it bigger, you must allocate a new, larger block and copy every element across, which is big O of n.
unit-07.opey6pxus5: Python hides raw arrays from you, so in this unit we'll simulate one with a list of a fixed length, such as [None] * capacity, and promise ourselves we'll never call append or insert on it. Only indexing and assignment, which are big O of 1, are allowed.
unit-07.y1eoh78tlw: A Python list can grow forever, yet indexing is big O of 1. It's built on an array using a simple trick. A dynamic array keeps:
unit-07.17qpy47jcqt: an underlying array with some capacity (the number of slots), and
unit-07.ull4ny4nqa: a size (how many slots are actually in use).
unit-07.1p9me2uywrm: To append, put the new item in slot size and add 1 to size. If the array is full, first allocate a new array with double the capacity, copy everything across, and then append. Most appends are a single big O of 1 step; occasionally one append costs big O of n for the copy.
unit-07.xgjwawfezf: Here is some code. Have a look at it on screen.
unit-07.ukkz7nf4o: If some appends cost big O of n, is append big O of n? In the worst case, a single append is. But look at a whole sequence of n appends, starting from capacity 1. Copies happen when the size reaches 1, 2, 4, 8, ..., so the total number of elements copied is
unit-07.y4lml0aaef: (each power of two is more than the sum of all the smaller ones; you proved sums like this in Lesson 6.5). So n appends do fewer than n placements plus 2n copies, about 3 steps per append on average. We say append is amortised big O of 1: expensive operations are rare enough that their cost, spread across all operations, is a constant per operation.
unit-07.7dwh9573h0: An analogy: a monthly £30 train pass. One day costs £30, the other 29 days cost nothing. Averaged over the month it's £1 a day.
unit-07.1z4pi4lsxj5: Doubling is essential. Suppose instead the array grows by a fixed 10 slots each time. Then copies happen every 10 appends, copying 10, 20, 30, ... elements, totalling about n²/20. That's big O of n per append on average, so a million appends would take around 50 billion copies. Growing by a constant factor (Python uses about 1.125, others use 1.5 or 2) is what keeps appends amortised big O of 1.
unit-07.2drmxg3o79y: Knowing that a list is a dynamic array explains every cost in this table:
unit-07.14qz0el6ehi: So a list is a great stack (add and remove at the end) but a terrible queue (remove from the front). The next two lessons build structures for each job.
unit-07.10k9h7ot3co: A Bag (a multiset) built two ways, with the same interface.
unit-07.5bm5q91nz6: Doubling the capacity when full, and counting the copies.
unit-07.16mo8vnojq0: Python's own list over-allocates too. sys.getsizeof reports how many bytes it's using.

unit-07.du2xdqje34: "A stack" doesn't mean "a list". It's a set of operations that could be built on a list, a linked list or something else. Design code against the operations, not the storage.
unit-07.nntt0pwa2g: Calling append amortised big O of 1 "always big O of 1"
unit-07.1f6sunldgyd: Any single append can cost big O of n when it triggers a resize. The guarantee is about the average over a sequence. That matters for real-time systems, where one slow operation can be a problem.
unit-07.10sm26uqat4: Adding k slots each time makes n appends cost big O of n²/k. Grow by a constant factor instead.
unit-07.1jhe8bk1wfj: It causes thrashing: alternating push and pop at the boundary resizes every time. Shrink at a quarter.
unit-07.1gav7b772k: Removing from the front of a dynamic array shifts every remaining element, big O of n each time. Use collections.deque (Lesson 7.3).
unit-07.ps3iz1gezp: An abstract data type says what operations a collection supports; a data structure says how they're implemented and what they cost.
unit-07.1up1e80pu1a: An array is contiguous fixed-size memory with big O of 1 indexing; growing it means allocating and copying.
unit-07.ik79ltyhz9: A dynamic array (Python's list) doubles its capacity when full, so append is amortised big O of 1: n appends cost big O of n in total.
unit-07.1hmj4ck1rdt: Grow by a constant factor, never a constant amount; shrink at a quarter full to avoid thrashing.
unit-07.1hrpc60dx0v: List operations at the end are big O of 1; inserting or deleting near the front shifts elements and costs big O of n.

unit-07.2e91e7ibw3f: Picture a stack of plates. You add a plate to the top, and you take a plate from the top. The plate you took is always the one most recently added. That's a stack: a collection where the last item in is the first item out (LIFO).
unit-07.2buomyytlp8: The stack ADT has just a few operations:
unit-07.24my7a3ne0k: There's deliberately no way to look at the middle. That restriction is the point: a stack is the right tool whenever only the most recent unfinished thing matters.
unit-07.14850slwq3y: Lesson 7.1 showed that a dynamic array (Python's list) adds and removes at the end in amortised big O of 1. So the end of a list makes a perfect top of stack:
unit-07.1kjuan1uqd5: Every operation is big O of 1 (push is amortised big O of 1). Using the front of the list as the top would make push and pop big O of n, because every element would shift.
unit-07.kdcslsdvip: Why wrap a list in a class at all, when a list already has append and pop? The class narrows the interface (Lesson 5.4): it states the intent ("this is a stack"), prevents accidental access to the middle, and gives clearer errors. In quick scripts, programmers often just use a list as a stack, and that's fine too.
unit-07.lvx4vts2l2: Undo, redo and the back button
unit-07.tnsxjg6bt7: Every time you edit a document, the editor pushes a record of the change onto an undo stack. Pressing undo pops the most recent change and reverses it. Undo again pops the one before. The most recent change is always undone first: LIFO.
unit-07.2g7sx4pi3re: Redo uses a second stack. When you undo a change, push it onto the redo stack; redo pops from there and re-applies it (pushing it back onto the undo stack). When you make a new edit, the redo stack is cleared, because the old future no longer makes sense.
unit-07.bong7ngvhz: A browser's back and forward buttons work the same way, with one stack of pages behind you and one ahead.
unit-07.wnh45fxzp1: Is { [ ( ) ] ( ) } correctly nested? What about ( [ ) ]? Every compiler checks this, and so does your code editor when it highlights a matching bracket.
unit-07.xqizefmlip: Scan left to right. When you see an opening bracket, push it: it's unfinished business. When you see a closing bracket, the most recent unfinished opener must match it, so pop and compare. The text is balanced if every closer matches and the stack is empty at the end.
unit-07.1xbvgq8m8hg: For ( [ ) ], the ) arrives while [ is on top, so it's a mismatch. Counting brackets alone can't catch this; you need to remember their order, which is exactly what a stack does.
unit-07.1kwhsskvin8: We normally write arithmetic in infix form, with operators between their operands: 3 + 4 * 2. That needs precedence rules and brackets. In postfix form (also called Reverse Polish Notation), operators come after their operands:
unit-07.1dymxik9ncg: Postfix needs no brackets and no precedence rules, and a stack evaluates it in one pass: push each number; for each operator, pop two numbers, apply the operator and push the result. At the end, the single value left is the answer.
unit-07.20s5zmjqpmt: Careful with order: the first number popped is the right operand. For 8 2 -, pop 2 then 8, and compute 8  minus  2.
unit-07.28v9tkb2wab: This is how stack machines work, including the Python virtual machine you met in Lesson 1.6: CPython's bytecode pushes operands and applies operators to the top of a stack.
unit-07.4gzyoy2yyp: How do you get from infix to postfix? Edsger Dijkstra's shunting-yard algorithm (named after railway yards that rearrange carriages) uses a stack of operators waiting to be output:
unit-07.24bxgax7dij: Number: send it straight to the output.
unit-07.rihqhsp2dd: Operator o: while the top of the stack is an operator with higher or equal precedence (for left-associative operators like + - * /), pop it to the output. Then push o.
unit-07.dbpm1zokez: ): pop operators to the output until you reach (, then discard the (.
unit-07.1gibc5cyjuu: At the end, pop all remaining operators to the output.
unit-07.2cgse0vjwzs: For 3 + 4 * 2: output 3; push +; output 4; * has higher precedence than +, so push it on top; output 2; at the end pop * then +. Result: 3 4 2 * +.
unit-07.vkwver9jcb: Together, shunting-yard and postfix evaluation make a calculator. Compilers do something similar when they parse expressions into syntax trees (Lesson 1.6).
unit-07.dogdrj8fdy: You met the call stack in Lesson 2.8. Each function call pushes a frame holding its local variables and where to return to; each return pops it. The most recently called function always finishes first, LIFO again. That's what makes recursion (Lesson 4.5) work: each recursive call gets its own frame on the stack.
unit-07.1avjalbyk30: It also means any recursive algorithm can be rewritten with an explicit stack that you manage yourself. You did this for graph reachability in Lesson 6.9 to avoid Python's recursion limit. Instead of calling the function on a smaller problem, push the smaller problem onto your stack, and loop while the stack isn't empty. The order of exploration can change slightly, but every subproblem is handled.
unit-07.1ojowlr8zax: Openers are pushed; each closer must match the most recent opener.
unit-07.24bucdhbxz9: Numbers are pushed; operators pop two and push the result.

Operating systems (Unit 10) and networks (Unit 11) are full of them. Breadth-first search (Lesson 7.9) uses a queue to explore a graph in rings of increasing distance.

A queue that has held a million items does a million shifts per dequeue. The opposite choice, insert(0, x) to enqueue, has the same problem.
unit-07.e0i4s6m72y: We need both ends to be cheap. There are three standard solutions.
unit-07.u0ine8yvxy: A neat trick uses two stacks (lists used at their ends):
unit-07.na9pq6ex15: outbox: dequeue pops from here. If the outbox is empty, first pour all of the inbox into it, one pop and push at a time.
unit-07.iawa53tkvq: Pouring reverses the order, so the oldest item ends up on top of the outbox, ready to leave first.
unit-07.3yfidddukr: A single dequeue can cost big O of n when it pours. But each item is moved from inbox to outbox at most once in its lifetime, so over any sequence of operations the total work is big O of n: amortised big O of 1 per operation, the same argument as the dynamic array in Lesson 7.1.
unit-07.1u9outsqlwy: If you know the maximum size in advance, a circular buffer (or ring buffer) uses one fixed array with no shifting at all. Keep the index of the front item (head) and the number of items (size). The back is at (head + size) % capacity: the modulo (Lesson 6.8) makes the index wrap around to the start of the array when it passes the end, as if the array were bent into a ring.
unit-07.471zftd58r: Every operation is big O of 1 in the worst case, not just amortised, and there's no memory allocation after the start. That makes circular buffers popular in operating systems, audio processing and embedded devices, wherever timing must be predictable. The cost is a fixed capacity: when it's full, you must refuse new items, overwrite the oldest, or grow the array.
unit-07.pxdzrwqerh: A deque (pronounced "deck", short for double-ended queue) allows adding and removing at both ends in big O of 1. It can act as a stack, a queue, or both at once.

unit-07.23y0fqs85zp: deque(maxlen=n) keeps only the last n items. Appending to a full one silently drops an item from the other end, perfect for "the last 10 log lines" or a moving average.
unit-07.xqtgc6dkiw: rotate(k) turns the deque k steps to the right (negative k turns it left).
unit-07.y08gy2r1rp: Indexing into the middle of a deque is big O of n, so it isn't a replacement for a list. But whenever you need a queue in Python, use collections.deque.
unit-07.18grcrm0wng: How many tills does a supermarket need on a Saturday? Building a store to find out would be expensive, so we simulate: model customers arriving over time, each needing some minutes of service, and track the queue minute by minute.
unit-07.1zindaq4b6y: Each minute: customers arriving now join the back of the queue; each free till takes the customer at the front, and stays busy for their service time. Record how long each customer waited. Change the number of tills and run it again.
unit-07.b19fyc14op: This style of program is called discrete-event simulation, and queues are at its heart. Combined with random arrival times (Lesson 6.7), it's how engineers plan call centres, hospital wards, network routers and traffic lights.
unit-07.1e8u2xl65qt: A deque also solves a classic efficiency problem: given a list of numbers and a window size k, find the maximum of every window of k consecutive numbers (say, the highest temperature over each week of a year).
unit-07.2bw6mtuila: Computing each window's maximum separately costs big O of k per window, big O of nk in total. A deque can do it in big O of n. Keep a deque of indexes, whose values decrease from front to back:
unit-07.1te4brfezsg: When a new value arrives, pop from the back every index whose value is less than or equal to the new value. They can never be a window's maximum again, because the new value is larger and will stay in the window longer.
unit-07.ax1tazw9cw: Append the new index at the back.
unit-07.1r05zuxjj37: If the front index has slid out of the window, pop it from the front.
unit-07.9u8ff1zkxg: The front is now the maximum of the current window.
unit-07.17jjv5zgpqo: Each index is added once and removed at most once, so the total work is big O of n. This "monotonic deque" idea appears in many algorithm problems.

unit-07.1z31qvhnypu: Remember from Lesson 3.4 that variables and attributes hold references to objects. node.next doesn't contain the next node; it refers to it, so nodes can be anywhere in memory. unit-07.24047vtzi18: This is the core loop of almost every linked-list operation. There's no way to jump straight to item i, so finding the item at position i takes big O of i steps, and searching for a value is big O of n. That's the big weakness compared with an array's big O of 1 indexing.

unit-07.ljkb4gzuxx: Some neat linked-list techniques use two references moving at different speeds:
unit-07.nrzk0zsh0j: Finding the middle: move slow one step and fast two steps at a time. When fast reaches the end, slow is in the middle, after a single pass.
unit-07.1qkb7xqk0in: Detecting a cycle: if a bug makes a node's next point back to an earlier node, walking the list loops forever. Floyd's tortoise and hare algorithm moves slow and fast pointers the same way. If there's no cycle, fast reaches the end. If there is one, both pointers end up going round the loop, and fast gains one step on slow each round, so it must eventually land exactly on slow. It uses big O of 1 extra memory, unlike remembering every node visited in a set.
unit-07.7b9ecm9rgw: Reversing a list in place is a different three-pointer dance: walk through the list, turning each next arrow round to point backwards, keeping references to the previous, current and next nodes so nothing is lost.
unit-07.1pq5mh5t6bj: In a singly linked list you can only move forwards, so removing a node requires the node before it. A doubly linked list gives each node both next and prev references:
unit-07.q7cg2gzgwt: Now, given any node, you can remove it in big O of 1 by connecting its neighbours to each other, and you can walk the list backwards. The cost is one extra reference per node and more rewiring per operation.
unit-07.1myo51ft9dn: Edge cases (empty list, removing the head, removing the tail) make the code fiddly. A classic trick removes them: add two sentinel (dummy) nodes that are always present, one before the first real node and one after the last. Every real node then always has a real prev and next, so the code needs no special cases:
unit-07.1uy2lqd3b1n: Doubly linked lists power the browser history, the undo history in some editors, and LRU caches (Lesson 7.5), which must move any item to the front in big O of 1.
unit-07.19jo7ig92ca: In practice, dynamic arrays win more often than the table suggests. Their items sit together in memory, so the CPU cache (Lesson 1.5) loads many at once; a linked list's nodes are scattered, so walking one causes many slow trips to main memory. Python's own list is an array for this reason. Choose a linked list when you genuinely need fast insertion and removal in the middle at positions you already hold, or a structure that can grow at both ends with no occasional resize pause. Linked structures are also the basis of the trees and graphs in the rest of this unit.
