unit-08.2112vu7u2e9: Find counterexamples to greedy rules that sound plausible but are wrong
unit-08.eg26xc0wy7: In Lesson 4.8 you met greedy algorithms: build a solution one piece at a time, always taking the choice that looks best right now, and never reconsider. Making change by taking the largest coin first is the classic example.
unit-08.154s37jdvjj: Greedy algorithms are attractive because they are usually simple and fast: often a sort or a priority queue, followed by one pass, for big O of n log n in total. The difficulty is that they're not always correct. For coins of 1, 3 and 4, greedy makes 6 as 4 + 1 + 1 (three coins), but 3 + 3 (two coins) is better. A greedy algorithm needs a proof, because testing a few examples can't show that no counterexample exists.
unit-08.13a3xjbctob: Two properties are what make a greedy algorithm work:
unit-08.2btu1qrx26b: Greedy-choice property. There is an optimal solution that includes the greedy first choice. So making that choice never loses anything.
unit-08.1w7fktllg2q: Optimal substructure. After making the choice, what remains is a smaller problem of the same kind, and an optimal solution to it combines with the choice to give an optimal solution to the original.
unit-08.1igq26h47sv: If both hold, a simple induction shows that the greedy algorithm is optimal: choose greedily, solve the remainder by induction.
unit-08.gy98c2s1nn: The standard way to prove the greedy-choice property is the exchange argument:
unit-08.12vidhsofms: Take any optimal solution O. (You can't assume anything about how it looks.)
unit-08.1euc9w4wxig: Show that you can exchange part of O for the greedy choice without making it worse, producing another solution O′ that contains the greedy choice and is still optimal.
unit-08.w4b3co2i4t: Conclude that some optimal solution contains the greedy choice.
unit-08.1spdfc650rc: Example: interval scheduling. You have a room and a list of requests, each with a start and end time. Choose as many non-overlapping requests as possible. The greedy rule is to always pick the request that finishes earliest (among those that don't clash with ones already chosen).
unit-08.21tzji37wmc: Proof. Let g be the request that finishes earliest of all, and let O be any optimal schedule, with first request f. Because g finishes no later than f, swapping f for g in O keeps O conflict-free (g ends before the rest of O's requests start, because f did). The number of requests is unchanged, so O′ is still optimal and contains g. After picking g, discard everything that overlaps it and repeat on what's left: the same argument applies by induction. ∎
unit-08.2a0ox51ppws: Notice that the proof tells you why this rule and no other. Rules that also sound sensible, like "earliest start" or "shortest request", have counterexamples (in the exercises you'll find them). The exchange argument is what separates a correct greedy algorithm from a plausible-sounding one.
unit-08.16egjbzqrbb: A related technique is "greedy stays ahead": show that after each step the greedy solution is at least as good as any other solution at the same step, and conclude it's best at the end.
unit-08.j52460vh7a: Minimising maximum lateness. You have jobs, each with a duration and a deadline, to run one after another on a single machine. A job's lateness is how long after its deadline it finishes (zero if on time). Order the jobs to minimise the largest lateness. The greedy rule: earliest deadline first (EDF). Exchange argument: if two adjacent jobs are out of deadline order, swapping them can't increase the maximum lateness. So repeatedly fixing such pairs, which is just sorting, reaches an optimal schedule. (Shortest-job-first sounds plausible, but is wrong for this goal.)
unit-08.2bz38xxnxsv: Interval partitioning. You have a list of lectures with start and end times and want the fewest rooms so that no two lectures in one room overlap. Sort lectures by start time. For each lecture, if some room has become free (its last lecture has already ended), reuse it; otherwise open a new room. Keeping the end times of the rooms in a min-heap (Lesson 7.8) finds the earliest-finishing room in big O of log n, so the whole algorithm is big O of n log n. The number of rooms used equals the maximum number of lectures running at the same moment, which is obviously a lower bound, so the greedy answer is optimal.
unit-08.1g5ve8u4x84: Knapsack and where greedy stops working
unit-08.1wwskw05gek: You have a bag of capacity W and items with a weight and a value. You want the most valuable load.
unit-08.1u7g4xdhgmm: In the fractional knapsack problem you may take part of an item (think of gold dust, flour or time). The greedy rule: sort by value per unit weight and take the best-ratio items first, splitting the last one if needed. The exchange argument is easy: if the best-ratio item isn't fully used in an optimal load but something worse is, swap some of the worse for more of the better and the value can only go up.
unit-08.16ftwd2xlcj: In the 0/1 knapsack problem each item must be taken whole or not at all. The same greedy rule fails. With capacity 50 and items (weight 10, value 60), (20, 100), (30, 120), the best ratios are 6, 5, 4, so greedy takes the first two (value 160, weight 30) and can't fit the third; but items 2 and 3 together weigh exactly 50 and are worth 220. The choice "take the best ratio" isn't safe, because the leftover space it leaves can be wasted. This problem is solved by dynamic programming (Lesson 8.7).
unit-08.phzofyw6hx: Greedy failing for 0/1 knapsack and coin change with unusual denominations is a warning: when a choice can leave awkward leftovers, greedy fails. (Coin systems like 1, 5, 10, 25, 100 happen to be well behaved, which is why cashiers get away with greedy.)
unit-08.qnm5py2mgy: Computers normally store each character of text in a fixed number of bits (8 for ASCII). But letters are not equally common: in English, e is far more frequent than z. Huffman coding assigns short codes to frequent symbols and long codes to rare ones, saving space overall.
unit-08.14kb9acqxt9: The codes must be a prefix code: no code may be the start of another, or you couldn't tell where one symbol ends and the next begins. (0 and 01 can't both be codes; 0 and 10 can.) A prefix code is the same as a binary tree with the symbols at the leaves, where a symbol's code is the path from the root: 0 for left, 1 for right. Decoding just follows the bits down the tree.
unit-08.16nwcv36j1j: Huffman's algorithm builds the best tree greedily:
unit-08.2c9v9hxg68d: Make a leaf for every symbol, with its frequency as weight, and put them all in a min-heap.
unit-08.1a8r5b2wui: Repeatedly remove the two lightest trees, join them under a new parent whose weight is their sum, and put the parent back.
unit-08.26v3w35e2rz: When one tree is left, it is the Huffman tree.
unit-08.14zd9u8lgbd: Rare symbols are merged first, so they end up deepest (longest codes). The cost of the finished code, the total number of bits used, equals the sum of all the merged weights (every symbol's frequency is counted once for each level it sits below the root). With n symbols the algorithm does n  minus  1 merges, each big O of log n: big O of n log n.
unit-08.1xlzzreu5vj: Why is it optimal? An exchange argument: in some optimal tree the two rarest symbols are siblings at the deepest level (if not, swap them down: a rarer symbol moved deeper and a more frequent one moved up can only reduce the total). So merging them first, as Huffman does, is a safe greedy choice, and the problem that remains (with the merged pair treated as one symbol) has the same form. Huffman codes are used inside ZIP, GZIP, JPEG and MP3 compression.
unit-08.l3h3g587rk: Example 1: Interval scheduling by earliest finish
unit-08.u792llo4q0: Compare the earliest-finish rule with the plausible-looking earliest-start rule on the same requests.
unit-08.9sqtd728vv: Take the best value-per-kilo first, splitting the last item if needed.
unit-08.zufh6k1r42: Merge the two lightest trees until one is left. The frequent letter gets the shortest code.
unit-08.1m7imcajfb5: Trusting a greedy rule because it works on the examples
unit-08.lfzmv1jhyv: Greedy rules often work on small cases and fail on tricky ones (coins 1, 3, 4 for the amount 6). Check against brute force on many small random inputs, then find an exchange argument.
unit-08.1kstk5ioiql: Interval scheduling needs earliest finish, not earliest start or shortest length. Lateness needs earliest deadline, not shortest job. The right criterion is the one the exchange argument supports.
unit-08.fq4ljzy378: Best ratio first is optimal for the fractional version only. With whole items, the leftover space can be wasted. Use dynamic programming.
unit-08.2w7y6ndpc2: When two heap entries have equal weights Python compares the next tuple element. If that element is a tree or a custom object, it may raise an error. Add a unique counter as the second element.
unit-08.3c34obf9bl: Making Huffman codes that aren't prefix-free
unit-08.htj9mwrvhq: Symbols must be at the leaves of the tree. If a symbol also sits at an internal node, its code is a prefix of other codes and decoding breaks.
unit-08.1npntknpgcz: A greedy algorithm makes the best-looking choice at each step and never revisits it. It works when the problem has the greedy-choice property and optimal substructure.
unit-08.fao6m7zqe4: Prove it with an exchange argument (swap part of any optimal solution for the greedy choice without making it worse) or by showing greedy stays ahead.
unit-08.1rk5qiioagj: Correct greedy algorithms: interval scheduling by earliest finish, minimising lateness by earliest deadline, interval partitioning with a min-heap of room end times, fractional knapsack by value per weight.
unit-08.1jkqs3ay27u: Huffman coding repeatedly merges the two lightest trees with a min-heap, giving an optimal prefix code in big O of n log n.
unit-08.17ufv5t5m9g: Greedy fails for 0/1 knapsack and general coin change, where choices leave awkward leftovers. Those need dynamic programming.
unit-08.sqbqpoqjxt: Always test a greedy rule against brute force on small inputs; a sensible-sounding rule is not a proof.
unit-08.1e5v69x8i1a: Greedy algorithms commit to a choice and move on. When that's not safe, you need a method that tries every possibility without redoing work: dynamic programming. Lesson 8.6 starts with the idea that makes it work, overlapping subproblems, using memoisation (top-down) and tabulation (bottom-up), and applies it to Fibonacci, climbing stairs, coin change done right, and the longest increasing subsequence.
unit-08.1kqrfv9y3w9: Recognise when a recursive solution repeats the same work, and remove the repetition with memoisation (top-down) or tabulation (bottom-up). Use it for Fibonacci, climbing stairs, coin change done correctly, and the longest increasing subsequence.
unit-08.fvukd89bhx: Explain overlapping subproblems and why they make plain recursion exponential
unit-08.1jrmvq9fsmk: Speed up a recursion with memoisation using a dictionary or functools.cache
unit-08.1oh6vr4e6iw: Convert a recursion into a bottom-up table and choose the order to fill it
unit-08.cotswkeuta: Define a DP state and a recurrence for a new problem
unit-08.2cj5w69w6js: Solve coin change (fewest coins and number of ways) and the longest increasing subsequence
unit-08.2d4pr18dza2: Count the subproblems and the work per subproblem to get the running time
unit-08.18k7jstfqig: In Lesson 8.3 divide and conquer split a problem into independent pieces: merge sort's two halves share nothing. Some problems split into pieces that overlap, so the same subproblem gets solved again and again.
unit-08.1ej83bi2nzl: The classic case is Fibonacci: fib(n) = fib(n-1) + fib(n-2). A direct recursion computes fib(n-2) once for fib(n) and again inside fib(n-1), and every one of those repeats itself. The number of calls roughly multiplies by 1.6 for each step in n, so fib(40) takes hundreds of millions of calls even though there are only 41 different questions to answer.
unit-08.1du1gjkc9yr: Dynamic programming (DP) is the cure: solve each distinct subproblem once, remember the answer, and look it up whenever it is needed again. The name is historical and says little. Think of it as recursion plus a memory.
unit-08.eumgm5o41a: DP applies when a problem has:
unit-08.1s33b1ndvd2: Optimal substructure: the answer is built from answers to smaller subproblems, so you can write a recurrence.
unit-08.ns3vl2z5zj: Overlapping subproblems: the number of distinct subproblems is small, even though the recursion tree is huge.
unit-08.64k7ocxv0l: Memoisation keeps the recursive code and adds a cache: before computing, check whether this subproblem has been solved; after computing, store the answer.
unit-08.1dtt3czhioy: @cache (from functools) does the bookkeeping for you: it stores the result for every set of arguments it has seen. Each distinct n is computed once, so fib(n) takes big O of n time instead of exponential.
unit-08.1k5gn6oib2y: Memoisation is the easiest way to write a DP: first write the correct recursion (getting the state and the recurrence right is the whole difficulty), then add the cache. Arguments must be hashable (numbers, strings, tuples; not lists). Python's recursion limit (about 1000) can be a problem for very deep recursions.
unit-08.1hxc7887sfz: Tabulation fills a table in an order such that everything a cell depends on is already filled. No recursion is needed.
unit-08.1ql5xgxo81: A tabulated solution is usually faster in practice (no function-call overhead, no recursion limit) and often lets you throw away old rows: Fibonacci only needs the last two values, so big O of 1 memory suffices. The price is that you must work out a valid filling order.
unit-08.x7sb9htz18: Both styles compute the same thing. A useful way to find the running time is:
unit-08.16l8ft32jyt: time = (number of distinct subproblems)  times  (work to combine per subproblem)
unit-08.1nq36a59mnb: For Fibonacci that is n  times  big O of 1 = big O of n.
unit-08.1iqgp6q86dy: A recipe for designing a DP
unit-08.1sp9oszt9ih: Define the state: what do you need to know to describe a subproblem? Write it as a sentence: "ways[i] is the number of ways to climb i stairs".
unit-08.178tgpm3bse: Write the recurrence for a state in terms of smaller states, with the base cases.
unit-08.vq4pspyoxv: Choose an order (bottom-up) or add a cache (top-down).
unit-08.1b0kqghtbd5: Read off the answer, which is usually one particular state.
unit-08.1s6f279r89m: Count states  times  work per state for the running time.
unit-08.26kbfsix476: Climbing stairs. You climb n steps, taking 1 or 2 at a time. State: ways[i] = the number of ways to reach step i. The last move was a 1-step from i-1 or a 2-step from i-2, so ways[i] = ways[i-1] + ways[i-2], with ways[0] = 1. It is the Fibonacci recurrence again.
unit-08.12oso50phf0: In Lesson 8.5 greedy failed for coins 1, 3, 4 and the amount 6. DP always works. State: best[a] = the fewest coins that make amount a. The last coin used is some coin c, leaving a - c to make, so
unit-08.1hb194l9lth: best[a] = 1 + min(best[a - c] for each coin c <= a)
unit-08.37w9hiv2k6: with best[0] = 0 and "impossible" represented by infinity. There are amount states and len(coins) choices each, so the time is big O of amount  times  coins, and it is correct for any set of coins.
unit-08.ydb71gryij: A second question has a different recurrence: in how many ways can you make an amount, where 1+3 and 3+1 count as the same? Process the coins one kind at a time, in an outer loop; for each coin, update ways[a] += ways[a - coin]. Putting the coin loop outside is what stops different orderings from being counted separately. (Swap the loops and you count sequences instead.)
unit-08.1nc4k5e3jf4: A subsequence keeps elements in order but may skip some. In [3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2, 6] the longest strictly increasing subsequence is 1, 4, 5, 9 or 3, 4, 5, 6, so its length is 4.
unit-08.k44j8uqv5d: State: length[i] = the length of the longest increasing subsequence that ends at index i. It is 1 plus the best length[j] over earlier j with a[j] < a[i] (or just 1 if there is none). The answer is the maximum over all i. With n states and big O of n work each, that is big O of n².
unit-08.1lxn2vhd3bs: Notice the idea: the state is defined so the last element is fixed. Choosing a state that makes the next decision easy is the creative part of DP, and it improves with practice. (A cleverer big O of n log n method uses binary search on the tails of the best subsequences, but the big O of n² DP is the one to learn first.)
unit-08.1tjhxz1vbsj: Count how often a plain recursion runs, then see the same calculation with a cache.
unit-08.1kdshf8f7t6: Greedy gives 3 coins for 6 with coins 1, 3, 4; the table finds 2.
unit-08.lhlm3mf1ry: length[i] is the longest increasing subsequence that ends at position i.
unit-08.1grr49hck86: Memoising something that has no overlap
unit-08.2522fbtqzhh: A cache only helps when the same arguments recur. Merge sort's halves never repeat, so caching them just wastes memory.
unit-08.g7v9qeby4j: A state that is missing information
unit-08.qlb039h517: If the recurrence needs something your state does not record (for example, which coin was used last), the table gives wrong answers. Ask "what must I know to continue from here?" and put exactly that in the state.
unit-08.9f9qxbvear: Filling the table in the wrong order
unit-08.2wbn5p9jex: A cell must be computed after the cells it depends on. In coin change the amounts increase; in grids it is row by row.
unit-08.dwq7he12qz: For "number of ways" with coins, the coin loop must be the outer loop. With the amount loop outside, 1+3 and 3+1 are counted separately.
unit-08.sn5h2t31oc: functools.cache cannot key on a list. Convert to a tuple or use indexes instead.
unit-08.1dqng27wcay: Dynamic programming solves each distinct subproblem once and reuses the answer. It applies when there is optimal substructure and overlapping subproblems.
unit-08.16aywbql0e5: Memoisation adds a cache to a recursion (@cache). Tabulation fills a table bottom-up in an order that respects dependencies.
unit-08.22rmp6vmaoz: Design recipe: define the state, write the recurrence and base cases, choose the order, read the answer, and count states  times  work per state.
unit-08.2bzcx2t64zk: Fewest-coins DP is correct for any coin system, unlike greedy. For counting combinations, loop over coins on the outside.
unit-08.iw3ikghjzf: Longest increasing subsequence uses the state 'best subsequence ending at i' and takes big O of n² time.
unit-08.18jun7ic1ue: Store a back-pointer next to each value to reconstruct the solution, not just its value.
unit-08.26v5uio5fxl: So far each state has had one or two numbers. Lesson 8.7 moves to two-sequence problems: edit distance, longest common subsequence, and the 0/1 knapsack that greedy could not solve. You will also see how to save memory by keeping only the rows you need.
unit-08.2dy21l9j26r: Apply dynamic programming to problems with two sequences or two limits: the longest common subsequence, edit distance and the 0/1 knapsack. Rebuild the actual answer from the table, and save memory by keeping only the rows you need.
unit-08.scd8xqobee: Define a two-index state and fill a two-dimensional table in a valid order
unit-08.29zcp7uxbsq: Solve longest common subsequence and edit distance, and explain each cell's three or four options
unit-08.4t5crup4hx: Solve 0/1 knapsack and explain why its running time is pseudo-polynomial
unit-08.5xxnpr8ajj: Trace back through a table to recover the actual subsequence, edit script or chosen items
unit-08.roa9oq3z0o: Reduce memory by keeping a single row or two
unit-08.1k8asulg2ko: Use the subset-sum idea to answer yes or no questions with a table of booleans
unit-08.znxv32rr9w: Lesson 8.6 used one number as the state. Many problems involve two sequences, such as two strings, and the natural state has two indexes: (i, j) stands for "the problem on the first i items of one sequence and the first j items of the other". The table is two-dimensional, filled row by row, and the answer is usually the bottom-right cell.
unit-08.s9lat7gkzw: The same four steps apply: state, recurrence, order, answer. The recurrence usually looks at the last item of each prefix and asks "how do these two items relate?".
unit-08.1m2fbcdkhnr: A common subsequence of two strings is a sequence that appears (in order, not necessarily next to each other) in both. For "ABCBDAB" and "BDCABA" the longest common subsequence (LCS) has length 4, for example "BCBA". It's the idea behind diff, which finds the unchanged lines between two versions of a file.
unit-08.dgrvlpzcdb: State: L[i][j] = the length of the LCS of the first i characters of a and the first j characters of b.
unit-08.1xyqoxu0zhr: If the last characters a[i-1] and b[j-1] are equal, they can be matched: L[i][j] = L[i-1][j-1] + 1.
unit-08.s9p6qqqoym: If they differ, at least one of them isn't in the LCS: L[i][j] = max(L[i-1][j], L[i][j-1]).
unit-08.29o1musl2ux: Base case: L[0][j] = L[i][0] = 0 (an empty string has nothing in common with anything).
unit-08.1iy4s9bffq9: The table has (m+1)(n+1) cells with big O of 1 work each, so the time is big O of mn.
unit-08.fs4lnag5de: Recovering the subsequence. Start at the bottom-right. If the characters match, include one and move diagonally up-left; otherwise move toward the neighbour with the larger value (up or left). Reverse what you collected at the end.
unit-08.19xpnjjj96o: The edit distance (Levenshtein distance) between two strings is the fewest single-character insertions, deletions and substitutions that turn one into the other. It's used in spell checkers, DNA comparison and fuzzy search. "kitten" becomes "sitting" in 3 edits: substitute k to s, substitute e to i, insert g.
unit-08.1il86h3gae9: State: D[i][j] = the edit distance between the first i characters of a and the first j characters of b.
unit-08.bomzkkkrh7: Base: D[i][0] = i (delete everything) and D[0][j] = j (insert everything).
unit-08.17ycnkqoqvi: If a[i-1] == b[j-1]: no edit is needed for the last characters, D[i][j] = D[i-1][j-1].
unit-08.190034kbjr6: Otherwise take the cheapest of three options, each costing one edit: delete a[i-1]: D[i-1][j] + 1 insert b[j-1]: D[i][j-1] + 1 substitute: D[i-1][j-1] + 1
unit-08.1kr2vo70hm6: Again big O of mn time. To list the edits, trace back from D[m][n], at each step choosing a neighbour that explains the value.
unit-08.17q6n1coco9: Now the problem that greedy couldn't solve (Lesson 8.5). Items have an integer weight and a value, and the bag holds weight W. Each item is taken whole or not at all.
unit-08.1lxh76612yk: State: best[i][w] = the greatest value using only the first i items with capacity w.
unit-08.1k16p1ord02: For item i (weight wt, value v) there are two choices:
unit-08.23oh89wq3np: take it (only if wt <= w): best[i-1][w - wt] + v
unit-08.qr6d2ay46m: and best[i][w] is the larger. The base row is all zeros. The table has n  times  W cells, so the time is big O of nW.
unit-08.1236s9ukxsi: That looks polynomial, but it's only pseudo-polynomial: the running time depends on the number W, and W can be huge. Doubling the number of digits in W squares the table size. In terms of the size of the input in bits, big O of nW is exponential. (In fact 0/1 knapsack is NP-complete, which you'll meet in Unit 9, so no truly polynomial algorithm is known.)
unit-08.1fe71r3tdk6: Saving memory. Row i depends only on row i-1, so you can keep a single array and update w from high to low (so you don't use item i twice): best[w] = max(best[w], best[w - wt] + v). That uses big O of W memory instead of big O of nW, but then you can't trace back which items were chosen, unless you keep the full table.
unit-08.25vccl2c5dm: Subset sum and other yes or no versions
unit-08.uuh5dkf0xg: Subset sum asks: can some of these numbers be added to give exactly target? It is knapsack with only booleans. can[s] is True if some subset sums to s. Start with can[0] = True; for each number x, update s from high to low: can[s] = can[s] or can[s - x]. Time big O of n  times  target, again pseudo-polynomial.
unit-08.h7nmw7qzj9: A famous application is partition: can a list of numbers be split into two groups of equal total? That is subset sum with target total / 2 (and the total must be even).
unit-08.6v889hklig: Spot the pattern across the whole of the lesson: the state is a prefix of each input (or a prefix plus a numeric budget); the recurrence looks at the last decision; the table is filled in increasing order; and the cell you want is the corner. When you meet a new optimisation problem, ask "what small description of a subproblem would let the last decision be made?"
unit-08.1yofnkirvrc: Fill the table, then walk back from the corner to recover a longest common subsequence.
unit-08.ogq17h0fn4: Three options for each pair of prefixes: delete, insert or substitute.
unit-08.hde8dziiw8: Update the capacities from high to low so that each item is used at most once.
unit-08.wddlhzkda3: Updating the knapsack row from low to high
unit-08.kxmdlepeu1: With one row, going upward lets an item be used again in the same pass (it becomes an unbounded knapsack). Go from high weights to low for 0/1 knapsack.
unit-08.1lkfu282cw5: Off-by-one between table indexes and string indexes
unit-08.2cw8d1qak7q: Row i of the table is about the first i characters, so its last character is a[i - 1]. Mixing these up is the most common bug in LCS and edit distance.
unit-08.7pie0zusj3: Forgetting the base row and column
unit-08.1w12i91cju3: In edit distance D[i][0] = i and D[0][j] = j. Leaving them as 0 makes inserting and deleting free.
unit-08.h4x52npmzw: Saving memory and losing the traceback
unit-08.23984i110oa: Two rows give the value; recovering the solution needs the whole table (or a smarter divide-and-conquer method). Decide which you need before you optimise.
unit-08.1utdejid64f: big O of nW depends on the numeric value of W, not on the length of its digits, so it is pseudo-polynomial.
unit-08.4h1wkb4ba2: Two-sequence problems use a state (i, j) for the prefixes, a 2D table filled row by row, and the answer in the corner.
unit-08.21ita3xsap: LCS: equal last characters extend the diagonal; otherwise take the max of dropping one character. Edit distance: base row/column i and j, then match, delete, insert or substitute. Both are big O of mn.
unit-08.io1zzcjv72: 0/1 knapsack: skip or take each item, big O of nW time. Use a 1D array updated from high to low to save memory.
unit-08.1cpmyi1nuq7: big O of nW is pseudo-polynomial: it depends on the value of W, so it is exponential in the number of digits.
unit-08.2hh9z1qyl8: Subset sum and partition are knapsack with booleans.
unit-08.10rwryaq85n: A traceback through the table (or stored back-pointers) recovers the actual answer; keeping only a few rows saves memory but loses it.
unit-08.xruuw9gn8s: Dynamic programming handles problems where the choices are limited. Lesson 8.8 returns to graphs with weights: shortest paths. You will meet Dijkstra's algorithm (a greedy method with a priority queue), the Bellman-Ford algorithm (dynamic programming over edge counts, which copes with negative weights), and Floyd-Warshall for all pairs.
unit-08.7emybe82jh: Find the cheapest route through a graph whose edges have weights. Use Dijkstra's algorithm (greedy plus a heap) when weights are non-negative, Bellman-Ford (dynamic programming over edge counts) when weights may be negative, and Floyd-Warshall to get every pair at once.
unit-08.1jjvmcfqq3: Explain why breadth-first search is not enough once edges have different weights
unit-08.2emcseiskk6: Implement Dijkstra's algorithm with a heap and explain why it needs non-negative weights
unit-08.2eqidrgf3g5: Reconstruct the actual shortest path from a table of predecessors
unit-08.13a5av4yqdx: Implement Bellman-Ford and use it to detect a negative cycle
unit-08.w9eve180nb: Implement Floyd-Warshall for all-pairs shortest paths
unit-08.3poyq2weyg: Choose the right algorithm from the graph's properties and give each one's running time
unit-08.1y42pppngqa: In Lesson 7.9 breadth-first search found the path with the fewest edges. Real networks have different costs per edge: roads have lengths, flights have prices, network links have delays. In a weighted graph each edge has a number, and the length of a path is the sum of its edge weights. The shortest path problem asks for the cheapest path from a start to a target (or to every vertex).
unit-08.ibfua2nwx1: We store the graph as a dictionary mapping each vertex to a list of (neighbour, weight) pairs:
unit-08.pmzkt9lnrs: Breadth-first search can fail: the route A to B has 1 edge but cost 4, while A to C to B has 2 edges and cost 3. We need an algorithm that cares about weights.
unit-08.1sw1x93oj0e: The key fact is optimal substructure: every piece of a shortest path is itself a shortest path (if a better route to an intermediate vertex existed, you could splice it in). It's what makes both greedy (Dijkstra) and dynamic programming (Bellman-Ford) work.
unit-08.kvvia4kyyj: Dijkstra's algorithm finds the shortest distance from one source to every vertex when all weights are non-negative. The idea is breadth-first search with a priority queue instead of an ordinary queue:
unit-08.3f89br6zqf: Set dist[source] = 0 and everything else to infinity. Put (0, source) in a min-heap.
unit-08.1otfy53x98i: Pop the vertex u with the smallest tentative distance. If it was already finalised, skip it.
unit-08.2gbbkmcnohg: For each edge u  to  v with weight w, relax it: if dist[u] + w < dist[v], update dist[v] and push (dist[v], v).
unit-08.bdrguf9zqg: Repeat until the heap is empty.
unit-08.1bc9sjni6gl: Why it is correct. When a vertex is popped with the smallest distance on the heap, nothing cheaper can reach it: any other route must leave the finalised set through an edge to a vertex that is still at least as far (the heap's minimum), and adding non-negative weights can only increase it. It's a greedy algorithm with an exchange-style argument (Lesson 8.5).
unit-08.owjbv68e0g: Why negative edges break it. A later, longer-looking path might become cheaper through a negative edge, after a vertex has already been finalised.
unit-08.2dxwbtvflxn: Running time. Each edge causes at most one push (big O of log E), and each pop is big O of log E. With a binary heap the total is big O of (V + E log V). We skip stale heap entries instead of using a decrease-key operation, because Python's heapq has none.
unit-08.q4bi1ql810: To rebuild the actual path, store parent[v] = the vertex you came from when you last improved dist[v], then follow parents back from the target and reverse.
unit-08.10em8hd0xiv: Bellman-Ford handles negative edge weights. It's dynamic programming over the number of edges: let dist_k[v] be the shortest distance to v using at most k edges. A shortest path in a graph with V vertices that has no negative cycle uses at most V  minus  1 edges, so after V  minus  1 rounds of relaxing every edge, all distances are final:
unit-08.17wzgutrpra: The running time is big O of V  times  E: slower than Dijkstra, but more general.
unit-08.y3lb2brwzs: Negative cycles. If a cycle's total weight is negative, you can go around it forever and the "shortest" distance is minus infinity. Run one more round: if any edge can still be relaxed, there's a reachable negative cycle. (In an undirected graph, a single negative edge is already a negative cycle, since you can walk back and forth along it.)
unit-08.14z7gn0xzcu: To get the shortest distance between every pair of vertices, you could run Dijkstra from each vertex, or use Floyd-Warshall, a small and beautiful DP. Number the vertices 0 to V  minus  1 and define d_k[i][j] as the shortest path from i to j whose intermediate vertices are all among the first k. For each new vertex k there are two options: the path doesn't use k (d[i][j] stays) or it goes i  to  k  to  j:
unit-08.ez6ft21m6d: Time big O of V³, memory big O of V², and it works with negative edges (but not negative cycles: a negative number on the diagonal d[i][i] < 0 reveals one). Notice that the vertex loop k is outermost, a classic place to get it wrong.
unit-08.sarx9a7vme: A heap always hands us the closest unfinished vertex. Stale entries are skipped.
unit-08.1hto1us4nlt: Example 2: Bellman-Ford and a negative cycle
unit-08.139dy3qcq70: Relax every edge V  minus  1 times. One extra pass tells us whether a negative cycle exists.
unit-08.1t1ym29yk52: Three nested loops, with the middle vertex k on the outside.
unit-08.wvpfvjws2r: Dijkstra finalises a vertex when it is popped. A negative edge discovered later can make an already-finalised vertex cheaper. Use Bellman-Ford.
unit-08.26qtu2u7d8c: BFS minimises the number of edges, not the total weight.
unit-08.1qugiob7r70: Floyd-Warshall with the wrong loop order
unit-08.1ro6w8tj1ff: The intermediate vertex k must be the outermost loop. Putting it innermost computes something different and gives wrong answers.
unit-08.19v33qejoq1: infinity + negative is still infinity in Python, but in some languages or with sentinel numbers it wraps or looks reachable. Check dist[u] != INF before relaxing in Bellman-Ford.
unit-08.237evl4ruvu: Forgetting to skip stale heap entries
unit-08.dx0a2i4l2d: Without if d > dist[u]: continue, the same vertex is expanded several times. The answer stays correct but the running time can blow up.
unit-08.1adl7f4ihgr: In a weighted graph the shortest path minimises the sum of edge weights, not the number of edges. Every piece of a shortest path is itself shortest.
unit-08.16vhcpc7qdg: Dijkstra (non-negative weights): repeatedly finalise the closest unfinished vertex using a min-heap and relax its edges. big O of (V + E log V).
unit-08.vtucn45afn: Keep a parent for each vertex to rebuild the path itself.
unit-08.192d2ruve11: Bellman-Ford relaxes every edge V  minus  1 times, tolerates negative edges, detects negative cycles with one extra pass, and takes big O of VE.
unit-08.1lbpuj1alc8: Floyd-Warshall finds all pairs in big O of V³ by allowing one more stopover vertex at a time (the stopover loop is outermost).
unit-08.14uisrpi8fg: Pick by situation: BFS for unweighted, Dijkstra for non-negative, Bellman-Ford for negative edges, Floyd-Warshall for all pairs on small graphs.
unit-08.vepktkd7cc: One more classic graph problem remains. Instead of the cheapest route between two places, Lesson 8.9 asks for the cheapest way to connect everything: the minimum spanning tree. You will meet Kruskal's algorithm, which needs the clever union-find data structure, and Prim's algorithm, which looks a lot like Dijkstra.
unit-08.yhe3ao0rdb: Connect every vertex of a weighted graph as cheaply as possible. Learn the cut property that makes greedy work, implement Kruskal's and Prim's algorithms, and build the union-find (disjoint set) data structure that makes Kruskal fast.
unit-08.2dctos1zaik: Define a spanning tree and a minimum spanning tree, and say how many edges a spanning tree has
unit-08.1wdrlkepqrc: State the cut property and use it to justify why greedy algorithms find minimum spanning trees
unit-08.19zua44v7ud: Implement union-find with path compression and union by size
unit-08.xc26owa1rb: Implement Kruskal's algorithm and state its running time
unit-08.1lid2z8fd23: Implement Prim's algorithm with a heap and explain how it differs from Dijkstra
unit-08.2e2mbnf42lp: Use a spanning tree algorithm to solve problems such as clustering and detecting cycles
unit-08.5xtz8ckukn: The cheapest way to connect everything
unit-08.2byz57cimud: Suppose you must lay cable between several towns. Each possible link has a cost, and you want every town connected, directly or through others, for the smallest total cost. You never need a cycle: a cycle means one link is redundant, and removing it still leaves everything connected.
unit-08.wgbwacwmnw: A spanning tree of a connected graph with V vertices is a set of edges that connects all the vertices with no cycles. Every spanning tree has exactly V  minus  1 edges. (Fewer would leave something disconnected; more would create a cycle.) A minimum spanning tree (MST) is a spanning tree with the smallest possible total weight. There may be several with equal weight, but if all the weights are distinct the MST is unique.
unit-08.24gbr2uexk1: The MST is not the same thing as the shortest-path tree of Lesson 8.8. Shortest paths minimise the distance from one source; the MST minimises the total weight of the connecting network.
unit-08.ga01khq6o5: MST has a rare property: the greedy choices are always safe. The reason is the cut property.
unit-08.1wd9vw6ykvq: A cut divides the vertices into two non-empty groups. Cut property: among the edges that cross a cut, the one with the smallest weight belongs to some minimum spanning tree (to all of them, if it is the unique cheapest).
unit-08.1bcpy3te3gf: Exchange argument. Take any MST T that doesn't contain the cheapest crossing edge e. Adding e to T creates a cycle, and the cycle must cross the cut again by some other edge f, which is at least as heavy as e. Swap f for e: the result is still a spanning tree and it is no heavier. So there is an MST containing e. ∎
unit-08.1qtbvlopmzg: Both algorithms below are just different ways of picking cuts and always choosing the cheapest crossing edge.
unit-08.d1rcmra5gj: Kruskal's algorithm needs to answer one question, quickly and many times: are these two vertices already connected? The union-find (or disjoint-set) data structure keeps track of groups of items, and supports:
unit-08.16ivkavusit: find(x): which group is x in? (returns a representative, the "root" of the group)
unit-08.1onapjqkfec: union(x, y): merge the groups of x and y.
unit-08.hb8wpcd563: Each group is stored as a tree where every item points to a parent, and the root points to itself. find follows parents up to the root. Two items are in the same group when find gives the same root.
unit-08.2a339bug3us: Two small tricks make it astonishingly fast:
unit-08.pu2aodeh2i: Path compression: during find, point every visited item directly at the root, so later finds are short.
unit-08.rgbrdg78eu: Union by size (or rank): when merging, attach the smaller tree under the root of the larger, which keeps trees shallow.
unit-08.155un88t20a: With both, a sequence of m operations on n items takes big O of m α(n), where α is the inverse Ackermann function. It grows so slowly that α(n) is at most 4 for any n you could ever store in the universe. In practice each operation is constant time.
unit-08.1kztsdfycyv: Kruskal's algorithm builds the MST edge by edge:
unit-08.1cbr09gopfn: For each edge in order: if its endpoints are in different groups (find(u) != find(v)), add the edge to the tree and union the groups. Otherwise skip it, because it would form a cycle.
unit-08.6pvhne8umr: Stop when V  minus  1 edges have been chosen.
unit-08.1eb20zhi9cr: Why is it correct? When Kruskal adds an edge, it is the lightest edge leaving the group containing one endpoint: a cut-property edge. The edges it skips connect vertices that are already joined, so they can't be needed.
unit-08.1ddiah0gz0q: The running time is dominated by the sort: big O of E log E, which is the same as big O of E log V. Union-find adds almost nothing.
unit-08.fw8bfzxtro: If the graph isn't connected, Kruskal produces a minimum spanning forest, one tree per component.
unit-08.2cw0wzzjngs: Prim's algorithm grows a single tree from a starting vertex. The cut is always "inside the tree" versus "outside":
unit-08.215i4qcgu1g: Start with one vertex in the tree. Put its edges in a min-heap.
unit-08.lftnnis45x: Pop the cheapest edge. If it leads to a vertex not yet in the tree, add the vertex and the edge, and push that vertex's edges onto the heap.
unit-08.gqj6weezt8: Repeat until V vertices are in the tree.
unit-08.2dhiziil7lt: It looks almost identical to Dijkstra, with one difference: Dijkstra's priority is distance from the source (dist[u] + w), while Prim's is just the edge weight w. The time with a binary heap is big O of E log V.
unit-08.gov2w6zja6: Which is better? Kruskal is simple when you have a list of edges and works well on sparse graphs; Prim is natural for dense graphs or when the graph is already stored as adjacency lists.
unit-08.1peftwsi2h6: Applications. Network design (cables, pipes, roads), approximating the travelling salesman problem, clustering (stop Kruskal early, at k groups, and the groups are the clusters), image segmentation and building mazes.
unit-08.20jp7eo6eny: Each item points at a parent. find follows the pointers and flattens the path.
unit-08.151e4hw1y7j: Go through edges from cheapest to most expensive and keep those that join two different groups.
unit-08.2ae3gp61j9e: Grow one tree from vertex 0, always taking the cheapest edge that leaves it.
unit-08.10e52ll20s8: Confusing the MST with the shortest-path tree
unit-08.27mpqq8u1m9: The MST minimises total weight of the whole network. Shortest paths from a source minimise each individual distance. The trees can be different.
unit-08.2a9zn9t7fer: Forgetting that a graph may be disconnected
unit-08.2481rbyfjn2: A spanning tree exists only for a connected graph. Otherwise Kruskal and Prim from one vertex give a spanning forest or just one component. Check the number of chosen edges against V  minus  1.
unit-08.6z52dy5meu: In Prim the heap key is the edge weight alone. Adding the distance travelled so far turns it into Dijkstra and gives a different tree.
unit-08.1me5tqq8fqf: A naive union-find can degrade into a long chain, making each find big O of n. Add path compression and union by size.
unit-08.1hroaw9jrzp: Comparing groups by find on the stale parent
unit-08.1b11jx06mal: Always compare roots (find(a) == find(b)), never parent[a] == parent[b]: parents change as trees are merged and compressed.
unit-08.1fo52r4jkwy: A spanning tree connects all V vertices with V  minus  1 edges and no cycle; a minimum spanning tree has the smallest total weight.
unit-08.l8q2myh0w2: The cut property says the cheapest edge crossing any cut belongs to some MST, so greedy choices are safe.
unit-08.21tslyfovge: Union-find supports find and union in almost constant time with path compression and union by size.
unit-08.873ww1v8ra: Kruskal: sort edges, add each one that joins two different groups. big O of E log E.
unit-08.172s7lv20uy: Prim: grow one tree from a start vertex, always taking the cheapest edge leaving it. big O of E log V. It resembles Dijkstra, but the key is the edge weight alone.
unit-08.18xg9bi758y: Uses: network design, clustering (stop Kruskal at k groups), cycle detection, and bottleneck (minimax) paths.
unit-08.1idvfbl9f4p: That completes the tools of Unit 8. The unit project brings them together: you will build a route planner that answers questions about a small road network using Dijkstra's shortest paths, a minimum spanning tree for the cheapest set of roads to keep, and dynamic programming for a trip budget.

unit-09.7hhk8parq9: Write and run your first C programs. See how C differs from Python (compiled, statically typed, no safety net), learn the basic types and how many bytes each takes, and print values precisely with printf.
unit-09.1j3cv4qgrm: By the end you will be able to:
unit-09.8zqr4m0f1d: Explain what makes C different from Python and why systems software is still written in it
unit-09.onujblx6wk: Read the parts of a C program, including the include line, main, statements and the return value
unit-09.1n6d6qq1puo: Choose between char, short, int, long, float and double, and say how many bytes each uses
unit-09.v43puvpcpz: Predict what happens when an integer goes past its largest value
unit-09.2azkqydzg8k: Use printf format codes to print integers, characters, strings, decimals and hexadecimal
unit-09.vkat2qssz1: Use casts and integer division correctly
unit-09.sw6rahr5rc: Python is wonderful for getting ideas working, but it hides almost everything the computer does. When you write x = 5 in Python, an object is created somewhere in memory, a name is attached to it, and a clean-up system deletes it later, all without you seeing any of it. The Python program itself is run by another program (the interpreter), and that interpreter is written in C.
unit-09.1hmjwv073eg: C was created in the early 1970s to write the Unix operating system. It is still the language underneath Linux, Windows, macOS, most databases, web browsers, and the firmware in cars and phones. Learning it shows you what the machine is really doing:
unit-09.1ue5k1js4yh: Compiled: a C program is translated by a compiler into machine instructions before it runs, so there is no interpreter in the way and it can be very fast. (Lesson 9.9 follows that translation.)
unit-09.gm9559drpw: Statically typed: every variable has a declared type, such as int, fixed when you write the program.
unit-09.lwauzsg3vo: Close to memory: you see addresses, bytes and sizes, and you decide when memory is created and destroyed.
unit-09.1zu9v4cngzw: No safety net: C trusts you completely. Reading past the end of an array does not raise an error; it just reads whatever is in memory there. Many of the world's security bugs are exactly this.
unit-09.15sc5wr7f6n: Everything from Units 1 to 8 still applies. This unit shows what lies beneath it.
unit-09.nziq9gu5fj: How C runs in this app
unit-09.2ra5doofq9: Real C is turned into a program by a compiler such as gcc or clang. To let you run C straight in the browser with nothing to install, this app uses PicoC, a small C interpreter. It handles the core of the language very well (everything this unit teaches), but it is not a full compiler, so a few things differ from gcc:
unit-09.139cnh8btgr: Always end a printf line with \n. Text without a newline at the end may not show.
unit-09.vi3zczy7y8: It models a 32-bit machine, so pointers and long are 4 bytes. On a modern 64-bit computer both are 8 bytes. Each lesson says when this matters.
unit-09.1ueveqytp9x: A few features are missing (for example const on local variables, long long, and function pointers). Where that affects a topic, the lesson shows the real C as plain text for you to read and tells you what to expect.
unit-09.2b37k64l60b: Where real C says "undefined behaviour" (it may do anything), PicoC just does something. Never rely on it.
unit-09.26qoqiywkfa: If you later want the real thing, installing gcc takes a few minutes, and everything you learn here carries over directly.
unit-09.xgjwawfezf: Here is some code. Have a look at it on screen.
unit-09.rp8dcvfj2h: #include <stdio.h> asks the preprocessor to paste in the description of the standard input/output functions, such as printf, before compiling.
unit-09.2cbqn3nwo4s: int main(void) is where every C program starts. The int says it returns a whole number to the operating system.
unit-09.1o3jfdore1s: Curly braces { } mark a block. C ignores indentation; the braces and semicolons give the structure.
unit-09.1otcqm6tc5r: Every statement ends with a semicolon.
unit-09.1a5fbd1c6p2: printf prints text. \n is the newline character.
unit-09.katp8d85my: return 0; means "finished successfully". Any other number tells the operating system something went wrong (the "exit code").
unit-09.9gmany0url: Comments are // to the end of the line or /* between these marks */.
unit-09.1fiyfgr7r9b: In Python, print("a") needs no setup. In C, you must declare what you use, spell out the types, and finish with a clean return.
unit-09.2d7wo7ldrte: A variable is declared with its type first: int count = 3;. The type decides how many bytes the variable occupies and how those bytes are read (Lesson 1.3).
unit-09.18hplixvl6p: There is a table here. Have a look at it on screen.
unit-09.2e8p2e5f1w7: Put unsigned in front of an integer type to forbid negative numbers and double the positive range: an unsigned char holds 0 to 255. Unsigned types are used for sizes, counts, bit patterns and bytes.
unit-09.1jq5w5go127: The operator sizeof tells you the size of a type or variable in bytes. In this runner int is 4 bytes and long is also 4; on a 64-bit Linux or Mac computer long is 8 (and on 64-bit Windows it is still 4). C only promises minimum sizes, which is why careful programs use sizeof rather than assuming.
unit-09.kza6d5d7uf: There is no real text type. A character such as 'A' is simply a char holding the number 65 (its ASCII code, Lesson 1.3). 'A' + 1 is 66, which prints as 'B' if you ask for a character. Strings come in Lesson 9.3.
unit-09.1lt8su1krdb: There is no true/false type in the basic language: 0 means false and any other number means true. (A comparison like a < b gives 1 or 0.)
unit-09.23374kzb26f: A 4-byte int holds one of only 2³² patterns, so there is a largest value, 2,147,483,647. In Python, an integer simply grows. In C, adding 1 to the largest int goes around to the most negative number,  minus 2,147,483,648, because the bits roll over exactly as in the two's complement arithmetic of Lesson 1.3.
unit-09.1go28zxis2s: Unsigned types wrap in a clean, guaranteed way: an unsigned char of 255 plus 1 is 0. For signed types, the C standard calls overflow undefined behaviour, meaning the compiler is free to assume it never happens, and optimised programs can behave strangely. The safe habits are: choose a type big enough for the largest value you expect; use unsigned types when you want wrap-around on purpose; and check before adding if the numbers could be huge.
unit-09.6uv8m7ng5c: This is not a rare corner case. Overflow is behind real disasters such as the 1996 Ariane 5 rocket failure and countless security bugs.
unit-09.227vqmhwe0z: printf takes a format string with placeholders, followed by the values to put in them. Each placeholder starts with %:
unit-09.26h3rcc79bb: Between % and the letter you may put a width and flags: %5d pads to 5 characters on the left, %-5d pads on the right, %05d pads with zeros, and %08x gives 8 hex digits with leading zeros. The number of placeholders must match the values, and each type must match too: printing a decimal with %d or the other way round gives nonsense and the compiler will not stop you (good compilers warn).
unit-09.25wjlwdrnq4: C has the arithmetic operators you know: + - * / and % for the remainder, plus ++ and -- to add or subtract 1.
unit-09.9jbxphynty: Integer division. If both sides of / are integers, the answer is an integer with the fraction thrown away: 7 / 2 is 3, -7 / 2 is  minus 3 (C truncates towards zero; Python's // would give  minus 4). To get a decimal answer at least one side must be a decimal: 7.0 / 2 is 3.5.
unit-09.s5m02l0wr1: A cast converts a value to another type: (double)a / b first turns a into a double, so the division keeps its fraction. Write the cast before dividing; (double)(a / b) has already lost the fraction by the time the cast happens.
unit-09.11hd87s13mh: Comparison (== != < > <= >=) and logic (&& || !) operators give 1 or 0. Take care: = assigns and == compares. Writing if (x = 5) assigns 5 to x and is always true, a classic and nasty mistake that the compiler accepts without complaint.
unit-09.m9dhbuu29: The smallest complete program, and a few kinds of output.
unit-09.1kfeccye0cl: sizeof reports the bytes used by each type in this runner.
unit-09.j6a8a0y9i3: Unsigned values wrap cleanly; a signed int rolls over to a negative number.
unit-09.11ssqc8styb: The same value in several formats, a char used as a number, and integer versus decimal division.
unit-09.1akh2t91skt: Forgetting the semicolon or the newline
unit-09.1fs3so0vfpp: A missing ; is a compile error and the message often points to the next line. A missing \n runs your output together or, in this runner, hides the last line.
unit-09.1hpzfjq616t: if (x = 5) assigns 5 and is always true. Many programmers write the constant first (if (5 == x)) so a slip becomes an error.
unit-09.745op7ywxh: Integer division where a decimal was wanted
unit-09.zg7tfcje47: 1 / 2 is 0. Make at least one side a decimal (1.0 / 2) or cast before dividing.
unit-09.1suwfr7jfxu: printf("%d", 2.5) prints garbage, and printf("%f", 3) does too. The format code must match the real type of the value.
unit-09.2e133jvekmk: Assuming a type has a particular size
unit-09.dcqrsoeujs: Only char is guaranteed to be 1 byte. Use sizeof instead of writing numbers like 4 or 8 into your program.
unit-09.1zur6vq6di9: C is compiled, statically typed, close to memory and has no safety net. The Python interpreter itself is written in C.
unit-09.2bd9b5lo0h3: A program starts in main, ends statements with ;, and returns 0 for success. #include <stdio.h> brings in printf.
unit-09.nzihx4pa9p: Types have sizes: char 1 byte, short 2, int 4, double 8. sizeof reports them. unsigned doubles the positive range.
unit-09.1sk3a049ixr: Integers have a fixed number of bits and wrap around; signed overflow is undefined behaviour in real C.
unit-09.ynxcckd0jv: A char is just a small number, and 0 is false while anything else is true.
unit-09.zcz3gcu5nk: printf format codes (%d %u %c %s %f %x %o) must match the argument types; width and flags such as %5d, %-5d, %05d and %.2f control layout.
unit-09.1ja1dbt4lk4: / on two integers truncates; cast before dividing to keep the fraction. = assigns and == compares.
unit-09.1tcn95vzpwo: So far everything has run top to bottom. Lesson 9.2 adds the control flow and functions that give programs structure: if, switch, loops, prototypes, scope, and how each function call gets its own stack frame in memory, including what happens when recursion goes too deep.
unit-09.k34qxbw440: Use C's decisions and loops, write functions with prototypes, understand scope and why arguments are copies, and see how every function call gets its own stack frame in memory, including what happens when recursion goes too deep.
unit-09.1shc5tl9cut: Write if, else if, switch, while, do-while and for statements in C
unit-09.1jbrhptzi34: Explain that 0 is false and everything else is true, and use && and || correctly
unit-09.1qnvs2cc4zl: Declare functions with prototypes and explain why C needs them
unit-09.6p5pz4auel: Explain scope, local variables, global variables and static locals
unit-09.253bupzzc2p: Explain pass by value and why a function cannot change its caller's variable by assigning to a parameter
unit-09.1mdviig7hct: Describe a stack frame and explain what a stack overflow is
unit-09.1jw6s0nmxcn: The condition goes in parentheses and there is no colon. Remember that any number can be a condition: 0 is false, everything else is true. && means and, || means or, and ! means not. Python's words and, or, not do not exist in C.
unit-09.1g0xb6fyt0q: Short-circuit evaluation. && and || stop as soon as the answer is known. In if (n != 0 && total / n > 5) the division is never attempted when n is 0. This is guaranteed by the language and is the standard way to guard against dividing by zero or following a null pointer. (PicoC, the runner in this app, does not short-circuit, so a guarded division like that would crash here but is safe in real C. Run such code with a real compiler.)
unit-09.28geavopa0: The conditional operator condition ? a : b picks one of two values: int bigger = (a > b) ? a : b;.
unit-09.ldt35pasqa: switch chooses between many whole-number cases:
unit-09.ndcvomwv9o: Each case must end with break; or execution falls through into the next case. That is sometimes useful (cases B and C share one action above) but forgetting break is a classic bug.
unit-09.1e7nvyo40ks: C has the same three loops you know, with different spelling:
unit-09.k8zxd7sir0: The for loop has three parts: initialisation, condition and update. i++ means "add 1 to i". break leaves the loop and continue jumps to the next iteration. A do-while tests at the end, so the body always runs at least once.
unit-09.1jost993qhv: There is no range(); the for loop is the counting machine. Be careful with the classic off-by-one: i < 5 runs 5 times (0 to 4) while i <= 5 runs 6 times.
unit-09.18zug5s1bpq: An accidental semicolon is a famous trap: for (i = 0; i < 3; i++); has an empty body, and the block after it runs once. The compiler accepts it.
unit-09.vf6xk3sadj: A C function states its return type, name and the type of every parameter:
unit-09.nmfkora2tm: A function that returns nothing has the return type void. A function with no parameters is written (void).
unit-09.2fos8qr1fb5: The compiler reads a file top to bottom and must know a function before it is used. If main is at the top and calls square defined below it, the compiler will complain (or guess wrongly). The fix is a prototype, a declaration that gives the signature without the body:
unit-09.2707n15zuq7: Prototypes are why C programs have header files (.h): a header is a list of prototypes that other files include so they can call the functions. #include <stdio.h> is exactly that for printf.
unit-09.1wrtscuv740: C functions return one value. To hand back more, use a struct (Lesson 9.6) or pointers (Lesson 9.4).
unit-09.1yh223vf995: A variable declared inside a function (or inside any { } block) is local: it exists only there. Two functions can each have a variable named i without clashing. Local variables are not initialised: until you assign them, they contain whatever happened to be left in that memory. Reading one is a bug.
unit-09.nq462i0a7h: A variable declared outside every function is global. It lives for the whole run and every function can change it, which makes programs hard to reason about. Use globals sparingly.
unit-09.1v7a7vbjjgn: A local declared static keeps its value between calls but is visible only inside its function:

unit-09.2x8ccu3plt: Loops and if become compares and jumps. There are no for or while instructions: the compiler writes a label at the top, a cmp and a conditional jump out, the body, and a jmp back. That is what a loop is at the lowest level.

unit-10.1bp5mr6i4lb: Imagine a computer with no operating system. Every program you wrote would have to know how to talk to the exact disk, keyboard, screen and network card in that machine. Only one program could run at a time, because nothing would stop a second program from overwriting the first. A bug in any program could crash everything, and one user could read another's files.
unit-10.1aaa3s45fcj: An operating system (OS) solves these problems with two jobs:
unit-10.omqs821a65: Resource manager. The machine has a limited supply of CPU time, memory, disk space and devices. The OS decides who gets what and when, and enforces that programs cannot interfere with each other. This is the unit's main theme: scheduling (Lessons 10.3 to 10.5), memory (10.7 and 10.8) and storage (10.9).
unit-10.oi49vmpds1: Abstraction provider. The OS presents simple, uniform ideas on top of complicated hardware. A process is an abstraction of a CPU. A virtual address space is an abstraction of memory. A file is an abstraction of disk blocks. A socket is an abstraction of a network card. Your program says "write these bytes to this file" and never needs to know whether the disk is a spinning platter or flash.
unit-10.2a8euz7ssp0: Everything else you think of as part of "the OS", such as the desktop, the window manager, the file browser and the web browser, is just ordinary programs that run on top. The part that really is special is the kernel.
unit-10.1o53ok5nnql: The kernel and the two modes
unit-10.d7qzrt2mru: The kernel is the core of the OS: the one program that is always loaded, runs with full control of the hardware, and manages everything else. Linux, the Windows NT kernel and XNU (macOS and iOS) are kernels.
unit-10.tgmg616fj4: To protect the kernel from other programs, the CPU itself has (at least) two privilege modes:
unit-10.2fbzrsnb0bx: User mode: where every ordinary program runs. A program in user mode can compute, and read and write its own memory, but it cannot talk directly to devices, change the memory map, switch off interrupts or halt the machine. Trying to run such a privileged instruction makes the CPU raise an exception and hand control to the kernel, which usually terminates the offending program.
unit-10.9w2ijifx8u: Kernel mode (also called supervisor mode): where the kernel runs. Everything is allowed.
unit-10.11j3z4kg1z5: On x86 these are called ring 3 and ring 0; ARM calls them EL0 and EL1.
unit-10.1cj2dfxz2dq: This makes the OS a referee that cannot be bypassed. A buggy or malicious program can crash only itself. Two more pieces of hardware make it work:
unit-10.3vliup7199: Memory protection: the memory management unit (MMU) lets the kernel mark which memory each process may touch (Lesson 10.7).
unit-10.9o1wzdtpfl: A timer interrupt: a clock that interrupts the CPU every few milliseconds and forces control back to the kernel. Without it a program stuck in while True: pass would own the machine forever. This is how the OS regains the CPU to do preemptive scheduling (Lesson 10.3).
unit-10.2mvu9mktss: A user program often needs something only the kernel can do: open a file, send network data, create a process, allocate more memory. It asks through a system call (syscall). The sequence:
unit-10.1rv9mv1240a: The program puts the syscall number and arguments in agreed registers (Lesson 9.9 described the same idea for ordinary calls).
unit-10.1f4k6e2tscv: It executes a special instruction (syscall on x86-64, svc on ARM). This is a trap: the CPU switches to kernel mode and jumps to a fixed entry point that the kernel set up at boot. A program cannot choose where it lands, only which syscall it asks for.
unit-10.1dk821vpnlg: The kernel validates the arguments (never trusting the caller: is that pointer valid? may this user open this file?), does the work, and puts the result in a register.
unit-10.20smsr9tpcc: The kernel returns to user mode, to the instruction after the trap. A negative result is an error code (the C library turns it into -1 and sets errno).
unit-10.101oh9j52kt: A trap costs more than an ordinary function call, typically hundreds of CPU cycles, because the CPU must switch modes and the kernel must check everything. That is why library functions like printf and Python's print buffer output: gather many characters, then make one write call.

unit-10.flp8c0oc0c: When you open a file, the kernel returns a small non-negative integer called a file descriptor (fd). It is an index into a table that the kernel keeps for each process. Later calls (read(fd, ...), write(fd, ...), close(fd)) use that number, so the program never gets a pointer into kernel memory and cannot forge one.
unit-10.pb306ukl6o: Three descriptors are open when a program starts: 0 is standard input, 1 is standard output and 2 is standard error. That is why print goes to the screen: it writes to fd 1. A shell can redirect fd 1 to a file (cmd > out.txt) without the program knowing, because the program only ever says "write to 1".
unit-10.1okan47z2qv: The kernel hands out the lowest unused number, so the first file you open is usually fd 3. dup(fd) returns a new descriptor that refers to the same open file, including its current position. This one trick builds shells' pipes and redirections.
unit-10.17nwi1frvxe: Unix extends the idea: devices, pipes, sockets and even some kernel information are accessed through the same read and write, which is the Unix slogan "everything is a file". It means a tool like grep works on a file, a pipe, or a terminal without change.

unit-10.26qkwa0lqlx: A monolithic kernel (Linux, BSD) puts schedulers, memory management, file systems and device drivers all in one large program running in kernel mode. Calls between parts are fast, but a bug in any driver can take down the whole system.
unit-10.240fz4dj80i: A microkernel (QNX, seL4, MINIX) keeps only the bare minimum in kernel mode (scheduling, memory, messages between processes) and runs file systems and drivers as separate user-mode servers. It is safer and easier to verify, but every request needs extra messages between processes, which costs time.
unit-10.1bwcuy4noe8: Real systems are hybrids: macOS and Windows keep most services in the kernel but use user-mode processes for others. Linux can load code at run time as kernel modules.
unit-10.1fsuyvda4jg: Booting. When the power comes on, nothing is in memory yet, so a tiny program in firmware (BIOS or UEFI) runs first. It tests the hardware, finds a boot loader on disk, and hands over to it. The boot loader loads the kernel into memory and starts it. The kernel sets up memory management and interrupts, mounts the root file system, and starts the first user process (init, or systemd on modern Linux, always process 1). That process starts everything else: login screens, network services, your desktop. Services are started in an order determined by their dependencies, which you will code in an exercise.

unit-10.sd1zcjz8t8: Each process lives in its own address space, a private view of memory (Lesson 10.7 shows how the OS builds that illusion). A typical layout, from low addresses to high:
unit-10.bdllruvo8l: The heap and stack grow toward each other. A process cannot see another process's memory at all: address 1000 in one process is a different piece of RAM from address 1000 in another. This isolation is why one crashing program cannot corrupt another.
unit-10.1dxqtg1negb: The kernel keeps a record for every process called the process control block (PCB) (Linux calls it task_struct). It holds everything needed to stop the process and later resume it exactly where it left off:

unit-10.h3531l8sno: Scheduling info: priority, how much CPU it has used.
unit-10.287afhtudru: Owner (user id), permissions, current directory, signal handlers.
unit-10.2c5ivawyrwm: The kernel keeps all PCBs in a process table. On Linux you can read it in /proc; ps and top display it.
unit-10.fa50ht8n3v: At any moment a process is in one of a few states. The classic model has five:
unit-10.lmgtb45yme: Note what is not possible: a waiting process never goes straight to running (it becomes ready first, then the scheduler picks it), and a ready process never moves to waiting (only a running process can ask for I/O). With one CPU, at most one process is running at any moment, but many may be ready or waiting. Choosing which ready process runs next is scheduling (Lesson 10.3).
unit-10.og2l83gtwp: Processes spend a lot of time waiting. A text editor sits blocked on keyboard input nearly all the time. This is what makes multitasking pay off: while one process waits for the disk, another can use the CPU.
unit-10.jfzjm2cdcd: To move the CPU from process A to process B the kernel performs a context switch:
unit-10.1bf276eh28m: Save A's registers (program counter, stack pointer, general registers) into A's PCB.
unit-10.1xv2qzb1dwl: Update A's state (to ready if preempted, or waiting if it blocked).
unit-10.qznsds8fvv: Load B's registers from B's PCB, switch to B's address space, and set B to running.
unit-10.295gu8qn4n2: From B's point of view nothing happened: it resumes right where it was. The cost is real, though. Saving and restoring registers takes microseconds; switching address spaces can flush the CPU's translation cache (the TLB, Lesson 10.7) and cause cache misses afterwards. Time spent switching is pure overhead, since no user program makes progress during it. That is why a scheduler can't switch too often.
unit-10.1il0259j2bx: On Unix, a process is created by copying an existing one.
unit-10.lb8gbaambb: fork() creates a new process, the child, that is a near-exact copy of the caller, the parent: the same code, a copy of the memory, the same open files. It returns twice: in the parent it returns the child's pid, and in the child it returns 0. (Real systems use copy-on-write, Lesson 10.8, so the copy costs almost nothing until someone writes.)
unit-10.xijatvpcem: exec() replaces the calling process's code and memory with a different program. The pid stays the same. A shell runs a command by fork (make a child), then exec in the child (become the new program).
unit-10.2crimqjq9pd: exit(status) ends a process, closing its files and freeing its memory.
unit-10.uskz71mls5: wait() lets a parent block until a child exits and collect its exit status.
unit-10.18blyphwjji: Every process except the first has a parent, so processes form a tree. pstree shows it: init (pid 1) at the root, then login shells, then your commands.
unit-10.173tbh3qztb: Windows uses a different design (CreateProcess starts a new program directly), but the ideas of parent, child, exit status and wait are the same.
unit-10.26j2riu551f: Two special cases follow from the parent/child relationship.
unit-10.1xznuwibtth: A zombie is a process that has exited but whose parent hasn't yet called wait. It has released its memory, but its PCB stays so that the parent can still read the exit status. A zombie uses almost nothing, but it occupies a slot in the process table; a parent that never waits can fill the table with them. When the parent finally calls wait, the zombie is reaped and disappears.
unit-10.1nt7tn9dnn8: An orphan is a live process whose parent has exited. The kernel reparents it to init (pid 1), which calls wait in a loop, so orphans are cleaned up properly when they finish.
unit-10.zb70focl56: A daemon is a process that runs in the background, deliberately detached from any terminal: web servers, schedulers, the print spooler.

A process can also be interrupted by a signal, a tiny message from the kernel or another process: SIGINT (Ctrl+C), SIGTERM (polite request to quit), SIGKILL (immediate termination, cannot be caught or ignored), SIGSTOP (pause, also uncatchable), SIGCHLD (a child ended). A process may install a handler for most signals; if it doesn't, the default action applies.

unit-10.2dkjlsr28h1: Switching saves and restores state and disturbs caches. Switching every microsecond would leave no time for real work.
unit-10.1wqfpmf1c9n: A process is a program in execution with its own address space (text, data, heap, stack), registers, open files and state. Many processes can run the same program.
unit-10.6bhadctl0y: The kernel keeps a process control block for each process: pid, parent, state, saved registers, memory map, scheduling info and open files.
unit-10.q3nu442x86: A process is new, ready, running, waiting or terminated. Only a running process can block, and a waiting process must become ready before it can run again.
unit-10.xh6gh28elz: A context switch saves one process's registers in its PCB and loads another's. It is pure overhead.
unit-10.1uv752q0rum: fork copies a process, exec replaces its program, exit ends it and wait collects its status. An exited process whose parent hasn't waited is a zombie; a process whose parent died is an orphan, adopted by init.
unit-10.1wjxogxx2bv: Signals send small notifications to processes; SIGKILL and SIGSTOP cannot be caught.
unit-10.2e29edyp46r: Several processes are ready at once, but there is only one CPU (or a few). Which one runs next, and for how long? Lesson 10.3 compares the classic scheduling policies (first-come first-served, shortest job first, round robin and priorities), measures them, and shows that every choice trades fairness, speed and responsiveness against one another.
unit-10.1moicmalzzl: Learn how the OS decides which ready process gets the CPU next. Compare first-come first-served, shortest job first, shortest remaining time, round robin and priority scheduling, measure each with turnaround, waiting and response time, and see why no policy wins on every measure.
