unit-10.5gh9z7vg9h: At any moment several processes may be ready (Lesson 10.2) while only one CPU is available. The scheduler is the part of the kernel that picks which one runs next. It runs whenever a process blocks, exits, or becomes ready, and whenever the timer interrupt fires.
unit-10.2gadvcmvl24: Programs alternate between CPU bursts (computing) and I/O bursts (waiting for disk, keyboard or network). A text editor has very short CPU bursts; a video encoder has very long ones. A good scheduler keeps the CPU busy while giving every process a fair and responsive turn.
unit-10.1e0w9qcln5x: Non-preemptive: once a process gets the CPU, it keeps it until it blocks or finishes.
unit-10.ja8diusp6w: Preemptive: the OS can take the CPU away, using the timer interrupt, and give it to someone else. Every modern desktop and server OS is preemptive.
unit-10.izvi9lacrx: To compare schedulers we need numbers. For each process, with arrival time (when it became ready), burst time (CPU time it needs) and the time it completes:
unit-10.1qt410i4zmz: Systems also care about throughput (jobs finished per second), CPU utilisation, and fairness. These goals conflict, and that conflict is what makes scheduling interesting.
unit-10.20ujs6rpnwz: FCFS runs processes in the order they arrive, to completion. It is simple (a queue) and fair in the sense of arrival order. But it suffers from the convoy effect: one long job at the front makes every short job behind it wait.
unit-10.1yv9i5alqgj: Suppose a 24-unit job arrives just before two 3-unit jobs. The short jobs wait 24 and 27 units. If they had gone first, they would have waited 0 and 3 units, and the long job would barely have noticed.
unit-10.13mrorfjcwg: Shortest job first (SJF) picks, among the ready processes, the one with the smallest burst. It is provably optimal for average waiting time: swapping any two adjacent jobs so the shorter is first never hurts, the same exchange argument you used for greedy algorithms in Lesson 8.5.
unit-10.z7epuzjnyt: The OS doesn't know how long a burst will be. It estimates from history, typically with an exponential average: estimate = α  times  last_burst + (1  minus  α)  times  old_estimate.
unit-10.l45wwghkcv: Starvation. If short jobs keep arriving, a long job may wait forever.
unit-10.2bnhev3gazk: The preemptive version, shortest remaining time first (SRTF), switches whenever a newly arrived process has a shorter remaining time than the running one. It gives the best average waiting time of all, but needs more context switches.
unit-10.1umimhb5qkl: Round robin (RR) is the preemptive policy built for interactive systems. Each process gets the CPU for at most one time quantum (say 10 ms). If it hasn't finished, it goes to the back of the ready queue, and the next process runs.
unit-10.5hxej1crp8: Response time is excellent: with n ready processes and quantum q, nobody waits more than (n  minus  1)  times  q for a turn.
unit-10.1nezfa2ir55: It is fair: no starvation, since everyone is in the queue.
unit-10.d36hz135la: The quantum is a trade-off. If q is huge, RR becomes FCFS. If q is tiny, the machine spends its time context switching (Lesson 10.2) and little real work is done. A common rule: make q long enough that most CPU bursts finish within one quantum, typically 10 to 100 ms. If a switch costs 1 ms and q is 10 ms, about 9% of the CPU is lost.
unit-10.2d2wa3jlbsu: RR's turnaround time is worse than SJF for short jobs, and equal-sized jobs finish all together at the end.
unit-10.c2c3nbvzw2: When a process arrives during another's time slice, convention puts it in the queue before the process that was just preempted. The exercises use this rule.
unit-10.owktjuqy1p: Many systems give each process a priority and always run the highest-priority ready process. SJF is a priority scheme where priority is the burst length. Priorities can be assigned by the OS (interactive processes high, batch jobs low) or by users (nice on Unix lets you lower your own priority).
unit-10.nrmlopmjkn: The danger is starvation: a low-priority process may never run if higher-priority ones keep coming. The cure is aging: gradually raise the priority of any process that has waited a long time, so it eventually reaches the top. A famous (probably apocryphal) story says that when MIT shut down its IBM 7094 in 1973, a low-priority job submitted in 1967 had still not run.
unit-10.kwrlarjsaj: Priority inversion is a related problem: a low-priority process holds a lock that a high-priority process needs, while a medium-priority process runs and prevents the low one from releasing it. The 1997 Mars Pathfinder rover reset itself repeatedly because of this. The fix is priority inheritance: the lock holder temporarily takes the priority of the highest waiter.
unit-10.1ess9bmuhuc: How can a scheduler favour short jobs when it can't know job lengths? The multilevel feedback queue (MLFQ) learns them by observation. There are several queues, each with a priority and a quantum:
unit-10.c3b37tmvqg: A new process starts in the highest-priority queue with a short quantum.
unit-10.5fl9tnfhur: If it uses its whole quantum, it was probably CPU-bound, so it is demoted to the next queue (lower priority, longer quantum).
unit-10.1w1hota4umq: If it blocks for I/O before its quantum ends, it stays where it is (interactive jobs stay at the top).
unit-10.1vi9tp9gty7: Every so often, all processes are boosted back to the top, to prevent starvation and to adapt to changes in behaviour.
unit-10.wj62nuj0al: So interactive and short jobs naturally get quick service, while long computations sink to lower queues where they still run, just with less urgency. This idea is the ancestor of the schedulers in Windows, macOS and BSD. Linux's current default, the Completely Fair Scheduler (CFS) (and its successor EEVDF), takes another approach: each process receives a share of CPU time proportional to its weight, tracked as a "virtual runtime" in a red-black tree, with the least-served process chosen next.
unit-10.20ofyanswop: Multiple CPUs add more questions: should there be one shared ready queue or one per core? Per-core queues avoid lock contention and keep a process's data in its core's cache (processor affinity), but need load balancing to move work from busy cores to idle ones.
unit-10.1r7oqffxm3e: A schedule is a list of (name, start, end) slices. This helper draws it as text so you can see what the CPU did.
unit-10.2bgsw0i5gwi: Example 2: Four schedulers on the same workload
unit-10.2b6h4e3ogfe: The classic example: four jobs arriving close together. FCFS, SJF, SRTF and round robin give very different averages.
unit-10.2a12knvmwy7: With a fixed cost per context switch, a small quantum wastes more CPU. This computes the useful fraction.
unit-10.1dskv1yf6jn: Low priority jobs starve if high priority jobs keep arriving. Aging raises the priority of waiting jobs.
unit-10.x8830m2egi: Assuming shortest-job-first is always the best choice
unit-10.1y9nr78ivn2: It minimises average waiting time, but it can starve long jobs, and the OS rarely knows burst lengths in advance.
unit-10.yroy43mtno: Picking a time quantum that is too small
unit-10.29xg17cutrp: Context switches are not free. A quantum close to the switch cost wastes much of the CPU.
unit-10.swx9om2zrj: If no process has arrived, the CPU waits. The clock must jump to the next arrival, not stay put.
unit-10.15h3z4963fp: Mixing up waiting time and response time
unit-10.1wsyi8xahug: Waiting time counts all the time spent ready but not running. Response time only measures the wait until the first run.
unit-10.khjuro6k9z: Ignoring arrival order when processes tie
unit-10.w7gpti5k0g: A scheduling problem needs a clear tie-breaking rule, or different solutions legitimately disagree.
unit-10.1zaxdx7njud: The scheduler picks which ready process runs next. Preemptive schedulers can take the CPU away using the timer; non-preemptive ones wait until a process blocks or ends.
unit-10.qqa3yzqcr6: Measure with turnaround (completion  minus  arrival), waiting (turnaround  minus  burst) and response (first run  minus  arrival), alongside throughput and fairness.
unit-10.21o2p02640h: FCFS is simple but suffers the convoy effect. SJF and SRTF minimise average waiting time but need to know burst lengths and can starve long jobs.
unit-10.dms61iobcr: Round robin gives each process a quantum in turn. A small quantum gives good response but more switching overhead; a huge one becomes FCFS.
unit-10.22jj3zecl3t: Priority scheduling risks starvation, which aging fixes; priority inversion is fixed by priority inheritance.
unit-10.24pw0u6vd0i: A multilevel feedback queue learns which jobs are short by demoting those that use a full quantum; Linux's CFS shares the CPU in proportion to weights.
unit-10.lsy9anxi12: So far each process has run on its own. Lesson 10.4 turns to concurrency: several threads of control sharing the same memory. The result is powerful and treacherous: the timing of the scheduler you just built can make a program give different answers on different runs. You will see a race condition happen and learn why it does.
unit-10.1nfx5yw4ays: Understand what threads are, why programs use them, and why sharing memory between them is dangerous. See a race condition happen, enumerate every possible interleaving of two threads to find the bad ones, and learn the limits of parallel speed-up with Amdahl's law.

unit-10.pzuwq2n876: A process (Lesson 10.2) has its own private address space, which makes processes safe but heavy: creating one, switching between them and communicating across them all cost time. A thread is a lighter unit of execution inside a process. Several threads of one process share the same code, heap, global variables and open files, but each thread has its own:
unit-10.1yikqtoek07: stack (so its own local variables and call chain),
unit-10.6hxbwfbtet: state (ready, running, waiting) and scheduling priority.
unit-10.19v8vykujvv: Programs use threads for two reasons:
unit-10.1aw7chknx6l: Responsiveness. A GUI thread keeps handling clicks while another downloads a file. A web server handles each request in its own thread so that one slow client doesn't block the rest.
unit-10.txkzjuiy9k: Parallelism. Splitting a big computation across several CPU cores to finish sooner.
unit-10.fokhwhz3se: Concurrency and parallelism are different. Concurrency means several tasks are in progress at overlapping times, even on one core, by taking turns. Parallelism means several tasks are literally running at the same instant on different cores. You can have one without the other.
unit-10.j5qwpzi9j5: Shared memory is the great convenience of threads, and also the source of nearly all their bugs.
unit-10.atorzittuv: Consider two threads that each execute counter = counter + 1 on a shared variable. This looks like one operation, but the hardware does three:
unit-10.rmjttplwhk: The scheduler (Lesson 10.3) can switch between threads at any point, including in the middle of these three steps. Suppose counter is 0 and the threads interleave like this:
unit-10.vgqj1w8ne9: Two increments happened, but the counter is 1. One update was lost. This is a race condition: the result depends on the exact timing of the threads. The bug is also non-deterministic. Most of the time the threads happen not to overlap and the answer is right, so tests pass, until one day under load the timing is different. Such bugs are famously hard to reproduce and fix (programmers call them Heisenbugs). A race in the Therac-25 radiation machine killed patients in the 1980s; a race in the Northeast power grid's alarm software contributed to the 2003 blackout.
unit-10.1a1ihu601yh: A critical section is a stretch of code that touches shared data and must not be interleaved with another thread's use of the same data.
unit-10.17f7z8qi8xm: Atomic means indivisible: an operation that appears to happen all at once, with no thread able to see it half-done. Hardware provides a few atomic instructions (such as compare-and-swap), and locks (Lesson 10.5) build bigger atomic sections from them.
unit-10.jknt56tftu: A data race is two threads accessing the same memory at the same time, at least one writing, with no synchronisation. In C and C++ this is undefined behaviour.
unit-10.14ytqqijrkk: The lost update is not the only shape of race. Another common one is check-then-act: you test a condition, then act on it, but the condition can change in between.
unit-10.r4nqg6vrde: With a balance of 100, two threads each withdraw 80. Both check: 100  greater than or equal to  80, true. Both then subtract: the balance becomes  minus 60. Each thread's reasoning was valid when it made it, but wrong by the time it acted. The same pattern gives double-booked seats, files created twice, and security holes: the famous TOCTOU ("time of check to time of use") bug, where a program checks that a file is safe to open and an attacker swaps it before the open happens.
unit-10.17rt4g4p2tn: The fix is always to make the check and the act one atomic step, usually with a lock (next lesson).
unit-10.26a1n5k0rsg: How many ways can two threads interleave? If thread A has a steps and thread B has b steps, the steps within each thread keep their order, so an interleaving chooses which of the a + b time slots belong to A: (a + b)! / (a! b!) possibilities. Two threads of two steps each give 6; three threads of two steps each give 90; two threads with 50 steps each give about 10²⁹.
unit-10.oxuujzdnkx: Since the number explodes, you can't test every interleaving of a real program. In small models, though, we can enumerate them all and check each one, which is called model checking, and tools like TLA+ and SPIN do it for real protocols. It is also the way to be sure a design is correct.
unit-10.mms1fo9qu6: In this lesson we model a thread as a Python generator. Each yield is a point where the scheduler is allowed to switch to another thread, so we control the interleaving exactly. A schedule is the list of which thread takes each next step, for example [0, 1, 0, 1].
unit-10.28m9dnowkyn: The Python angle: GIL and real threads
unit-10.1x51nzhb04b: Python's standard implementation (CPython) has a global interpreter lock (GIL): only one thread executes Python bytecode at a time. This protects the interpreter's internals, but has two consequences you should know.
unit-10.1o3aa5n9aga: Threads don't speed up CPU-bound Python code; for that use the multiprocessing module (separate processes) or write the hot loop in C or NumPy. Threads are still useful for I/O-bound work, because a thread waiting on the network releases the GIL.
unit-10.2awxwgsxjwq: The GIL does not make your code race-free. A switch can still happen between the bytecodes of counter += 1, so Python programs still need locks for read-modify-write on shared data. (Recent Python versions even offer a build without the GIL.)
unit-10.8k60n51eok: Java, C#, Go and Rust threads do run in parallel on many cores, so races are even more visible there. Rust's ownership rules were designed to make data races impossible to compile.
unit-10.11erhtj37al: How much faster can parallelism make things?
unit-10.1fffb2o67yf: If a program takes time T on one core and you add more cores, you might hope for a speed-up proportional to the number of cores. But some part of the work is inherently sequential (reading input, combining results, waiting for a lock). Amdahl's law says that if a fraction p of the work can run in parallel and the rest cannot, the speed-up with n cores is
unit-10.18bqsuskx3c: Even with infinitely many cores the speed-up cannot exceed 1 / (1  minus  p). If 90% of the program is parallelisable, the best you can ever do is 10 times ; with 4 cores you get only 3.08 times . If only 50% is parallel, the ceiling is 2 times  no matter how many cores you buy. So reducing the sequential part is often worth more than adding hardware. (Gustafson's law gives a more optimistic view: in practice we often make the problem bigger as we add cores.)
unit-10.1pb96vc9s51: A thread is a generator that yields where a switch is allowed. A schedule says who goes next. The same threads can give different answers.
unit-10.1vlsf0izly4: With small threads we can try all schedules and collect every possible final value.
unit-10.w2mjhtkewf: Example 3: Check-then-act on a bank account
unit-10.2eokt63ikol: Each withdrawal checks the balance, then subtracts. A switch between the two lines is enough to overdraw.
unit-10.1k6gzi1dp3j: The same lost update with Python's threading module. It is non-deterministic, which is the point.
unit-10.ywhkd2xmk: It is a read, an add and a write. Two threads can interleave between the steps and lose an update. Use a lock or an atomic type.
unit-10.19sv6opyx6w: Testing once and concluding the code is thread-safe
unit-10.1uji3yzu7i5: Races depend on timing. A program can pass a thousand runs and fail on the next. Reason about all interleavings, or use tools made for the job.
unit-10.6sts25scu5: Anything of the form "if the condition holds, do the thing" on shared state needs the check and the action to be one atomic step.
unit-10.2aqe9lxba9a: Using threads to speed up CPU-bound Python
unit-10.s78rvsqksq: The GIL lets one thread run Python bytecode at a time. Use processes, or vectorised libraries, for CPU-bound work.
unit-10.un6bke4zr1: Expecting linear speed-up from more cores
unit-10.kk1ebqj44: The sequential fraction of a program caps the speed-up (Amdahl's law), and contention for locks lowers it further.
unit-10.18k2x2e4fto: Sharing mutable state when you do not have to
unit-10.295cyh5olec: The safest shared variable is one that doesn't exist. Prefer passing messages or giving each thread its own data and combining the results at the end.
unit-10.2ar9bqrvnff: A thread is a unit of execution inside a process. Threads share the heap, globals and files but each has its own stack and registers. They are cheaper than processes but share their failures.
unit-10.e5i0a9xtfa: Concurrency is tasks overlapping in time; parallelism is tasks running at the same instant on several cores.
unit-10.wrx5evljl8: A race condition occurs when the result depends on thread timing. The classic lost update comes from the non-atomic read-modify-write of counter += 1.
unit-10.akoo2pzalk: Check-then-act bugs (and TOCTOU) arise when a condition can change between the check and the action.
unit-10.3gppz78bq1: Two threads of a and b steps have (a+b)!/(a!b!) interleavings; testing a few cannot show the absence of races, but enumerating all of them in a small model can.
unit-10.jtdg5w5fmd: The Python GIL stops threads speeding up CPU-bound code but does not prevent races. Amdahl's law: speed-up = 1/((1 minus p)+p/n), with limit 1/(1 minus p).
unit-10.1d97wdazhwo: The cure for races is to make critical sections mutually exclusive. Lesson 10.5 introduces locks, semaphores and condition variables, builds them on top of a toy scheduler, and uses them to solve the famous producer-consumer problem correctly.
unit-10.u75jxzey1k: Learn the tools that make shared memory safe: mutual exclusion with locks, counting with semaphores, waiting for conditions, and lock-free updates with compare-and-swap. Build a semaphore and a mutex from scratch, run threads on a small cooperative kernel, and solve the classic producer-consumer problem correctly.

unit-10.2bm49dcfjqv: Lesson 10.4 showed that two threads updating shared data can lose updates. The fix is to make the critical section (the code touching the shared data) execute by one thread at a time. A correct solution must provide:
unit-10.faacazfg1h: Mutual exclusion: at most one thread inside the critical section at any moment.
unit-10.zmkukfsno8: Progress: if no thread is inside and some want to enter, one of them is allowed to, in finite time (nobody waits for a thread that isn't interested).
unit-10.1m6lw6ivy91: Bounded waiting: once a thread asks to enter, only a limited number of other threads may enter before it does (no starvation).
unit-10.1jzra8iml4x: The standard tool is a lock (also called a mutex, short for mutual exclusion). Before entering, a thread acquires the lock; if another thread holds it, the caller waits. After leaving, it releases the lock.
unit-10.iyfdov2dfq: In Python the safe way is with lock:, which releases automatically even if an exception happens. Forgetting to release, or releasing twice, are classic bugs.
unit-10.1dq1oo5gt8v: Keep critical sections short. While a thread holds a lock, every other thread that needs it is stuck. Lock the data for the shortest time possible, and never do slow things (disk, network) while holding a lock if you can avoid it.
unit-10.20nyl05u2ip: How can software build a lock out of nothing? A naive attempt (while locked: pass; locked = True) has the same check-then-act race it was meant to fix. Early solutions like Peterson's algorithm achieve mutual exclusion using only ordinary reads and writes, but they are subtle and break on modern CPUs that reorder memory operations.
unit-10.jjwybwrlfj: Real locks use special atomic instructions that the hardware guarantees cannot be interrupted, even across cores:
unit-10.qlbc5mc9zv: Test-and-set: atomically read a flag and set it to 1, returning the old value. Acquire: while test_and_set(flag) == 1: pass. This is a spinlock: it wastes CPU while waiting, but is good for very short waits on multi-core machines.
unit-10.3v3pdykyrc: Compare-and-swap (CAS): atomically do if x == expected: x = new; return True; else return False. It is the building block of nearly all lock-free programming.
unit-10.1hzunrzcrtr: A lock that makes the waiting thread sleep (the kernel marks it waiting and runs someone else, Lesson 10.2) saves CPU for long waits, but costs a context switch. Real locks (like Linux's futex) spin briefly and then sleep.
unit-10.1tahkjfhcic: Lock-free updates. With CAS you can update a shared value with no lock at all: read the old value, compute the new one, and CAS it in; if somebody else changed it meanwhile, the CAS fails and you simply retry. No thread can ever block another, which avoids deadlock (next lesson) and priority inversion. But it takes care to get right. A famous trap is the ABA problem: the value changes from A to B and back to A, so the CAS succeeds although the world changed underneath it.
unit-10.w2llekbr65: A semaphore, invented by Edsger Dijkstra in 1965, is an integer counter with a queue of sleeping threads and two atomic operations:
unit-10.in6iu8bisr: wait(s) (also called P, down, or acquire): if the counter is above 0, decrement it and continue. If it is 0, the thread blocks, joining the semaphore's queue.
unit-10.1uv1a8nzj3k: signal(s) (V, up, release, or post): if a thread is waiting, wake the first one in the queue (it takes the unit directly). Otherwise increment the counter.
unit-10.1f6tgf3ns3p: A semaphore initialised to 1 is a binary semaphore, which works as a mutex. A semaphore initialised to N is a counting semaphore, which lets up to N threads in at once: N database connections, N slots in a buffer, N licences. A semaphore initialised to 0 is a signal: one thread waits until another says "go".
unit-10.28c8nhuwf5e: A subtle difference from a mutex: a semaphore has no owner, so any thread may signal it. This makes semaphores flexible (one thread can signal an event for another), and also easier to misuse.
unit-10.1845wegyqu0: Producer-consumer (bounded buffer). Producers add items to a buffer of capacity N; consumers remove them. Producers must wait if the buffer is full; consumers must wait if it is empty; and the buffer itself must not be touched by two threads at once. Three semaphores solve it:
unit-10.1iejtnodlq5: Order matters. If the producer waited on mutex before empty, then a producer holding the mutex while the buffer is full would block forever, and no consumer could get the mutex to make room. That's a deadlock, the subject of the next lesson.
unit-10.ztrru8hk6z: Semaphores are low-level and easy to get wrong. A monitor packages shared data together with the code that accesses it, and guarantees that only one thread at a time executes inside the monitor. Java's synchronized methods and Python's threading.Condition work this way.
unit-10.vn4udt27ha: Inside a monitor, threads may need to wait for a condition ("buffer not empty"). A condition variable supports:
unit-10.5ji797f793: wait(): atomically release the monitor's lock and go to sleep; when woken, re-acquire the lock before continuing.
unit-10.14x49fyxs1r: notify() / notify_all(): wake one / all sleeping threads.
unit-10.2a2si4gg75u: Why a while and not an if? Another thread may have taken the item between the wake-up and your re-acquiring the lock, and some systems wake threads spuriously. Re-checking the condition makes the code correct either way.
unit-10.1xijxpni6mh: Readers and writers, and other classics
unit-10.1u19nr2ma6o: Many threads may safely read shared data at once, but a writer needs exclusive access. A readers-writers lock (Python has none built in; Java has ReadWriteLock) lets any number of readers in together, or one writer alone. The design question is who gets priority: if readers always win, writers may starve, and vice versa.
unit-10.n065zjz0e8: Other classic synchronisation problems you will meet:
unit-10.6kpikxbiv9: Dining philosophers: five philosophers share five forks and each needs two to eat. A trap for deadlock (Lesson 10.6).
unit-10.1b3860ff6vj: Barrier: all threads must reach a point before any continues (used in parallel simulations).
unit-10.wjzi6ohlkk: Sleeping barber, cigarette smokers: puzzles that exercise different coordination patterns.
unit-10.3wuzretj8y: Tips for real programs. (1) Prefer higher-level tools: queues (queue.Queue is a thread-safe bounded buffer), thread pools and message passing. (2) Share as little mutable state as you can. (3) Always acquire multiple locks in the same global order. (4) Hold locks briefly. (5) Test under stress and with tools like thread sanitizers; reasoning alone misses things.
unit-10.kj4nwoxzh6: Example 1: A semaphore and a small kernel
unit-10.1s1ajtkce56: Threads are generators that yield requests (step, wait, signal). The kernel runs them in turns and puts blocked threads to sleep on the semaphore's queue.
unit-10.10essxucvzl: Example 2: Producer and consumer with a bounded buffer
unit-10.ygovn1yeqt: Three semaphores: empty slots, filled slots, and a mutex for the buffer. The buffer never exceeds its capacity.
unit-10.1r7tg6imihn: Example 3: A deadlock from the wrong order
unit-10.jh9aujdw28: The consumer takes the mutex first and then waits for an item. The producer can never get the mutex to supply one.
unit-10.7s2hzwkzlt: The same ideas with the real threading module. Not run here, because the browser cannot start threads.
unit-10.29dcg8nvkwx: Waiting with an if instead of a while
unit-10.29dyl7qarf8: A condition may no longer hold by the time a woken thread runs. Re-check it in a loop.
unit-10.tmmmb5ncga: Taking the mutex before waiting on a counting semaphore
unit-10.1too9600ddk: Holding the mutex while sleeping blocks everyone who could wake you: deadlock. Wait on empty or full first, then lock.
unit-10.f3fyquwpbr: Forgetting to release a lock on an error path
unit-10.2dd59fb4pgq: An exception inside the critical section leaves the lock held forever. Use with lock: or try/finally.
unit-10.21cb08r2qx1: Holding a lock during slow work
unit-10.krq6aqurzv: Network or disk calls inside a critical section stall every other thread that needs the lock. Copy what you need, release, then do the slow part.
unit-10.1lqzu35oj90: Locking different data with different locks inconsistently
unit-10.1299nt2vlfn: If one code path protects a variable with lock A and another with lock B, nothing protects it. Each shared variable needs one lock that is always used.
unit-10.lqvsy920ov: Using a spinlock for long waits
unit-10.871dyh292c: Spinning burns CPU. Use it only when the wait is shorter than a context switch.
unit-10.1snj97psdap: A critical-section solution must give mutual exclusion, progress and bounded waiting. A mutex (lock) provides mutual exclusion; keep its sections short and always release it (with lock:).
unit-10.d9229ct5ex: Locks are built on atomic hardware instructions like test-and-set and compare-and-swap. A spinlock busy-waits; a sleeping lock lets the kernel run another thread. CAS enables lock-free retries.
unit-10.q3ddcb7zsq: A semaphore is a counter plus a wait queue: wait decrements or sleeps, signal wakes the first sleeper or increments. Value 1 is a mutex, value N limits access, value 0 signals an event.
unit-10.1n0lduv05tk: Bounded buffer: empty (free slots), full (items) and mutex. Wait on the counting semaphore before the mutex, or you can deadlock.
unit-10.8o56j781i9: A monitor bundles data with a lock; a condition variable lets a thread sleep until a condition is true. Always wait() in a while loop.
unit-10.k6e9ig4qx1: Prefer high-level tools (queues, thread pools, message passing), share little, and acquire multiple locks in one fixed order.
unit-10.14qqrbndvjz: Locks fix races but create a new danger: threads that wait for each other forever. Lesson 10.6 studies deadlock: the four conditions that cause it, how to draw and search a wait-for graph, Dijkstra's banker's algorithm for avoiding it, and the dining philosophers.
unit-10.1xpiuyci33u: Understand deadlock: a set of threads each waiting for something only another in the set can provide. Learn the four conditions that cause it, find deadlocks by searching a wait-for graph, prevent them with lock ordering, and avoid them with the banker's algorithm.
unit-10.58qg5whrga: State the four necessary conditions for deadlock and show how breaking each one prevents it
unit-10.2e6piccwzug: Build a wait-for graph from lock ownership and find the deadlocked threads
unit-10.1l6c74l65a8: Use a global lock order to prevent circular waits, and spot AB-BA lock orders in code
unit-10.u3errm9fkm: Apply the banker's algorithm to decide whether a state is safe and whether to grant a request
unit-10.w9xv52psej: Solve the dining philosophers problem without deadlock
unit-10.1zefuco25pt: Two cars meet on a one-lane bridge, each waiting for the other to back up. Neither can move, and neither ever will. In a computer, a set of threads is deadlocked when every one of them is waiting for a resource held by another thread in the set. Since each waits for another, none can ever release anything, so none ever proceeds.
unit-10.f5q6ot75lk: The smallest example uses two locks:
unit-10.1xwxwl8fag1: If thread 1 takes A and thread 2 takes B before either takes its second lock, then thread 1 waits for B (held by 2) and thread 2 waits for A (held by 1). Neither lock is ever released. If they happen to run one after the other the program works fine, which is why deadlocks lurk in tested code and appear once in a million runs on a customer's machine.
unit-10.1mu9cnfvzz7: Deadlock can involve any resource that is held exclusively: locks, files, database rows (databases detect and abort such transactions), printers, network connections, memory pages.
unit-10.192zpvfjo4i: In 1971 Coffman, Elphick and Shoshani showed that deadlock can occur only if all four of these hold at once:
unit-10.1ptpmxrrdvv: Mutual exclusion: a resource can be held by only one thread at a time.
unit-10.17v006aevqk: Hold and wait: a thread holding some resources can wait for others.
unit-10.2crbxkma30l: No preemption: a resource cannot be forcibly taken from the thread holding it; only the holder can release it.
unit-10.1rskifdezjp: Circular wait: there is a cycle of threads, each waiting for a resource held by the next.
unit-10.rx5libvdio: That list is useful because it gives four different ways to prevent deadlock: make sure at least one condition can never hold.
unit-10.25z9loz90wf: Lock ordering is the practical weapon. Number every lock (or sort by name or address) and require that any thread holding lock k may only request locks with numbers greater than k. Then a cycle of waits is impossible, since following the waits would need numbers to increase around a loop. Code review rule: whenever you see code that takes two locks, ask "who takes them in the other order?"
unit-10.us6gxp1ui8: Detecting deadlock with a wait-for graph
unit-10.c29lgu0vna: A resource-allocation graph has nodes for threads and resources, with an edge from a resource to the thread that holds it, and from a thread to the resource it wants. When every resource has a single instance, you can simplify it into a wait-for graph with only threads: an edge T1  to  T2 means "T1 is waiting for something T2 holds".
unit-10.25eqejfsamn: A cycle in the wait-for graph means deadlock (for single-instance resources). The threads on the cycle can never proceed, and any thread waiting (even indirectly) for them is stuck too. Finding cycles is the depth-first search you know from Lesson 7.8: from each node, follow edges and see whether you can get back to the starting node.
unit-10.1i6rwhx0r9i: Databases do exactly this. When the wait-for graph gets a cycle, the DBMS picks a victim transaction, aborts it (rolling back its changes, which breaks the no-preemption condition) and lets the others continue. General-purpose operating systems usually ignore the problem (jokingly called the ostrich algorithm), because deadlocks are rare and detecting them has a cost; the programmer is expected to avoid them. If a deadlock does happen, recovery means killing a process or rolling back.
unit-10.19lskhnh9se: Prevention restricts how locks are requested. Avoidance instead lets threads request freely but only grants a request if the system will still be safe afterwards. It needs advance knowledge: each thread declares its maximum need for each resource type.
unit-10.17f4vg3ryqk: A state is safe if there is some order, a safe sequence, in which the threads can all run to completion: each thread in turn can get everything it might still ask for from what is currently free plus what earlier threads have returned. An unsafe state doesn't mean deadlock has happened, only that it might; the system can no longer guarantee that it won't.
unit-10.pm6gijkl9x: Dijkstra's banker's algorithm (named for a banker who never lends out cash that would leave him unable to satisfy his customers) works with m resource types:
unit-10.2bf1gbyn290: available: how many units of each type are free.
unit-10.c3wtsaokla: max: each thread's maximum claim. allocation: what each thread holds now.
unit-10.eb34fyjrq9: Safety check: set work = available. Repeatedly find an unfinished thread whose need  less than or equal to  work; pretend it finishes and returns its allocation (work += allocation). If all threads can finish, the state is safe; if you get stuck with some unfinished, it's unsafe.
unit-10.hj0h5uzqu2: Request check for thread T asking for request: (1) if request > need, error (it exceeded its stated maximum); (2) if request > available, T must wait; (3) otherwise pretend to grant it and run the safety check; if safe, grant it; if not, make T wait.
unit-10.bp6klb20r7: The banker's algorithm is rarely used in real systems, as threads rarely know their maximum needs, and checking costs time. But it is the clearest example of avoidance, and the idea of keeping the system in a "safe state" returns in capacity planning and in cloud schedulers.
unit-10.28sxvhhslql: Five philosophers sit around a table, with one fork between each pair of neighbours (five forks in all). A philosopher needs both adjacent forks to eat, thinks otherwise, and puts both forks down after eating. The obvious protocol, "pick up the left fork, then the right fork", deadlocks if all five pick up their left fork at the same moment: each holds one fork and waits for a fork held by the neighbour, a circular wait.
unit-10.i63ekk7mb1: Solutions, each breaking a different condition:
unit-10.27vc2thovjc: Ordering. Number the forks 0 to 4 and have every philosopher pick up the lower-numbered fork first. The last philosopher (between fork 4 and fork 0) therefore takes fork 0 first, which breaks the cycle.
unit-10.fg1ttozaoo: A waiter. Allow at most four philosophers to sit down at once (a semaphore with value 4): someone can always eat.
unit-10.igv8x8kk9z: All or nothing. Pick up both forks atomically, or put back the first if the second is unavailable (but beware of livelock).
unit-10.1owsw4kowmp: Not every "nothing happens" bug is a deadlock.
unit-10.26yx2081yle: Livelock: threads are not blocked, but keep reacting to each other without making progress, like two people in a corridor who both step aside the same way, repeatedly. A backing-off lock protocol where both threads release and retry in lockstep is a livelock. The cure is randomised back-off, as in Ethernet.
unit-10.1x9yz033udx: Starvation: a thread is ready to proceed but is never chosen, because others keep going first (unfair locks, strict priorities; Lesson 10.3). Fairness (FIFO queues) and aging fix it.
unit-10.10y2qyu2472: Unlike deadlock, in livelock and starvation other threads may be running perfectly well, so the symptoms are different: deadlocked threads use no CPU; livelocked threads use a lot.
unit-10.21g0c7364hk: Debugging tip. If a program hangs, take a thread dump (jstack for Java, py-spy dump or faulthandler.dump_traceback for Python, gdb for C). Look for threads blocked on locks held by each other. The lock cycle is usually visible.
unit-10.1zz0hrkswmr: Example 1: A deadlock found in the wait-for graph
unit-10.2fq3y347b29: Each thread holds one lock and wants another. Build the graph, then search for threads that can reach themselves.
unit-10.14269kis1h: Five threads and three resource types (the textbook example). Is the state safe, and which requests may be granted?
unit-10.26sdj2poarm: If every philosopher grabs the left fork first, all five hold one fork each: a perfect cycle. Ordering the forks breaks it.
unit-10.25jmuwhn5gr: Example 4: Avoiding deadlock in real Python
unit-10.14jh6zb0mxc: Two practical techniques: a fixed lock order, and a timeout with retry. Not run here, because the browser has no threads.
unit-10.1gxrjfg00d6: Taking two locks in different orders in different places
unit-10.1lqi584xvho: The AB-BA pattern is the commonest deadlock. Pick a global order (for example by name or id) and always follow it.
unit-10.1rcb3ljvzu0: Holding a lock while calling unknown code
unit-10.28zszmefjnp: A callback or overridden method may try to take another lock, in an order you never planned. Release your lock before calling out, or document the order.
unit-10.1qw8hwunxb5: Calling a function that takes the same lock again
unit-10.glfvl1ajgj: A thread that locks a non-reentrant lock it already holds deadlocks with itself. Use a reentrant lock (RLock) or restructure.
unit-10.1n2q06rgwv5: Two threads that both back off and retry at the same moment can livelock. Add a random delay.
unit-10.1543n6pw85y: Thinking a hung program must be deadlocked
unit-10.herhqzbpjx: It could also be livelock, starvation, an infinite loop, or waiting on a slow network. Check whether the threads use CPU and what each is blocked on.
unit-10.1jkubdll645: Believing an unsafe state is a deadlock
unit-10.17mypo2z8tz: Unsafe means deadlock is possible, not that it has happened. The banker refuses unsafe grants to stay on the safe side.
unit-10.12my26o7izk: Deadlock is a set of threads each waiting for a resource held by another in the set, so none can ever proceed. Deadlocked threads use no CPU.
unit-10.1pjrmpo0ktt: It needs all four Coffman conditions: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption and circular wait. Break any one and deadlock is impossible.
unit-10.v37q741ugd: A global lock order prevents circular waits and is the standard practical defence; acquire(timeout=...) and rollback break no-preemption.
unit-10.1mcdmua89yk: A cycle in the wait-for graph means deadlock for single-instance resources. Databases detect it and abort a victim; most operating systems ignore it (the ostrich algorithm).
unit-10.1o01o7uo37t: The banker's algorithm avoids deadlock: grant a request only if a safe sequence still exists. It needs maximum claims in advance, so it is rare in practice.
unit-10.c2s0bes27w: Dining philosophers show the problem and its fixes (ordering, a waiter, all-or-nothing). Livelock (busy but no progress) and starvation (never chosen) are different failures.
unit-10.1trvucavsmi: So far the processes have shared a CPU. They also have to share memory, and each process needs to believe it has a large, private, contiguous address space. Lesson 10.7 begins memory management: contiguous allocation and fragmentation, then paging, page tables and the address translation hardware, which uses the bit operations from Unit 9.
unit-10.l8piij4zvr: See how the OS gives every process a private address space on top of shared physical memory. Compare contiguous allocation (and its fragmentation) with paging, translate virtual addresses to physical ones with page tables and bit operations, and measure what a TLB does for speed.
unit-10.1u7yx218h7t: Explain why programs use virtual addresses and what the MMU does
unit-10.1flx1lc9ja: Allocate memory with first-fit, best-fit and worst-fit, and measure internal and external fragmentation
unit-10.3q6bn5okoq: Split a virtual address into page number and offset, and translate it using a page table
unit-10.16od90ehm36: Compute the size of single-level and two-level page tables
unit-10.1dqhhbzeet: Explain how a TLB speeds translation, and compute effective access time
unit-10.xkxoqnbxqy: Describe protection bits and shared pages
unit-10.1sgpwdmesj5: Early computers ran one program at a time, which used physical addresses directly. With many processes the problems appear at once: where in RAM does each program go, what if two programs want the same addresses, how do you stop one program reading or writing another's memory, and what if the programs together need more memory than the machine has?
unit-10.6e9fb9cq7t: The solution is a layer of indirection, the oldest trick in computing. Every process uses virtual addresses (also called logical addresses): its code and data appear to live at addresses starting from 0, in a private address space. A piece of hardware, the memory management unit (MMU), translates each virtual address to a physical address in RAM as the instruction executes, using tables the OS maintains. The process never sees physical addresses.
unit-10.2c6expy3zvo: Isolation / protection: a process can only name addresses the OS has mapped for it. An attempt to touch anything else raises a fault (a segmentation fault in Unix).
unit-10.149cjec87m4: Relocation: the OS can put a process anywhere in RAM, and even move it, without the process noticing.
unit-10.2g9353oc398: Sharing: two processes can map the same physical memory (shared libraries, shared memory) at different virtual addresses.
unit-10.20l326urb1w: More memory than RAM (next lesson): not every virtual page has to be in RAM at once.
unit-10.nxw9ycodzr: Convenience: every program can be compiled assuming the same layout.
unit-10.1qn7oj787yb: The simplest scheme gives each process one contiguous block of physical memory, with a base register (where it starts) and a limit register (how long it is). The MMU adds the base to every virtual address and traps if the address is beyond the limit.
unit-10.16ztp4e9zoy: The OS must then track free holes and choose one when a process arrives. Common placement strategies:
unit-10.9a6hqaa99a: First fit: the first hole that is big enough (fast; tends to chew up the start of memory).
unit-10.1snpermht62: Best fit: the smallest hole that fits (leaves the smallest leftover, but leaves tiny useless slivers and needs a search).
unit-10.1lg0fl0subf: Worst fit: the largest hole (leftover is large enough to be useful, but destroys big holes).
unit-10.1woc99fodkk: Simulations show first fit and best fit perform similarly, and both beat worst fit.
unit-10.1u4iqxptxnb: Whatever you choose, memory becomes riddled with unusable holes as processes come and go. This is external fragmentation: enough total free memory exists, but not in one piece. A 100 KB request fails even though 300 KB is free, as three 100 KB  minus  1 byte holes. Freed neighbouring holes must be coalesced (merged) to fight it. The brute-force cure is compaction (sliding everything together), which costs a lot of copying.
unit-10.1lanmnvug76: Contiguous allocation has another weakness: a process must fit in one block, and growing (the heap, the stack) requires moving. Paging removes both problems.
unit-10.19qhi3ln19c: Paging cuts memory into fixed-size pieces. Virtual memory is divided into pages and physical memory into frames of the same size (commonly 4 KB = 4096 bytes). Any page can go in any frame, so a process's memory need not be contiguous in RAM. Because all pieces are the same size, there is no external fragmentation: any free frame is as good as any other.
unit-10.1bgito7w8u7: The OS keeps a page table for each process: an array indexed by page number, giving the frame number holding that page (plus flag bits). Translating an address is bit manipulation (Lesson 9.8):
unit-10.20vpc2d7tx8: Example: virtual address 0x1234 with 4 KB pages has page number 1 and offset 0x234. If page 1 lives in frame 7, the physical address is (7 << 12) | 0x234 = 0x7234.
unit-10.j9rsnwfc45: Each page table entry (PTE) also holds flag bits:
unit-10.1ir74wsnge2: Valid / present: is the page mapped (in RAM)? If not, the access causes a page fault and the OS takes over (Lesson 10.8).
unit-10.1stv3b6ztkk: Read / write / execute: permissions. Code pages are read-only and executable; data pages are not executable. This blocks many attacks (a buffer overflow that injects code can't run it).
unit-10.1293qwhn4iw: Dirty: written since it was loaded. Accessed: used recently.
unit-10.128jtxnws36: User / supervisor: whether user code may access it.
unit-10.18uuad0qtgu: Internal fragmentation. Memory is handed out in whole pages, so the last page of every region is partly wasted. A 4097-byte request takes two 4 KB pages and wastes 4095 bytes. On average, half a page per region is wasted, which is why page sizes are a compromise: small pages waste little but make big page tables; large pages (2 MB, 1 GB "huge pages") make small tables but waste more.
unit-10.240tu3xf1re: Page table size and multi-level tables
unit-10.2cu77w5r3pn: A flat page table can be huge. With 32-bit addresses and 4 KB pages there are 2²⁰ ≈ 1 million pages, so a table of 4-byte entries takes 4 MB per process. With 64-bit addresses the flat table would be astronomically large, and most of it would describe unused address space.
unit-10.gug4hx5rwd: The fix is a multi-level page table, a tree (like a trie, Lesson 7.7). A 32-bit address is split into three fields (the classic x86 layout): 10 bits for the directory index, 10 bits for the table index, 12 bits of offset.
unit-10.h6sxm9aevc: The top-level directory has 1024 entries, each pointing to a second-level table of 1024 entries, but a second-level table exists only if that part of the address space is used. A small program with a little code, heap and stack needs a directory plus maybe three or four small tables, a few tens of KB instead of 4 MB. x86-64 uses four levels (9 bits each); newer CPUs offer five.
unit-10.f6gbxmlx4l: The price: translation now takes several memory reads, one per level. Hardware makes this tolerable with a cache.
unit-10.11ymts6u0y3: Reading a page table entry from RAM for every memory access would at least double (or with four levels, quintuple) the cost of every load and store. The translation lookaside buffer (TLB) is a small, very fast cache inside the CPU holding recently used translations (page number to frame). Typical sizes: 64 to 2048 entries.
unit-10.18sx94deslj: TLB hit: translation takes about a cycle; just one memory access follows.
unit-10.1q347rz7yx3: TLB miss: the hardware (or on some architectures the OS) walks the page table, then loads the entry into the TLB, evicting an old one (often least recently used).
unit-10.2fsbpm8ratc: The effective access time is a weighted average. With hit ratio h, TLB lookup time t and memory access time m, using a single-level page table:
unit-10.b7dd3nrohl: EAT = h  times  (t + m) + (1  minus  h)  times  (t + 2m)
unit-10.1zjvz2lpnqg: With t = 10 ns, m = 100 ns and h = 90%: 0.9  times  110 + 0.1  times  210 = 120 ns, only 20% slower than raw memory instead of 100% slower. TLBs work because programs have locality of reference: they tend to reuse the same few pages over and over (Lesson 1.6). On a context switch the TLB entries of the old process are invalid, so either the TLB is flushed or entries are tagged with a process id; this is part of the hidden cost of context switches (Lesson 10.2).
unit-10.io9qlaczgl: Sharing and copy-on-write. Because mapping is by table, two processes can map the same frame. Shared libraries (such as libc) are loaded once and mapped into every process read-only. After fork (Lesson 10.2), parent and child share all frames, marked read-only; only when one writes does the OS copy that single page. That's why fork is cheap.
unit-10.2evsruwfdvw: Example 1: A memory allocator and fragmentation
unit-10.2e9ikri23z8: Allocate and free blocks in 1000 bytes of memory, then compare first-fit, best-fit and worst-fit on the same holes.
unit-10.18ni0lh68t8: The page number and offset are just the high and low bits of the address. Shifts and masks do the work.
unit-10.4e9lxw5j5n: Why a flat page table is too large, and how two levels save memory for a small program.
unit-10.1d509lc85nd: Example 4: The TLB and effective access time
unit-10.2ep3631t60t: A tiny LRU cache of translations. Locality gives a high hit rate; a poor access pattern defeats it.
unit-10.1syqwsq8z9k: Pages belong to the virtual address space; frames belong to physical memory. The page table maps pages to frames.
unit-10.1v1fossyfih: Frame 0 is a perfectly good frame. Use an explicit valid bit or compare with None.
unit-10.11c3mrcbpy0: Only the page number is translated. The low bits pass straight through.
unit-10.emfpclrpxt: Internal: waste inside an allocated block (the unused tail of a page). External: free memory scattered in pieces too small to use. Paging eliminates external fragmentation but has internal.
unit-10.25mn6najjht: Believing the TLB is just a bigger cache of data
unit-10.gildvi7aqi: It caches address translations, not the data itself. A TLB miss costs a page-table walk even if the data is in the CPU's data cache.
unit-10.1lhivxh50wk: Assuming a bigger page size is always better
unit-10.26r31u3gg33: Bigger pages shrink page tables and raise TLB reach, but waste more memory per allocation and make copy-on-write copies bigger.
unit-10.25ay76k3z18: Each process uses virtual addresses, which the MMU translates to physical addresses using tables set up by the OS. This gives isolation, relocation, sharing and (next lesson) more memory than RAM.
unit-10.15ok1m080fi: Contiguous allocation uses base and limit registers and a free list (first, best, worst fit). It suffers external fragmentation, partly cured by coalescing and compaction.
unit-10.fmdqomq9v2: Paging splits memory into equal pages and frames. A virtual address is page number | offset; the page table maps page to frame, and physical = (frame << offset_bits) | offset. It has no external fragmentation but some internal fragmentation.
unit-10.1v1tb1j24kt: Page-table entries carry valid, permission, dirty and accessed bits. An access to an invalid page causes a page fault.
unit-10.4r27fck7y5: A flat table for 32-bit addresses is 4 MB per process; multi-level tables allocate only the parts in use (x86-64 uses four levels).
unit-10.um7x90dz68: The TLB caches translations: EAT = h(t+m) + (1 minus h)(t+2m). Copy-on-write shares frames after fork until someone writes.
unit-10.24t1mcocix3: Paging makes it easy to keep only some of a program's pages in RAM and the rest on disk. Lesson 10.8 covers virtual memory proper: demand paging, handling page faults, and the page replacement algorithms (FIFO, LRU, optimal and clock) that decide which page to evict, including a surprising anomaly where giving a program more memory makes it fault more.
unit-10.13vbvoo7zlf: Understand how an OS lets programs use more memory than the machine has: load pages only when they are touched (demand paging), handle page faults, and choose which page to throw out when RAM is full. Compare the replacement algorithms FIFO, LRU, optimal and clock, see Belady's anomaly, and learn about the working set and thrashing.
unit-10.3yx3i3okgh: Describe demand paging and the sequence of steps in handling a page fault
unit-10.10s6pp26686: Compute the effective access time with page faults and see why the fault rate must be tiny
unit-10.18mlyto0qao: Simulate FIFO, LRU, optimal and clock page replacement and count faults
unit-10.28dvz8ytcv6: Explain Belady's anomaly and stack algorithms
unit-10.ijo59a6dc7: Define the working set and explain thrashing and how the OS prevents it
unit-10.1ib7t5p6f49: Describe swap space, memory-mapped files and the out-of-memory killer
unit-10.1ri8rhqujdu: Lesson 10.7 gave every process a page table. The final trick is to let the page table say "not present". A page can then be in RAM, or on disk (in a swap area or in the program's own file), and the process cannot tell the difference except by speed.
unit-10.20gqqwfsczi: With demand paging, a program's pages are loaded only when first touched. Starting a 100 MB program doesn't read 100 MB: the OS maps the file and loads the pages the program actually executes. Many pages of a large program (error handlers, rarely used features) are never loaded at all, so programs start faster and more of them fit in RAM. The total virtual memory of all processes can be far larger than physical RAM.
unit-10.cs2afvx1d: This works because of locality of reference (Lesson 1.6): at any moment a program uses only a small part of its memory, mostly the same pages again and again, so keeping that part in RAM is enough.
unit-10.23ey1v7df8i: When an instruction touches a page whose entry is not present, the MMU raises a page fault, a trap into the kernel. The handler does the following:
unit-10.zsoe2b5981: Check the address is legal for this process. If not (null pointer, outside any mapping), send SIGSEGV, the "segmentation fault" that kills the program.
unit-10.1rrezuf5028: Find a free frame. If none is free, run the page replacement algorithm to pick a victim frame. If the victim page is dirty (modified since loading), write it to disk first; a clean page can simply be dropped.
unit-10.1vhef44lojz: Start a disk read of the needed page into the frame. The process is put in the waiting state (Lesson 10.2) and another process runs while the disk works.
unit-10.1iuc78nopjn: When the read finishes, update the page table (frame number, present bit set), and make the process ready.
unit-10.8302chenf2: When the process runs again, restart the instruction that faulted. This time it succeeds.
unit-10.rm10y074zt: A page fault is very expensive: a disk read takes milliseconds, while a memory access takes about 100 nanoseconds, a ratio of tens of thousands. (SSDs are faster than spinning disks, but still hundreds of times slower than RAM.) That makes the fault rate the dominant factor in performance:
unit-10.o6gj137law: EAT = (1  minus  p)  times  memory_time + p  times  fault_time
unit-10.2cc2dl9817c: With memory time 200 ns, fault time 8 ms (8,000,000 ns) and a fault rate p of just 1 in 1,000, EAT = 0.999  times  200 + 0.001  times  8,000,000 ≈ 8,200 ns, forty times slower. To keep the slowdown under 10%, p must be below about 1 in 400,000. So the replacement algorithm has to be good at keeping the right pages in RAM.
unit-10.9akrebdok8: Given a reference string (the sequence of pages a process touches) and a fixed number of frames, which page should be evicted when a new page is needed and all frames are full? The measure is the number of page faults.
unit-10.1emjvap6xe0: FIFO: evict the page that has been in memory the longest. Simple, but it can evict a page that is in constant use just because it was loaded long ago.
unit-10.3nqeyjljxa: Optimal (OPT, or Belady's MIN): evict the page whose next use is farthest in the future (or never). It gives the fewest possible faults, but needs to know the future, so it cannot be implemented in a real OS. It is the yardstick to compare other algorithms against.
unit-10.23s17uf7pct: LRU (least recently used): evict the page that has not been used for the longest time, on the theory that the past predicts the future (locality). It performs close to optimal, but exact LRU needs a timestamp or list update on every memory access, which is far too slow for hardware.
unit-10.1sjskh45rln: Clock (second chance): an inexpensive approximation of LRU. Frames form a circle with a pointer (the "hand"). Each frame has a reference bit that the hardware sets whenever the page is used. To find a victim the hand sweeps: if the bit is 1, clear it (a second chance) and move on; if it is 0, evict that page. Used (in variants) by Linux, BSD and Windows.
unit-10.1sqpfyauzpq: On the classic reference string 7 0 1 2 0 3 0 4 2 3 0 3 2 1 2 0 1 7 0 1 with 3 frames: FIFO causes 15 faults, LRU 12, optimal 9. Where all 20 references are distinct pages, every algorithm faults 20 times; a reference to a page already in memory is a hit.
unit-10.x737kqfh20: Real systems also add: dirty-page preference (evicting a clean page is cheaper than a dirty one), page buffering (keep a pool of free frames so a fault never has to wait for a write-back), and prefetching (read neighbouring pages ahead).
unit-10.2flzzlnvlb9: You would expect that giving a process more frames can only reduce its page faults. For FIFO, it isn't so. On the reference string 1 2 3 4 1 2 5 1 2 3 4 5, FIFO with 3 frames causes 9 faults, but with 4 frames it causes 10. This is Belady's anomaly (1969).
unit-10.m8bwb874xm: LRU and OPT never show it, because they are stack algorithms: the set of pages held with n frames is always a subset of the set held with n + 1 frames, so adding memory can't hurt. FIFO lacks this property, since which page is oldest depends on the history in a way that changes with the number of frames.
unit-10.17ivbsgnkb0: How many frames does a process need? The working set W(t, Δ) is the set of distinct pages referenced in the last Δ memory references (the "window"). If a process has at least |W| frames, it runs with few faults; if not, it faults constantly.
unit-10.115ojnf2xfq: Thrashing happens when the total working sets of all running processes exceed physical memory. Each process keeps stealing frames from the others, every process spends its time waiting for the disk, the CPU sits idle, and, in an old naive design, the OS notices low CPU use and starts more processes, making it worse. Throughput collapses. A thrashing machine is almost unusable (the disk light stays on and the mouse crawls).
unit-10.88qba8decv: Remedies: use the working-set model to run only as many processes as will fit in memory (suspend others, i.e. swap out whole processes), use local replacement so one process can't steal everyone's frames, monitor the page-fault frequency and add or remove frames, and, ultimately, buy more RAM.
unit-10.283s642286f: Memory-mapped files, swap and the OOM killer
unit-10.9m9zzeu8zh: Virtual memory is also a general mechanism, not just a way to simulate extra RAM.
unit-10.g82lq243n3: Memory-mapped files (mmap): a file's contents appear as a range of virtual addresses, loaded by demand paging. Reading and writing memory reads and writes the file, and different processes mapping the same file share the same frames. Program loaders and databases use it constantly. Python has the mmap module.
unit-10.1urns789nqo: Shared libraries and copy-on-write (Lesson 10.7) are also page-table tricks.
unit-10.1ydmxaxo5wm: Swap space is the disk area where evicted anonymous pages (heap and stack, which have no file behind them) are saved. Systems start to "swap" heavily when RAM is overcommitted.
unit-10.51m0j1f2ym: Overcommit and the OOM killer. Linux lets programs allocate more virtual memory than exists, because most is never touched. If the system really does run out of both RAM and swap, the out-of-memory (OOM) killer picks a process to terminate, usually the one using the most memory. So malloc can return a pointer successfully and the process still be killed later when it touches the pages.
unit-10.23ifgfbj3cp: Guard pages: unmapped pages placed at the ends of stacks or buffers so that an overflow causes an immediate fault instead of silent corruption (the tools in Lesson 9.7 use this trick).
unit-10.piz6z195su: Example 1: Replacement algorithms on the classic reference string
unit-10.2fy7o7phwwx: Count the page faults of FIFO, LRU and optimal with 3 frames. This is the standard textbook comparison.
unit-10.p8hllavkql: More frames, more faults: it really happens for FIFO on this reference string.
unit-10.hkr8eiiq6u: A circular list with reference bits: pages used recently get a second chance.
unit-10.26gcpnpqghv: The working set is the set of distinct pages used in the last few references. If it is bigger than the frames available, the process thrashes.
unit-10.365hacueaw: Example 5: The cost of a page fault
unit-10.143ntiw29ee: Even a tiny fault rate ruins performance because disks are so much slower than memory.
unit-10.2g6dkztuy1s: Thinking more frames always means fewer faults
unit-10.366yop4d5v: That holds for LRU and optimal (stack algorithms) but not for FIFO: Belady's anomaly.
unit-10.1lf17u828o0: Treating LRU as free to implement
unit-10.wvnzivjfpx: Exact LRU needs bookkeeping on every memory access. Real systems approximate it with reference bits (clock).
unit-10.t76xtji0gf: Forgetting that faults are measured on page misses only
unit-10.2acigeb9nuu: A reference to a page already in memory is a hit, even if it is the first reference since the last fault.
unit-10.2e151u69oxd: Ignoring dirty pages when estimating fault cost
unit-10.wzbk7yfd0z: Evicting a modified page costs a disk write as well as a read, doubling the fault time.
unit-10.2122gcge8i3: Assuming malloc success means memory is available
unit-10.503zdyzdnf: With overcommit, pages are provided only when touched. The process can be killed later by the OOM killer.
unit-10.gaqs12vnmu: Blaming the CPU when the disk light is on
unit-10.122l0ltqrqa: A slow machine with constant disk activity and low CPU use is often thrashing: it needs more RAM or fewer programs.
unit-10.26mqd6g8b85: Demand paging loads pages only when touched; pages not in RAM live on disk. A reference to such a page causes a page fault: the kernel loads the page (evicting a victim if needed, writing it first if dirty) and restarts the instruction.
unit-10.23r8a0kc4m8: A fault costs milliseconds while a memory access costs nanoseconds, so the fault rate must be tiny: EAT = (1 minus p)·m + p·fault_time.
unit-10.2e1qx29zpmi: FIFO evicts the oldest page; LRU the least recently used; OPT the page used farthest in the future (a benchmark, not implementable); clock approximates LRU with a reference bit and a sweeping hand.
unit-10.e20jvbtxpi: Belady's anomaly: FIFO can fault more with more frames. LRU and OPT are stack algorithms and never do.
unit-10.25alpmibd5b: The working set is the set of pages used in the last Δ references. When working sets exceed RAM, the system thrashes; the cure is to run fewer processes or add memory.
unit-10.1osu5q4hab3: Virtual memory also provides memory-mapped files, swap, copy-on-write, and guard pages. Linux's OOM killer terminates a process when memory and swap run out.
unit-10.2xsu4zeve2: Memory is volatile. The last piece of the picture is persistent storage: how disks are organised into files and directories. Lesson 10.9 covers file-system structures (blocks, inodes, directories, links), how files are allocated on disk, journaling for crash safety, and disk-scheduling algorithms.
unit-10.2imq5lkblm: See how the OS turns a disk of numbered blocks into named files in folders. Learn the layout of a Unix-style file system (superblock, inodes, bitmaps, data blocks), how paths are resolved, what hard and symbolic links are, how permissions use bits, how a journal keeps the disk consistent through crashes, and how the OS orders disk requests.
unit-10.28b5qyjziht: Explain the file abstraction and the main operations on files and directories
unit-10.1ojk1pp50w2: Describe inodes, directory entries and block allocation, and compute the maximum file size from an inode layout
unit-10.1g97vsjfsut: Resolve paths, including ., .. and relative paths, and distinguish hard links from symbolic links
unit-10.1sb6y5es2du: Check Unix permission bits for a user and group
unit-10.2g88czcwz3w: Explain why crashes corrupt file systems and how journaling and copy-on-write prevent it
unit-10.1520gczjb7z: Simulate disk scheduling policies (FCFS, SSTF, SCAN, LOOK) and compare head movement
unit-10.1rqh0ko09zy: Disks (and SSDs) store fixed-size blocks, typically 512 bytes or 4 KB, addressed by number. Nobody wants to remember "my essay is in blocks 8812 to 8830". The file system provides the abstraction we all use instead: a file is a named, growable sequence of bytes with attributes (size, owner, permissions, timestamps), organised in a tree of directories.
unit-10.1holyl1kxfg: The basic operations (system calls, Lesson 10.1): open, read, write, lseek (move the current position), close, create, unlink (delete), rename, mkdir, stat (read the attributes). The kernel keeps a current position for each open file, so successive reads continue where the last stopped.
unit-10.1gvxab7ksx7: A directory is just a special file whose content is a table of (name  to  file number) entries. A path like /home/maya/notes.txt is resolved one component at a time: start at the root directory, look up home, then within it maya, then notes.txt. A path starting with / is absolute; otherwise it is relative to the process's current working directory. Two special names are in every directory: . (the directory itself) and .. (its parent; at the root, .. is the root).
unit-10.125zrarmurg: The file system also provides mounting: attaching another disk's file system at a directory of the tree (/mnt/usb), so everything appears as one tree.
unit-10.21zcnsnl1du: A Unix-style file system divides the disk into regions:
unit-10.yhxpdkmoo8: An inode (index node) is the file's real identity. It stores everything about the file except its name: type (file, directory, link), owner and group, permission bits, size, timestamps, link count, and pointers to the data blocks. Names live in directories, which map names to inode numbers. That separation is what makes hard links possible.
unit-10.1xol27ens0j: The pointers are arranged to handle both tiny and enormous files: the classic ext2/UFS inode has 12 direct pointers, then one single indirect pointer (to a block full of pointers), one double indirect and one triple indirect. With 4 KB blocks and 4-byte pointers, one block holds 1024 pointers, so:
unit-10.2gb9xiiazw4: Small files, which are most files, need no indirect blocks at all, and only huge files pay for the extra reads. Modern file systems use extents (a start block plus a length) instead of listing every block, which is more compact and keeps files contiguous.
unit-10.ffyd0mfand: Other ways to track the blocks of a file:
unit-10.r5sryr0ien: Contiguous allocation: fast, simple, but external fragmentation and growth problems (Lesson 10.7) apply. Good for read-only media like CDs.
unit-10.1uhn75ucqup: Linked allocation: each block holds a pointer to the next. No fragmentation, but random access is slow (follow the chain) and one bad pointer loses the rest.
unit-10.1n65mx3iecn: FAT (File Allocation Table): the pointers are collected into one table in memory, indexed by block number. Used by USB sticks and SD cards, so it is everywhere, but needs a lot of memory for big disks.
unit-10.23ms0iv4ub1: Indexed allocation (inodes): one index per file, as above.
unit-10.1he7u1w12qj: Because names are separate from inodes, a file can have several names:
unit-10.1hvwxyzrqwg: A hard link is another directory entry pointing to the same inode. The inode's link count goes up by one. Deleting a name (unlink) lowers the count, and only when it reaches zero (and no process still has the file open) are the data blocks freed. All the names are equal; there is no "original". Hard links cannot cross file systems (inode numbers are only unique within one) and cannot link directories.
unit-10.qi5mt2naym: A symbolic (soft) link is a tiny file whose content is another path. Following it means looking up that path. It can point anywhere, even to something that doesn't exist (a dangling link), and it can cross file systems. A chain of symlinks that loops back on itself is detected by limiting how many are followed (Linux stops after 40) and reports "too many levels of symbolic links".
unit-10.1z27g5j5cep: ls -l shows the link count in its second column; ls -i shows inode numbers.
unit-10.295jpdzt25e: Each inode holds an owner (user id), a group, and nine permission bits in three groups of three, which Lesson 9.8 used as an example of flags: read (4), write (2), execute (1) for the owner, the group and others. Mode 0o754 is rwxr-xr--: the owner can do everything, the group can read and execute, others can only read.
unit-10.2gazdey8fnw: The kernel checks access in this order: if the user is the owner, use the owner bits; else if the user is in the file's group, use the group bits; else use the others bits. (It does not combine them: an owner with no access bits is denied even if "others" have access.) The superuser (uid 0) bypasses read and write checks. For a directory, read means you can list its names, write means you can add or remove entries, and execute means you can pass through it (look up names inside). Extra bits are setuid (run with the file owner's privileges), setgid and the sticky bit (on /tmp: only a file's owner may delete it). More flexible access-control lists (ACLs) exist on top of this simple model.
unit-10.2ftzbmfssyk: Creating a file changes several places on disk: the inode bitmap, the inode, the data bitmap, the data block, and the directory. If power fails between those writes, the file system is inconsistent: a block marked used but belonging to nothing (a leak), or a directory entry pointing at an unused inode (dangerous). Old file systems ran fsck after a crash, scanning the entire disk to repair such problems, which took many minutes for large disks.
unit-10.122f1nuwsk7: Journaling (ext3/4, NTFS, XFS) borrows an idea from databases: write-ahead logging. Before changing the real structures, write a description of the whole change to a reserved journal area:
unit-10.cis3lnoo41: Write a begin record and the intended block updates to the journal.
unit-10.2f16lbrzxvg: Write a commit record. The change is now durable: it will happen.
unit-10.mh01sz0okv: Checkpoint: apply the updates to their real locations.
unit-10.26ca35q0jp7: After a crash, recovery reads only the journal: transactions that have a commit record are replayed (applying them again is harmless); those with no commit are ignored, as if they had never started. Either the whole change happens or none of it, the property called atomicity. Recovery takes seconds, not minutes.
unit-10.23g8o2yfstf: Another approach is copy-on-write file systems (ZFS, Btrfs, APFS): never overwrite data in place; write new versions elsewhere, and switch a single root pointer atomically. Old versions remain, so snapshots are nearly free.
unit-10.o5umcs760m: Finally, the OS keeps a page cache of recently used disk blocks in RAM (the unused memory you see in free is mostly cache), and delays writes (write-back), which is why you should eject a USB stick properly, and why fsync exists to force data to disk when a program really needs it.
unit-10.lr798biebw: A hard disk has a head that must seek to the right cylinder (several milliseconds), wait for the platter to rotate to the right sector, then transfer data. Seek time dominates, so the order in which pending requests are served matters. Disk-scheduling policies, with a request queue of cylinder numbers:
unit-10.18unsqn4orw: FCFS: first come, first served. Fair but the head zig-zags wildly.
unit-10.18khw696qrq: SSTF (shortest seek time first): always go to the nearest request. Less movement, but can starve far-away requests.
unit-10.1vjugqtlfdj: SCAN (the "elevator"): sweep the head in one direction to the end of the disk serving requests on the way, then reverse. LOOK is the same but reverses at the last request instead of the disk edge. C-SCAN only serves on the way up, then jumps back to the start, giving more uniform waiting.
unit-10.1xftuq98iko: For the classic queue 98 183 37 122 14 124 65 67 with the head at cylinder 53 on a 200-cylinder disk: FCFS moves 640 cylinders, SSTF 236, SCAN 331, LOOK 299.
unit-10.t759yhwspa: SSDs have no moving parts, so there is no seek time and the order matters much less. Their quirks are different: flash must be erased in large blocks before rewriting, so the controller does wear levelling and the OS issues TRIM hints about deleted blocks. For redundancy and speed, several disks can be combined into a RAID array: striping (RAID 0) for speed, mirroring (RAID 1) for safety, parity (RAID 5) for a compromise.
unit-10.1utojz37ngm: Example 1: Maximum file size from an inode layout
unit-10.jeqm62vao4: Direct pointers, then indirect blocks that are blocks full of pointers. Each level multiplies the reach by the pointers per block.
unit-10.tmi485io0g: Example 2: A tiny file system with inodes and hard links
unit-10.1ugz89a81j2: Names map to inodes; inodes own the blocks. Deleting one of two names keeps the file alive.
unit-10.1vp1htruwb2: Normalising turns relative paths, dots and double dots into one canonical absolute path. Then the walk goes one component at a time.
unit-10.1xjikdnoz5a: The same request queue served under four policies. Total head movement measures the work.
unit-10.6z83ffyzt4: Example 5: Journal replay after a crash
unit-10.2gfd5gnot61: Committed transactions are replayed; the transaction that never committed leaves no trace.
unit-10.2du7bndh4o3: Thinking a file's name is stored in the file
unit-10.1wvlc2knofn: The name lives in a directory entry; the inode has no name. That's why a file can have many names (hard links) or be renamed without touching its data.
unit-10.hzsxeuhcqp: Expecting deleting a hard link to delete the data
unit-10.u3mttndylw: unlink removes one name. The data is freed only when the link count reaches zero and no process holds the file open.
unit-10.2a91v605sjt: Using a path before normalising it
unit-10.in6zs70zc: Checking whether /uploads/../etc/passwd starts with /uploads passes a naive test. Normalise first, then check.
unit-10.26l2g3tfxme: Forgetting that permission classes do not combine
unit-10.1rukn5qkn0t: The owner is judged by the owner bits only, even if the group or others have more access.
unit-10.28cle6hsr52: Assuming writes reach the disk immediately
unit-10.1o6hjnmm3oq: The OS caches and delays writes. Use flush and os.fsync when you must be sure the data is durable (and unmount drives safely).
unit-10.181zdbp3xag: Treating SSD scheduling like hard-disk scheduling
unit-10.g0zksuxlm8: Seek-minimising policies matter on spinning disks. On flash, the controller and its internal parallelism dominate.
unit-10.18hef8rtfsg: A file is a named sequence of bytes; a directory maps names to files. Paths are resolved component by component, with ., .., and absolute versus relative forms.
unit-10.1w5323d3f0m: An inode holds a file's metadata and block pointers (not its name); directories map names to inode numbers; bitmaps track free inodes and blocks. Inodes use direct and indirect pointers, so file size reach grows by a factor of block-size/pointer-size per level.
unit-10.23czfn47nhe: Hard links are extra names for one inode (counted; the file is freed when the count hits zero). Symbolic links store a path and can dangle or loop.
unit-10.27goxrt8p50: Permissions are nine bits (rwx for owner, group, others); the kernel uses exactly one class: owner, else group, else others. Root bypasses read and write.
unit-10.2dkar0ioujv: Journaling logs changes before applying them: committed transactions are replayed after a crash, uncommitted ones ignored. Copy-on-write file systems never overwrite in place.
unit-10.l166yl42vm: Disk scheduling (FCFS, SSTF, SCAN/LOOK) reduces seek movement on hard disks; SSDs change the trade-offs.
unit-10.293y3u4igml: That completes the tour of the operating system: processes, scheduling, concurrency, deadlock, memory and storage. The Unit 10 project ties several of these together: you will build a small operating-system simulator that schedules processes, manages page frames and serves a simulated workload, and report statistics from it.

unit-11.1l9jzk5f4ix: Understand how a message gets from one program to another across the world: the idea of layered protocols, how each layer wraps data in its own header, how bytes are laid out in a header, how a checksum catches damage, and why delay has two separate parts, latency and bandwidth.
unit-11.1j3cv4qgrm: By the end you will be able to:
unit-11.6wvlbmxco1: Describe packet switching and why the internet breaks messages into packets
unit-11.nyn6nbi5zz: Name the four layers of the internet model and say what each is responsible for
unit-11.2g3cwoz2pl4: Explain encapsulation and decapsulation, and build and parse a header with struct
unit-11.1c6acj4cpyj: Compute an internet checksum and say which errors it can and cannot catch
unit-11.243ggnjs58i: Calculate transfer time from bandwidth and latency, including store-and-forward delay
unit-11.1g9jba6l9v6: A network is computers (called hosts) connected by links and by routers that pass traffic along. The internet is a network of networks: your home network, your internet provider's network, a company's network, all connected together.
unit-11.1o8q4fgcmz4: Old telephone networks used circuit switching: a call reserved a dedicated path for its whole length, even during silences. The internet uses packet switching instead. A message is cut into packets of at most a few thousand bytes. Each packet is sent separately, carrying the address of its destination, and each router along the way decides where to send it next. Packets from many conversations share the same links, so the links stay busy and nobody needs to reserve anything. The price is that packets can be delayed, reordered, duplicated or lost, and something else must cope with that. Most of this unit is about who does that and how.
unit-11.1z9sp1apuo3: To make the whole thing manageable, networking is built from protocols: agreed rules about the format of messages and what to do when you receive one. A web browser and a web server can talk because both follow HTTP. Your laptop and your router can talk because both follow Wi-Fi's rules. Nobody needs to understand the whole system, only the protocols at their own level.
unit-11.mxvgauq8w6: Protocols are organised in layers. Each layer uses the services of the layer below and offers a simpler service to the layer above, hiding everything underneath. The internet model has four:
unit-11.18hplixvl6p: There is a table here. Have a look at it on screen.
unit-11.do9ywjgede: A famous seven-layer teaching model called OSI splits these differently (it separates physical signals, sessions and presentation), and you will meet its numbers in job descriptions ("layer 2 switch", "layer 7 load balancer").
