Layer 2 is the link layer, layer 3 the network (internet) layer, layer 4 the transport layer and layer 7 the application layer.
unit-11.1sj7pypw2m: The point of layering is separation of concerns: the web does not care whether you are on Wi-Fi or a cable, and Wi-Fi does not care what the bytes mean. You can replace one layer, say moving from IPv4 to IPv6 or from Ethernet to 5G, without rewriting the others. The one narrow waist everything depends on is IP: every network speaks it.
unit-11.1kc3j4g2emw: When an application sends data, each layer on the way down wraps it by adding a header (and sometimes a trailer) in front. This is encapsulation:
unit-11.217sdc6dskm: The application produces a message, for example an HTTP request.
unit-11.295oabdn51o: TCP adds a header (source port, destination port, sequence number, ...) making a segment.
unit-11.p6m24z4r5x: IP adds a header (source address, destination address, time to live, ...) making a packet.
unit-11.dwipwlxtnt: Ethernet or Wi-Fi adds a header and trailer making a frame, and the hardware sends the bits.
unit-11.1esoantg5wy: At the receiver the process is reversed, decapsulation: the link layer checks the frame and strips its header, IP reads its header and strips it, TCP does the same, and finally the message reaches the application. A router in the middle only looks at the link and IP headers: it strips the old frame, picks the next hop using the destination address, and wraps the packet in a new frame for the next link. It never needs to understand the TCP or HTTP inside. Each layer talks to the same layer at the other end (TCP to TCP) while physically using the layer below.
unit-11.1su93a4l33r: This nesting is the same pattern as a function call stack or an envelope inside an envelope, and as the nested brackets you will parse in this lesson's first exercise.
unit-11.uh8pk8unx9: A header is not text; it is a precise layout of bytes and even single bits, so that every computer reads it identically. Network protocols use big-endian order for multi-byte numbers (the most significant byte first), called network byte order, which is why Lesson 9.8's endianness matters here.
unit-11.1vbpoa4hnp4: Python's struct module packs and unpacks these layouts. A format string describes the fields: > means big-endian, B is one unsigned byte, H an unsigned 16-bit integer, I an unsigned 32-bit integer.
unit-11.xgjwawfezf: Here is some code. Have a look at it on screen.
unit-11.24gv2r4u5mp: Often several fields share a byte. You extract them with the shifts and masks from Lesson 9.8: the IPv4 header's first byte holds the version (the top 4 bits, always 4) and the header length (the bottom 4 bits). byte >> 4 and byte & 0x0F pull them out. When you read a hex dump of a real packet, this is what you are doing.
unit-11.1drl6p97gzr: A header also needs a length field or a fixed size, so the receiver knows where the header ends and the payload begins. Protocols that forget this are hard to extend.
unit-11.7a65wgv3nr: Bits get flipped by noise, so protocols include a checksum: a small number computed from the data, sent along with it. The receiver recomputes it and discards the packet on a mismatch. The internet checksum (used by IP, TCP and UDP) is simple:
unit-11.mp5dd58r0d: Treat the data as a sequence of 16-bit big-endian words (pad an odd final byte with a zero byte).
unit-11.nfjuxxo5sw: Add them all up as ordinary integers.
unit-11.1uc1826q3g4: While the sum is larger than 16 bits, fold the carry back in: (sum & 0xFFFF) + (sum >> 16).
unit-11.1jgl85oa2z8: The checksum is the bitwise NOT (one's complement) of the result, in 16 bits.
unit-11.1o7htw56k9w: The receiver adds up all the words including the checksum, folds, and expects all ones (0xFFFF). It is cheap to compute, and it catches every single-bit error and most bursts. But it is weak: it cannot see two 16-bit words swapped, because addition ignores order, and a determined attacker can easily make a corrupted packet pass. Stronger checks (the CRC in Ethernet frames, cryptographic hashes) exist at other layers, and the checksum is a reminder that each layer checks only what it needs to.
unit-11.6uoy1jifpl: People say "fast internet" for two different things:
unit-11.28xi2v3b0tg: Bandwidth (or throughput) is how many bits per second a link can carry, like the width of a pipe. Units are bits per second: kbps, Mbps, Gbps. Note the bits: a file size is in bytes, so a 100 MB file is 800 megabits.
unit-11.1pm9qzud3kj: Latency is how long a single bit takes to get from one end to the other, like the length of the pipe. It is limited by the speed of light in cable (about 200,000 km/s, so roughly 5 ms per 1000 km), plus processing.
unit-11.9tkus0qa75: The time to deliver a message is roughly latency + size / bandwidth. Which term dominates depends on the size: for a tiny message latency is everything, so a 1 Gbps link does not make a chat message to Australia arrive sooner; for a huge file bandwidth is everything. A protocol that needs many round trips (a request and a reply) pays the latency every time, which is why much protocol design aims to reduce round trips.
unit-11.4lr7krv618: A router must receive a whole packet before forwarding it (store-and-forward). So the delay of a packet over a path adds, for each link, its transmission delay (packet bits divided by link rate) and its propagation delay (the latency of that link). With several packets, the links work like an assembly line (pipelining): the first packet takes the whole path delay, and each later one follows one slowest-link transmission time behind it. That is why splitting a big message into packets makes it arrive sooner than sending it as one huge block.
unit-11.209yi4man64: Each layer wraps what the layer above produced. Unwrapping goes in the reverse order.
unit-11.19gfkdvqnms: Example 2: Packing a header with struct
unit-11.84i71qbu2q: Fixed-size fields in network byte order, then unpacked again. The hex dump is how engineers read real packets.
unit-11.ctkfrjb4sc: Add 16-bit words, fold the carries, invert. One flipped bit changes the answer; swapped words do not.
unit-11.dw3orzd46s: Transfer time is the latency plus size over bandwidth, plus one latency for every extra round trip. Watch which term dominates.
unit-11.xnly8d5sg5: Link speeds are in bits per second, file sizes in bytes. A 100 Mbps link moves about 12.5 megabytes per second, not 100.
unit-11.1d73rn0mvxj: Assuming faster bandwidth means lower latency
unit-11.1bv762wd5ml: Bandwidth is the width of the pipe and latency its length. Upgrading to a faster plan does not move Sydney any closer to London.
unit-11.20rw5htvo82: Network protocols are big-endian. Packing with the machine's native order (no > or ! in struct) works on your computer and breaks on another.
unit-11.2388f19kz5w: Always compare a length claimed in a header with the number of bytes you actually have before using it.
unit-11.1b0ziciefgx: Thinking a router reads the whole packet
unit-11.4q1r3tkqru: Routers look at the link and IP headers only. The transport and application data are opaque payload to them (though some "deep packet inspection" devices peek anyway).
unit-11.648l9c4qpv: Believing a checksum protects against attackers
unit-11.14zieen0i7k: A checksum catches accidents, not malice. Anyone who can change the data can recompute the checksum. Security needs cryptography (Unit 16).
unit-11.gp1a6xigj3: The internet uses packet switching: messages are cut into packets that share links and may be delayed, reordered or lost.
unit-11.mdrokumy9g: Protocols are layered: link, internet (IP), transport (TCP/UDP) and application (HTTP, DNS, ...). Each layer uses the one below and hides it from the one above.
unit-11.j50jqndysc: Encapsulation wraps data in a header at each layer on the way down; decapsulation unwraps it on the way up. Routers handle only link and IP headers.
unit-11.2183sblsaac: Headers are precise byte layouts in network byte order (big-endian). Python's struct packs and unpacks them, and shifts and masks extract fields that share a byte.
unit-11.17ftdtp2q7e: The internet checksum adds 16-bit words, folds carries and inverts. It catches single-bit errors but not reordered words, and offers no protection against an attacker.
unit-11.1aoccpucm7o: Delay is latency + size / bandwidth, plus a latency per round trip. Store-and-forward adds each link's transmission and propagation delay, and pipelining packets overlaps the links.
unit-11.ny1lufp6o6: Packets need addresses. Next is IP: how addresses are written and divided into networks, how a router chooses the next hop with a forwarding table, and how many devices share one address.
unit-11.2o3lhmsfp1: Learn how hosts are named on the internet. Read and write IPv4 addresses as 32-bit numbers, split them into a network part and a host part with a prefix length, compute subnet ranges, recognise private and special addresses, and see how a router uses the longest matching prefix to choose where to send a packet.
unit-11.oi728my8bx: Convert an IPv4 address between dotted-quad text and a 32-bit integer
unit-11.uy69mdigfn: Read CIDR notation and compute a subnet's network address, mask, broadcast address and number of usable hosts
unit-11.1sty1bj99z: Recognise private, loopback and link-local address ranges
unit-11.o65ip09rqq: Apply longest-prefix match to a forwarding table
unit-11.15qiq3js5rd: Explain NAT, DHCP, ARP and why IPv6 exists
unit-11.879fz5qt94: Every interface on the internet has an IP address. An IPv4 address is a 32-bit number, written as four bytes in decimal separated by dots, the dotted quad: 192.168.1.10 is the bytes 192, 168, 1 and 10. As a single integer it is 192 times 2²⁴ + 168 times 2¹⁶ + 1 times 2⁸ + 10, or 0xC0A8010A. Each part is 0 to 255 because it is one byte. There are 2³² = 4,294,967,296 possible addresses, roughly one for every person on Earth in 1983, which is why we ran out (see IPv6 below).
unit-11.ls2fq8hjqh: Treating an address as an integer is the key to every calculation in this lesson, using the shifts and masks of Lesson 9.8:
unit-11.215fi5v54e9: Addresses are not given out at random. They are hierarchical like phone numbers: a front part identifies a network and a back part a host on it. That is what lets a router store a few hundred thousand entries instead of four billion.
unit-11.17nmqp30tvu: The address is split into a network part (the first p bits, called the prefix) and a host part (the remaining 32  minus  p bits). The split is written after a slash: CIDR notation (Classless Inter-Domain Routing). 192.168.1.0/24 means the first 24 bits (192.168.1) name the network and the last 8 bits are for hosts.
unit-11.28bog0wduwg: The same information as a subnet mask: a 32-bit number with p ones followed by zeros. For /24 it is 255.255.255.0; for /26 it is 255.255.255.192. Using the mask:
unit-11.24g8uw58ggq: network address = ip & mask (host bits zeroed),
unit-11.1m3d94ifi6n: broadcast address = network | ~mask & 0xFFFFFFFF (host bits all ones): packets sent there go to every host on the network,
unit-11.1l8qp63a9or: the usable host addresses are everything in between, so a /p network has 2^(32-p)  minus  2 of them. The " minus 2" removes the network and broadcast addresses. (A /31 is a special point-to-point link with 2 usable addresses, and a /32 names a single host.)
unit-11.27yogsrjz4j: Two addresses are on the same network exactly when a & mask == b & mask. A host uses this test to decide whether the destination is local (send it directly) or remote (send it to the default gateway, the router).
unit-11.1tbf4a27au9: Worked example: 192.168.1.130/26. The mask is 255.255.255.192; the block size is 2⁶ = 64; the host is in the block starting at 128, so the network is 192.168.1.128, the broadcast is 192.168.1.191 and the usable hosts are .129 to .190, which is 62 of them.
unit-11.1y1a3gtw5yb: Subnetting divides a network into smaller ones by lengthening the prefix: a /24 splits into four /26 blocks. Aggregation (supernetting) does the reverse, so the rest of the internet can know a whole company as one route.
unit-11.cwwsmkoz6j: Your home has one public address from your provider, but every phone and laptop has a private one like 192.168.1.23. The router performs NAT (network address translation): when a private host sends a packet out, the router rewrites the source to its own public address and a fresh port number, remembers the mapping in a table, and reverses the rewrite for replies. Many devices share one public address. NAT also means outside computers cannot start connections to your devices, which is a side effect, not real security.
unit-11.2avpuvo3wf4: Getting an address, and finding a neighbour
unit-11.mf4dt40snr: A device usually learns its address using DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol): it broadcasts "I need an address", and a server answers with an address, the subnet mask, the default gateway, the DNS server address and a lease time. When the lease runs out the device renews or gets another.
unit-11.162k840groy: On a local link the frame must carry a hardware (MAC) address, not an IP address. ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) bridges the two: to send to 192.168.1.1, a host broadcasts "who has 192.168.1.1?", the owner replies with its MAC address, and the host caches the answer in its ARP table.
unit-11.2cqpy3twbe3: A router has a forwarding table: a list of (prefix, next hop) entries. For each packet it finds every entry whose prefix contains the destination address, and uses the one with the longest prefix (the most specific). A route with the prefix 0.0.0.0/0 matches every address and is the default route, used when nothing more specific applies.
unit-11.1ibdxj4jhqc: 10.1.2.7 matches all four; the longest is /24, so it goes to C,
unit-11.11odqdxlj7v: 10.1.9.9 matches /16, /8 and /0, so it goes to B,
unit-11.dw5thjsff0: 10.9.9.9 goes to A, and 8.8.8.8 to the default G.
unit-11.1opyfw9dhew: This rule lets a small specific route override a broad one (a company can announce a more specific route for one office), and is why internet routing tables work at all. Real routers use special data structures (tries, Lesson 7.x style, and dedicated hardware) rather than scanning, but the rule is the same. How the table gets filled in is the subject of the next lesson.
unit-11.1pvrwb47fz5: IPv4's 4.3 billion addresses ran out (the last blocks were given out in 2011), and NAT stretched them. IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses, enough for about 3.4  times  10³⁸. They are written as eight groups of four hex digits, 2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:ff00:0042:8329, with leading zeros dropped and one run of zero groups replaced by ::, giving 2001:db8::ff00:42:8329. The prefix idea is identical (2001:db8::/32), and in IPv6 every device can have its own public address again, so NAT is unnecessary. IPv4 and IPv6 run side by side during a long transition, a good example of how hard it is to change the "narrow waist".
unit-11.1b4hfx8en9b: Four bytes make a 32-bit number. Shifts pack them and shifts with a mask unpack them.
unit-11.1nklbfwe4d5: The mask, the network address and the broadcast address are all bit operations on the integer form.
unit-11.2a3hht5ih6h: Python's standard library already does all of this. It is worth knowing, and a good cross-check of your own code.
unit-11.ur619gf1ey: Among all prefixes that contain the address, the most specific one wins.
unit-11.47bpd6t6xy: The router rewrites private sources to its public address and a fresh port, and reverses it for replies.
unit-11.1lup6rkoaqr: In a /24 there are 256 addresses but 254 usable hosts: the all-zeros host part is the network address and the all-ones part is the broadcast address.
unit-11.ihpy9e1is6: As text "10.0.0.9" > "10.0.0.10" is true because "9" sorts after "1". Compare integers (or use the ipaddress module).
unit-11.ic1lp9h66n: ip.startswith("172.16") misses 172.17 through 172.31, which are also in 172.16.0.0/12. Prefixes live in bits, not in decimal digits.
unit-11.ekg27tab0v: Choosing the first match instead of the longest
unit-11.1pqqgqqjk7h: A router that stops at the first matching route can send traffic the wrong way when a broader route is listed before a more specific one.
unit-11.1jku4rdt7vi: NAT blocks unsolicited incoming connections as a side effect, but it was designed to save addresses. A real firewall is a deliberate set of rules.
unit-11.188f38rpyr: Using a /24 mask for every network
unit-11.zcnrhsfzhr: Prefix lengths are anything from 0 to 32. Check the mask of the network you are on rather than assuming.
unit-11.18zasj3jh4h: An IPv4 address is a 32-bit number written as four bytes (192.168.1.10). Work with it as an integer using shifts and masks.
unit-11.28azzoijblr: CIDR notation a.b.c.d/p gives a network part (the first p bits) and a host part. The mask, network address (ip & mask) and broadcast address (host bits all ones) follow from it, and a network has 2^(32-p) - 2 usable hosts.
unit-11.3d9qlwwskf: Private ranges (10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16), loopback (127/8) and link-local (169.254/16) are special. NAT lets many private hosts share one public address.
unit-11.11k5h3yomut: DHCP assigns addresses automatically; ARP maps an IP address on the local link to a hardware address.
unit-11.1uyildrs508: Routers forward by longest-prefix match: of all table entries containing the destination, the most specific wins, and 0.0.0.0/0 is the default route.
unit-11.e57emnp2fy: IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses, with the same prefix idea, to end address shortage.
unit-11.1jaif3i9790: A forwarding table has to come from somewhere. Next: routing. How do routers learn the shape of the network, find the shortest paths with the algorithms from Unit 8, and react when a link fails?
unit-11.1pj94sv4mqk: Learn how routers build their forwarding tables. Distinguish forwarding from routing, see how link-state routing runs Dijkstra on a map every router shares, how distance-vector routing computes the same thing with only neighbour-to-neighbour gossip, why loops and "counting to infinity" happen, and how the internet links thousands of independently run networks with BGP.
unit-11.1x4snpcxrs5: Distinguish forwarding (per packet) from routing (building the tables)
unit-11.17gr674ej4l: Compute next hops with a link-state calculation (Dijkstra) over a network graph
unit-11.21gi1nnew60: Simulate distance-vector routing, including the Bellman-Ford update rule and convergence
unit-11.1ydfqvop9d4: Explain routing loops, TTL, counting to infinity and split horizon
unit-11.38dswaxnum: Describe autonomous systems and how BGP chooses routes using policy and path length
unit-11.26rcg6vsmtk: Two jobs are easily confused. Forwarding is what a router does to every packet: look at the destination address, find the longest matching prefix in the forwarding table (Lesson 11.2) and send the packet out of the right link. It must happen in nanoseconds. Routing is the slower job of building that table: working out which neighbour leads to each destination, and keeping the answer current when links break or appear.
unit-11.2adzkeu9mt6: We can model a network as a weighted graph (Unit 6 and Unit 8): routers are nodes, links are edges, and each link has a cost (distance, delay, or a number the operator chooses). The goal of routing is each router's next hop for every destination, such that following the next hops from router to router gives the cheapest path. The two classic approaches differ in what each router knows.
unit-11.17wm9rbglfp: In link-state routing (OSPF, IS-IS), every router learns the whole map:
unit-11.1eywzuy6ly9: Each router discovers its neighbours and the cost of the links to them.
unit-11.j8tfc14w6w: It floods this link-state advertisement to every other router. Each router passes on a new advertisement to all neighbours except the one it came from, and remembers the latest sequence number so that each advertisement is flooded once.
unit-11.6hueuciv5o: Now every router holds the same graph, and runs Dijkstra's algorithm (Lesson 8.8) from itself. Instead of storing the whole path to each destination, it records only the first hop.
unit-11.eob9fcvz4a: Because everyone computes from identical data, the tables are consistent. When a link fails, its neighbours flood a new advertisement and every router recomputes. The price is memory and CPU proportional to the whole network, so link-state is used inside one organisation, not across the whole internet.
unit-11.1v9ystyp9ii: One practical detail: when two paths cost the same (equal-cost multipath), all routers must break ties the same way (or deliberately split traffic) or packets may loop. Our exercises always pick the lexicographically smallest path.
unit-11.kw7q53e8fw: In distance-vector routing (RIP and the classic Bellman-Ford approach), a router does not know the map. It only knows its neighbours and what they tell it. Each router keeps a table of destination  to  (cost, next hop) and periodically sends its vector of costs to its neighbours. On receiving neighbour N's vector, with c the link cost to N, the router applies the Bellman-Ford update for each destination d:
unit-11.14cjh3r9k1j: A cheaper route replaces the old one, with N as the new next hop. Repeating this, good news spreads one hop per round, and after at most (number of routers  minus  1) rounds every table is correct. No router needs the map, which makes distance-vector simple and cheap. But there is a famous weakness.
unit-11.8vuatfdzkb: Counting to infinity. Suppose A reaches C through B, and the link B–C breaks. B now has no route to C, but A still advertises "I can reach C at cost 2", so B decides to route through A, at cost 3. A then hears B's new cost and updates to 4, then B to 5, and so on: the two routers keep adding to each other's cost, each stuck in a routing loop in which packets bounce between them. Bad news travels slowly. Protocols mitigate this with:
unit-11.1nux1dvl9u7: a small maximum that counts as infinity (RIP uses 16), so the counting stops;
unit-11.24d31ozq3vn: split horizon: never advertise a route back to the neighbour it came through (and poison reverse: advertise it with cost infinity);
unit-11.mmuv83ye60: triggered updates: send news of a change immediately instead of waiting for the next periodic update.
unit-11.12uygqiozga: Split horizon cures the two-router loop but not all loops, which is one reason large networks prefer link-state.
unit-11.16223lo8vdy: Routing tables can be briefly inconsistent while news propagates, so packets may travel in circles. To stop a looping packet from living forever, every IP packet carries a TTL (time to live), a counter that each router decrements. When it reaches zero the router drops the packet and sends back an error message (ICMP "time exceeded").
unit-11.1e21qd6o5d6: The traceroute tool turns this into a map: it sends probes with TTL 1, 2, 3, ... and each router along the path reports itself when it discards the packet that expired there. Seeing the list of routers (and the delay to each) shows where a slow link is.
unit-11.11o0tx1y4da: The internet is a network of networks
unit-11.1bmw7jcdlfc: No single protocol can run the whole internet: it is too large for link-state, and different organisations want to keep their internals private and apply their own policies. The internet is divided into about 100,000 autonomous systems (AS): networks under one administration, such as an ISP, a university or a cloud provider, each with an AS number.
unit-11.lih1olwnaa: Inside an AS, an interior gateway protocol (OSPF, RIP) finds the best paths by cost.
unit-11.krcg9huqzy: Between ASes, BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) exchanges reachability. A BGP router tells its neighbours: "I can reach this prefix, via this AS path" such as AS 64500  to  AS 64510  to  AS 64520. Receivers prepend their own AS number before passing the route on.
unit-11.a47f9dwklp: BGP is a path-vector protocol. Seeing the whole AS path has two benefits. It prevents loops: a router discards any route whose AS path already contains its own AS number. And it lets operators apply policy: ASes prefer routes through customers (who pay them) over peers over providers, and often choose by business reasons, not shortest path. Among otherwise equal routes, the shorter AS path wins.
unit-11.2073r8jx87j: Because BGP is built on trust, a mistaken or malicious announcement can divert the traffic of the world: in 2008 a Pakistani ISP's attempt to block YouTube accidentally took it offline globally, and similar leaks still happen. Securing BGP is an ongoing effort (Unit 16).
unit-11.xkllu9hsnd: Example 1: Link-state: Dijkstra from each router
unit-11.1mj4xupd0ss: Every router has the same map. Each runs Dijkstra and keeps only the first hop toward every destination.
unit-11.1duschltnm2: Example 2: Distance-vector: gossip until nothing changes
unit-11.25g0cflwmia: Each round, every router looks at its neighbours' tables from the last round. News travels one hop per round.
unit-11.nre0tf87s: After the B–C link breaks, A and B keep feeding each other stale news. Infinity is capped at 16, as in RIP.
unit-11.3rpcqzknwa: Example 4: A forwarding loop and TTL
unit-11.ws5twa9k8c: Two routers with inconsistent tables each think the other is the way. The TTL ends the loop.
unit-11.1ksrdeixsom: Routes carry the list of ASes they cross. Discard routes that already contain your own AS, then prefer the shortest.
unit-11.1rogqh7ldvt: Routing builds the table (slowly, occasionally). Forwarding uses it (for every packet, very fast).
unit-11.ory2mbacky: A distance-vector router never sees the whole graph, only its neighbours' cost vectors. If your code needs the full graph to compute a router's table, it is link-state.
unit-11.10dt8frfm2l: Ignoring worse news from the next hop
unit-11.21893l86vo1: If your next hop says the route got more expensive, believe it. Refusing bad news from the next hop leaves a stale, cheap-looking route in place.
unit-11.msgz8pgif9: Without a TTL a looping packet would circulate forever and clog the links. Every router decrements it and drops the packet at zero.
unit-11.k2nfkqt816: Believing BGP finds the shortest path
unit-11.1ezm1b4ya5o: BGP follows business policy first. The path chosen may be longer in hops or in miles.
unit-11.o1kwtova1e: When two paths cost the same, routers that break the tie differently can create loops. Use one deterministic rule everywhere.
unit-11.u6lb8ionwi: Forwarding moves each packet using the table; routing builds the table. Costs make the network a weighted graph and routers compute next hops.
unit-11.1ry115yznho: Link-state routing floods every link to every router, which then runs Dijkstra on the full map and keeps the first hop to each destination.
unit-11.bqoqgq4uny: Distance-vector routing uses only neighbour gossip and the Bellman-Ford update cost = min(cost, link + neighbour's cost), converging in at most n - 1 rounds.
unit-11.26tflxjc10u: Distance-vector can count to infinity after a failure. A small infinity (RIP's 16), split horizon and triggered updates limit the damage.
unit-11.chziwj59ea: Each packet's TTL is decremented per hop and the packet is dropped at zero, ending loops and powering traceroute.
unit-11.28p8xw2joag: The internet is thousands of autonomous systems. BGP is a path-vector protocol: it carries AS paths, rejects routes containing its own AS, and chooses by policy first and path length second.
unit-11.1fo3af68pce: Now packets can reach the right host. The next lesson covers what the hosts do with them: the transport layer, ports, UDP and the TCP connection.
unit-11.26dcuwpc6l3: See how data gets from a program on one machine to a program on another. Learn what ports are and how a host sorts arriving packets, how simple and fast UDP is, and how TCP turns an unreliable packet network into a reliable, ordered byte stream using sequence numbers, acknowledgements, a three-way handshake and a state machine.
unit-11.1qibcf80uib: Explain ports, multiplexing and the (address, port) pairs that identify a connection
unit-11.29ojo6oczbf: Build and parse a UDP datagram and say what UDP does and does not guarantee
unit-11.md6mbv5nz4: Describe TCP segments, flags, sequence and acknowledgement numbers, and trace a handshake and a teardown
unit-11.2fxx31nphpv: Split a byte stream into segments and reassemble it from out-of-order arrivals
unit-11.s3cqqg8oep: Walk a TCP connection through its states
unit-11.21njgpsbcql: Choose between TCP and UDP for an application
unit-11.1l4im0jjvmf: IP delivers a packet to a host. But a host runs many programs at once: a browser with twenty tabs, a music app, a mail client. The transport layer finishes the delivery to the right program. The mechanism is the port: a 16-bit number (0 to 65535) that names an endpoint on a host.
unit-11.29kuuuk7olq: A server listens on a well-known port so clients know where to find it: 80 for HTTP, 443 for HTTPS, 22 for SSH, 25 for email, 53 for DNS. Ports below 1024 are "well-known", reserved for services run by the system. A client program does not need a fixed port: the operating system gives it a random ephemeral port (typically in the 49152 to 65535 range) for each connection.
unit-11.22gek9xu0a6: A TCP connection is therefore identified by four numbers, the 4-tuple (source address, source port, destination address, destination port). Two browser tabs talking to the same web server share the server's address and port 443, but their ephemeral source ports differ, so the server (and the OS) can tell the conversations apart. Sending incoming data to the right program is called demultiplexing; letting many programs share one network connection is multiplexing.
unit-11.2cv8p9y9tya: The transport layer offers two main services:
unit-11.kkbckvvzwp: UDP: a thin wrapper that adds ports and a checksum to IP's "best effort" delivery.
unit-11.om8mkxxylr: TCP: a full, reliable, ordered byte stream between two programs, built from UDP-like pieces plus a great deal of machinery.
unit-11.1oax40bgyox: The User Datagram Protocol has an 8-byte header with four 16-bit fields:
unit-11.4sjnqrmv1t: That is all. UDP has no connection, no acknowledgements, no retransmission and no ordering. Each datagram is sent independently, may be lost, duplicated or reordered, and keeps its boundaries (one send is one receive). A damaged datagram is silently dropped.
unit-11.1jmhtt50pef: This sounds like a bad deal, but it is exactly right for some jobs. It adds no setup delay (nothing to negotiate), no waiting for retransmissions (an old video frame is worthless anyway), and little overhead. So UDP carries DNS queries (one tiny question, one tiny answer; the application just asks again if there is no reply), voice and video calls, online games, and QUIC, the newer transport that HTTP/3 uses, which builds its own reliability on top of UDP.
unit-11.19v6x0n4520: The Transmission Control Protocol gives programs the illusion of a pipe: bytes written at one end come out of the other complete, in order and without duplicates, even though the network underneath loses, reorders and duplicates packets. TCP is connection-oriented: the two ends first agree to talk, and keep state for the connection.
unit-11.og2kia6o5v: A TCP segment has a header of at least 20 bytes. The fields that matter most:
unit-11.2otrxoec92: source and destination port (16 bits each),
unit-11.1ftia9fscij: sequence number (32 bits): the position in the stream of the first data byte in this segment,
unit-11.ooe3bz2bbc: acknowledgement number (32 bits): the position of the next byte the sender of this segment expects to receive,
unit-11.1eakc2yv268: flags: SYN (open a connection), ACK (the acknowledgement number is valid), FIN (I have finished sending), RST (abort), PSH and URG,
unit-11.z132cy26j5: window: how many more bytes the sender of this segment is willing to receive (flow control, next lesson),
unit-11.mj0fjijv6x: Sequence numbers count bytes, not segments. If a segment has sequence number 1000 and carries 500 bytes, it covers bytes 1000 to 1499, and the receiver acknowledges with 1500: "I have everything up to 1499 and want 1500 next". That is a cumulative acknowledgement. SYN and FIN each consume one sequence number, as if they were a byte, so that they too can be acknowledged. Sequence numbers are 32 bits and wrap around, so arithmetic on them is done modulo 2³².
unit-11.m7djbvshf9: Segmentation. The application hands TCP any amount of data. TCP cuts it into segments no larger than the MSS (maximum segment size), usually 1460 bytes, so each fits in a 1500-byte Ethernet frame after the IP and TCP headers. The receiver puts segments back in order by their sequence numbers (reassembly), holds on to early arrivals, and delivers bytes to the program only up to the first gap.
unit-11.28xjn13dwr1: Before data flows, the two ends synchronise their sequence numbers. Each side picks a random initial sequence number (ISN), which prevents old stray segments of a previous connection from being mistaken for new ones (and makes blind spoofing harder). The exchange takes three segments, the three-way handshake:
unit-11.1koj214rc04: Client  to  server: SYN, seq = x. "I'd like to connect; my numbers start at x."
unit-11.182lo6dnypo: Server  to  client: SYN+ACK, seq = y, ack = x + 1. "OK; mine start at y, and I expect your next byte to be x + 1."
unit-11.14szardmvpm: Client  to  server: ACK, seq = x + 1, ack = y + 1. "Got it."
unit-11.15m7u3pemvt: Now the connection is established. The client can send data in the very next segment. Notice the cost: one full round trip before any data moves, which is why latency (Lesson 11.1) makes opening connections expensive, and why HTTP keeps connections open for reuse.
unit-11.264dgxb5w7b: Closing is done with FINs. Each direction is closed independently: the side finished with its data sends FIN, the other ACKs it; later the other side sends its own FIN and receives an ACK. So a normal close takes four segments. The side that closes first lingers in TIME_WAIT for a couple of minutes, so that late stray segments cannot confuse a new connection that reuses the same 4-tuple. A RST aborts a connection immediately, for example when a segment arrives for a port nobody is listening on.
unit-11.2fh3gs0lmc4: Each end of a connection keeps a state and moves between states when events happen: the application calls something, or a segment arrives. The main states for a client and a server:
unit-11.4hp0pz7i44: When you see thousands of connections stuck in CLOSE_WAIT on a server, it usually means the program forgot to close its sockets: the state tells you whose fault it is. netstat and ss show these states.
unit-11.gqjea5kp3l: Choose TCP when every byte must arrive correctly and in order and you can afford some delay: web pages, email, file transfers, SSH, databases. Choose UDP when timeliness matters more than completeness, when messages are tiny and independent, or when you want to design your own reliability: DNS lookups, live audio and video, games, streaming telemetry. A lost frame in a video call is better skipped than waited for. The next lesson shows how TCP detects loss and what it does about it.

unit-11.1ema1b58zc6: TCP promises reliability on an unreliable network. How does it actually notice a lost segment and fix it, and how does it avoid flooding a slow receiver or an overloaded network? That is the next lesson: retransmission, flow control and congestion control.

Then learn how TCP chooses its timeout, how fast retransmit reacts to duplicate acknowledgements, how flow control protects the receiver, and how congestion control (slow start and AIMD) protects the network.

unit-11.1glv5j6hx7q: Packets are lost for several reasons: a router's queue is full and drops them, a bit error is caught by a checksum, a wireless signal fades. The sender cannot see this directly. All it can observe is the absence of an acknowledgement. The general technique is ARQ (automatic repeat request): the receiver acknowledges what it gets, and the sender retransmits whatever is not acknowledged within a timeout.
unit-11.139221ngzj1: The simplest ARQ is stop-and-wait: send one packet, wait for its ACK, then send the next. If no ACK comes before the timeout, send the same packet again. Each packet carries a sequence number so that the receiver can recognise a duplicate (the ACK was lost, so the sender sent it twice) and ignore the extra copy while still acknowledging it. This works, and the protocol is easy to get right. But it is dreadfully slow on long links.
unit-11.13de15ggwex: Suppose a 100 Mbps link with a 40 ms round-trip time. A 1500-byte packet takes 12,000 bits / 100 Mbps = 0.12 ms to transmit, and then the sender sits idle for the 40 ms it takes the ACK to return. The link is busy 0.12 ms out of every 40.12 ms. That is a utilisation of 0.3%, or 300 kbps on a 100 Mbps link.
unit-11.cx5bu01ya: utilisation = transmit time / (transmit time + round-trip time)
unit-11.268p6vs2slp: The cure is pipelining: allow several packets to be in flight (sent but not yet acknowledged). The amount of data needed to keep the pipe full is the bandwidth-delay product (BDP): bandwidth  times  round-trip time. For our example, 100 Mbps  times  40 ms = 4,000,000 bits = 500,000 bytes, about 334 packets. That is the window the sender needs for full speed. Fast, long ("long fat") networks need huge windows, which is why TCP window sizes have grown over the years.
unit-11.bvak6eol0w: A sliding window protocol lets the sender have up to W unacknowledged packets outstanding. The window covers sequence numbers from base (the oldest unacknowledged) to base + W - 1. As acknowledgements arrive the window slides forward and new packets become eligible. There are two classic ways to deal with loss inside a window.
unit-11.hwnos6hyzr: Go-back-N (GBN). The receiver accepts packets only in order and discards any that arrive after a gap. It acknowledges cumulatively ("everything up to k"). When the sender times out on the oldest packet, it goes back and resends the whole window starting from base. It is simple (the receiver needs no buffer), but one loss makes the sender resend packets that had actually arrived.
unit-11.1zbpkl2uc70: Selective repeat (SR). The receiver buffers out-of-order packets and acknowledges each one individually. The sender retransmits only the packets that were lost. It uses the link more efficiently, at the price of a buffer and more bookkeeping at both ends.
unit-11.227tj8ji0np: TCP is a hybrid. Its acknowledgements are cumulative like go-back-N, but modern TCP adds SACK (selective acknowledgements) so the receiver can say "I also have bytes 5000 to 6000", letting the sender retransmit only what is missing, like selective repeat.
unit-11.10s4e506lxm: Waiting for a timeout is slow. TCP has a faster signal. If segment 2 is lost but segments 3, 4 and 5 arrive, the receiver keeps acknowledging "I still want 2": it sends duplicate ACKs. When the sender sees three duplicate ACKs (four ACKs in a row for the same number) it concludes that the segment was lost, not merely delayed, and retransmits immediately without waiting for the timer. This is fast retransmit.
unit-11.1bsz3bq6g1r: The timer still matters, and its value is a judgement call. Too short, and the sender retransmits packets that were merely slow (wasting bandwidth, and feeding congestion). Too long, and a loss stalls the connection. TCP measures the round-trip time (RTT) of each acknowledged segment and keeps a smoothed average with an exponentially weighted moving average (EWMA):
unit-11.203f2quohyl: srtt = 7/8 · srtt + 1/8 · sample rttvar = 3/4 · rttvar + 1/4 · |srtt  minus  sample| (computed with the old srtt) rto = srtt + 4 · rttvar
unit-11.10aj5t2t6hh: The first sample sets srtt = sample and rttvar = sample / 2. The variation term makes the timeout generous when the network is jittery. If a timeout does occur, the RTO is doubled (exponential backoff) each time until an ACK arrives, so a dead path is not hammered. Also, Karn's rule: never use the RTT of a retransmitted segment as a sample, since you cannot tell which transmission the ACK answers.
unit-11.1oxihc97ran: A fast sender could overwhelm a slow receiver whose buffer is full. TCP's flow control prevents this: in every segment the receiver advertises its receive window (rwnd), the number of bytes it has room for. The sender never allows more than rwnd bytes to be unacknowledged. If the receiver's application is slow to read, rwnd shrinks, possibly to zero, and the sender pauses (and probes occasionally to see if space has opened up). Flow control protects the receiver.
unit-11.ithe50g07p: A different danger is the network itself. If every sender transmits as fast as the receivers allow, routers' queues overflow and packets are dropped, causing retransmissions that add even more traffic: congestion collapse, which actually happened to the early internet in 1986. The fix, by Van Jacobson, was to make TCP infer congestion from loss and slow down.
unit-11.17yb9fpsc5u: Each sender keeps a congestion window (cwnd, measured here in segments), and may have at most min(cwnd, rwnd) unacknowledged. It adjusts cwnd like this:
unit-11.1mbi9cddw11: Slow start. Start with cwnd = 1 and double it every RTT (every ACK adds one segment) until it reaches a threshold ssthresh. Despite the name, this is exponential growth: the sender is quickly probing for the available capacity.
unit-11.okbok9hton: Congestion avoidance. Beyond ssthresh, grow linearly: add 1 segment per RTT.
unit-11.1sl1apled4r: On loss, reduce. Tahoe: set ssthresh = cwnd / 2 and restart slow start from cwnd = 1. Reno: if the loss was signalled by three duplicate ACKs (the network is still delivering something), do fast recovery: set ssthresh = cwnd / 2 and cwnd = ssthresh, staying in congestion avoidance. A timeout is a more serious sign and still resets cwnd to 1.
unit-11.24yvore541t: Increase by one, decrease by half: additive increase, multiplicative decrease (AIMD). This rule has a lovely property: when several connections share a bottleneck, AIMD drives them to fair, equal shares of the link, with no central coordinator. The cwnd graph looks like a sawtooth. Newer algorithms (CUBIC, the Linux default, and BBR from Google, which measures bandwidth and RTT instead of waiting for loss) change the curve but not the idea.
unit-11.dx1e2es64n: A connection's throughput is bounded by cwnd  times  MSS / RTT. So distance (a larger RTT) directly reduces the speed of a single TCP connection, which is why content delivery networks put servers close to users.

unit-11.1nshrs1s35y: It doubles every round trip. It is "slow" only compared with starting at full speed, which would risk overwhelming the network.
unit-11.1igmgokouj3: ARQ repeats what is not acknowledged. Stop-and-wait sends one packet per round trip, so utilisation is tx / (tx + RTT), tiny on long links.
unit-11.80736dgo89: The bandwidth-delay product is the data needed in flight to fill the pipe. Sliding windows keep many packets outstanding.
unit-11.mvtu0tt3cb: Go-back-N resends the whole window from the first loss; selective repeat resends only lost packets. TCP uses cumulative ACKs plus SACK.
unit-11.gz8abf9e4i: Three duplicate ACKs trigger fast retransmit. Otherwise a retransmission timeout srtt + 4 * rttvar fires, doubling on each failure.
unit-11.pwbvv3exzw: Flow control uses the receiver's advertised window; congestion control uses cwnd: slow start (doubling), congestion avoidance (+1 per RTT) and a multiplicative decrease on loss (AIMD). Tahoe restarts from 1; Reno halves and continues.

unit-11.bscno2omuo: Computers route by IP address, but people remember names. And names carry a second benefit: they can stay the same while the address changes. A website can move to a new server, or be spread over a hundred servers around the world, and its name stays example.com. The Domain Name System (DNS) is the global, distributed database that maps names to the information needed to reach them, mostly IP addresses.
unit-11.1wxurvrx0d: A single file listing every name could not work for a billion names, and in the early internet it nearly did (a file called HOSTS.TXT was copied around by hand). DNS replaced it in 1983 with a design that scales: the database is split into zones, each managed by whoever owns that part of the name space, and queries are answered by a hierarchy of servers with heavy caching. DNS is one of the internet's most-used services: almost every connection begins with a lookup.
unit-11.25cezn9l3vn: A domain name is a list of labels separated by dots, read from right to left from the most general to the most specific. In www.example.com:
unit-11.1j74ptvi71o: example is a second-level name that someone registered under com,
unit-11.77keibc6nu: www is a host name chosen by the owner of example.com.
unit-11.18s94f832qg: The full form ends with a dot, www.example.com., where the final empty label stands for the root of the tree. Each label is 1 to 63 characters of letters, digits and hyphens (not starting or ending with a hyphen), and the whole name is at most 253 characters. Names are case-insensitive: Example.COM is example.com.
unit-11.1eii1nr2kne: The name tree is mirrored by a tree of servers, and each level delegates authority to the next:
unit-11.spmf9p4pww: The root servers (13 named addresses, each replicated at hundreds of sites) know only who runs each TLD: "for anything under com, ask these servers".
unit-11.1o07c8vrciq: The TLD servers (com, org, uk, ...) know who runs each registered name beneath them: "for example.com, ask ns1.example.com".
unit-11.1w5si0x2ure: The authoritative servers of a domain hold its actual records and give the final answers.
unit-11.1k7n8a6lsv: A pointer from one level to the next is a delegation, stored as an NS record. The owner of a zone can create subdomains freely (mail.example.com, a.b.c.example.com) without asking anyone.
unit-11.2rtxfa1vy3: Your program calls a library function such as getaddrinfo. This stub resolver is deliberately simple: it asks one recursive resolver (usually run by your ISP, your company, or a public service) and waits for the answer. The recursive resolver does the work:
unit-11.1a9y9s771oz: It asks a root server: "who knows www.example.com?" The root replies with a referral: the servers for com.
unit-11.qfkzwc6qh9: It asks a com server, which replies with a referral to the servers for example.com.
unit-11.8398383b5o: It asks one of those authoritative servers, which answers: www.example.com is 93.184.216.34.
unit-11.k52gs1osut: It returns the answer to the stub resolver and remembers all of it.
unit-11.4furk8wvth: Asking one server after another and following referrals is iterative resolution. The stub's request to the recursive resolver ("do it all for me") is a recursive query. Queries are normally sent in a single UDP datagram to port 53 (Lesson 11.4); if the answer is too large, or for zone transfers, DNS switches to TCP.
unit-11.j2d0h5sqrs: A name can also be an alias: a CNAME record says "blog.example.com is really www.example.com". The resolver restarts the search with the canonical name. A CNAME may chain, but not loop.
unit-11.ly4t4h0jzr: If every lookup went to the root, the root servers would melt. Instead every record in an answer carries a TTL (time to live): the number of seconds the answer may be reused. Resolvers (and your operating system, and your browser) keep answers in a cache until the TTL runs out. Popular names are answered instantly from memory; the root servers are asked only rarely, because the referral to com stays cached for a day or two.
unit-11.1qbevq24qg1: The TTL is a trade-off made by the domain's owner:
unit-11.713jgztmqv: A long TTL (a day) means fewer queries and faster lookups, but changes are slow to take effect: after moving a website to a new server, some visitors keep going to the old address until their cached copy expires.
unit-11.6pgng2t7v1: A short TTL (a minute) allows quick changes and fast failover but increases load and latency. Operators lower the TTL a day before a planned migration.
unit-11.2z6u7gspos: Resolvers also cache negative answers. A reply of NXDOMAIN ("that name does not exist") is cached too, for a time given by the zone, so repeated lookups of a mistyped name do not hammer the servers.
unit-11.2bnhgnxjq3m: A zone is a set of resource records, each with a name, a type, a TTL and a value:
unit-11.1hy50qptfty: One name can have several records of the same type. Returning several A records and rotating their order (round-robin DNS) crudely spreads load over several servers, and content delivery networks answer with the address of a server near the asker, using the resolver's location.
unit-11.7kmgrp7l5f: A DNS message, query or reply, starts with a 12-byte header of six 16-bit big-endian fields:
unit-11.2gjkz189qyd: After the header come the question (name, type, class) and the records. Types are numbers: A = 1, NS = 2, CNAME = 5, MX = 15, TXT = 16, AAAA = 28. Class 1 is "Internet".
unit-11.1kapgok553q: A name is encoded as a sequence of length-prefixed labels ending with a zero byte: www.example.com becomes 03 77 77 77 07 65 78 61 6d 70 6c 65 03 63 6f 6d 00. Replies repeat names a lot, so DNS offers compression: a length byte whose top two bits are 11 is a pointer. The remaining 14 bits give an offset elsewhere in the message where the rest of the name can be found. Decoding must follow pointers carefully, and reject pointers that form a loop.
unit-11.1rlbzos1lh3: Plain DNS has no authentication, so a forged reply that reaches the resolver first, carrying the right ID, is accepted: cache poisoning. A poisoned cache sends every user of that resolver to an attacker's server. Defences are random IDs and random source ports (so the attacker must guess about 32 bits), and DNSSEC, which signs records with public-key cryptography (Unit 16) so that a resolver can verify an answer really came from the zone's owner. DNS queries are also visible to anyone on the path, so DNS over HTTPS (DoH) and DNS over TLS encrypt them. Finally, DNS is used in attacks: a small spoofed query can trigger a large reply aimed at a victim (amplification), and when a major DNS provider was attacked in 2016, large parts of the web became unreachable though their servers were fine.
