unit-11.2f9tyy1k6f6: A CNAME cannot coexist with other records for the same name, and the apex (example.com) needs NS and SOA records, so aliasing it breaks the zone. Providers offer special "ALIAS" records instead.
unit-11.1urp2667fwg: DNS maps names to addresses (and more) with a distributed, hierarchical database: the root, TLD and authoritative servers, linked by delegations.
unit-11.1h2pfnypxaz: A stub resolver asks a recursive resolver, which iteratively follows referrals from the root. A CNAME alias restarts the search with a new name.
unit-11.t6sabodb4r: Every answer has a TTL; resolvers cache answers (and NXDOMAIN results) until it expires. Short TTLs allow fast changes at the cost of more traffic.
unit-11.rix5v8tz8r: Common records: A, AAAA, CNAME, NS, MX (lower preference first), TXT, PTR (reverse lookup under in-addr.arpa).
unit-11.1b13hs1rrr2: A DNS message is a 12-byte header plus questions and records. Names are length-prefixed labels ending in zero, with compression pointers that must be decoded safely.
unit-11.2b7sxczkdby: Plain DNS can be forged (cache poisoning). Defences: random IDs and ports, DNSSEC signatures, and encrypted transports (DoH, DoT).
unit-11.82cpbhzo7f: With a name resolved and a connection open, programs finally talk to each other. Next is the most widely used application protocol of all: HTTP, the language of the web, with requests, responses, status codes, headers and cookies.
unit-11.1p52yw2edd4: Learn the protocol that carries the web. Take a URL apart, read and write HTTP requests and responses as plain text, understand methods, status codes and headers, see how cookies add memory to a stateless protocol, how caching and conditional requests save bandwidth, and build a small REST-style API.
unit-11.1ljf4b2t7ku: Split a URL into scheme, host, port, path, query and fragment, and apply percent-encoding
unit-11.1wnijxp7tl1: Read and write HTTP/1.1 request and response messages, including headers and bodies
unit-11.1i66o0a5lp7: Choose appropriate methods and status codes, and explain safe and idempotent methods
unit-11.12xtyqx2d26: Explain cookies, caching headers, ETags and conditional requests
unit-11.1sxa4wxodzm: Implement a small REST-style API with routing, JSON bodies and proper error responses
unit-11.15xhqpzr7tz: Describe how HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 improve on HTTP/1.1
unit-11.v9obrj2h8k: A URL (uniform resource locator) names a thing on the web and says how to fetch it:
unit-11.fz4bj89wr5: The scheme is the protocol: http, https, ftp, mailto, ...
unit-11.16y87mwg6m9: The host is a domain name (resolved through DNS, Lesson 11.6) or an IP address.
unit-11.tnx9iq9w5c: The port is optional; the default is 80 for http and 443 for https.
unit-11.xgllaydijx: The path names the resource on the server; an empty path means /.
unit-11.11olikh02gw: The query after ? is a list of key=value pairs separated by &.
unit-11.uu2h3yzwwl: The fragment after # points inside the page and is never sent to the server; the browser uses it locally.
unit-11.1rb8hyjv7es: URLs can only contain a limited set of characters. Anything else, such as spaces, & inside a value, or non-English letters, is written as percent-encoding: each byte of its UTF-8 form becomes % and two hex digits. A space is %20 (in query strings + is also used for a space), é is %C3%A9, and & inside a value is %26, so it cannot be mistaken for a separator. Forgetting to encode user input is how many bugs and security holes begin.
unit-11.1ppof309o30: HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol) is a request/response protocol over TCP. The client opens a connection to the server's port (Lesson 11.4), sends one request, and the server sends back one response. The messages are plain text (in HTTP/1.1), which is why you can type one by hand and why they are easy to debug. A request:
unit-11.1qtdcroln3h: The first line is the request line: a method, the target (path and query), and the HTTP version.
unit-11.1ar1t6wf8cj: Then come headers, one Name: value per line. Names are case-insensitive. Host is required in HTTP/1.1, because one server (one IP address) often hosts many websites.
unit-11.m1u2jc5wcb: A blank line ends the headers. Every line ends with the two characters CRLF (\r\n).
unit-11.bjea8ietd: An optional body follows. Its length is given by a Content-Length header (or by chunked transfer encoding).
unit-11.1j1ccckha8x: The first line is the status line: version, a numeric status code and a human-readable reason. Then headers, a blank line and the body. Content-Type tells the client how to interpret the bytes: text/html, application/json, image/png, ...
unit-11.1xpnnrafu6o: The method says what the client wants to do:
unit-11.1a8yanu2lnf: A safe method does not change anything on the server, so it can be repeated, prefetched and cached freely. An idempotent method has the same effect whether you do it once or ten times: deleting something twice leaves it deleted. This matters when a request times out and the client does not know if it arrived: retrying a PUT or DELETE is harmless, but retrying a POST might charge a credit card twice. That is why "Do not click twice" warnings exist and why payment APIs ask for an idempotency key.
unit-11.14bbw01xe6p: A form that only searches should use GET (the data goes in the URL, so the result can be bookmarked and shared). A form that changes things should use POST (the data goes in the body). Never put passwords in a URL: URLs end up in logs and browser history.
unit-11.addxfyo8xt: The three-digit status code groups by its first digit:
unit-11.r13lvbvijf: A redirect carries a Location header giving the new URL. The difference between 301 (permanent, caches may remember it) and 302 (temporary) matters for search engines and caches. A 405 must include an Allow header listing the methods that do work on that URL. Choosing the right status code is part of designing an API: clients (and automatic retry logic) act on the code, not the text.
unit-11.5nhy09ii5g: HTTP is stateless: each request stands alone, and the server keeps no memory of earlier ones. But shops have baskets and sites have logins. The solution is the cookie:
unit-11.4ntwzk6kxz: The server's response includes Set-Cookie: session=abc123; HttpOnly; Secure; Max-Age=3600.
unit-11.571xmq8x6o: The browser stores it and sends Cookie: session=abc123 with every later request to that site.
unit-11.1nvhmwiu6n4: The server uses the value as a key into its own data about you.
unit-11.21rgskrr57n: So the state lives on the server (or is signed inside the cookie); the cookie is just a ticket. Cookie attributes matter for security: HttpOnly hides it from JavaScript (limiting what a script-injection attack can steal), Secure sends it only over HTTPS, SameSite stops it being sent on requests triggered by other sites (defending against cross-site request forgery), and Max-Age or Expires sets how long it lasts. Cookies are also how advertisers track you across sites, which is why browsers now restrict third-party cookies. Passing credentials with each request in an Authorization header (for example a bearer token) is the usual alternative for APIs.
unit-11.1en0m1p9255: The fastest request is the one never sent. A response can say how long it may be reused with Cache-Control: max-age=3600 (one hour); until then the browser, or any cache between, serves the stored copy without asking. no-store forbids storing, no-cache means "store it but check with the server before reuse", and private allows only the user's own browser to keep it, not shared caches.
unit-11.26mtbn05n6o: After the copy goes stale, the client does not have to download it again. The server includes a validator, usually an ETag (a fingerprint, such as a hash of the content). The client's next request asks conditionally:
unit-11.1e8crm2414c: If the ETag still matches, the server replies 304 Not Modified with no body, and the client reuses its copy; otherwise it sends 200 with the new content and a new ETag. This is a conditional GET. The best practice for static files is to give them a fingerprint in their file name (app.3f9c2e.js) and a very long max-age, so they are cached for a year and a new version simply has a new URL.
unit-11.3s0x9w48n6: Most web services today expose an API over HTTP, usually in the REST style: every kind of thing is a resource with its own URL, and the standard methods act on it.
unit-11.kxjwy4300u: Bodies are usually JSON (JavaScript Object Notation): objects {"name": "pen"}, arrays, strings, numbers, true, false, null. In Python the json module converts between JSON text and dictionaries and lists. A good API validates input (a malformed body is 400, not a crash), uses the correct status codes, and answers a wrong method with 405 and an Allow header.
unit-11.1ueicflyqjb: HTTP/1.1 sends one request at a time per connection; opening several connections is the way to get parallelism, and a slow response blocks the ones behind it (head-of-line blocking). HTTP/2 keeps the same methods, headers and status codes but changes the transport format: messages are binary frames carrying numbered streams, so many requests and responses are multiplexed over one TCP connection, and headers are compressed. HTTP/3 runs over QUIC, built on UDP (Lesson 11.4), which gives each stream its own loss recovery so a lost packet no longer stalls the others, and which merges the transport and encryption handshakes to save round trips (Lesson 11.5 explained why those matter). The application sees the same HTTP semantics throughout.
unit-11.w8ijcygq4g: The standard library does the splitting; the pieces are the ones in the diagram.
unit-11.1cw39vr1dv3: Example 2: A request and a response as text
unit-11.1x4wiyang8k: Just lines of text joined with CRLF. This is exactly what travels over the TCP connection.
unit-11.22rgq9z5zls: The first digit tells you who is at fault and what to do next.
unit-11.1beu88wcm41: Routes map a method and a path to a handler. Wrong methods get 405; unknown paths get 404.
unit-11.1amwcq96l95: The client says which version it has. If it is current, the server sends no body at all.
unit-11.1tg4d80j7rg: A value containing &, =, # or a space breaks the URL, or worse, injects extra parameters. Percent-encode each part.
unit-11.frnbgnvgyb: URLs are logged by servers and proxies and saved in browser history. Send credentials in headers or the body, over HTTPS.
unit-11.10yj843bali: Using GET for actions that change data
unit-11.1tfy6st1lrw: Browsers and crawlers freely repeat and prefetch GETs. A "delete" link that uses GET can be triggered by a search-engine bot.
unit-11.e1bqme3iqf: Clients, caches and monitoring tools rely on the status code. An error page with status 200 is treated as success.
unit-11.215u5m18qfn: 401 means "I do not know who you are" (authenticate). 403 means "I know who you are, and you may not".
unit-11.23seie36ol1: POST is not idempotent. Retrying after a timeout can create duplicates unless the API supports an idempotency key.
unit-11.18lefmdsspt: A URL has a scheme, host, optional port, path, query and fragment (never sent to the server). Unsafe characters are percent-encoded (% plus two hex digits of each UTF-8 byte).
unit-11.l4pf0mzabj: HTTP/1.1 is a text protocol over TCP: a request line, headers, a blank line and an optional body (sized by Content-Length); the response starts with a status line. Host is required.
unit-11.1lvs0t9y6mb: Methods have meaning: GET and HEAD are safe; PUT and DELETE are idempotent; POST is neither. Status codes (2xx success, 3xx redirect, 4xx client error, 5xx server error) drive client behaviour.
unit-11.22dzl32053y: HTTP is stateless; cookies (Set-Cookie / Cookie) carry a session key, protected by HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite.
unit-11.8l2asq89me: Caching uses Cache-Control: max-age, and ETags with If-None-Match allow a 304 Not Modified response with no body.
unit-11.2ckl10mzn7h: REST APIs map resources to URLs and use the right methods and codes with JSON bodies. HTTP/2 multiplexes streams over one connection; HTTP/3 uses QUIC over UDP.
unit-11.4egaepiw4k: Until now the network has been a pile of messages in strings. Next we put it into practice with sockets: the programming interface that lets a program open connections, listen for them, and send and receive bytes, with a simulated network to build a real client and server on.
unit-11.srnivzmred: Learn how programs actually use the network: the socket API with its bind, listen, accept, connect, send and receive calls. Understand why TCP gives you a stream with no message boundaries and how to frame messages, how a server handles many clients, and how to write clients that survive failures with timeouts, retries, backoff and rate limits. Everything is practised on a simulated network.
unit-11.gqe56zq0j1: Describe the socket lifecycle for a TCP server and client
unit-11.1o2hb81j0mt: Explain why a TCP stream has no message boundaries, and frame messages with length prefixes or delimiters
unit-11.1yqzl58i0pb: Build and test an in-memory network with listening, connecting, sending, receiving and closing
unit-11.5irmv59nm7: Design a simple line-based chat protocol as a state machine
unit-11.cvt9cb6cju: Write a client that retries with exponential backoff, and a token-bucket rate limiter
unit-11.27k451anvfd: Compare threads, event loops and asynchronous I/O for serving many clients
unit-11.ti0429k8zu: A socket is the operating system's handle for one end of a network conversation (Lesson 10.1 called such handles file descriptors; a socket is one). Every network program, from a browser to a game server, is built on this small API, which first appeared in Berkeley Unix in 1983.
unit-11.20lrpio9sy6: A TCP server goes through these steps:
unit-11.scomys11mr: bind(address, port) attaches it to a local address and port, such as ("0.0.0.0", 8080), where 0.0.0.0 means "any of my addresses". If the port is already taken the call fails with "address already in use".
unit-11.gkzxq7pl7w: listen() turns it into a listening socket and starts a queue (the backlog) of connections waiting to be accepted.
unit-11.29tlpd4bpt2: accept() takes the next waiting connection and returns a new socket for it, plus the client's address. The listening socket keeps listening; each client gets its own connected socket.
unit-11.1fyyzpzxn3g: recv(n) and send(data) move bytes. close() finishes.
unit-11.fhw775tjif: A TCP client is shorter: socket(), connect((host, port)) (which performs the three-way handshake of Lesson 11.4), then send and recv, then close. The client never calls bind: the OS picks an ephemeral port for it.
unit-11.265rczjnp3q: A UDP socket skips the connection: it uses sendto(data, address) and recvfrom(n), and each call is one datagram.
unit-11.298ghnxy5ac: Our browser-based Python cannot open real sockets, so in this lesson you will build a simulated network with the same shape of API. The code you write in the exercises has the same logic as the real thing.
unit-11.16nmwfgr7k8: A stream has no message boundaries
unit-11.35e6ymm7f7: This is the most important fact about TCP programming. TCP delivers a stream of bytes, not messages. If a client calls send(b"hello") and then send(b"world"), the server's recv(100) might return b"helloworld", or b"hello" then b"world", or b"hel" then b"loworld". The network may split and merge data in any way, and it can differ from run to run. Code that assumes "one send equals one recv" works on a developer's laptop and fails in production.
unit-11.25lk7t0y0cp: recv(n) returns up to n bytes: whatever has arrived, at least one byte. It returns an empty b"" only when the other side has closed the connection (end of file). To read exactly n bytes you must loop.
unit-11.203rclsrgdu: Your protocol must mark where messages end. The usual methods are: Delimiter: messages end with a special byte, typically a newline (\n), as in HTTP headers, SMTP and Redis. Simple to read and debug; the data cannot contain the delimiter without escaping. Length prefix: each message begins with its length, for example 4 bytes in network byte order, then that many bytes. Works for binary data; the reader needs to buffer partial messages. Fixed size, or closing the connection to mean "done" (HTTP/1.0 did that).
unit-11.11e5ih5yq5s: The receiving side keeps a buffer: append every recv result, and repeatedly extract any complete messages from the front, keeping the incomplete remainder for next time. Always cap the length you will accept: a hostile client can announce a four-gigabyte message to exhaust your memory.
unit-11.1iyc6apih5e: A basic server handles one client at a time: while it is talking to one connection, others wait in the backlog. Real servers need concurrency, and there are three classic designs (using ideas from Unit 10):
unit-11.21zv4npxakt: A thread (or process) per connection. The simplest to write: each connection has its own code path that can block freely. It costs memory (a stack per thread) and scheduling overhead, so a few thousand connections is the limit.
unit-11.130wvxlztpz: An event loop with non-blocking sockets. One thread asks the OS, with select, poll or epoll, "which of my sockets are ready to read or write?", and handles each ready one briefly without waiting. This is how nginx and Redis serve tens of thousands of connections on one thread. The cost is that the code is split into pieces driven by events.
unit-11.1copnuxi5l: Asynchronous I/O (async/await). A language-level version of the event loop where await conn.read() suspends only that task. Python's asyncio, JavaScript's await and Rust's tokio are of this kind. This is the generator machinery from Lesson 10.4, with a loop that resumes tasks when their I/O is ready.
unit-11.2ieatf8toc: In our simulation recv returns None when nothing has arrived yet, instead of waiting: a non-blocking socket. The event-loop idea then becomes visible, since the program has to check again later.
unit-11.1lbz0ips93z: A protocol is the agreement between client and server about what messages exist and what they mean. Text protocols (HTTP/1.1, SMTP, IRC) are easy to try by hand with telnet or nc and to debug. Binary protocols (DNS, TCP itself, gRPC) are compact and fast to parse. When you design one:
unit-11.u1t209e5q6: Define every message and every error. A server must reply to nonsense with a clear error, never crash.
unit-11.nda83bkb36: Be strict in what you send, careful in what you accept: validate everything that arrives, since the bytes come from strangers (Unit 16).
unit-11.24n2avrzk3f: Include a version so the protocol can change.
unit-11.13vezehubjg: Think about state: what messages are legal now? (Lesson 11.4's TCP state machine, and the chat server in this lesson's exercises.)
unit-11.15wj4i86kr1: Networks fail constantly: connections are refused (nobody is listening), reset (the other side crashed), or simply go silent. A robust client assumes failure.
unit-11.1blpmtvssaa: Set a timeout on every network call. A call with no timeout can block forever.
unit-11.1kwbj54cueb: Retry failures that are likely to be temporary (timeouts, connection resets, 503 responses), but never retry blindly something that is not idempotent (Lesson 11.7).
unit-11.29utrmy33u: Use exponential backoff: wait 0.5 s, then 1 s, 2 s, 4 s, capped at some maximum, so that a recovering server is not buried under retries from thousands of clients at once. Add random jitter in real systems so that clients do not retry in lockstep.
unit-11.fugnw51h14: Give up after a bounded number of attempts and report the error.
unit-11.1oneejdgoai: Servers protect themselves with rate limiting. The classic algorithm is the token bucket: a bucket holds up to capacity tokens and is refilled at a steady rate per second; each request removes a token, and a request that finds the bucket empty is refused (HTTP 429 Too Many Requests). It allows short bursts up to the capacity while enforcing the long-run average rate.
unit-11.uf83zwmmby: Example 1: A real TCP echo server and client
unit-11.1a6vmpelm3: This is the genuine socket API in Python. It needs a real operating system, so read it here and run it on your own computer.
unit-11.178yealk4jy: The same lifecycle on an in-memory network. recv returns None when no data has arrived yet, standing in for blocking.
unit-11.axf6id86oc: A delimiter and a length prefix, each with a receive buffer that copes with partial and merged data.
unit-11.24xibj9qrud: A flaky operation, a bounded number of attempts, and growing pauses between them. The pauses are recorded instead of slept.
unit-11.u98hw13mtj: A steady refill, a burst allowance, and a refusal when the bucket is empty.
unit-11.22snn31f68a: Assuming one send is one recv
unit-11.1n8qjrvk0bd: TCP has no message boundaries. Loop, buffer and frame your messages.
unit-11.2fisgnrd3zz: It returns up to n bytes. An empty result means the connection closed, not "no data yet".
unit-11.2qzojyugzs: Cap it. A malicious or buggy peer can announce a gigantic message and exhaust your memory.
unit-11.14zbxjd9vag: A network call without a timeout can block forever when the other side disappears. Set one on every socket.
unit-11.7cxolv2vag: Retries without backoff and a limit turn a small outage into a big one. Wait longer each time, add jitter, and give up eventually.
unit-11.2auozskly6o: Using send when you mean sendall
unit-11.1y0tbkawbk0: send may transmit only part of your data and returns how many bytes it took. sendall loops until everything has gone.
unit-11.14rwof8by5t: A socket is the program's handle on a network endpoint. A TCP server does socket, bind, listen and accept (which returns a new socket per client); a client does connect. UDP uses sendto and recvfrom.
unit-11.1xdscfe93ev: TCP is a byte stream with no message boundaries: recv(n) returns up to n bytes, and b"" means the peer closed. Protocols need framing: a delimiter such as a newline, or a length prefix, with a receive buffer and a size cap.
unit-11.1dugo1nrmqs: Servers handle many clients with a thread per connection, an event loop (select, epoll) with non-blocking sockets, or async/await.
unit-11.9f5smwc80k: A good protocol has framing, a defined message for every case including errors, validation of all input, a version number and clear state.
unit-11.4lfk8ffaoy: Networks fail: use timeouts, retries with exponential backoff (and jitter) for transient errors and idempotent operations, and a bounded number of attempts.
unit-11.24t6q91y6or: A token bucket rate limiter permits bursts up to its capacity and a steady average rate, and tells clients how long to wait (HTTP 429, Retry-After).
unit-11.gdkyej8qxy: Everything so far assumed the network is honest. It is not: anyone on the path can read, change or fake packets. The last networking lesson covers security: encryption, TLS and certificates, firewalls and the attacks that target each layer.
unit-11.nxa6kbq75s: See why the network cannot be trusted and how we build trust on top of it anyway. Learn the main attacks at each layer, the ideas of encryption, hashing and message authentication, how two strangers agree a secret key in public (Diffie-Hellman), how TLS and certificates make HTTPS work, and how firewalls and monitoring defend a network.
unit-11.1ge3bqy38gj: Describe common network attacks (sniffing, spoofing, man-in-the-middle, replay, DNS poisoning, SYN flood, scanning) and where each happens
unit-11.23agh7vjryr: Distinguish encryption, hashing, message authentication codes and digital signatures, and what each guarantees
unit-11.4izj53ry84: Carry out a Diffie-Hellman exchange and explain why an eavesdropper cannot easily break it
unit-11.2goktkcybfw: Walk through a TLS handshake and validate a certificate chain
unit-11.2201mhxln7o: Write firewall rules with first-match semantics and a stateful allowance for replies
unit-11.1cs99s4faap: Detect port scans in a connection log
unit-11.gzrgzj8897: Everything in this unit so far assumed that packets arrive as sent. In reality a packet crosses a dozen networks owned by strangers: the coffee-shop Wi-Fi, your ISP, backbone carriers, the hosting company. Anyone on that path can try to read it, change it, forge one, replay an old one, or just block it. Security rests on three goals, the CIA triad:
unit-11.1hg29bn9gn4: Confidentiality: only the intended parties can read the data.
unit-11.1dlb6rzgbe1: Integrity: the data cannot be altered without detection.
unit-11.bktfd8u4ls: Authenticity (and availability): you are talking to who you think you are, and the service works when needed.
unit-11.kx1v2bkkmx: Typical attacks, by where they happen:
unit-11.b53cyrl5a0: The lasting lesson: security must be added deliberately. The original internet protocols had none, and almost every defence is a layer built on top. The next Unit 16 goes deeper; here we study the networking part.
unit-11.mbj43sp66x: Four building blocks do the work.
unit-11.1lcmx3xm3ez: Hash functions (SHA-256) turn any data into a fixed-size fingerprint. They are one-way (you cannot recover the input), and any change to the input changes the output completely. A hash proves nothing about who made the data, though: anyone can hash anything.
unit-11.1ot56hzrxqe: Symmetric encryption (AES) uses one shared secret key to scramble and unscramble data, and is fast enough for gigabytes. Its problem is key distribution: how do two strangers agree on a key without already having a secure channel?
unit-11.203fwxlaat9: A message authentication code (MAC), for example HMAC-SHA256, is a hash that also mixes in a shared secret key. Only someone holding the key can compute a valid tag, so a matching tag proves the message is unmodified and came from a key-holder. Compare tags in constant time (hmac.compare_digest) so that timing does not reveal how many leading characters matched.
unit-11.wd1qdobua4: Asymmetric (public-key) cryptography uses a pair of keys: what one key does the other undoes. Anyone can use the public key; only the owner has the private key. This provides two things: encryption to the owner (encrypt with the public key, decrypt with the private one), and digital signatures (sign with the private key, anyone verifies with the public key), which prove that a certain private-key owner produced a message. It is slow, so it is used only to set up a key for the fast symmetric cipher. Choosing a good algorithm and implementing it correctly is very hard: never invent your own cryptography; use a vetted library.
unit-11.1shtvispiuv: A MAC authenticates a message against replay only if the message includes something fresh. Signing "transfer 100 to Sam" lets an attacker replay the whole signed message on Tuesday that was valid on Monday. Defences are a timestamp (reject old ones), a nonce (a number used once, which the receiver remembers) and sequence numbers.
unit-11.a6fjdzxc3l: Agreeing on a secret in public
unit-11.6oexqr9hy6: Diffie-Hellman key exchange (1976) lets two parties build a shared secret by talking over a channel that an eavesdropper can fully read. The idea uses a one-way function from modular arithmetic (Lesson 6.6):
unit-11.99ogf4rnbg: Alice and Bob publicly agree on a large prime p and a base g.
unit-11.1o0rrye8s8: Alice picks a secret number a and sends A = gᵃ mod p. Bob picks b and sends B = gᵇ mod p.
unit-11.25k7kiotitt: Alice computes Bᵃ mod p. Bob computes Aᵇ mod p. Both equal gᵃᵇ mod p: the shared secret.
unit-11.u913ewfl7m: The eavesdropper sees p, g, A and B, but computing a from A is the discrete logarithm problem, which for a prime of thousands of bits is infeasible, while computing pow(g, a, p) in the other direction is fast (square-and-multiply). With a tiny prime like 23 you can simply try every exponent, as one of the exercises shows.
unit-11.2f76s9pknrs: Diffie-Hellman alone does not stop a man in the middle, who can run one exchange with Alice and another with Bob. The parties must also authenticate each other, which is the job of certificates.
unit-11.29l3qvk5kx0: TLS (Transport Layer Security, the successor of SSL) is the protocol that turns HTTP into HTTPS. It sits between the application and TCP (Lesson 11.4) and provides confidentiality, integrity and server authentication. A simplified TLS handshake:
unit-11.12tbza1ompv: ClientHello: the client lists the TLS version and ciphers it supports and sends a random number and its key-exchange share.
unit-11.21ou2rhfw8h: ServerHello + Certificate: the server picks a cipher, sends its own random value and key share, and its certificate: a document stating "this public key belongs to www.example.com", signed by a certificate authority.
unit-11.1l4pqpf9may: Both compute the shared secret by key exchange (Diffie-Hellman) and derive the symmetric session keys from it. The server proves it holds the private key matching the certificate by signing the handshake.
unit-11.1qwd6n26kxq: Each side sends Finished, a MAC over the whole handshake, which detects any tampering. From now on all data is encrypted and authenticated with the session keys.
unit-11.1mn9hvhav89: Where does trust come from? Your browser or operating system ships with a list of about 150 root certificate authorities (CAs) that it trusts. A website's certificate is rarely signed by a root directly. It is signed by an intermediate CA, which is certified by the root, forming a chain of trust: leaf (the website)  to  intermediate  to  root. The client checks, at the current time:
unit-11.1r4xd9v2uh7: every certificate is within its validity period (not before to not after),
unit-11.m2xkoh5c1b: each certificate's issuer is the subject of the next one, and its signature verifies with the next certificate's public key,
unit-11.1doe6qd9mbm: every certificate that signs another is allowed to be a CA,
unit-11.1yzpryjv9qu: the chain ends at a trusted root,
unit-11.1oeuiqrsfcg: and the leaf certificate names the host the client is connecting to. A name may be exact (www.example.com) or a wildcard (*.example.com), which stands for exactly one label, so it covers www.example.com but neither example.com nor a.b.example.com.
unit-11.1l2755c23xg: If any check fails the browser shows a warning. Never click through it casually: that warning is the only sign of a man in the middle. Certificates expire (now at most about 13 months) to limit the damage of stolen keys. Certificate Transparency logs make every issued certificate publicly auditable. The lock icon means the connection is encrypted and the name matched a certificate, not that the site is honest.
unit-11.141y7au4m44: A firewall filters traffic by rules. A packet filter examines each packet's protocol, addresses and ports and applies an ordered list of rules: the first rule that matches decides (allow or deny), and if none match a default applies. The safe default is deny: list what is permitted and block everything else. A stateful firewall also remembers connections: if an inside host opens a connection to a web server, the matching reply packets are allowed in automatically, though a fresh inbound packet to the same port would be blocked. This is much of what NAT (Lesson 11.2) gives a home router. Firewalls cannot stop an attack carried in traffic they allow (a malicious web page), which is why they are one layer among several, the idea of defence in depth.
unit-11.422sbhy47c: A VPN (virtual private network) wraps your packets in an encrypted tunnel to a gateway, so that the local network sees only the tunnel. It protects against local eavesdropping, but then the VPN operator sees your traffic instead. Intrusion detection systems watch for suspicious patterns. One classic signal is a port scan: one source touching many different ports in a short time, which ordinary clients never do.
unit-11.1en49l6k2qv: A closing note on ethics and law: probing networks you do not own is illegal in many places even if you "just look". Security practice means testing your own systems or having written permission; the exercises here detect scans in a log and never perform them.

unit-11.204qw3iicx: Packets cross networks you do not control. Attackers can read, change, forge, replay or block them. The goals are confidentiality, integrity and authenticity.
unit-11.q7cg4goyet: Hashes fingerprint data; symmetric ciphers are fast but need a shared key; a MAC (HMAC) adds integrity and authenticity; public-key cryptography gives key exchange and digital signatures. Never invent your own.

unit-12.1j6rgafetet: So far your programs kept data in variables and, at best, in files. That works for a to-do list. It stops working when many people use the data at once, when the data is far bigger than memory, when a crash must never leave it half-written, or when you need to answer questions such as "which students got an A in a course taught by the Computer Science department?" without writing a new program each time.
unit-12.wum95lo3z0: A database is an organised collection of data. A database management system (DBMS) is the program that looks after it: it stores the data safely on disk, lets many users read and change it at once without corrupting it, keeps it consistent by enforcing rules, finds things quickly using indexes, and answers questions written in a query language. Well-known systems are PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server, Oracle and SQLite, a tiny one that lives in a single file and is built into phones, browsers and your operating system. This unit uses SQLite, compiled to run right here in your browser, so everything you type really executes.
unit-12.16ox7rvte8h: Most databases you will meet are relational: all data is stored in tables. The language for working with them is SQL (say "sequel" or "S-Q-L"), standardised since the 1980s and still the most widely used data language in the world. It is declarative: you describe what you want ("the names of third-year students, best grade first") and the database works out how to get it. That is a very different way of thinking from the step-by-step code you have written so far, and it is why SQL feels strange for a few days and then feels like a superpower.
unit-12.15rubveqvm4: A table (formally a relation) stores one kind of thing: students, courses, orders. Each column (attribute) is one property with a name and a type. Each row (record, tuple) is one particular thing. In our university database the student table has columns id, name, major_id, year, gpa and email, and one row per student.
unit-12.1pbg2i1m70c: Two ideas make tables work together:
unit-12.kbkoc11lay: A primary key is a column (or columns) whose value is unique for every row and never missing. It is the row's identity. student.id is a primary key: two students may share a name, but never an id. Choose keys that never change; an email address looks unique but people change it.
unit-12.1uk48s3hnck: A foreign key is a column that holds the primary key of a row in another table, linking them. student.major_id holds a department.id. Rather than writing "Computer Science" into every student's row (and fixing hundreds of rows when the department is renamed), we store the department once and refer to it by number. The database can enforce that a foreign key always points at a row that really exists.
unit-12.22iwfdg0ysm: The enrollment table connects students and courses. A student takes many courses and a course has many students, so each row says "this student took this course in this term and got this grade". Its primary key is three columns together, a composite key: the same student may retake a course in another term, but not enroll twice in the same term.
unit-12.eja3t8pcy: The set of all tables and their columns, types and keys is the database's schema. The rows currently in them are the data. Schemas change rarely; data changes constantly.
unit-12.cznvydsg88: A query asks a question; the answer is itself a table (a result set). The core is SELECT ... FROM ... WHERE ...:
unit-12.xgjwawfezf: Here is some code. Have a look at it on screen.
unit-12.13a2ej6rtiy: SELECT * means "all columns". The WHERE clause keeps only rows for which its condition is true. Conditions use = (a single equals sign, not two), <> or != (not equal), <, >, <=, >=, and combine with AND, OR and NOT. Text goes in single quotes ('Physics'; double quotes are for column names). Keywords are not case sensitive, but writing them in capitals and putting each clause on its own line makes queries far easier to read. Statements end with a semicolon.
unit-12.1qh21kie93k: Although you write SELECT first, the database reads the query in a different order: first FROM (find the table), then WHERE (filter rows), then SELECT (pick columns), and finally ORDER BY and LIMIT. Keeping that order in mind explains many puzzling errors later.
unit-12.suc2mi9q7u: Rows in a table have no guaranteed order. If you care about order, say so with ORDER BY, which sorts ascending by default; add DESC for descending, and list several columns to break ties: ORDER BY year DESC, name. LIMIT n keeps only the first n rows of the (sorted) result, which is how "top 3" queries are written. OFFSET k skips k rows first, useful for paging through results.
unit-12.1e7zkjw6ako: DISTINCT removes duplicate rows from the result: SELECT DISTINCT year FROM student lists each year once. You can rename a column in the output with an alias: SELECT gpa * 25 AS percent_scale. You can compute with columns (+ - * /), join text with ||, and call functions such as UPPER(name), LENGTH(name) or ROUND(gpa, 1). The result still has one row per input row; computing does not change how many rows come back.
unit-12.1ryvvj107vb: Real data has gaps: Carl has no email, Barbara has no GPA yet. SQL represents "unknown or missing" with the special value NULL. It is not zero and not an empty string; it means no value here. Because the truth about a NULL is unknown, SQL uses three-valued logic: a condition can be true, false or unknown, and WHERE keeps only rows where it is true.
unit-12.26w9i534aoi: Any comparison with NULL is unknown: gpa > 3.5 is unknown when gpa is NULL, and so is gpa = NULL, and even NULL = NULL.
unit-12.12d0b8007fy: Therefore WHERE email = NULL returns nothing, ever. The right test is WHERE email IS NULL (or IS NOT NULL).
unit-12.u974ms0d3r: Arithmetic with NULL gives NULL, and NOT (unknown) is still unknown, so WHERE NOT gpa > 3.5 does not return the students whose GPA is missing.
unit-12.1pbhd6edpfz: COALESCE(a, b, ...) returns its first non-NULL argument, handy for substituting a default: COALESCE(email, 'none').
unit-12.5k2dt8x1jt: In ORDER BY, SQLite sorts NULLs first.
unit-12.2anc2dxj9h3: NULL is the biggest source of silent mistakes in SQL: queries run without error and return a plausible, wrong answer. Whenever a column can be NULL, ask yourself what should happen to those rows.

unit-12.1hp3kmhlpt3: SQLite has no special date type. Dates are stored as text in the ISO format YYYY-MM-DD (or YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS), as numbers or as Unix timestamps. The department's name would repeat in every row of every student. Rename a department and you must find and fix hundreds of rows; miss one and the data contradicts itself. This is why relational designs store each fact once, in its own table, and link tables with keys. The next-but-one lesson turns that into a systematic method called normalisation.
unit-12.11eqotxxq5u: The price is that the answer to a question is often spread over several tables. A join combines rows from two tables into wider rows, pairing them according to a condition, normally foreign key = primary key:
unit-12.1xojqmzkuxo: Think of it as: for each student row, look for department rows where the ON condition holds, and output one combined row for each match. Because both tables have a column called name (and id), you must say which you mean by qualifying it with the table name. Long names get tedious, so give each table a short alias after its name: FROM student s JOIN department d ON s.major_id = d.id.
unit-12.29gr303t7i6: A plain JOIN (short for INNER JOIN) keeps only combined rows where the condition matched. A student with no major (major_id is NULL) has no match, so that student disappears from the result. Sometimes that is right; sometimes it silently loses data.
unit-12.1z1lz3ij7jl: A LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the left table. Where there is no match, the right table's columns are filled with NULL:
unit-12.1rynlq1mn74: Now Linus appears with a NULL major. (RIGHT JOIN and FULL OUTER JOIN exist in many databases, but swapping the table order turns a RIGHT into a LEFT, and SQLite added both only recently, so LEFT is all you need.) There is also the CROSS JOIN, every row of one table paired with every row of the other, with no condition; the result has n  times  m rows, which is occasionally useful and often a bug.
unit-12.1pn10tfj4rp: A rule of thumb: ON says how rows are matched; WHERE filters the result afterwards. For a LEFT JOIN that difference matters. A condition on the right table put in WHERE (like WHERE d.name = 'History') throws away the NULL-filled rows and quietly turns your LEFT join into an inner one. Put it in ON if you want to keep the unmatched left rows.
unit-12.16hrr630fo7: Relationships come in three shapes. One-to-many: one department has many students (the foreign key lives on the "many" side). One-to-one: rare, usually two tables describing the same thing. Many-to-many: students and courses, where each can have many of the other. A many-to-many relationship always needs a third link table (also called a junction or association table), here enrollment, with a foreign key to each side. Its own columns, like term and grade, describe the relationship.

unit-12.1i7kyafd9l1: So far each input row produced one output row. An aggregate function collapses many rows into one value:
unit-12.2fzqsi6iczl: Aggregates ignore NULL. With twelve students and one missing GPA, COUNT(*) is 12 but COUNT(gpa) is 11, and AVG(gpa) divides by 11, not 12. If every value is NULL, SUM and AVG return NULL (and COUNT(col) returns 0). Without a GROUP BY, an aggregate query returns exactly one row for the whole table, even if the table is empty. Mixing an aggregate with an ordinary column (SELECT name, MAX(gpa)) is meaningless: which name? Some databases refuse; SQLite picks an arbitrary row and says nothing, so do not do it.
unit-12.l51x1p1xuw: To summarise each category separately, add GROUP BY. The database sorts the rows into groups, one per distinct value of the grouping columns, and the aggregates are computed once per group:
unit-12.12u6chvxahb: The rule that keeps queries meaningful: every column in the SELECT list must either be in the GROUP BY or be inside an aggregate function. You can group by several columns (GROUP BY major_id, year) and each distinct combination becomes a group. NULL values form a group of their own. Groups come back in no particular order, so add ORDER BY when you need one; you may sort by an aggregate (ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC).
unit-12.1vh8jqskwbq: Sometimes you want to keep only some groups: "years with more than two students". You cannot write that in WHERE, because WHERE runs before the groups exist. HAVING filters groups after aggregation:
unit-12.1cvvsc6p4u5: The full order in which the database evaluates a query is therefore: FROM and JOIN, then WHERE, then GROUP BY, then HAVING, then SELECT, then DISTINCT, then ORDER BY, then LIMIT. This single list explains most "why can't I use that here?" questions. For example, a column alias defined in SELECT is not available in WHERE (SELECT has not run yet) though SQLite lets you use it in ORDER BY. As a habit, filter rows in WHERE whenever you can, because discarding rows early is cheaper than grouping them first.
unit-12.1tddqn5j1pu: Aggregation and joins combine naturally: join the tables first, then group the wide rows. "How many students are enrolled in each course?" joins course with enrollment and groups by course:
unit-12.2arck54ztid: Notice two details. Using a LEFT JOIN and counting a column from the right table (COUNT(e.student_id), not COUNT(*)) gives 0 for a course with no enrollments, because COUNT(*) would count the single NULL-filled row as 1. And the name is grouped along with the code to make the SELECT legal.
unit-12.1ui07fq0ebg: Beware double counting. If you join a student to both their enrollments and some other many-valued table, every enrollment row is repeated once per row of the other table, and SUM or COUNT inflate. Aggregate each many-side separately (in a subquery, next lesson) and then combine, or use COUNT(DISTINCT ...).
unit-12.21h7zrqcrgd: GROUP BY collapses rows. Sometimes you want a per-group number next to every row: each student's GPA beside their department's average, or each student's rank. Window functions do this: an aggregate or ranking function followed by OVER (...), which describes the window of rows to look at, without removing any rows.
unit-12.2s923jh7za: PARTITION BY splits the rows into independent groups (like GROUP BY, but all rows stay); ORDER BY inside OVER orders each partition. ROW_NUMBER() numbers rows 1, 2, 3...; RANK() gives ties the same number and skips ahead (1, 1, 3); DENSE_RANK() does not skip (1, 1, 2). SUM(x) OVER (ORDER BY ...) is a running total. Window functions are evaluated after WHERE, GROUP BY and HAVING, so you cannot filter on them directly; wrap the query in a subquery to do that (next lesson).

unit-12.9nfvxsp2yf: Any SELECT can appear inside another. The inner one is a subquery, written in parentheses. It comes in three useful shapes, depending on what it returns:
unit-12.151ad0pwkxy: A scalar subquery returns one row with one column, and can be used wherever a single value could: WHERE gpa > (SELECT AVG(gpa) FROM student) finds students above average. If it returns more than one row SQLite quietly uses the first, which is a bug waiting to happen; make sure it returns exactly one.
unit-12.gpfmi1t9ws: A list subquery returns one column of many rows and is used with IN: WHERE major_id IN (SELECT id FROM department WHERE building LIKE '%Hall').
unit-12.23m21l71j0r: A table subquery returns a full result and is used in the FROM clause as if it were a table (it needs an alias): FROM (SELECT year, AVG(gpa) AS avg_gpa FROM student GROUP BY year) AS y. This is the way to filter on a window function or aggregate, or to aggregate twice, such as "the average of the per-year averages".
unit-12.se0m8hod72: Subqueries let you ask a question in steps: first compute the number you need, then use it. Often a join does the same job; use whichever reads more clearly.
unit-12.1ccda534wyz: A subquery that mentions a column of the outer query is correlated. It cannot be computed once; conceptually it is re-run for every outer row:
unit-12.1zwao2frpuz: "Students whose GPA is above the average of their own major." For each student the inner query averages only that student's major. (Databases are clever and often avoid literally repeating the work, but the meaning is "for each row".)
unit-12.1gullawpzua: EXISTS (subquery) is true when the subquery returns at least one row; what it selects does not matter (people write SELECT 1). It is the natural way to say "has some matching row":
unit-12.c82neb74mn: NOT EXISTS finds rows with no match, the clean version of the LEFT JOIN anti-join. It is also safer than NOT IN: if the list inside NOT IN (...) contains a single NULL, no row can pass (last lesson's trap), whereas NOT EXISTS has no such problem.
unit-12.bkzxspgf6m: Deeply nested subqueries are hard to read. A common table expression (CTE), introduced by WITH, gives a subquery a name, defined before the main query that uses it:
unit-12.hfsblu4m3h: Read top to bottom like a recipe: compute per_student, then use it. You can define several CTEs separated by commas, and later ones may use earlier ones. A CTE exists only for that one statement. Think of it as a temporary, named view of your own making.
unit-12.23y9ibrr0bv: A CTE can also be recursive: it refers to itself, which is how SQL walks trees and counts. WITH RECURSIVE n(x) AS (SELECT 1 UNION ALL SELECT x + 1 FROM n WHERE x < 5) SELECT x FROM n; produces 1 to 5. The first part is the starting row, the part after UNION ALL is the step, and it repeats until the step produces nothing. Recursive CTEs follow chains such as "manager of a manager of...", and you will use one in the project.

unit-12.2d7jgs2jezn: Columns are matched by position, not name, and the names of the result come from the first query. ORDER BY goes once, at the very end. Set operations treat NULLs as equal to each other (unlike =), and the "remove duplicates" versions are really set operations in the mathematical sense. A typical use: "students who took a CS course but never a Math course" is EXCEPT; "students who took both" is INTERSECT; "all names that appear as a student or as a department" is UNION.

unit-12.17q4mm0wk7z: Queries only read. Three statements change the data (together with SELECT they are the CRUD operations: create, read, update, delete):
unit-12.cz7a8ncepn: Always list the column names in INSERT; relying on their position breaks the day someone adds a column. Several rows can be given at once: VALUES (...), (...), and INSERT INTO t SELECT ... copies the result of a query. Columns you leave out get their default value (NULL unless the table says otherwise).
unit-12.pren3znd2n: UPDATE and DELETE without a WHERE change every row. DELETE FROM student; empties the table instantly and there is no "are you sure?". The habit of experienced people: write the WHERE, then run it as a SELECT first to see exactly which rows it will touch, then turn it into the UPDATE or DELETE. UPDATE can compute from the old value: SET credits = credits + 1. Each statement is atomic, meaning it either changes all the rows it matches or none; the next-but-one lesson explains how to extend that to groups of statements.
unit-12.1ozsao09qzf: CREATE TABLE defines a table's name, columns and rules. Each column has a type. SQLite is relaxed about types (it uses type affinity: a column of declared type INTEGER tries to store numbers as integers but will accept text), while other databases are strict. The main families are INTEGER, REAL (floating point), TEXT and BLOB (raw bytes). Money should be stored as an integer count of cents, never as floating point, for the same reason you met in Unit 9: 0.1 + 0.2 is not 0.3.
unit-12.cyvcsoa67i: An INTEGER PRIMARY KEY in SQLite is special: if you omit it on insert, the database assigns the next free number (an auto-increment key). DROP TABLE name deletes a table and its data for good, so be careful; DROP TABLE IF EXISTS does not complain when it is already gone.
unit-12.1inc9d49ipn: Constraints are rules the database enforces on every change, whoever or whatever makes it: your app, a script, a colleague at 2 a.m. That is far stronger than hoping every program remembers to check.
unit-12.18hh3ppoytc: A statement that breaks a constraint fails with an error and changes nothing. This is a feature: it turns a silent data corruption into a loud, immediate bug.
unit-12.gg5ibojju7: Foreign keys need one extra step in SQLite: run PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON; for each connection (for historical reasons it is off by default; most other databases always enforce them). With enforcement on you cannot insert an enrollment for a student who does not exist, and you cannot delete a department that students still reference, unless you chose a rule for it: ON DELETE CASCADE deletes the referencing rows too, ON DELETE SET NULL clears the reference, ON DELETE RESTRICT (the default behaviour) refuses.
unit-12.21wiir9jz3x: Schemas evolve. ALTER TABLE student ADD COLUMN phone TEXT; adds a column (existing rows get NULL or the default); ALTER TABLE student RENAME TO pupil; and RENAME COLUMN rename; DROP COLUMN removes one. Bigger changes (such as adding a constraint to an existing column) are done in SQLite by creating a new table, copying the rows with INSERT INTO ... SELECT, dropping the old table and renaming the new one. Real systems keep such changes in numbered migration scripts so every copy of the database can be brought to the same version.
unit-12.1enaxqu9rrc: A view is a saved query with a name. It stores no data of its own; each time you query the view the database runs the saved SELECT:
unit-12.3omkrem3ec: Views hide complexity (a join written once, used everywhere), restrict access (show some columns of a table, hide others) and give old programs a stable face while the tables underneath change. Because a view is just a stored query, it is always up to date.
unit-12.16g1b5tib1d: Three changes, then a SELECT to see the result. Only the last SELECT is displayed.
unit-12.4axkgfjjvl: A new table with rules. The failing insert is the point: the error message names the rule.
unit-12.7komsxh9ey: With enforcement turned on, a row cannot point at something that does not exist.

unit-12.w67ry29k3k: Floating point cannot represent most decimals exactly. Store whole cents as an integer.
unit-12.t7byp0mxol: INSERT INTO t VALUES (...) depends on column order. Name the columns.

unit-12.23g023flqb9: Good schemas begin on paper, not in SQL. List the entities (the things the system must remember: students, courses, departments), their attributes (properties: a student's name and year) and the relationships between them (a student enrolls in a course). Each relationship has a cardinality: one-to-one, one-to-many or many-to-many, and each side may be mandatory or optional (must a student have a major? In our data, no).
unit-12.1lh1c0dmf63: A diagram of entities as boxes and relationships as lines is an entity-relationship (ER) diagram. Turning it into tables follows three rules you already know from the last lessons: each entity becomes a table with a primary key; a one-to-many relationship becomes a foreign key on the "many" side; a many-to-many relationship becomes a link table holding two foreign keys (and any attributes of the relationship itself, like a grade).
unit-12.1krcsen3n5q: Choosing keys. A natural key is a real-world identifier (course code, passport number); a surrogate key is a meaningless number invented by the database (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY). Natural keys are readable but real-world identifiers do change, get reused, or turn out not to be unique. Most designs use a surrogate key for the primary key and keep natural identifiers as UNIQUE columns.
unit-12.2ahejbh01f0: What goes wrong with one big table
unit-12.3liooo2ztf: The table flat_sale in this lesson's database records sales with the customer's name and city and the product's name and price repeated on every row. That redundancy causes three kinds of anomaly:
unit-12.1jx9lz5cl4v: Update anomaly. Asha's city is stored three times. One was typed as Puna, the other two as Pune. Change a city and you must change every row; miss one and the data contradicts itself. (Look at sales 6 and 8: the notebook costs 120 in one row and 125 in another. Which is right?)
unit-12.1rp56cbbjo6: Insert anomaly. You cannot record a new product until somebody buys it, because a product only exists inside a sale row. You would have to invent a sale or leave sale columns empty.
unit-12.7ek6fwphbw: Delete anomaly. If Chloe's only purchase is cancelled and its row deleted, the fact that Chloe lives in Oslo disappears with it.
unit-12.5spqs7268n: The cure is to give every fact its own home: a customer's city lives in one row of a customer table, a product's price in one row of a product table. A sale refers to them by key.
unit-12.nmijq6z6d7: The theory behind this is the functional dependency (FD). We write A  to  B ("A determines B") when any two rows that agree on A must also agree on B. Examples that should hold in real life: customer_name  to  customer_city (a customer lives in one city, assuming names are unique), product_name  to  product_price, and sale_id  to  everything (the key).
unit-12.yz2pswvbqn: You can test a dependency in the data with a query. If a dependency holds, no value of A can map to two different values of B:
unit-12.o34stm3jjt: Any row returned is a violation, either a data error (the Puna typo) or proof that the dependency does not really hold. Remember that data can only refute a dependency; whether it is true is a fact about the real world, which you must decide by understanding the domain.
unit-12.13t5xg6kk73: A key is a set of columns that determines every other column in the row, and is minimal (no column can be removed). The problem tables above have the key sale_id, yet customer and product facts depend on only part of the row's meaning, which is what the normal forms address.
unit-12.72te7bbo6p: Normal forms are checklists for removing redundancy, each stricter than the last.
unit-12.26ehmioo9so: First normal form (1NF). Every cell holds a single, atomic value, and rows are distinct. A column such as courses = 'CS101,CS201,MA101' violates it: you cannot index it, join it, count it, or enforce that each course exists. Move each value to its own row in a related table. Repeating columns (course1, course2, course3) violate the spirit too.
unit-12.1avarraijvt: Second normal form (2NF). In 1NF, and no column depends on only part of a composite key. Consider enrollment(student_id, course_code, student_name, grade) with the key (student_id, course_code): student_name depends on student_id alone, so it does not belong here. Move it to the student table. (A table with a single-column key is automatically in 2NF.)
unit-12.95zgq2ixgw: Third normal form (3NF). In 2NF, and no non-key column depends on another non-key column. In student(id, major_id, major_name), major_name is determined by major_id, which is not the key. This is a transitive dependency (id  to  major_id  to  major_name). Move major_name to department. A catchphrase: every column depends on the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key.
unit-12.awjhi05kqf: Boyce-Codd normal form (BCNF) is a slightly stricter 3NF that handles rare overlapping-key cases. Most practical designs aim for 3NF.
unit-12.ggfcd4cmgo: Splitting must be lossless: joining the pieces back must give exactly the original rows. Splitting on a genuine functional dependency guarantees that.
unit-12.xreywqz9m6: Normalisation optimises for correctness: each fact in one place. It costs joins at query time. Data warehouses and reporting systems often deliberately denormalise, copying values into one wide table so reads need no joins and are fast, accepting that a loader process must keep the copies consistent. Caches and summary tables are the same trade. A sound approach: normalise first to get a correct model; denormalise later, deliberately, where measurements show a real read bottleneck, and know which copy is the source of truth.
unit-12.16j0pwhasgx: Other design habits worth knowing: name tables in the singular and columns clearly (created_at, not d1); never put two facts in one column; store each fact in the units you will compute with; add NOT NULL, UNIQUE, CHECK and foreign keys so the database defends the design; and keep a column for each real thing you will search by.
unit-12.2akf38vxnbi: The same customer and product facts repeat on many rows. Counting distinct combinations shows how few separate facts there really are.
unit-12.jemhf50uhx: Does customer_name determine customer_city? A query finds the counter-examples.
unit-12.14jyp0rd7gw: The same test for product_name  to  product_price finds the inconsistent notebook price.
unit-12.1ppbeto00f3: Create customer and product tables from the data (after deciding which values are right), then a sale table that refers to them. The final SELECT shows the result.
unit-12.r7bs2vqyon: Joining the three tables back must give the original nine rows, apart from the two conflicts we resolved.
unit-12.5vjon8ws3q: A comma-separated list in one cell is hard to query correctly.
unit-12.1omc3yii36a: Storing a list in one column
unit-12.1xdh65ne3sr: Comma-separated values defeat joins, constraints and indexes. Use a related table with one row per value.
unit-12.16orjfmycu6: Using a changeable real-world value as the primary key
unit-12.cnsnnshiic: Emails, names and phone numbers change. Use a surrogate key and keep the natural value UNIQUE.
unit-12.184u4gjiyr6: Copying a value into several tables 'for convenience'
unit-12.1fsf2yw61b5: Each copy can drift. Store it once and join, or document the copy as deliberate denormalisation.
unit-12.113gjpwcqe0: Normalising is a means to correctness. Do not split a street, a city and a postcode into three tables unless your queries need that.
unit-12.1fra3dm451a: Model entities, attributes and relationships first; one-to-many becomes a foreign key and many-to-many a link table.
unit-12.gkns3bhcqy: Redundancy causes update, insert and delete anomalies.
unit-12.1draffrw2zl: A functional dependency A  to  B means equal A implies equal B; queries can refute but not prove one.
unit-12.1jze7yxq0re: 1NF: atomic cells. 2NF: no dependence on part of a key. 3NF: nothing but the key determines a column.
unit-12.h04e1of3rz: Splits must be lossless; denormalise deliberately and only for measured read performance.

unit-12.1t3gjelhjlz: Moving 100 from Ada to Ben takes (at least) two changes: subtract 100 from Ada, add 100 to Ben. Between them there is a moment when 100 has vanished from the world. If the program crashes there, or the power fails, or the second statement is rejected, the money is gone and nobody can say what happened. Real systems have many such multi-step changes: placing an order (create the order, reduce the stock, charge the card), or enrolling a student (insert the enrollment, reduce the seat count).
unit-12.6166svqju: A transaction groups statements into one logical unit that either happens completely or not at all. You mark it with:
unit-12.129a4f6ybz9: COMMIT makes all the changes permanent at once. ROLLBACK undoes everything since BEGIN, as if it never happened. If a statement inside breaks a constraint you roll back and no half-done work remains. Outside an explicit transaction, each statement is its own tiny automatic transaction (which is why a single UPDATE of a thousand rows never stops halfway).
unit-12.uhhne65gb4: The guarantees a database makes about transactions are summarised as ACID:
unit-12.8zmko2gv0u: Atomicity: all of a transaction's changes happen, or none do. There is no visible half-way state, even after a crash.
unit-12.1tpjovs3rvf: Consistency: a transaction moves the database from one valid state to another. Constraints (CHECK, FOREIGN KEY, UNIQUE) are checked, and a transaction that would violate one fails. Rules the database cannot express (the total money in the system is constant) are the programmer's duty; atomicity is what makes them achievable.
unit-12.1elfaz9ouia: Isolation: concurrent transactions do not see each other's unfinished work; the result is as if they ran one at a time (to a degree you can choose, below).
unit-12.bee2gr3t0u: Durability: once COMMIT returns, the change survives power failure and crashes.
unit-12.9fpcb6j71u: A bank transfer is the classic example, but the same needs appear in booking a seat, writing a blog post with its tags, or moving a student between sections. Whenever a business fact is stored in more than one row, wrap the change in a transaction.
unit-12.c9189gw4po: A busy database serves many users at once. Without isolation, their statements interleave and produce surprising results. The classic anomalies:
unit-12.1ry3dq1jo9u: Dirty read: you read data another transaction has changed but not yet committed; if it rolls back, you acted on something that never existed.
unit-12.1g3apnkei6l: Non-repeatable read: you read a row twice in one transaction and get different answers because someone committed a change in between.
unit-12.1tdr52y6p5i: Phantom: you run the same query twice and a new row matching your condition appears the second time.
unit-12.1ssdzd27qew: Lost update: two transactions read the same value, both compute a new value from it, and both write; the second write overwrites the first and one change disappears.
unit-12.1gy84d6nryv: The lost update is the one that hurts most in practice. Suppose two clerks each add 50 to a balance of 100. Both read 100, both write 150, and the balance is 150 instead of 200. The fix is to do the read and the write in a single statement so the database applies it atomically to the current value: UPDATE account SET balance = balance + 50 WHERE id = 1. Do not read the balance into your program, add in your program, and write back.
unit-12.3rfh60dxyj: Isolation is usually implemented with locks: a transaction that writes a row holds a lock until it commits, and others who need that row wait. Too much locking makes users queue, so databases offer isolation levels, trading safety for speed: read uncommitted (dirty reads possible), read committed (no dirty reads; PostgreSQL's default), repeatable read, and serializable (the strongest: the result equals some one-at-a-time order). Many systems use multiversion concurrency control (MVCC): readers see a consistent snapshot while writers create new versions, so readers never block writers. SQLite is simple: one writer at a time for the whole database, which is plenty for an app but not for a busy web site.
unit-12.18sjjase1: Locks bring a risk you met in the operating systems unit: deadlock. Transaction A locks row 1 and wants row 2; B holds row 2 and wants row 1. Databases detect the cycle and abort one transaction (the victim), which your program must be ready to retry. Keeping a transaction's rows locked briefly, and always touching rows in the same order, avoids most deadlocks.
unit-12.2rkid6ysb3: Durability and atomicity are usually implemented with a write-ahead log (WAL). Before changing the data pages, the database appends a record of the change to a log file and forces it to disk. If it crashes, on restart it replays committed changes from the log that had not reached the data files, and undoes those of transactions that never committed. The log is written sequentially (fast) while the data files are updated lazily. This is the same journaling idea as the file system in Lesson 10.9.
unit-12.na8vqyka0c: Two practical rules: keep transactions short (never wait for a human in the middle of one), and remember that long transactions hold locks and block others.
unit-12.licbzoffdm: Both updates are made permanent together. The total stays 800.
unit-12.1oeq8ww54hu: We start a transfer, change our mind, and roll back. The balances are as before.
unit-12.11lwgqtrm5x: Example 3: A constraint protects the total
unit-12.geom01jg8a: Ben only has 300. The second update would make a balance negative, which the CHECK constraint forbids, so the statement fails.
unit-12.1xesh559qvw: A SAVEPOINT marks a place inside a transaction that you can roll back to without abandoning the whole transaction.
unit-12.cbb2n1r6tm: Example 5: The lost update, and its fix
unit-12.u76mqwd224: Two clerks each add 50. We simulate both reading the balance first (the unsafe way), then show the atomic way.
unit-12.8hrp9946ko: Example 6: Atomic change inside the database
unit-12.20c89h0a0ol: The same two additions written as single statements cannot lose an update.
unit-12.2f8vuuq3zit: Reading a value, computing in the program, writing it back
unit-12.okowknvjng: Another user can change the row in between and one update is lost. Write SET balance = balance + x so the database does it atomically.
unit-12.19dwejbkh32: Forgetting COMMIT or ROLLBACK keeps locks held and blocks other users. Keep transactions short and always end them.
unit-12.1gzkjdcasjf: Waiting for user input inside a transaction
unit-12.1edp4ovqi5m: A person can take minutes to answer. Hold locks only while doing database work.
unit-12.25t17jswch3: Assuming each statement in a script commits separately
unit-12.5c7a710cdf: After BEGIN, nothing is permanent until COMMIT. If the program stops first, the work is rolled back.
unit-12.233xzz44jzt: A transaction groups statements so they happen completely or not at all: BEGIN, then COMMIT or ROLLBACK.
unit-12.8quo69bcj2: Concurrency can cause dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, phantoms and lost updates; isolation levels trade safety for speed.
unit-12.188m5w2nv5w: Do the read and the write in one statement (balance = balance + x) to avoid lost updates.
unit-12.qmsmhvc3r: Locks or MVCC provide isolation; a write-ahead log provides atomicity and durability across crashes; deadlocks are detected and one transaction is retried.
unit-12.1ttvpamgu5z: Make queries fast and safe: understand how an index (a B-tree) turns a scan into a search, read query plans with EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN, create single-column, composite and unique indexes, know what makes an index useful or useless, and prevent SQL injection with parameters.
unit-12.owg7nbqawz: Explain why scanning a big table is slow and how a B-tree index avoids it
unit-12.14crchlgw63: Create indexes and read EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN to see whether they are used
unit-12.t2u3c8bpqr: Choose columns and column order for composite indexes, and recognise queries an index cannot help
unit-12.pb0n9mzd0h: Describe the costs of indexes and the idea of a covering index
unit-12.amrhwuakhy: Explain SQL injection and prevent it with parameterised queries
unit-12.19eylf1nyvm: The event table in this lesson's database has 3,000 rows (real tables have millions or billions). To answer SELECT * FROM event WHERE user_id = 42 the database has no clue where user 42's rows are, so it must read every row and check each one: a full table scan. The work grows in proportion to the table size. Double the data, double the time.
unit-12.u0l8z77xa7: An index is an extra data structure that finds rows by the value of a column without scanning, like the index at the back of a textbook: instead of reading every page for "Dijkstra", you look the word up in a sorted list and jump to the page numbers. The database keeps the index in sync as rows change.
unit-12.1luofz6tn33: Most databases implement an index as a B-tree (balanced tree), a sorted tree where each node holds many keys, so that it is only a few levels deep. With a branching factor of a few hundred, a billion rows need only about four levels. Looking up a value means reading about four nodes: logarithmic time instead of linear. The tree is sorted, so an index also supports range searches (day BETWEEN 100 AND 110) and returns rows already in order, which can save a sort. You met the same idea in the data structures unit; this is where it earns its living. (Hash indexes exist, but are only good for equality.)
unit-12.1ma1lpvyl08: You do not tell a query to use an index. The query planner decides, estimating the cost of each way to run the query, and chooses. To see its decision, put EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN in front:
unit-12.o6im2ww6f7: Before the index the plan says SCAN event (every row); afterwards SEARCH event USING INDEX idx_event_user (user_id=?). Learn these two words. In PostgreSQL and MySQL the command is EXPLAIN (or EXPLAIN ANALYZE to also measure real time). Reading plans is the main skill of performance tuning: measure and look, do not guess.
unit-12.1gsysi6o910: Two things get an index automatically: a primary key and a UNIQUE constraint. A UNIQUE index also enforces the rule. A lookup by id is therefore always fast. Foreign key columns are not indexed by default in most databases, but joins and deletes constantly search by them, so they usually deserve an index.
unit-12.1rqq28qr4jf: Composite indexes and what defeats an index
unit-12.25syrawihp6: An index can cover several columns: CREATE INDEX idx_kind_day ON event (kind, day) sorts rows by kind, and within each kind by day, like a phone book sorted by last name then first name. Column order matters. It helps queries that give the leftmost columns: WHERE kind = 'buy' and WHERE kind = 'buy' AND day = 10, and a range on the last used column WHERE kind = 'buy' AND day > 300. It does not help WHERE day = 10 alone (just as a phone book is no use for finding everyone called Anna). Put equality columns first and the range column last.
unit-12.bcqsqmn5nh: Things that stop an index being used:
unit-12.7zxbj2qy4j: Applying a function to the column: WHERE ABS(amount) = 5 or WHERE day + 1 = 100 must compute for every row. Rewrite as WHERE day = 99, or create an index on the expression.
unit-12.104ujlsajdk: A leading wildcard: LIKE '%abc' cannot use the sort order; LIKE 'abc%' can (in databases with suitable collation settings).
unit-12.2g5xwr416o8: Low selectivity: if kind has only four values, each matching a quarter of the table, the planner may rightly prefer scanning, since jumping back and forth for a quarter of all rows is slower than reading them in order.
unit-12.27fcrv85v8m: A type mismatch between the column and the value.
unit-12.xeih2fit7w: If an index contains all the columns a query needs, the database can answer from the index alone and never touch the table. That is a covering index.
unit-12.1iotrc0r2tj: Indexes are not free. Each one takes space, and every INSERT, DELETE and UPDATE of an indexed column must also update the index, so heavy writing gets slower with each index added. The rule: index the columns you search, join and sort by in your real queries, check the plan to confirm they help, and drop indexes nobody uses. Do not index every column "just in case". Tables you only read (reports) can carry many indexes; tables that take thousands of writes a second carry few.
unit-12.zl06no5m5p: Other ways of making queries fast: select only the columns you need instead of SELECT *; filter early; avoid doing a query inside a loop in your program (the "N+1 queries" mistake: one query per row instead of one join); and use LIMIT with an ordered index for paging.
unit-12.1k2mg57lqkf: SQL injection and using SQL from programs
unit-12.2ddtxw530dd: Programs usually build queries from user input. The dangerous way is to paste the input into the SQL text:
unit-12.289fi6jixg1: If a user types x' OR '1'='1, the text becomes ... WHERE name = 'x' OR '1'='1' and returns every student. Worse input, such as '; DROP TABLE student; --, can change or destroy data or leak other tables. This is SQL injection, one of the most common and costly security holes in history. The cause is mixing code (SQL) and data (the user's text) in one string.
unit-12.1b5zgxp59dd: The fix is parameterised queries (prepared statements): send the SQL with placeholders and the values separately. The database treats the values only as data, never as SQL:
unit-12.6306pe0kgq: Every language's database library offers this (? or :name or $1). Never build SQL with string formatting or concatenation. Also run the application with a database account that has only the permissions it needs, so that even a mistake cannot drop tables. Parameters also let the database reuse the plan for repeated queries.
unit-12.s405427vl9: That completes the tour: you can model data, define it, write queries from simple to subtle, change it safely, and make it fast. The unit project asks you to do all of it.
unit-12.2bqutfzshbb: Without an index, the plan is a full scan of the event table.

unit-12.1mljxm6bigk: Results do not change when you add an index, only the work done. Rows for user 42:
unit-12.148embc9yw2: A query built by pasting text. The 'user input' closes the quote and adds a condition that is always true.
unit-12.1x591zcga2: Each index slows writes and uses space. Index what real queries filter, join and sort by.
unit-12.8v6tm4dvgn: Wrapping an indexed column in a function
unit-12.1oet3i1xukk: WHERE LOWER(name) = 'ada' cannot use an index on name. Store normalised data or create an index on the expression.
unit-12.2e2ar3qe0mm: Putting the range column first in a composite index
unit-12.16w25nen9zm: Equality columns come first, the range column last. A range on the first column stops the later columns from narrowing the search.
unit-12.10y4v0u9aum: It invites SQL injection. Always use parameters (? placeholders).
unit-12.1haa6meaoil: Without an index a query scans every row; a B-tree index finds rows in logarithmic time and supports ranges and ordering.
unit-12.1e7p2i737i9: EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN shows SCAN or SEARCH ... USING INDEX; measure instead of guessing.
unit-12.kogek3gupx: In a composite index put equality columns first and the range column last; functions on the column, leading wildcards and low selectivity defeat an index.
unit-12.265r641h6ox: Indexes cost space and slow writes; a covering index answers from the index alone.

unit-12.1h4efc56iy8: That completes the tour of databases, from tables and queries to design, transactions and speed. The Unit 12 project puts the pieces together: you will turn a messy flat export into a clean, constrained, indexed registrar database and report on it.
